The post Top 10 Best Security Service Edge (SSE) Solutions in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security Service Edge is the security portion of SASE SWG, CASB, ZTNA, and increasingly DLP and browser isolation, all delivered from the cloud and most organisations deploy it well before they take on the networking half.

The solutions below separate on service convergence under one policy engine, data-protection depth, and threat-prevention model.

Zscaler takes 1; Netskope and Palo Alto complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Zscaler the scale-first proxy benchmark.

• Podium: Zscaler, Netskope (data-centric control), Palo Alto Prisma Access (platform-estate fit).

• Model split: inline-proxy fabrics (Zscaler, Netskope, Prisma) versus platform-estate SSE (Cisco, Fortinet) versus isolation/data specialists (Skyhigh, Forcepoint ONE, iboss, Lookout).

• 2026 theme: one policy engine the unification that actually cuts operational overhead versus stitched point tools.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: service convergence (one policy), CASB/DLP depth, ZTNA strength, threat-prevention model, global performance, and pricing clarity.

Weights: convergence/one-policy 25%, CASB/DLP depth 20%, ZTNA 20%, threat prevention 20%, performance 15%.

The 2026 SSE Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Zscaler — Best Scale-First Proxy Benchmark

Snapshot: Per-user enterprise | Inline proxy inspecting every connection | ZTNA at global scale

Why it earns 1: Zscaler was an early mover on the cloud-proxy model: every connection inspected inline, users routed to apps without network exposure, at global scale and with the longest track record.

For organizations wanting the deepest cloud-security pedigree under one policy, it sets the benchmark.

Pros: Inline proxy; ZTNA core; global scale.

Cons: Fullest value as the primary access fabric.

Bottom line: The scale-and-pedigree SSE benchmark.

2. Netskope — Best Data-Centric Control

Snapshot: Enterprise | Inline data + cloud control | Deep CASB/DLP

Why it ranks here: Netskope leads with inline visibility and granular control over data across sanctioned and shadow SaaS, with deep CASB and DLP. For organizations whose core concern is data in motion, it’s the data-centric anchor.

Pros: Inline data control; CASB/DLP depth; cloud visibility.

Cons: Best value when data governance is the priority.

Bottom line: The data-centric SSE anchor.

3. Palo Alto (Prisma Access) — Best Platform-Estate Fit

Snapshot: Enterprise | Stack extension into cloud SSE | Consistent policy

Why it ranks here: Prisma Access extends Palo Alto’s security stack into a cloud-delivered SSE with consistent policy from on-prem firewalls to the edge. For Palo Alto estates, SSE arrives as an extension of the platform they run.

Pros: Stack extension; consistent policy; breadth.

Cons: Breadth carries cost.

Bottom line: SSE for the Palo Alto estate.

4. Cisco — Best Infrastructure-Estate SSE

Snapshot: Enterprise | Umbrella/Secure Access lineage | Identity integration

Why it ranks here: Cisco provides SSE from the Umbrella/Secure Access line, wired into its identity and network estate.

For Cisco-standardized organizations, SSE shares context with the broader stack.

Pros: Umbrella lineage; identity integration; estate fit.

Cons: Fullest value inside the Cisco estate.

Bottom line: SSE for the Cisco-centric estate.

5. Cloudflare One — Best Performance-First Edge

Snapshot: Per-user/bundled | Vast edge network | Low latency, ZTNA

Why it ranks here: Cloudflare One runs on one of the biggest edge networks, serving SSE near users to keep latency low. For globally distributed, performance-sensitive organizations, it’s the network pick.

Pros: Vast edge; low latency; ZTNA.

Cons: Some enterprise SSE depth still maturing.

Bottom line: The global-performance SSE lane.

6. Skyhigh Security — Best CASB-Heritage Data Lane

Snapshot: Enterprise | McAfee/Skyhigh CASB lineage | Deep data protection

Why it ranks here: Skyhigh, from the McAfee Enterprise/Skyhigh CASB line, is built around deep data protection and CASB spanning cloud and web.

For organizations prioritizing CASB-grade data control, it’s the heritage pick.

Pros: CASB depth; data protection; cloud DLP.

Cons: Networking/ZTNA breadth versus the fabric leaders.

Bottom line: The CASB-and-data-protection lane.

7. Forcepoint ONE — Best Data-Plus-Identity Control

Snapshot: Enterprise | Converged SWG/CASB/ZTNA + data protection | Risk-adaptive

Why it ranks here: Forcepoint ONE converges SWG, CASB, and ZTNA with the company’s behavior-based data protection at the center, enforcing dynamically on user risk. For data-plus-identity SSE, it’s the adaptive pick.

Pros: Converged SSE; risk-adaptive enforcement; data protection.

Cons: Confirm converged-platform scope.

Bottom line: The data-and-identity SSE benchmark.

8. Broadcom (Symantec) — Best Existing-Symantec-Estate Lane

Snapshot: Enterprise (renewal-oriented) | Symantec SSE lineage | Estate continuity

Why it ranks here scoped honestly: The Symantec SSE lineage, now within Broadcom, suits large existing Symantec estates; evaluate on renewal given the portfolio’s acquisition-era focus. Ranked as the estate-continuity lane.

Pros: Symantec data/web heritage; estate continuity.

Cons: Evaluate on renewal; greenfield momentum versus challengers.

Bottom line: SSE for existing Symantec estates, on renewal.

9. iboss — Best Dedicated-Cloud Lane

Snapshot: Per-user | Containerized dedicated cloud | Isolation focus

Why it ranks here: iboss serves SSE on a containerised, dedicated-cloud architecture for organisations that want isolated cloud-delivered security. For dedicated-cloud SSE, it’s the isolation pick.

Pros: Containerized cloud; isolation; scalability.

Cons: Brand scale versus the leaders.

Bottom line: The dedicated cloud-security SSE lane.

10. Fortinet FortiSASE — Best Unified-Security Estate Lane

Snapshot: Enterprise | Unified SSE + Fortinet Security Fabric | Cloud-delivered security with global enforcement

Why it ranks here: Fortinet FortiSASE combines SWG, ZTNA, CASB, DLP, FWaaS, and browser security in a unified cloud-delivered platform, with particularly strong integration for organizations already using Fortinet networking and endpoint products.

For Fortinet-centric estates, it’s the unified-security pick.

Pros: Broad SSE coverage; strong ZTNA; integrated CASB and DLP; Fortinet Security Fabric integration.

Cons: Strongest value inside the broader Fortinet ecosystem.

Bottom line: The unified SSE lane for Fortinet-centric enterprises.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Start From Your Platform, Demand One Policy Engine

Begin SSE from the platform you already run Palo Alto, Cisco, Netskope, and Symantec estates each come with a home-field option then let the decider break the tie: governing data (Netskope, Skyhigh, Forcepoint ONE), the prevention model (inline proxy against isolation), or outright global speed (Cloudflare One, Zscaler).

In the pilot, refuse to settle for less than one policy engine and one console spanning every pillar, because it’s that unification never a longer spec sheet that actually shrinks operational overhead next to lashing point tools together.

Because SSE is usually the first step toward SASE, pick a vendor whose networking trajectory you’d also adopt, and validate the ZTNA implementation against our ZTNA ranking.

Evaluate Broadcom/Symantec on renewal, pilot with your riskiest SaaS data flows and most distributed users, and track the metric that renews the contract: policy-exception count and data-loss incidents trending down.

FAQs

What are the best SSE solutions in 2026? Zscaler as the scale-first benchmark, Netskope for data governance, Prisma Access for platform estates, Cloudflare One for performance, with Cisco, Skyhigh, Forcepoint ONE, Broadcom (Symantec), iboss, and Lookout by model.

How is SSE different from SASE? SSE is the security half SWG, CASB, ZTNA; SASE adds SD-WAN networking. Most organizations adopt SSE first.

Inline-proxy or isolation SSE? Inline-proxy platforms inspect all traffic in the cloud path; isolation executes risky content in a remote container. Most full SSE platforms offer both, in different depths.

Does SSE include ZTNA? Yes zero-trust network access is a core SSE pillar, replacing VPN with identity-aware app access; implementations vary.

What proves SSE value? Fewer data-loss incidents and policy exceptions, with one policy engine cutting the operational overhead of stitched point tools measured in your pilot.

Verdict

Ten solutions, one unification test: a single policy engine across SWG, CASB, and ZTNA. Zscaler benchmarks scale, Netskope governs data, Prisma fits the Palo Alto estate, Cloudflare One brings global performance, and Forcepoint ONE adapts to user risk start from your platform’s home-field, demand one console, pilot your riskiest flows, and let falling data-loss incidents renew the contract.

articles.description:
SASE fuses SD-WAN networking with a cloud security stack in one fabric, yet the term papers over a genuine divide: some vendors grew up in networking and bolted security on, others grew up in security and tacked on the network, and a handful engineered the whole thing single-pass from day one. The post Top 10 Best SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) Solutions in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
SASE fuses SD-WAN networking with a cloud security stack in one fabric, yet the term papers over a genuine divide: some vendors grew up in networking and bolted security on, others grew up in security and tacked on the network, and a handful engineered the whole thing single-pass from day one.

The solutions below separate on genuine convergence (one console, one policy model), global PoP performance, and ZTNA depth. Palo Alto (Prisma SASE) takes 1; Zscaler and Netskope complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Palo Alto (Prisma SASE) the single-vendor platform benchmark.

• Podium: Prisma SASE, Zscaler (security-first ZTNA scale), Netskope (data-centric control).

• Model split: single-vendor platforms (Prisma, Fortinet, Cato) versus security-first fabrics (Zscaler, Netskope) versus networking-led (Fortinet, Versa, Broadcom/VMware, HPE Aruba).

• 2026 theme: genuine convergence one policy engine versus two acquired stacks sharing a logo.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: convergence depth (one platform/policy), heritage strength (network vs security), global PoP performance, ZTNA and data-protection depth, operating model, and pricing clarity.

Weights: convergence 25%, ZTNA/data depth 20%, global performance 20%, heritage strength 20%, operating model 15%.

The 2026 SASE Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Palo Alto (Prisma SASE) — Best Single-Vendor Platform Benchmark

Snapshot: Enterprise | Full security stack + SD-WAN, unified management | Broadest surface

Why it earns 1: Prisma SASE brings Palo Alto’s full security stack and SD-WAN into one converged platform with unified management the broadest consolidator surface, with deep ZTNA and data protection.

For enterprises wanting one vendor to own networking and security end to end, it sets the benchmark.

Pros: Full stack + SD-WAN; unified management; breadth.

Cons: Breadth carries cost and complexity.

Bottom line: The single-vendor consolidation benchmark.

2. Zscaler — Best Security-First ZTNA Scale

Snapshot: Per-user enterprise | Zero-trust access at global scale | Inline security

Why it ranks here: Zscaler pioneered cloud security at scale; its SASE leads with zero-trust access proxying users to apps without network exposure layered with inline security. For security-first estates anchoring SASE on ZTNA, it’s the pedigree pick.

Pros: ZTNA pedigree; inline inspection; global scale.

Cons: Networking convergence younger than its security core.

Bottom line: The ZTNA-led security estate lane.

3. Netskope — Best Data-Centric Control

Snapshot: Enterprise | Inline data + cloud control | Deep CASB/DLP

Why it ranks here: Netskope leads with inline data and cloud control deep CASB and DLP woven into the fabric for organizations whose SASE priority is governing data, not just connecting sites. For data-centric SASE, it’s the governance pick.

Pros: Inline data control; CASB/DLP depth; cloud visibility.

Cons: Networking heritage younger than security.

Bottom line: The data-governance-led SASE lane.

4. Cisco — Best Infrastructure-Breadth

Snapshot: Enterprise | SD-WAN + security + identity portfolio | Estate integration

Why it ranks here: Cisco brings SD-WAN (the Meraki/Viptela line), security, and identity together across a wide portfolio, fitting organisations built around Cisco infrastructure. For infrastructure-led SASE, it’s the breadth pick.

Pros: SD-WAN breadth; identity (Duo); portfolio reach.

Cons: Integration work across the portfolio.

Bottom line: SASE for the Cisco-centric estate.

5. Fortinet — Best Networking-Led Edge

Snapshot: Enterprise | FortiGate security + SD-WAN on one OS | Own silicon

Why it ranks here: Fortinet converges its FortiGate security and SD-WAN on a single operating system and often its own silicon, giving networking-driven organizations one stack from branch to cloud. For networking-led SASE, it’s the edge pick.

Pros: Integrated OS; own silicon; branch-to-cloud stack.

Cons: Fullest value inside the Fortinet ecosystem.

Bottom line: The networking-led edge benchmark.

6. Cato Networks — Best Single-Pass Convergence

Snapshot: Subscription | Single-pass cloud-native engine | Own global backbone

Why it ranks here: Cato engineered SASE single-pass from scratch on its own global backbone networking and security in a single cloud-native engine instead of bolted-together acquisitions. For genuine from-scratch convergence, it’s the purpose-built pick.

Pros: Single-pass architecture; own backbone; real convergence.

Cons: Enterprise-feature depth versus the incumbents in places.

Bottom line: The built-from-scratch convergence pick.

7. Cloudflare — Best Performance-First Network

Snapshot: Per-user/bundled | Vast global edge | Low latency, ZTNA

Why it ranks here: Cloudflare runs one of the largest global edge networks, delivering SASE services close to users for low latency at scale. For performance-first, distributed estates, it’s the network pick.

Pros: Vast edge network; low latency; ZTNA.

Cons: Some enterprise SASE features still maturing versus incumbents.

Bottom line: The global-performance lane.

8. Broadcom (VMware) — Best SD-WAN-Estate Lane

Snapshot: Enterprise | VMware SD-WAN lineage | Estate integration

Why it ranks here scoped honestly: The VMware SD-WAN lineage, now within Broadcom, suits estates standardized on VMware networking extending toward SASE. Ranked as the estate-continuity lane; confirm post-acquisition roadmap and packaging.

Pros: VMware SD-WAN heritage; estate integration.

Cons: Confirm Broadcom roadmap and packaging.

Bottom line: SASE for the VMware-networking estate.

9. Versa Networks — Best Full-Stack Flexibility

Snapshot: Enterprise | Flexible single-stack SASE | Cloud/on-prem/managed

Why it ranks here: Versa provides a broad, adaptable single-stack SASE with solid SD-WAN and security, deployable in the cloud, on-prem, or as a managed service. For deployment flexibility, it’s the full-stack pick.

Pros: Flexible deployment; full stack; managed option.

Cons: Brand scale versus the platform giants.

Bottom line: The deployment-flexibility lane.

10. HPE Aruba — Best Campus-Plus-SASE Lane

Snapshot: Enterprise | SASE joined to Aruba campus/edge networking | EdgeConnect SD-WAN

Why it ranks here: HPE Aruba pairs SASE (EdgeConnect SD-WAN plus security partnerships/SSE) with its strong campus and edge networking, suiting organizations standardized on Aruba infrastructure. For campus-led estates, it’s the networking-plus pick.

Pros: Campus/edge strength; EdgeConnect SD-WAN; Aruba integration.

Cons: Security-stack depth versus the security-first leaders.

Bottom line: SASE for the Aruba campus estate.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Ask Which Team Owns It, Test for Real Convergence

SASE deliberately merges networking and security, so the first question is which team owns the project and the best outcomes come from both co-owning it.

Network-led initiatives favor deep SD-WAN heritage and edge integration (Fortinet, Cloudflare, Versa); security-led initiatives favor the ZTNA and data anchors (Zscaler, Netskope); consolidation mandates favor the broadest single platform (Prisma, Cato).

Judge genuine convergence one console, one policy model over two acquired stacks sharing a logo, which is exactly why single-pass architectures (Cato) and true single-vendor platforms matter; make finalists prove one policy engine across networking and security in the pilot.

Sequence the migration where pain and payoff are highest VPN replacement with ZTNA, or a branch whose circuit is up for renewal so the first phase funds itself, and keep a hybrid state as the norm rather than a big-bang cutover.

Confirm the Broadcom/VMware roadmap, narrow the security layer with our SSE and ZTNA rankings, and track the metric that renews the contract: sites migrated and incidents/latency trending the right way.

FAQs

What are the best SASE solutions in 2026?

Prisma SASE as the single-vendor benchmark, Zscaler and Netskope for security-led estates, Fortinet and Cloudflare for networking-led ones, Cato for single-pass convergence, with Cisco, Broadcom (VMware), Versa, and HPE Aruba by model.

How is SASE different from SSE?

SSE is the security half SWG, CASB, ZTNA; SASE adds the SD-WAN networking layer. Many buyers adopt SSE first.

Single vendor or best-of-breed?

Single-vendor platforms (Prisma, Fortinet, Cato) simplify operations; best-of-breed goes deeper per function but you integrate it. Most enterprises consolidate over time.

Is SASE a product or a journey?

A journey a multi-year migration from datacenter-hub to edge-delivered access, rolled out site by site.

Does SASE replace firewalls and VPN?

Over time it replaces the datacenter-hub firewall and VPN model with FWaaS and ZTNA, gradually, with hybrid states normal.

Verdict

Ten solutions, one test: real convergence versus two stacks under a logo.

Prisma benchmarks the single-vendor platform, Zscaler and Netskope lead security-first estates, Fortinet and Cloudflare lead networking-led ones, and Cato proves from-scratch single-pass convergence ask which team owns it, make finalists prove one policy engine, sequence so phase one funds itself, and let sites-migrated-cleanly renew the contract.

articles.title: Hackers Turn Trusted Windows Software Downloads Into Tools for Secretly Controlling PCs
articles.description:
Tampered installers for two Windows utilities, Q-Dir and DesktopOK, turned official SoftwareOK downloads into a way for hackers to take remote control of PCs. The installers launched the genuine applications, giving users little reason to suspect anything was wrong. In the background, they downloaded a Python-based remote access trojan, or RAT, that could run commands, […]

The post Hackers Turn Trusted Windows Software Downloads Into Tools for Secretly Controlling PCs appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Tampered installers for two Windows utilities, Q-Dir and DesktopOK, turned official SoftwareOK downloads into a way for hackers to take remote control of PCs.

The installers launched the genuine applications, giving users little reason to suspect anything was wrong. In the background, they downloaded a Python-based remote access trojan, or RAT, that could run commands, transfer files, and capture screenshots.

The risk extended beyond people who manually downloaded a fresh installer. Logs showed that malicious files also appeared during updates of previously legitimate installations.

That makes this a software supply chain attack: the delivery route users already trusted was itself a source of the malicious files. In the separate Silver Fox download campaign, a working app also helped hide malware, but that installer came through a third-party download portal.

Researchers from AhnLab Security Intelligence Center (ASEC) identified the Python malware and published their technical findings on November 26, 2026.

They confirmed tampered installers for Q-Dir versions 12.85.0.0, 12.84.0.0, and 12.83.0.0, and DesktopOK versions 12.85.0.0 and 12.82.0.0.

ASEC did not establish how the files were replaced and cautioned that the confirmed versions may not cover everyone exposed during the distribution period.

Trusted Windows Software Downloads

Investigators spotted a discrepancy that users would not see just by opening the app: some installers did not match the SHA-256 hashes published on the download page.

A SHA-256 hash acts as a fingerprint for a file. The genuine executables embedded inside the malicious installers did match the published hashes and still carried developer Nenad Hrg’s valid digital signature.

The distinction matters: the signature verified the embedded app, not the installer that delivered it. The installer opened the genuine utility and retrieved two files from an external server: a legitimate 7-Zip extraction tool and an archive containing the trojan.

The archive included its own Python runtime, so the malware could run even if the user had never installed Python. It then registered a Windows scheduled task to keep running independently of Q-Dir or DesktopOK.

In a separate incident, the Notepad++ update server hijacking also exposed users through a trusted update channel, though ASEC did not establish that SoftwareOK was compromised in the same way.

Once running, the trojan contacted a command-and-control server, which sent instructions to the infected PC. Operators could execute shell commands or Python code, upload and download files, capture the screen, and collect system details.

The malware also checked running processes against 1,206 names associated with security products and sent its findings back. The separate SilverFox trusted software case illustrates how genuine software can provide cover for a different remote-access threat.

ASEC identified Chinese-language comments in the SoftwareOK malware, but did not attribute the campaign to a named group.

What Q-Dir and DesktopOK Users Should Check

ASEC recommends uninstalling the existing utility and reinstalling the latest verified release. Before running the replacement installer, compare its SHA-256 hash with the value on the official download page.

A mismatch is a reason to stop, even if the filename and version look right. The separate Notepad++ update verification changes show how an updater can enforce this principle by rejecting downloads that fail signature or certificate checks.

Reinstalling the utility does not remove a trojan that is already running separately. Check for the scheduled task, unexpected Python files, and connections to the addresses below, then update your antivirus and run a full scan.

If you confirm signs of infection, isolate the PC from the network and investigate whether the operators ran additional malware or accessed sensitive files.

Screenshot and file-transfer capabilities show what the malware could do; they do not establish what happened on any individual machine.

The post Top 10 Best DMARC & Email Authentication Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
DMARC’s entire value is reaching an enforcement policy p=reject without blocking your own legitimate mail, and that journey is where most programs stall.

Every tool here parses aggregate reports; they separate on how much of the SPF/DKIM/DMARC gauntlet they automate, how well they discover the sprawl of third-party senders, and who they’re priced for.

Valimail takes 1; Proofpoint and Red Sift complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Valimail the zero-maintenance automation benchmark.

• Podium: Valimail, Proofpoint (enterprise suite depth), Red Sift (guided-enforcement).

• Model split: automation-first platforms (Valimail, Red Sift, EasyDMARC) versus enterprise suites (Proofpoint, Mimecast) versus value/SMB tools (EasyDMARC, Skysnag, Fraudmarc).

• 2026 theme: time-to-enforcement the metric that separates a reporting dashboard from a tool that actually gets you to reject.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: time-to-enforcement (automation to p=reject), hosted SPF/DKIM flattening, third-party-sender discovery, BIMI readiness, and pricing clarity.

Weights: automation to enforcement 30%, sender discovery 20%, hosted SPF/DKIM 20%, BIMI/reporting 15%, pricing 15%.

The 2026 DMARC Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Valimail — Best Zero-Maintenance Automation

Snapshot: Enterprise tiers | Automated sender authentication | Durable enforcement

Why it earns 1: Valimail automates the authentication problem end to end identifying and authenticating sending services without manual DNS churn, so enforcement holds as the sender list changes.

For organizations that want to reach and stay at p=reject without a standing DNS project, it sets the benchmark.

Pros: Automated authentication; durable enforcement; BIMI.

Cons: Automation-first model suits larger estates.

Bottom line: The zero-maintenance enforcement benchmark.

2. Proofpoint — Best Enterprise Suite Depth

Snapshot: Enterprise | DMARC within the email-security program | Impersonation defense

Why it ranks here: Proofpoint folds DMARC into its wider email-security program, managing authentication alongside impersonation defense and VAP intelligence. For Proofpoint estates, DMARC arrives inside the suite.

Pros: Suite integration; impersonation defense; hosted services.

Cons: Standalone DMARC specialists go deeper on the journey.

Bottom line: DMARC inside the Proofpoint program.

3. Red Sift (OnDMARC) — Best Guided-Enforcement

Snapshot: Tiers | Guided path to p=reject + hosted records | BIMI tooling

Why it ranks here: OnDMARC guides the whole journey sender discovery, hosted SPF/DKIM to dodge the 10-lookup limit, and a confident path to p=reject, with BIMI tooling adjacent. For the fastest safe path to enforcement, it’s the guided pick.

Pros: Guided path; hosted records; BIMI; discovery.

Cons: Premium positioning.

Bottom line: The fastest safe path to enforcement.

4. Fortra (Agari) — Best Portfolio-Lineage Defense

Snapshot: Enterprise | Agari lineage within Fortra | DMARC + brand protection

Why it ranks here: Agari’s authentication lineage now ships within Fortra’s portfolio, pairing DMARC with broader email and brand-protection tooling.

Buyers searching “Agari” evaluate the Fortra product. For Fortra estates, it’s the portfolio pick.

Pros: DMARC + brand protection; portfolio integration.

Cons: Portfolio-era packaging confirm.

Bottom line: Authentication within the Fortra portfolio.

5. dmarcian — Best Methodology-Led Program

Snapshot: Tiers | Source categorization + expert guidance | Co-author lineage

Why it ranks here: dmarcian founded by a DMARC co-author is the methodology house: deep reporting, source categorization, and managed guidance for teams wanting expertise alongside the platform. For expertise-led programs, it’s the methodology pick.

Pros: Source categorization; managed guidance; co-author lineage.

Cons: Services-flavored delivery.

Bottom line: The expertise-led program lane.

6. Mimecast — Best Suite-Integrated DMARC

Snapshot: Per-user bundles | DMARC within the email suite | Managed support

Why it ranks here: Mimecast manages DMARC within its email-security suite, suiting estates consolidating gateway, continuity, and authentication under one vendor. For suite consolidation, it’s the integrated pick.

Pros: Suite integration; reporting; managed support.

Cons: Journey depth versus the specialists.

Bottom line: DMARC folded into the Mimecast suite.

7. EasyDMARC — Best SMB Value

Snapshot: Value + free | Hosted records + guided enforcement | Free entry

Why it ranks here: EasyDMARC delivers report parsing, source visibility, hosted records, and guided enforcement at accessible economics with a genuinely useful free entry. For SMB-to-mid-market value, it’s the economics pick.

Pros: Hosted records; guided enforcement; free tier; BIMI.

Cons: Enterprise-depth versus the anchors.

Bottom line: The SMB-to-mid-market value pick.

8. Cloudflare — Best Infra-Native Management

Snapshot: Low-cost/bundled | DMARC within DNS/email routing | Accessible entry

Why it ranks here: Cloudflare offers DMARC management within its DNS and email-routing platform, convenient for organizations already running Cloudflare. For infra-native management, it’s the convenience pick.

Pros: DNS-native; email routing; accessible entry.

Cons: Journey-automation depth versus the specialists.

Bottom line: DMARC where your DNS already lives.

9. Skysnag — Best Automation-for-SMB

Snapshot: Tiers | Automated continuous authentication | SMB fit

Why it ranks here: Skysnag emphasizes automated, continuous authentication for smaller teams wanting enforcement without ongoing manual DNS work. For SMB automation, it’s the hands-off pick.

Pros: Automated enforcement; continuous monitoring; SMB fit.

Cons: Enterprise-scale depth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: Automation for the smaller estate.

10. Fraudmarc — Best Reporting-Focused Value

Snapshot: Value tiers | DMARC reporting + SPF management | Accessible

Why it ranks here: Fraudmarc focuses on clear DMARC reporting and SPF management at accessible economics for teams wanting visibility and basic enforcement support. For reporting-focused value, it’s the accessible pick; confirm current scope.

Pros: Clear reporting; SPF management; value economics.

Cons: Full journey-automation versus the leaders.

Bottom line: Reporting-focused DMARC value.

Buying Advice: Measure Time-to-Enforcement, Mind the 10-Lookup Limit

DMARC success is measured by safe arrival at p=reject, so buy for the journey, not the dashboard pilot finalists on your real sending estate and measure how quickly they discover every legitimate sender and move you toward enforcement without breaking mail.

Match the lane: enterprises racing to reject without disruption want hosted SPF/DKIM and sender discovery (Valimail, Red Sift), teams wanting expertise want the methodology house (dmarcian), and SMBs should start on value tiers (EasyDMARC) before over-buying.

Watch the 10-lookup SPF limit hosted flattening solves it and plan BIMI only after you’ve reached enforcement, since it requires p=reject first.

Move through the policy stages deliberately (monitor at p=none, then quarantine, then reject), authenticate every sender before enforcing, and route “Agari” searches to the Fortra product.

Pair DMARC with anti-phishing and BEC protection since exact-domain spoofing is one technique among several, and track the metric that renews the contract: reaching and holding enforcement across all domains.

What happened to Agari? Agari’s DMARC lineage now ships within Fortra’s security portfolio evaluate the Fortra-backed product.

Does DMARC need BIMI? BIMI needs DMARC, not the reverse displaying your logo requires reaching enforcement first, so p=reject is the prerequisite.

Verdict

Ten tools, one destination: p=reject without breaking your own mail. Valimail automates the whole journey, Red Sift guides it, Proofpoint and Mimecast consolidate it in a suite, and EasyDMARC delivers value measure time-to-enforcement on your real senders, flatten SPF to beat the 10-lookup limit, authenticate every sender before enforcing, and let durable enforcement across all domains renew the contract.

articles.title: Top 10 Best Business Email Compromise (BEC) Protection Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored]
articles.description:
BEC is the most expensive attack in email precisely because there’s nothing to scan no malware, no malicious link, just a perfectly worded message asking finance to change a wire or an executive to approve a payment. Stopping it means modeling who normally talks to whom about what, catching the deviation, and defending the vendor […]

The post Top 10 Best Business Email Compromise (BEC) Protection Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
BEC is the most expensive attack in email precisely because there’s nothing to scan no malware, no malicious link, just a perfectly worded message asking finance to change a wire or an executive to approve a payment.

Stopping it means modeling who normally talks to whom about what, catching the deviation, and defending the vendor relationships attackers hijack.

The tools below separate on behavioral catch rate, vendor and supply-chain fraud defense, and how they close the loop with payment verification. Abnormal Security takes 1; Proofpoint and Mimecast complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Abnormal Security the behavioral-AI BEC benchmark.

• Podium: Abnormal, Proofpoint (intel-led enterprise depth), Mimecast (suite breadth).

• Model split: behavioral-AI layers (Abnormal, IRONSCALES) versus intel-led gateways (Proofpoint, Microsoft) versus specialist fraud/vendor defense (Cloudflare Area 1, Vade, Tessian-Proofpoint).

• 2026 theme: vendor-fraud and the compromised-thread problem the hardest BEC comes from a real account on a real thread.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: behavioral/AI BEC detection, vendor/supply-chain fraud defense, account-takeover detection, remediation speed, financial-process integration, and pricing clarity.

Weights: behavioral BEC detection 30%, vendor-fraud defense 20%, ATO detection 20%, remediation 15%, process integration 15%.

The 2026 BEC Protection Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Abnormal Security — Best Behavioral-AI BEC Benchmark

Snapshot: API subscription | Behavioral AI modeling communication patterns | Vendor-fraud + ATO focus

Why it earns 1: Abnormal is built for exactly this: modeling who normally communicates with whom about what, so the out-of-pattern wire request, the hijacked vendor thread, and the compromised internal account all surface as anomalies with automatic remediation.

For the payload-less attack that defeats everything else, it sets the benchmark.

Pros: Behavioral-AI depth; vendor-fraud detection; ATO catch + clawback.

Cons: Complements the full email-security stack.

Bottom line: The behavioral benchmark for BEC.

2. Proofpoint — Best Intel-Led Enterprise Depth

Snapshot: Enterprise tiers | Threat intel + impersonation + VAP | Broad remediation

Why it ranks here: Proofpoint brings deep threat intelligence and impersonation defense to BEC, with VAP targeting of the executives and finance staff attackers hit, and estate-wide remediation. For enterprise-depth BEC defense, it’s the intel pick.

Pros: Threat-intel depth; impersonation defense; VAP targeting.

Cons: Enterprise complexity versus the API specialists.

Bottom line: Enterprise BEC defense with intel behind it.

3. Mimecast — Best Suite-Breadth BEC Defense

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | Gateway + impersonation + awareness | Suite breadth

Why it ranks here: Mimecast defends BEC with gateway impersonation controls and awareness training, so technical and human layers run together across its suite.

For organizations wanting BEC defense inside a broader email program, it’s the suite pick.

Pros: Impersonation controls; awareness linkage; suite breadth.

Cons: Behavioral-AI depth versus the API leaders.

Bottom line: BEC defense across the email suite.

4. Microsoft — Best Native Baseline

Snapshot: Bundled (E5/add-on) | Native impersonation/spoof defense | Stack-wide signal

Why it ranks here: Microsoft’s native defense flags impersonation and spoofing across M365, improving at scale, though BEC’s payload-less nature leads many estates to add a behavioral layer. Ranked as the native foundation.

Pros: Native integration; bundled economics; stack signal.

Cons: Payload-less BEC often supplemented by behavioral AI.

Bottom line: The native BEC baseline.

5. IRONSCALES — Best Mailbox-AI + Crowdsource

Snapshot: Per-mailbox tiers | Mailbox AI + crowdsourced intel | Automated remediation

Why it ranks here: IRONSCALES applies mailbox-level AI and crowdsourced intelligence to catch impersonation and BEC, remediating automatically across the estate.

For fast, collaborative BEC defense, it’s the crowdsource pick.

Pros: Mailbox AI; crowdsourced intel; automated remediation.

Cons: Enterprise-program breadth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: Mailbox AI against BEC.

6. Cloudflare (Area 1) — Best Preemptive-Infrastructure Defense

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | Area 1 campaign/infrastructure discovery | Early blocking

Why it ranks here: Cloudflare’s Area 1 identifies BEC and phishing infrastructure before campaigns launch, blocking the attacker domains and staging early on Cloudflare’s network. For preemptive, infrastructure-level BEC defense, it’s the early-warning pick.

Pros: Preemptive discovery; infrastructure intel; global network.

Cons: Confirm Area 1 packaging within Cloudflare.

Bottom line: Blocking BEC infrastructure early.

7. Material Security — Best Workspace-Native BEC Defense

Snapshot: SaaS / enterprise tiers | Native Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace protection | Post-delivery remediation

Why it ranks here: Material Security protects cloud email and collaboration environments by combining behavioral signals, identity context, and post-delivery controls to detect BEC, account compromise, and suspicious mailbox activity.

For organizations that want BEC protection built around the modern cloud workspace, it’s the workspace-native pick.

Pros: M365 and Google Workspace fit; account-compromise detection; strong post-delivery remediation.

Cons: Less focused on traditional gateway-style email filtering than some broader email-security suites.

Bottom line: Workspace-native BEC defense with strong account and remediation context.

8. Trend Micro — Best Research-Backed Detection

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | BEC detection backed by threat research | Writing-style analysis

Why it ranks here: Trend Micro backs BEC detection with threat research and writing-style analysis that flags impersonation of known senders. For research-backed detection, it’s the analysis pick.

Pros: Research backing; writing-style analysis; impersonation detection.

Cons: Behavioral-graph depth versus the API leaders.

Bottom line: Research-backed BEC detection.

9. Barracuda — Best Mid-Market Value

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | API impersonation defense | Mid-market economics

Why it ranks here: Barracuda delivers API-based impersonation and BEC defense at mid-market economics, giving smaller teams behavioral protection without enterprise pricing. For value BEC defense, it’s the mid-market pick.

Pros: API impersonation defense; value economics; simplicity.

Cons: Enterprise depth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: BEC defense at value scale.

10. Darktrace / EMAIL — Best Self-Learning Behavioral Detection

Snapshot: Enterprise subscription | Self-learning AI | Behavioral anomaly detection across email

Why it ranks here: Darktrace / EMAIL learns normal communication patterns across users and organizations then flags unusual behavior linked to BEC, impersonation, compromised accounts, and supply-chain attacks.

For organizations that want adaptive behavioral detection rather than static rules, it’s the self-learning AI pick.

Pros: Self-learning behavioral analysis; anomaly detection; strong impersonation and account-compromise coverage.

Cons: Premium enterprise positioning and less pricing transparency than simpler email-security products.

Bottom line: Self-learning behavioral AI for detecting BEC and anomalous email activity.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Weight the Compromised Thread, Close the Payment Loop

The hardest BEC isn’t a spoofed stranger it’s a real vendor account, compromised, replying on a genuine thread to redirect a wire, so test finalists specifically on vendor-fraud and compromised-account scenarios, not just display-name spoofing, because that’s where the losses come from.

Weight behavioral modeling that understands relationships (who normally asks whom for what), since static rules can’t catch a legitimate-looking request on a real thread.

Decide your architecture: a behavioral-AI layer (Abnormal, IRONSCALES) catches the payload-less deviation, intel gateways and native defense form the baseline, and preemptive infrastructure defense (Area 1) blocks campaigns early most estates run native plus a behavioral layer.

Crucially, close the loop outside email: no tool should be the only thing between a message and a wire, so pair detection with mandatory out-of-band payment verification in finance.

Pair with email security, anti-phishing, and security awareness training, and track the metric that renews the contract: BEC attempts reaching finance and executives trending down.

FAQs

What are the best BEC protection tools in 2026? Abnormal as the behavioral-AI benchmark, Proofpoint for intel-led depth, Mimecast for suite breadth, Microsoft as the native baseline, with IRONSCALES, Area 1, Vade, Trend Micro, Barracuda, and Tessian-Proofpoint by model.

Why is BEC so hard to stop? It carries no malware or malicious link just a well-worded request so signature engines have nothing to scan; only behavioral modeling of normal communication catches the deviation.

What’s the hardest form of BEC? Vendor fraud and compromised-account attacks a real account replying on a genuine thread to redirect payment — because nothing about the message looks fake.

Can a tool fully prevent BEC losses? No single tool should be the only thing between a message and a wire pair behavioral detection with mandatory out-of-band payment verification in finance processes.

What proves BEC-protection value? BEC attempts reaching finance and executives trending down, plus fast remediation of compromised-account activity tested on vendor-fraud scenarios, not just spoofing.

Verdict

Ten tools, one unscannable attack: a perfect message asking for money. Abnormal benchmarks behavioral modeling, Proofpoint brings intel depth, IRONSCALES adds crowdsourced catch, and Area 1 blocks the infrastructure early but no tool stands alone, so weight vendor-fraud scenarios, layer native plus behavioral, close the loop with out-of-band payment verification, and let falling BEC attempts to finance renew the contract.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Human risk management is awareness training all grown up: instead of annual compliance clips, it assigns each person a risk figure, intervenes adaptively, and in the newest tools folds in technical signals like which mailboxes are actually in the crosshairs.

The platforms below separate on per-person measurement, adaptive intervention, and whether they catch modern vectors like shadow SaaS and inbox attacks. Mimecast takes 1; KnowBe4 and Hoxhunt complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Mimecast the suite-integrated human-risk benchmark.

• Podium: Mimecast, KnowBe4 (breadth ecosystem), Hoxhunt (adaptive behavior change).

• Model split: suite/breadth platforms (Mimecast, KnowBe4, Proofpoint) versus adaptive engines (Hoxhunt) versus technical-HRM and unified-risk lanes (CultureAI, Living Security, Abnormal).

• 2026 theme: signal fusion the frontier is joining behavioral training to real technical attack signals.

How We Scored (Methodology)

This is a research-led assessment rather than lab testing, with no paid placement and editorial scores held back from structured data.

We judged each platform on how it scores individual risk, how adaptively it intervenes, how well it fuses technical signals, how far it covers modern vectors such as shadow SaaS and inbox attacks, how much it automates, and how clear its pricing is.

Weights: per-person scoring 25%, adaptive intervention 25%, signal fusion 20%, vector coverage 15%, automation 15%.

The 2026 Human Risk Management Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Mimecast — Best Suite-Integrated Human-Risk

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | Awareness + risk scoring in the email suite | Human-risk scoring

Why it earns 1: Mimecast anchors human-risk management to its email-security estate awareness, simulation, and per-user risk scoring bundled where the gateway already bills, with the attack telemetry to target it.

For organizations wanting human risk joined to the email defenses that see the actual attacks, it sets the benchmark.

Pros: Suite integration; attack-telemetry targeting; risk scoring.

Cons: Pure-play adaptive depth versus Hoxhunt-class.

Bottom line: The suite-integrated human-risk benchmark.

2. KnowBe4 — Best Breadth-and-Ecosystem

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | Largest content + HRM analytics | SecurityCoach lineage

Why it ranks here: KnowBe4 brings the largest content library, simulation breadth, and human-risk analytics (SecurityCoach lineage) into one ecosystem. For breadth-first programs, it’s the ecosystem pick.

Pros: Library scale; risk analytics; ecosystem.

Cons: Content volume needs curation.

Bottom line: The breadth-and-ecosystem default.

3. Hoxhunt — Best Adaptive Behavior Change

Snapshot: Per-user | Adaptive, gamified per-person training | Measurable reduction

Why it ranks here: Hoxhunt tailors everything to the individual adaptive lures and bite-size trainings that follow each person’s observed behaviour, wrapped in game mechanics that build a lasting habit of reporting, with per-user risk reduction a board will understand.

When the goal is a measurable shift rather than course completions, it’s the adaptive choice.

Pros: Individual adaptivity; gamification; measurable change.

Cons: Premium positioning.

Bottom line: The behavior-change benchmark.

4. Living Security — Best Unified Human-Risk Metrics

Snapshot: Enterprise | Aggregated human-risk scoring (Unify) | Data-driven targeting

Why it ranks here: Living Security pulls signals from across the stack into one human-risk score, aiming interventions by the data instead of running blanket campaigns. For metrics-driven programs, it’s the unified-risk choice.

Pros: Cross-stack aggregation; unified risk score; targeted action.

Cons: Content-library breadth versus the giants.

Bottom line: The unified human-risk scoreboard.

5. Proofpoint — Best Threat-Informed Targeting

Snapshot: Enterprise | VAP-targeted interventions | Telemetry fusion

Why it ranks here: Proofpoint grounds human risk in its threat telemetry VAP intelligence identifying who’s actually attacked, with training targeted accordingly. For threat-informed targeting, it’s the telemetry pick.

Pros: VAP targeting; telemetry fusion; program scale.

Cons: Fullest value inside the Proofpoint estate.

Bottom line: Human risk aimed by the live threat picture.

6. CultureAI — Best Technical-Signal HRM

Snapshot: Enterprise | Real-time intervention + SaaS/identity risk | Technical-signal fusion

Why it ranks here: CultureAI blends behaviour with hard technical signals risky SaaS activity, misconfigurations, and nudges delivered at the moment of risk pushing past simulation into live human-risk management. For technical-HRM, it’s the fusion pick.

Pros: Real-time intervention; SaaS/identity risk; technical-signal fusion.

Cons: Content-library breadth versus the giants.

Bottom line: The technical, intervene-in-the-moment benchmark.

7. Abnormal Security — Best Detection-Derived Risk

Snapshot: Enterprise | AI inbox behavior scoring | Detection-derived risk

Why it ranks here: Abnormal rates human risk from the detection side its AI learns inbox behaviour to stop socially engineered attacks, then shows which people are most targeted and most exposed.

For detection-derived risk, it’s the behavioral-AI pick.

Pros: Behavioral AI; targeted-user surfacing; detection-derived risk.

Cons: Best as part of the broader email-security buy.

Bottom line: Human risk derived from real detection.

8. OutThink — Best Risk-Intelligence Lane

Snapshot: Enterprise | Human-risk intelligence + profiling | Behavioral insight

Why it ranks here: OutThink casts itself as a human-risk intelligence platform, pairing training with data-led risk profiling and an emphasis on the reasons behind user behaviour. For risk-intelligence programs, it’s the profiling pick.

Pros: Risk profiling; behavioral insight; targeted training.

Cons: Ecosystem breadth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: The risk-intelligence lane.

9. CybSafe — Best Evidence-Based Behavioral Risk Reduction

Snapshot: Human-risk analytics | Behavioral-science-driven interventions | Adaptive security guidance

Why it ranks here: CybSafe combines behavioral analytics, security awareness, phishing simulations, and personalized interventions to identify and reduce risky employee behaviors.

Its platform uses behavior-based risk insights to tailor guidance and measure improvements rather than relying solely on training completion metrics.

For organizations wanting measurable behavior change through personalized interventions and evidence-based human-risk insights, it’s the behavioral risk reduction pick.

Pros: Behavioral risk measurement; adaptive interventions; automated nudges; phishing simulation; data-driven reporting.

Cons: Requires integration and configuration to get meaningful risk insights; enterprise capabilities may require higher-tier plans.

Bottom line: Evidence-based human-risk reduction through measurable behavioral change.

10. Right-Hand — Best Real-Time-Nudge Lane

Snapshot: Per-user | In-the-moment security nudges | Behavioral focus

Why it ranks here: Right-Hand focuses on real-time security nudges and micro-interventions at the point of risky behavior, reinforcing good habits in context. For nudge-driven programs, it’s the in-context pick.

Pros: Real-time nudges; micro-interventions; behavioral focus.

Cons: Platform breadth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: The real-time-nudge lane.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Define “Human Risk,” Then Measure Per Person

Pin down what “human risk” means for you before you shop, because the platforms optimise for different vectors: if it’s susceptibility to phishing, favour adaptive simulation and genuine behaviour change (Hoxhunt); if it’s unmanaged SaaS and loose OAuth, that’s a discovery-and-intervention job training can’t do (CultureAI); if it’s inbox attacks, let the detection layer rate the risk (Abnormal); and if you want it all rolled into one score, begin with the aggregators (Living Security, Proofpoint, Mimecast).

Demand per-person measurement instead of completion rates, deliver interventions in the moment rather than annually, and keep the program blame-free so staff report instead of hiding.

Prove it to leadership with trend lines click rate down, report rate up, highest-risk cohort shrinking not module counts. Connect HRM to your security awareness training and phishing simulation programs, feed the risk signal into anti-phishing so the riskiest users get more coaching and more technical protection, and track the metric that renews the contract: per-person risk trending down.

FAQs

What are the best human risk management platforms in 2026?

Mimecast as the suite-integrated benchmark, KnowBe4 for breadth, Hoxhunt for adaptive change, Living Security for unified risk, CultureAI for technical-signal HRM, with Proofpoint, Abnormal, OutThink, Mimecast Elevate, and Right-Hand by model.

How is HRM different from awareness training?

Awareness training pushes out content; HRM rates each person’s risk, intervenes adaptively, and increasingly weds behavioural training to live technical attack signals.

What should I measure?

Per-person risk trends a falling click rate, a rising report rate, fewer risky actions rather than course-completion percentages.

Can one platform cover all human risk?

No single tool covers phishing, SaaS sprawl, and inbox attacks equally map your dominant vector and consider complementary tools.

Does detection-based HRM replace training?

No platforms such as Abnormal rate risk off live attacks, yet shifting behaviour still takes adaptive training; the two feed each other.

Verdict

Ten platforms, one evolution: from annual modules to measured, adaptive, signal-fused human risk.

Mimecast integrates it with the email suite, KnowBe4 brings breadth, Hoxhunt personalizes for change, Living Security unifies the score, and CultureAI fuses technical signals define your dominant vector, measure per person, stay blameless, and let a falling human-risk score renew the contract.

articles.title: Hackers Test Malware Against Microsoft Defender Until It Runs Without Triggering an Alert
articles.description:
A Russian-speaking ransomware crew tested its Windows malware against Microsoft Defender for Endpoint in a lab it controlled. On October 16, 2026, Defender flagged one build and automatically isolated the test machine. Five days later, a revised build reached the crew’s command-and-control server without triggering an alert in the exported device timeline. That second test […]

The post Hackers Test Malware Against Microsoft Defender Until It Runs Without Triggering an Alert appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Russian-speaking ransomware crew tested its Windows malware against Microsoft Defender for Endpoint in a lab it controlled. On October 16, 2026, Defender flagged one build and automatically isolated the test machine.

Five days later, a revised build reached the crew’s command-and-control server without triggering an alert in the exported device timeline.

That second test was not invisible. Defender recorded the outbound connection, data preparation and attempts to discover accounts. None of the 659 events in the export carried an alert ID.

The distinction matters for security teams: an empty alert queue does not mean the endpoint has nothing worth investigating.

Analysts from SOCRadar identified the malware as Streamer, a Windows implant written in Rust. The November 26 report drew on files, screenshots and Defender exports tied to the operators’ infrastructure.

Researchers said they took no action against victim systems and notified affected organizations and relevant authorities.

Hackers Test Malware Against Microsoft Defender

The October 16 test produced one high-severity incident containing 10 alerts. Four concerned an executable loading an unexpected library, a pattern known as DLL side-loading. Defender then isolated the device.

Microsoft’s automatic device isolation feature is designed to cut a compromised workstation off from the network while preserving its connection to the Defender service.

On October 21, the revised Streamer build presented itself as a security product component. Defender recorded it as an unknown process and marked the file as obfuscated, meaning its contents were made harder to inspect.

The device page still showed no known risks. This differs from the Gentlemen ransomware Defender tampering case, where malware actively tried to turn off protection. Here, Defender kept collecting events.

The report does not establish which change accounted for the different outcome or whether the same build would go unflagged on another endpoint.

What it does show is that investigators had several clues to work with. A process contacting an unfamiliar server may not stand out on its own.

The same process making that connection after gathering account information and preparing data is a stronger reason to investigate.

LostTrust, Eclipse and What Defenders Can Hunt For

The same build server held deployment files for the MetaEncryptor/LostTrust extortion platform. SOCRadar also found overlap with an Eclipse ransomware server examined by the Atos Threat Research Center, including the Streamer framework and a matching developer handle.

Researchers assessed with high confidence that the two servers shared a developer and toolkit, but could not determine whether the ransomware brands were run by the same crew.

The operators’ records named 17 organizations across four countries, 14 of them in the United States. They included a federal agency, three energy cooperatives and a healthcare provider.

The federal case showed sustained access and theft of source repository files and an API private key. The records range from confirmed activity to operator claims and one reconnaissance-only case, so the count does not represent 17 confirmed breaches or ransomware deployments.

SOCRadar recommends hunting in endpoint timelines rather than relying on alerts alone. Review unexpected library loads by trusted programs, then correlate them with unfamiliar outbound connections or bulk directory queries.

Earlier coverage of trusted software loading malware shows why investigators should examine the libraries a signed program loads, not just the program’s signature.

Microsoft’s Defender behavior monitoring documentation explains how the product observes processes, files and services as they run.

For this case, the practical step is to use a match on a hash or domain to pivot into the device timeline and check what the process did before and after the match. Validate infrastructure indicators before blocking them, especially the suspected front end that appeared only in a lab firewall allow-list.

Researchers also observed reconnaissance against more than 30 Indonesian government organizations but found […]

The post Hackers Breach Military and Government Networks Across Southeast Asia, Stealing Sensitive Documents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers stole gigabytes of sensitive documents and exposed government credentials in a cyber espionage campaign that breached military, government and legislative organizations in Thailand and the Philippines.

The operation, called RedOps, ran from August to September 2026 and involved five confirmed intrusions. Researchers also observed reconnaissance against more than 30 Indonesian government organizations but found no evidence that the attackers breached those networks.

The records point to an interest in South China Sea defense ties and military agreements. The attackers searched public sources for information on regional military cooperation before collecting government material that was not publicly available.

The stolen files included legislative records and military logistics documents, while a separate breach exposed records on national strategy and budget planning.

Analysts from SOCRadar identified malicious tools used in the campaign, including a custom component that let the operators send instructions to a compromised JasperReports server and receive results.

The researchers tracked the group as WeaveLotus and assessed Vietnamese state sponsorship with moderate confidence, but said the evidence was not conclusive.

The team cited Vietnamese-language comments in scripts, activity consistent with UTC+7 working hours and the group’s choice of targets.

Hackers Breach Military and Government Networks

At a Thai military-affiliated organization, researchers believe the attackers entered through CVE-2024-36401, a critical flaw in GeoServer, an open-source platform for sharing mapping data.

The same flaw enabled a separate U.S. federal agency breach that CISA documented. In Thailand, the attackers used the compromised server to reach a Directus content management system that allowed file access without a login.

They downloaded about 31,418 files totaling 575 MB, including documents on logistics, disaster response and military operations.

The largest verified transfer came from a Thai legislative organization. The group signed in to an internet-facing JasperReports server with default credentials and reached a third-party document management system that relied on it.

Researchers verified about 19 GB of stolen data against transfer logs. The haul included meeting agendas, expenditure records, appointments and asset disclosure outcomes.

The attackers also captured administrator credentials for a separate Thai government organization, turning one breach into a route to another agency.

Those credentials gave the group access to a server running Keycloak, an identity management platform. The attackers copied a database containing more than 40,000 user records and used recovered passwords to reach a connected application.

They retrieved 349,782 records covering policy, fiscal plans and budget allocations. In the Philippines, a vulnerable osTicket deployment exposed staff usernames, email addresses and password hashes.

At a second Philippine organization, a Laravel application running in debug mode exposed server paths and snippets of source code.

What Defenders Can Learn From RedOps

The targeting fits a wider pattern of Southeast Asian government espionage, but similar targets do not mean the same group was responsible.

SOCRadar assessed a direct link to OceanLotus, also known as APT32, with low confidence. Unlike the OceanLotus supply chain attack involving FireAnt MetaKit, RedOps relied on exposed applications and weak configurations rather than a tampered software update.

Researchers did not observe known APT32 malware in the campaign. Security teams should prioritize patching exposed GeoServer and osTicket instances, replacing default JasperReports credentials, disabling debug mode in production Laravel applications and checking whether sensitive file APIs allow anonymous access.

They should also look for unexpected outbound SSH sessions over port 443 and unusually large file transfers. For public agencies and their vendors, the Thai legislative breach shows why that review should extend to shared reporting systems and identity trusts: access to one supporting service exposed documents and credentials beyond the original server.

articles.title: Cacti 4HTTP2ROOT Zero-Day Lets Hackers Execute Commands on Network Monitoring Servers Without Login
articles.description:
A zero-day vulnerability in Cacti, an open-source network monitoring tool, lets attackers run operating system commands without logging in if guest access is enabled. Security researcher ek0ms savi0r disclosed the flaw, dubbed 4HTTP2ROOT, on November 26, 2026. A public proof of concept demonstrated command execution in four HTTP requests against Cacti 1.2.31, and Previdian reported […]

The post Cacti 4HTTP2ROOT Zero-Day Lets Hackers Execute Commands on Network Monitoring Servers Without Login appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A zero-day vulnerability in Cacti, an open-source network monitoring tool, lets attackers run operating system commands without logging in if guest access is enabled. Security researcher ek0ms savi0r disclosed the flaw, dubbed 4HTTP2ROOT, on November 26, 2026.

A public proof of concept demonstrated command execution in four HTTP requests against Cacti 1.2.31, and Previdian reported verifying the result in a lab. No exploitation in the wild had been reported as of November 27.

The flaw is a stored SQL injection, which means Cacti saves untrusted input and later treats it as part of a database command. The application does not properly check settings that a guest can control.

The resulting database changes can affect Cacti’s polling configuration, which governs how it collects monitoring data. In the lab, that led to remote code execution, meaning someone who could reach the web interface could run commands on the server without a valid account.

The researcher demonstrated root-level command execution on a test system where Cacti was already running as root. That result does not mean the flaw grants root privileges on every server.

Commands run with the permissions of the affected process. Even without root access, a compromised monitoring server could expose credentials Cacti uses to reach network devices, giving an attacker a possible route into other systems.

Cacti 4HTTP2ROOT Vulnerability

Cyber Security News previously covered a Cacti command injection flaw and a separate remote code execution flaw in Cacti’s SNMP parser. Both required authenticated access. The new disclosure matters because the demonstrated attack requires no login when anonymous guest access is enabled.

According to Previdian, Cacti 1.2.31 is the confirmed affected version, but the full scope remains unknown, with no public CVE, official severity rating, or confirmed patch available at the time of reporting.

Guest access is off by default, but administrators can enable it to share monitoring graphs without requiring users to sign in. Teams should verify the setting on each deployment rather than assume it is still off.

Administrators should remove the designated Guest User from Cacti’s authentication settings and deactivate the guest account under Console > Configuration > Users.

Then open a fresh browser session without signing in and confirm anonymous visitors can no longer access protected features. Restrict the web interface to trusted management networks or authenticated VPN users. Turning off guest access blocks the demonstrated attack path, but it does not repair the underlying SQL injection.

Security teams should review unexpected changes to user settings and polling configurations and look for unusual processes started by Cacti. Make sure the application and its polling processes do not run as root unless required.

If compromise is suspected, assess which network device credentials the server could access and rotate those that may have been exposed. Follow the official Cacti security advisories and release notes for a confirmed fix.

articles.title: Hackers Hide PolinRider Malware in 375 GitHub Repositories to Execute Malicious Code
articles.description:
Hackers planted PolinRider malware in 375 GitHub repositories, hiding a Python loader in ordinary-looking project files. The loader retrieves JavaScript stored in an Ethereum transaction and runs it through Node.js. In some projects, running tests is enough to trigger the loader. In others, it can run when the application starts and imports the planted module. […]

The post Hackers Hide PolinRider Malware in 375 GitHub Repositories to Execute Malicious Code appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers planted PolinRider malware in 375 GitHub repositories, hiding a Python loader in ordinary-looking project files. The loader retrieves JavaScript stored in an Ethereum transaction and runs it through Node.js.

In some projects, running tests is enough to trigger the loader. In others, it can run when the application starts and imports the planted module.

The affected public repositories belonged to 260 accounts, and 370 had received a push in November 2026. Those figures describe the reach of the malicious code, not the number of machines infected.

Unlike the earlier PolinRider npm package compromises, this Python variant was found in repository source files, not in packages published to PyPI or npm.

Researchers at SafeDep.io identified the loader on the repositories’ default branches on November 24, 2026, after Jay Maier of Rising Sun Solutions first reported it that day.

The team traced the Python code to an Ethereum wallet and found a second wallet that pointed the malware to its command-and-control (C2) server. The server supplied additional code, but SafeDep did not retrieve it during this investigation.

Hackers Hide PolinRider Malware in 375 GitHub Repositories

SafeDep found the same 58-line loader in all 375 repositories. In 363 cases, it sat inside a planted package, often in a utils folder. The most common filename was session.py, which accounted for 183 copies.

The other 12 loaders appeared in conftest.py, a configuration file that pytest imports while collecting tests. That means the loader can run before a test case starts.

The risk resembles other GitHub repository malware traps that turn routine development work into a trigger. But opening or cloning a repository is not the same as executing this loader.

In three applications SafeDep checked, the documented startup commands failed because Python could not find the planted package.

That distinction matters: the import error prevented execution in those tests, but fixing the import path without inspecting the code could activate the loader.

Once loaded, the Python code reads the input data of the latest transaction an Ethereum wallet sent to itself. As of November 24, that transaction held roughly 31 KB of JavaScript.

The JavaScript used a second wallet to locate the C2 server, then handed further code to a separate Node.js process. The use of blockchain command and control lets operators change the server address without editing each planted file.

What Developers Should Check Before Running Tests

SafeDep also tied the second wallet to malicious changes in two AsyncAPI Generator pull requests. Maintainers did not merge the changes, and no automated build ran them.

Separate reporting on PolinRider in pull requests found that CircuitVerse’s build workflow did execute a loader. The contrast shows why incident responders should check what a workflow actually ran, rather than treating every malicious commit as proof of execution.

Start with a static review of the working tree and Git history before running tests or starting a suspect project. Look for unfamiliar conftest.py changes, new utility modules, and unexpected imports in application entry points.

A dependency scan alone can miss this variant because the loader uses Python’s standard library. Commit messages are not reliable proof of cleanup either: SafeDep found two repositories where commits claiming to remove malware still contained the loader.

If a suspect project ran on a machine with Node.js, SafeDep recommends treating the host as compromised. Isolate it and review process and network logs, then rotate exposed secrets from a clean machine.

Revoke affected GitHub tokens and SSH keys, invalidate browser sessions, and check automated build runners that handled the same code. Cleaning the branch without securing the machines and credentials that can push to it leaves the repository open to reinfection.

SafeDep observed the latest C2 address using plain HTTP on port 443. That protocol mismatch is worth checking alongside unexpected Node.js activity.

Earlier PolinRider stages stole browser passwords, cookies, environment secrets, and wallet data, but SafeDep did not verify what the server delivered in this Python wave. Responders should investigate possible exposure without reporting theft as a confirmed outcome.

Indicators of compromise (IoCs);-

articles.title: SAP Confirms Security Incident as Hackers Reportedly Steal GitHub Tokens and Alter Code
articles.description:
SAP has confirmed an IT security incident after detecting suspicious activity. DER SPIEGEL reported that attackers stole authentication tokens belonging to SAP employees and used them to alter and copy source code on GitHub. The German software maker said it took immediate steps to protect customers and secure its services. It said investigators had found […]

The post SAP Confirms Security Incident as Hackers Reportedly Steal GitHub Tokens and Alter Code appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
SAP has confirmed an IT security incident after detecting suspicious activity. DER SPIEGEL reported that attackers stole authentication tokens belonging to SAP employees and used them to alter and copy source code on GitHub. The German software maker said it took immediate steps to protect customers and secure its services.

It said investigators had found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data at that stage. SAP did not answer detailed questions about the incident.

An internal memo cited by DER SPIEGEL described the incident as active. SAP is reportedly handling the investigation under the name “Project Granite.” The magazine, citing sources inside the company, said the attackers may have used AI agents. SAP has not confirmed that detail, and the reporting does not explain what role, if any, AI played in the incident.

Stolen GitHub Tokens Used to Alter SAP Code

An authentication token is a digital credential that gives a person or tool access to an account or service. On GitHub, the permissions tied to a token help determine whether its holder can read a repository, a project’s code and change history, or also make changes.

Cybersecurity News recently covered a separate case in which a malicious VS Code extension stole GitHub tokens. The method used to obtain the SAP employees’ tokens has not been disclosed.

SAP publishes source code for products and open-source projects on GitHub. The report did not name the affected repositories or say whether the copied code was public or private. Those details matter.

SAP’s statement addresses unauthorized access to customer business data. It does not establish whether any code changes reached software that customers use

In a separate case, Cybersecurity News reported how hijacked GitHub accounts targeted automated build workflows. That case shows why investigators look beyond the changed files to check whether automated systems used the altered code. There is no public evidence tying that campaign to SAP.

GitHub’s audit log guidance explains how organizations can trace recorded actions back to a compromised token. GitHub also lets administrators revoke credentials by user and token type.

SAP has not publicly described which steps it took or which repositories it reviewed. The most useful details for customers and developers would be the affected repository names, whether any published builds contained unauthorized changes, and whether users need to take action.

Until SAP shares those details, the reported code changes should not be treated as evidence that customer software or business data was compromised.

articles.title: Bitcoin Privacy Flaw Could Let Hackers Trace Wallet Addresses to IP Addresses for Just 35 Cents
articles.description:
A privacy flaw in Bitcoin Core could let an observer link a public Bitcoin address to the IP address of a node that tracks it. Bitcoin Core contributor Abubakar Sadiq Ismail reported on November 25 that the link could be made with a payment costing less than 35 cents in his estimate. His test identified […]

The post Bitcoin Privacy Flaw Could Let Hackers Trace Wallet Addresses to IP Addresses for Just 35 Cents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A privacy flaw in Bitcoin Core could let an observer link a public Bitcoin address to the IP address of a node that tracks it. Bitcoin Core contributor Abubakar Sadiq Ismail reported on November 25 that the link could be made with a payment costing less than 35 cents in his estimate.

His test identified the correct node in 30 out of 30 attempts on a private test network. The result has not been measured on Bitcoin’s live network.

The finding does not show that anyone can steal funds or recover private keys. It exposes a different kind of information: which computer’s wallet recognizes a Bitcoin address.

That link matters because it connects a public payment record to network activity, a privacy risk also seen in the reported Wagyu crypto platform breach, though the two cases involve different ways of exposing the data.

Bitcoin Privacy Flaw

In his Delving Bitcoin research post, Ismail traced the leak to wallet rebroadcast, the process of announcing an unconfirmed payment again. The behavior is meant to help payments stay visible to the network.

But Bitcoin Core can resend both outgoing and incoming payments held by its wallet. That means a node can reveal that it tracks a receiving address even when its operator did not send the payment.

Ismail used standard Bitcoin Core software on regtest, a local Bitcoin test network, with five wallets across six trials. The estimated payment cost ranged from about 18 to 34 cents, depending on the address type and the Bitcoin price used in the report.

That figure covers the small payment and its fee, not the cost of monitoring the network. On the live network, which nodes an observer can see and whether other nodes also relay the payment could make attribution less clear.

The flaw is in the wallet, not in every Bitcoin Core node. It can affect a watch-only wallet, which tracks addresses without holding the private keys needed to spend their funds. Third-party wallets can also inherit the behavior when they load addresses into a Bitcoin Core wallet. Ismail cited Sparrow in Bitcoin Core mode and Specter Desktop as examples.

A match therefore identifies a node that tracks the address, not necessarily the person who owns the bitcoin. A shared service can track addresses for many users, and an IP address alone does not establish a person’s identity. The distinction matters when grouping cryptocurrency addresses during investigations.

Operators can set -walletbroadcast=0 to stop the wallet from announcing transactions. The trade-off is that it also stops the first announcement of their own outgoing payments, so those transactions must be broadcast separately.

Ismail also noted that using Tor alongside peers on the public internet does not shield the public IP from this leak. A Tor-only setup avoids exposing that IP through rebroadcast, but it can still link the wallet address to the node’s Tor identity.

The Bitcoin Core developer discussion points to a longer-term option: make automatic rebroadcast of incoming payments opt-in. Developers cautioned that a narrower proposed change would not close every path. For operators, the first step is to check whether their setup loads a Bitcoin Core wallet at all, including one used only to watch addresses.
