articles.description:
Nothing in security is trickier than insider risk, because the person triggering it is already logged in, already permitted, and often acting in good faith the resignee copying files and the sloppy uploader set off identical alarms. The solutions below separate on where they center detection (user behavior, data movement, or analytics), whether they tell […]

The post Top 10 Best Insider Threat Management Solutions in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Nothing in security is trickier than insider risk, because the person triggering it is already logged in, already permitted, and often acting in good faith the resignee copying files and the sloppy uploader set off identical alarms.

The solutions below separate on where they center detection (user behavior, data movement, or analytics), whether they tell malice from carelessness, and how proportionately they can be run. Proofpoint takes 1; Microsoft and Forcepoint complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Proofpoint the people-centric ITM benchmark.

• Podium: Proofpoint, Microsoft (M365-native Purview), Forcepoint (risk-adaptive enforcement).

• Model split: user-centric monitoring (Proofpoint, Teramind, DTEX) versus data-centric (Varonis) versus analytics-centric UEBA (Gurucul).

• 2026 theme: proportionality the programs that work pair strong detection with governance that keeps employee trust intact.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: detection approach (user, data, analytics), behavioral context (intent vs accident), data-movement visibility, forensic depth, privacy/proportionality controls, and pricing clarity.

Weights: behavioral context 25%, data-movement visibility 25%, detection approach 20%, forensic depth 15%, proportionality controls 15%.

The 2026 Insider Threat Management Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Proofpoint — Best People-Centric ITM Benchmark

Snapshot: Enterprise | ITM (ObserveIT lineage) with context | People-centric lens

Why it earns 1: Proofpoint’s ITM captures user activity with context screen, file, and application timeline centered on the people most likely to pose or attract risk, inside its people-centric security program.

For organizations wanting insider risk in the same lens as their email and data defense, it sets the benchmark.

Pros: Activity capture with context; timeline forensics; people-centric lens.

Cons: Endpoint-agent footprint.

Bottom line: The people-centric ITM benchmark.

2. Microsoft (Purview IRM) — Best M365-Native Insider Risk

Snapshot: Bundled (E5/add-on) | Native Microsoft 365 signals | Policy templates + HR context

Why it ranks here: Purview Insider Risk Management runs natively across Microsoft 365, correlating signals from email, SharePoint, Teams, and endpoints with policy templates and HR-connector context.

For Microsoft-stack estates, insider risk arrives without a new agent or vendor.

Pros: Native M365 signals; policy templates; HR connectors.

Cons: Value concentrates in the Microsoft stack.

Bottom line: Insider risk native to Microsoft 365.

3. Forcepoint — Best Risk-Adaptive Enforcement

Snapshot: Enterprise | Risk-adaptive protection | Behavioral scoring + DLP

Why it ranks here: Forcepoint scores user behavior continuously and dials enforcement up or down in response, tightening automatically as behavior drifts toward exfiltration.

For programs wanting DLP that responds to intent rather than blanket-blocking, it’s the risk-adaptive pick.

Pros: Risk-adaptive enforcement; behavioral scoring; integrated DLP.

Cons: Tuning investment to calibrate scoring.

Bottom line: DLP that responds to intent.

4. DTEX Systems — Best Behavioral-Analytics Lens

Snapshot: Per-user | Privacy-conscious behavioral analytics | Lightweight telemetry

Why it ranks here: DTEX centers human-behavior analytics with a privacy-respecting, lightweight model building behavioral baselines and surfacing intent without heavy surveillance.

For programs wanting analytics-led insight with proportionality built in, it’s the behavioral pick.

Pros: Behavioral baselining; privacy-conscious telemetry; intent scoring.

Cons: Deep session-forensics versus the UAM specialists.

Bottom line: The privacy-conscious behavioral lens.

5. Teramind — Best Forensic User Monitoring

Snapshot: Per-seat tiers | Granular UAM + session playback | Forensic depth

Why it ranks here: Teramind goes fine-grained keystroke, screen, application, and session capture with policy alerts and forensic replay the depth you want when an investigation must reconstruct exactly what someone did.

For forensic-grade monitoring (with proportionality controls), it’s the UAM pick.

Pros: Granular UAM; forensic playback; policy automation.

Cons: Monitoring depth demands proportionality governance.

Bottom line: The forensic-depth monitoring lane.

6. Mimecast (Code42) — Best Data-Exfiltration Detection

Snapshot: Per-user | Code42 Incydr within Mimecast | Exfiltration focus

Why it ranks here: Code42’s Incydr, now under Mimecast, is purpose-built to catch file exfiltration across endpoint, cloud, and email with little policy setup. Buyers searching “Code42” evaluate the Mimecast product. For data-movement detection, it’s the exfiltration pick.

Pros: Exfiltration detection; low-policy model; broad egress coverage.

Cons: Confirm packaging within Mimecast.

Bottom line: File-exfiltration detection, Mimecast-backed.

7. Varonis — Best Data-Centric Defense

Snapshot: Enterprise | Permissions mapping + data-access anomalies | Data-first

Why it ranks here: Varonis starts from the asset who can access what data, who actually does, and when access patterns go anomalous catching over-permissioning and exfiltration that user-watching tools miss. For data-first organizations, it’s the data-centric anchor.

Pros: Permissions mapping; data-access anomaly detection; DSP breadth.

Cons: User-behavior forensics versus the UAM tools.

Bottom line: The data-first insider benchmark.

8. Gurucul — Best UEBA Analytics

Snapshot: Enterprise | ML UEBA across identities and data | Risk scoring

Why it ranks here: Gurucul applies ML UEBA across identities and data, scoring insider risk through behavioral baselines and anomaly detection spanning on-prem and cloud. For analytics-first programs, it’s the UEBA pick.

Pros: ML UEBA; identity analytics; risk scoring.

Cons: Model tuning and data onboarding.

Bottom line: The UEBA-centric insider lane.

9. Netwrix — Best Audit-and-Governance Lane

Snapshot: Tiers | Data-access auditing + change tracking | Governance focus

Why it ranks here: Netwrix offers data-access auditing and change tracking through a governance lens, fitting organisations that anchor insider oversight on access audit. For audit-led programs, it’s the governance pick.

Pros: Access auditing; change tracking; governance reporting.

Cons: Behavioral-analytics depth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: The audit-and-governance lane.

10. Veriato — Best SMB Behavioral Monitoring

Snapshot: Per-user | User-activity monitoring + behavioral analytics | SMB fit

Why it ranks here: Veriato delivers user-activity monitoring and behavioral analytics at economics suiting smaller organizations wanting insider visibility without enterprise platforms. For SMB monitoring, it’s the accessible pick.

Pros: User-activity monitoring; behavioral analytics; SMB economics.

Cons: Enterprise-scale depth versus the leaders.

articles.title: Microsoft Warns State-Backed Hackers Are Using ARTEX AI Agents to Steal Credentials and Breach Networks
articles.description:

The post Microsoft Warns State-Backed Hackers Are Using ARTEX AI Agents to Steal Credentials and Breach Networks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
State-backed hackers and financially motivated groups are using ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework, to find exposed systems, steal credentials, and break into enterprise networks and cloud environments.

In a November 25 report, Microsoft warned that the framework can move from scanning to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on the target’s defenses and how the operator uses it.

The report does not describe a new exploit or a flaw in an AI model. Instead, ARTEX speeds up familiar techniques and reduces the need for an operator to intervene between steps.

In one case, an AI agent went from searching public GitHub repositories for application secrets to extracting data from Azure Key Vault, Microsoft’s cloud service for storing secrets, in five minutes.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence researchers identified six threat actors using ARTEX: Storm-0940, Storm-3358, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Crystal Typhoon, and Salt Typhoon.

Microsoft Warns State-Backed Hackers Are Using ARTEX AI Agents

They describe ARTEX as a security testing framework abused by attackers, not a standalone malware family. As earlier coverage of internet-exposed AI hacking frameworks showed, these tools can support authorized security testing, but the same automation can also speed up intrusions.

ARTEX divides work among several AI agents. A planner reviews what the framework has discovered, workers carry out assigned tasks, and a reporter documents confirmed findings.

The framework updates a shared record of systems and findings as work progresses. That matters because an agent can act on a discovery while other tasks are still running, rather than waiting for a person to review the results.

Microsoft’s ConnectWise supply chain investigation found that China-aligned Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate intrusions.

The ConnectWise Microsoft 365 campaign involved stolen application credentials and sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 customer environments, not 2,250 confirmed breaches.

The attackers relied on permissions customers had already granted to trusted applications. In multiple Storm-0940 intrusions, Microsoft observed the group reach privileged cloud access less than three hours after initial targeting.

Microsoft recorded more than 151,000 failed sign-ins in one Storm-0940 campaign, with a peak of 2,900 failures per minute. Other activity was less obvious: ARTEX agents added credentials to applications to maintain access, and one application assigned itself the Global Administrator role.

The previously reported ARTEX GitHub credential theft case illustrates a separate risk: a leaked application secret can expose cloud data without an employee account being compromised.

How Defenders Can Detect and Contain ARTEX Activity

Microsoft says the strongest signal is a sequence of events, not a single IP address or browser identifier. Look for bursts of web requests or failed sign-ins followed quickly by successful access, unusual server processes, or changes to cloud application permissions.

A web server unexpectedly launching a command shell is worth investigating, especially if it coincides with new scripts in a web folder or rapid reads of files that hold credentials.

For cloud investigations, collect application identity sign-in logs as well as employee sign-in logs. Microsoft Entra records those events separately.

Teams should correlate them with audit logs for new application credentials and privileged role assignments. The FBI’s ARTEX security warning also underscores why defenders should check what an internet-facing service or trusted application can reach after it is compromised.

Microsoft recommends patching exposed systems first, using web application firewalls in prevention mode after tuning, and rate-limiting bursts of requests. Enable secret scanning and push protection to catch credentials before they enter repositories.

Revoke and replace exposed secrets, move workloads to managed identities where possible, and require phishing-resistant multifactor authentication for administrators.

Microsoft also recommends enabling automatic attack disruption in Defender XDR to help contain compromised assets before attackers move to other systems.

Why it ranks here: NetSPI combines expert-led penetration testing with a mature penetration-testing-as-a-service platform, covering applications, APIs, cloud environments, networks, and enterprise infrastructure.

For organizations that want traditional penetration-testing depth combined with continuous visibility, remediation tracking, and retesting, it’s the enterprise-PTaaS pick.

Pros: Broad testing coverage; mature PTaaS platform; remediation and retesting workflows.

Cons: Enterprise-focused positioning may be more than smaller organizations require.

Bottom line: Enterprise-scale penetration testing with a strong PTaaS delivery model.

6. Google (Mandiant) — Best Incident-Informed Offense

Snapshot: Services | Offense informed by frontline IR | Elite reputation

Why it ranks here: Mandiant within Google tests with the authority of a firm that works the biggest breaches, so its offensive engagements reflect how real intrusions unfold.

For organizations wanting offense informed by frontline incident response, it’s the incident-informed pick.

Pros: IR-informed realism; elite reputation; threat-actor fluency.

Cons: Premium; demand-driven scheduling.

Bottom line: Offense shaped by real intrusions.

7. Cobalt — Best Agile PTaaS Delivery

Snapshot: PTaaS platform | Vetted pentester community | Fast, flexible testing delivery

Why it ranks here: Cobalt delivers penetration testing through a PTaaS model that connects organizations with vetted security researchers while centralizing findings, collaboration, remediation, and retesting within its platform.

For teams that need faster testing cycles across web applications, APIs, cloud environments, mobile applications, and networks, it’s the agile-PTaaS pick.

Pros: Flexible engagement model; broad testing coverage; centralized remediation and retesting.

Cons: Less traditional consultancy depth than specialist research-led firms for highly bespoke engagements.

Bottom line: Agile penetration testing built around a modern PTaaS workflow.

8. Optiv — Best Large-Scale Program Delivery

Snapshot: Services + advisory | Large program delivery | Advisory integration

Why it ranks here: Optiv delivers penetration testing within large security programs, pairing testing with advisory and integration services
for enterprises running multi-year engagements.

For organizations wanting testing inside a broader program relationship, it’s the scale-delivery pick.

Pros: Program-scale delivery; advisory integration; enterprise fit.

Cons: Research-boutique depth versus the specialists.

Bottom line: Testing inside the big program.

9. Synack — Best Crowd-Blended Assurance

Snapshot: Platform + vetted researchers | Crowd testing on a controlled platform | Continuous option

Why it ranks here: Synack blends a vetted researcher crowd with a controlled platform, delivering testing coverage and continuous assessment with the governance enterprises need.

For organizations wanting crowd breadth under control, it’s the crowd-blended pick.

Pros: Crowd breadth; platform governance; continuous coverage.

Cons: Bespoke consultancy depth versus the research leaders.

Bottom line: Crowd scale, enterprise control.

10. IBM X-Force — Best Enterprise-Scale Engagements

Snapshot: Services | X-Force Red offensive team | Enterprise delivery

Why it ranks here: IBM’s X-Force Red brings offensive testing within IBM’s enterprise delivery machine, covering application, network, hardware, and adversary simulation at large-account scale.

For IBM-estate enterprises, it’s the scale-engagement pick.

Pros: X-Force Red offense; enterprise delivery; broad scope.

Cons: Boutique agility versus the specialists.

Bottom line: Offensive testing at IBM scale.

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Vet the Testers, Demand the Retest

A pentest is bought on the testers assigned and the fixes it drives, not the firm’s logo, so before you sign, ask who will actually be on your engagement, read a sample report, and confirm a retest is included because a finding without a verified fix is half a deliverable.

Match the firm to your scope: compliance-driven testing wants assessor heritage (Coalfire), adversary realism wants intel- and IR-informed offense (Secureworks, Mandiant), and continuous coverage wants a crowd or attack-surface model (Synack, Bishop Fox).

Insist on reproducible findings with clear remediation paths over raw CVE dumps, scope the hard assets (cloud, OT, identity) to specialists who’ve done them, and treat the readout as the start of remediation, not the end of the engagement.

Track the metric that justifies the spend: repeat findings closed and not recurring at the next test. Feed results into your vulnerability management and attack path management programs so testing, exposure, and fix share one picture.

FAQs

What are the best penetration testing companies in 2026? NCC Group as the research-depth benchmark, Bishop Fox for offensive reputation, Rapid7 for platform-plus-services, Coalfire for compliance alignment, Mandiant for IR-informed offense, with Secureworks, Trustwave, Optiv, Synack, and IBM X-Force by model.

How do I judge a pentest firm? On the testers assigned to your engagement, the reproducibility and remediation guidance in a sample report, and whether a retest is included not on brand or price alone.

Pentest or PTaaS? Point-in-time pentests suit compliance milestones and deep bespoke scope; PTaaS and continuous models suit ongoing coverage as code ships many programs use both.

Is a retest important? Yes a finding is only closed when a retest verifies the fix; a report without one leaves you guessing whether the risk is actually gone.

What proves pentest value? Repeat findings that close and don’t recur at the next engagement, and fixes driven by clear remediation guidance not the raw count of findings.

Verdict

Ten firms, one truth: the report is only as good as the testers and only as valuable as the fixes it drives. NCC Group benchmarks the research depth, Bishop Fox owns the offensive reputation, Rapid7 wires it into a platform, Coalfire feeds the audit, and Mandiant brings frontline realism vet the people on your engagement, demand reproducible findings and a retest, and judge by repeat findings that stay closed.

articles.description:
The grammar-mistake era of phishing is over. AI now writes flawless lures, clones brands pixel-perfect, and personalizes at scale so anti-phishing has shifted from spotting typos to modeling behavior, verifying sender identity, and killing the malicious link or message after it lands. cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The grammar-mistake era of phishing is over. AI now writes flawless lures, clones brands pixel-perfect, and personalizes at scale so anti-phishing has shifted from spotting typos to modeling behavior, verifying sender identity, and killing the malicious link or message after it lands.

The solutions below separate on detection depth against modern lures, impersonation and lookalike defense, and remediation speed. Proofpoint takes 1; Abnormal and Mimecast complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Proofpoint the threat-intel and impersonation-defense benchmark.

• Podium: Proofpoint, Abnormal Security (behavioral-AI catch), Mimecast (gateway-plus-awareness).

• Model split: intel-led gateways (Proofpoint, Mimecast, Microsoft) versus behavioral-AI layers (Abnormal, IRONSCALES) versus specialist link/isolation defense (Cloudflare Area 1, Vade, INKY).

• 2026 theme: AI-versus-AI the defining fight is machine-generated lures against machine-behavioral detection.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: phishing detection depth, impersonation/lookalike defense, behavioral/AI capability, remediation speed, user-reporting integration, and pricing clarity.

Weights: detection depth 25%, impersonation defense 25%, behavioral/AI 20%, remediation 15%, reporting integration 15%.

The 2026 Anti-Phishing Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Proofpoint — Best Intel + Impersonation Benchmark

Snapshot: Enterprise tiers | Threat intel + impersonation defense + VAP | Broad remediation

Why it earns 1: Proofpoint pairs the deepest threat intelligence with strong impersonation and lookalike-domain defense, VAP targeting of attacked users, and estate-wide remediation.

For organizations wanting the most comprehensive anti-phishing program, it sets the benchmark.

Pros: Threat-intel depth; impersonation defense; VAP targeting.

Cons: Enterprise positioning and complexity.

Bottom line: The anti-phishing benchmark.

2. Abnormal Security — Best Behavioral-AI Catch

Snapshot: API subscription | Behavioral AI over the mailbox | Payload-less lure detection

Why it ranks here: Abnormal catches the AI-written, payload-less phish by modeling normal behavior and flagging the deviations unusual senders, tone, and requests then remediating post-delivery.

For organizations whose gap is modern social-engineering lures, it’s the behavioral pick.

Pros: Behavioral-AI detection; payload-less catch; fast API deploy.

Cons: Complements the full gateway stack.

Bottom line: The behavioral answer to AI-written phish.

3. Mimecast — Best Gateway-Plus-Awareness

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | Gateway detection + awareness training | Suite breadth

Why it ranks here: Mimecast pairs gateway-grade phishing detection with built-in awareness training, so technical defense and human conditioning run together. For organizations wanting detection plus the human layer, it’s the gateway-awareness pick.

Pros: Gateway detection; awareness integration; suite breadth.

Cons: Behavioral-AI depth versus the API specialists.

Bottom line: Detection plus the human layer.

4. Cofense — Best Report-to-Remediate Network

Snapshot: Subscription| Report button + triage + global sensor network | Human-reporting focus

Why it ranks here: Cofense turns employees into sensors: the report button feeds triage and automated remediation, and confirmed reports become intelligence shared across its network. For organizations building a human-reporting defense, it’s the network pick.

Pros: Report-to-remediate loop; sensor network; shared intel.

Cons: Behavioral-AI inbound depth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: Employees as a phishing sensor network.

5. IRONSCALES — Best Mailbox-AI + Crowdsource

Snapshot: Per-mailbox tiers | Mailbox-level AI + crowdsourced intel | Automated remediation

Why it ranks here: IRONSCALES blends mailbox-level AI with crowdsourced intelligence so a phish caught anywhere helps everyone, with automated remediation across the estate. For fast, collaborative defense, it’s the crowdsource pick.

Pros: Mailbox AI; crowdsourced intel; automated remediation.

Cons: Enterprise-program breadth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: Mailbox AI with a crowdsourced edge.

6. Microsoft — Best Native Baseline Defense

Snapshot: Bundled (E5/add-on) | Native Defender anti-phishing | Stack-wide signal

Why it ranks here: Microsoft’s native anti-phishing protects M365 mailboxes with impersonation and spoof defense, improving at Microsoft scale, though many estates layer a behavioral tool over it. Ranked as the native foundation.

Pros: Native integration; bundled economics; stack signal.

Cons: Behavioral depth often supplemented.

Bottom line: The native anti-phishing baseline.

7. Barracuda — Best Mid-Market Layered Defense

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | Gateway + API impersonation defense | Mid-market economics

Why it ranks here: Barracuda layers gateway and API-based impersonation defense with awareness at mid-market economics, giving smaller teams solid phishing protection without enterprise complexity. For value-layered defense, it’s the mid-market pick.

Pros: Layered defense; value economics; awareness linkage.

Cons: Enterprise depth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: Layered phishing defense at value scale.

8. Cloudflare (Area 1) — Best Preemptive-Infrastructure Defense

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | Area 1 preemptive campaign discovery | Infrastructure intelligence

Why it ranks here: Cloudflare’s Area 1 maps phishing infrastructure before campaigns launch discovering attacker domains and staging sites early to block at the source, delivered on Cloudflare’s global network.

For preemptive, infrastructure-level defense, it’s the early-warning pick.

Pros: Preemptive campaign discovery; infrastructure intel; global network.

Cons: Confirm current Area 1 packaging within Cloudflare.

Bottom line: Blocking phishing before it launches.

9. Vade — Best ISP-Scale AI Filtering

Snapshot: Per-user / MSP tiers| AI filtering at ISP scale | MSP channel focus

Why it ranks here: Vade filters phishing with AI filteringtrained on enormous ISP-scale mail volume, delivered strongly through the MSP channel for M365 protection. For MSP-served and value-conscious estates, it’s the scale-filtering pick.

Pros: ISP-scale AI training; MSP delivery; M365 fit.

Cons: Enterprise-program breadth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: AI filtering at ISP scale.

10. INKY — Best Visual-Impersonation Banners

Snapshot: Per-user tiers| In-email warning banners + visual detection | Impersonation focus

Why it ranks here: INKY flags suspicious mail with in-email warning banners and computer-vision detection of brand impersonation, giving users context at the moment of risk. For banner-driven, visual-impersonation defense, it’s the in-context pick.

Pros: Warning banners; visual impersonation detection; user context.

Cons: Deep behavioral modeling versus the AI leaders.

Bottom line: Warnings and visual-impersonation catch in the inbox.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Test Against Modern Lures, Weight Impersonation and Remediation

Anti-phishing is now an AI-versus-AI problem, so test finalists against the lures you actually receive AI-written, brand-cloned, personalized not a canned sample set, and measure catch rate on the social-engineering messages that carry no payload.

Weight impersonation and lookalike-domain defense heavily, because display-name spoofing and near-miss domains are the most common successful techniques, and confirm the tool catches them, not just malware.

Decide your architecture: intel-led gateways and native defense form the baseline, behavioral-AI layers (Abnormal, IRONSCALES) catch what they miss, and preemptive infrastructure defense (Area 1) blocks campaigns early many estates run native plus a behavioral layer.

Make remediation a priority: when a phish reaches a hundred inboxes, automatic clawback beats one more detection.

Wire user reporting into triage so employees become sensors (Cofense-class), pair with security awareness training and DMARC, and track the metric that renews the contract: successful-phish rate per user trending down.

FAQs

What are the best anti-phishing solutions in 2026?

Proofpoint as the intel-and-impersonation benchmark, Abnormal for behavioral AI, Mimecast for gateway-plus-awareness, Cofense for report-driven defense, with IRONSCALES, Microsoft, Barracuda, Area 1, Vade, and INKY by model.

How has phishing changed with AI?

AI writes flawless, personalized, brand-cloned lures at scale, so detection has shifted from spotting typos to modeling behavior, verifying identity, and remediating fast.

Gateway or behavioral anti-phishing?

Gateways and native defense form the baseline; behavioral-AI layers catch the payload-less social engineering they miss. Many estates run both.

What stops impersonation and lookalike domains?

Impersonation defense plus DMARC at enforcement and lookalike-domain monitoring display-name spoofing and near-miss domains are the most common successful techniques.

What proves anti-phishing value?

Successful-phish rate per user trending down and faster remediation of messages that land tested against your real lure mix, not canned samples.

Verdict

Ten solutions, one AI-versus-AI fight: machine-written lures against machine-behavioral detection.

Proofpoint benchmarks intel and impersonation, Abnormal and IRONSCALES bring behavioral AI, Cofense builds the sensor network, and Area 1 blocks campaigns before they launch test against modern lures, weight impersonation and remediation, layer native plus behavioral, and let a falling successful-phish rate renew the contract.

articles.description:
The Shadowserver Foundation found around 4,200 internet-exposed instances of AI hacking frameworks on November 23, 2026, up from just under 3,700 a day earlier. Its November 25 report also documented more than 10,000 events from over 80 IP addresses identified as running these tools between November 9 and 23. The larger figure measures exposure. The […]

The post 4,000+ Servers Running AI Hacking Agents Are Exposed to the Internet and Actively Attacking appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Shadowserver Foundation found around 4,200 internet-exposed instances of AI hacking frameworks on November 23, 2026, up from just under 3,700 a day earlier.

Its November 25 report also documented more than 10,000 events from over 80 IP addresses identified as running these tools between November 9 and 23. The larger figure measures exposure.

The smaller one counts sources that sent traffic to Shadowserver’s honeypots. The findings do not show that all 4,200 instances were attacking.

Shadowserver scans the internet daily for 15 AI attack frameworks and tracks exposure on its public dashboard. These tools use large language models to guide tasks such as finding exposed services and testing for known flaws with limited human input.

4,000+ Servers Expose AI Hacking Agents

Security teams can use them for authorized testing. A public instance alone does not tell researchers who runs it or whether its activity is approved.

ARTEX accounted for around 70% of exposed instances on most days. AntiFox, a version based on ARTEX, grew from a handful of instances to around 200. Together, they made up about three-quarters of observed instances on November 22.

A jump in PentestCode deployments helped drive the next day’s increase. Nearly half of the exposed instances were in Asia, more than a third were in North America, and most of the rest were in Europe.

The FBI’s November 13 advisory said some ARTEX-assisted intrusions moved from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.

In a separate case, Cyber Security News reported on a CyberStrikeAI intrusion that exposed 3,392 user accounts. Those cases show what the tools can do in real intrusions. Shadowserver’s honeypot data measures attempted activity, not confirmed breaches.

Honeypots are decoy systems that record suspicious traffic. Nearly nine in ten source IP addresses seen by Shadowserver were identified as running ARTEX Gateway.

A handful generated most of the events, and the busiest address was linked to PentAGI. Almost all sources were on cloud networks. Activity was concentrated in the United States and Hong Kong, but that likely reflects where the servers were hosted, not where the operators were based.

About six in ten source addresses tried to relay traffic through the sensors. Direct requests often probed VPN gateways, web apps, and developer tools such as Jenkins. About one in ten source addresses sent exploit or injection attempts, most often targeting the Metabase flaw CVE-2023-38646.

Some also looked for .env files, which can contain database passwords and cloud API keys. The focus on known flaws echoes earlier reporting on ARTEX attacks.

Shadowserver recommends checking its free Device Identification report for the ai-attack-framework label. If a deployment is approved, limit access to trusted addresses or a VPN, require strong authentication, and keep the software updated. If no one can verify that the deployment is approved, isolate it and investigate possible misuse.

Most sources operated in short bursts, but a few sent traffic during every hour of the day over several days. Shadowserver advises teams to rate-limit repeated probes and make sure alerts are handled outside business hours.

Before blocking an address, check it against recent logs. Cloud IP addresses can be reassigned, and an old report may no longer describe the system using that address.

articles.title: Roundcube Webmail Flaws Could Let Hackers Execute Malicious Code and Expose Sensitive Data
articles.description:
Roundcube released Webmail versions 1.6.22 and 1.7.7 on November 23, 2026, to address 12 security flaws. The updates fix weaknesses in how the browser-based email client handles attachments, displays messages, and connects to mail servers. The release notes describe flaws that could expose data and allow unauthorized email filter code to run. However, they do […]

The post Roundcube Webmail Flaws Could Let Hackers Execute Malicious Code and Expose Sensitive Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Roundcube released Webmail versions 1.6.22 and 1.7.7 on November 23, 2026, to address 12 security flaws. The updates fix weaknesses in how the browser-based email client handles attachments, displays messages, and connects to mail servers.

The release notes describe flaws that could expose data and allow unauthorized email filter code to run. However, they do not confirm remote code execution on the webmail server or report active exploitation of these bugs.

One fix stops Roundcube from passing unsafe PDF, PostScript, and SVG attachment content to ImageMagick, a tool used to process images. Roundcube had previously attempted to fix this issue.

The project also revisited an HTTP request injection flaw in its ATD spellcheck backend, which could allow unintended requests. The release notes do not say which configurations are most at risk or whether either flaw could give an attacker control of the server.

Several fixes address how Roundcube displays HTML email. Two flaws let message styling break out of the limits meant to keep it separate from the webmail interface.

Another let SVG content load external resources despite the user’s remote-content settings, weakening a privacy control that helps prevent email tracking.

Roundcube Webmail Flaws

The update also closes a flaw that could expose responses handled by the CSS proxy. It fixes a gap in the HTML filter on systems running PHP versions earlier than 8.4.

Two separate flaws could let unauthorized instructions enter Sieve scripts, which mail servers use to run rules such as sorting incoming messages. Another fix addresses XML injection in the XIMSS driver of Roundcube’s password plugin.

The release also closes a denial-of-service flaw where the decoder for TNEF attachments, a format associated with Microsoft Outlook, could spend too long processing attachment data.

The updates also stop Roundcube from falling back to unencrypted IMAP, SMTP, or ManageSieve connections when TLS encryption is configured.

However, the mail server does not advertise the required capability. That matters because a setting that appears to require encryption did not always prevent an unencrypted connection.

Administrators should back up their data and patch production systems promptly. The official Roundcube 1.6.22 release notes identify it as the final release in the 1.6 long-term support branch.

Teams that cannot move to 1.7 immediately should apply 1.6.22 rather than wait for the migration. The Roundcube 1.7.7 release notes list the same security fixes, and Roundcube says only the 1.7 branch will receive future security updates.

Cyber Security News previously covered CISA’s warning about exploited Roundcube vulnerabilities and a separate Roundcube flaw that let attackers track email opens. Those reports concern earlier bugs, not the flaws fixed in November.

They offer two reasons to keep webmail current: attackers have targeted Roundcube before, and a flaw does not have to take over a server to compromise user privacy. For teams still on 1.6, this update closes the current gaps, but moving to 1.7 is what keeps future fixes available.

articles.description:
SolarWinds released Serv-U 2026.4 on November 24, 2026, fixing 18 vulnerabilities, including nine critical flaws, two of which could grant attackers root access on Linux servers, while the risk is lower on Windows. However, the same update also fixes a high-severity command injection flaw that affects only Windows installations. The Serv-U 2026.4 release notes identify […]

The post Critical SolarWinds Serv-U Flaws Could Let Hackers Gain Root Access and Take Control of Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
SolarWinds released Serv-U 2026.4 on November 24, 2026, fixing 18 vulnerabilities, including nine critical flaws, two of which could grant attackers root access on Linux servers, while the risk is lower on Windows.

However, the same update also fixes a high-severity command injection flaw that affects only Windows installations. The Serv-U 2026.4 release notes identify CVE-2026-123172 and CVE-2026-123168 as the two flaws that could grant Linux root privileges.

Both received severity scores of 9.1 out of 10. Root access goes beyond the control of the Serv-U application. It could let an attacker read or change protected files and alter settings on the host.

Several other critical flaws let users with existing administrative access gain more power than their roles should allow. CVE-2026-82322 could let a domain group administrator become a Serv-U server administrator.

Two separate flaws, CVE-2026-82320 and CVE-2026-82321, could let domain administrators gain system administrator rights. CVE-2026-123167 could let a domain administrator reach files that normally require higher privileges.

These are not the only ways someone without an account could break in. Several instead increase the damage a compromised admin account could cause.

Critical SolarWinds Serv-U Flaws

Three more critical flaws affect how Serv-U checks file access. SolarWinds says CVE-2026-82315 and CVE-2026-82316 could let a domain administrator or someone with higher privileges access or modify protected files outside the intended directory, potentially allowing code execution.

CVE-2026-82319 could let a similarly privileged user read and write application files. SolarWinds credited the Intigriti Bug Bounty Program for all nine critical reports.

The update also fixes weak protections against repeated password and one-time code guesses, a flaw that exposes whether specific usernames exist, and a separate SSH flaw that could disclose data from server memory.

The release notes do not report active exploitation of the newly disclosed flaws. Cyber Security News previously covered the Serv-U 2026.3 security fixes and CISA’s warning about a separate Serv-U flaw exploited in attacks.

Administrators should prioritize upgrading to Serv-U 2026.4, starting with internet-facing Linux servers. Windows deployments also need the update because the lower risk from the critical flaws does not remove the Windows-only command injection risk. The Serv-U 2026.4 release includes OpenSSL 3.5 LTS and stops Serv-U from writing multi-factor authentication codes to its logs.

Before installing the update, follow the SolarWinds Serv-U upgrade guide to back up the configuration and export the server identifier. If you are skipping more than one version, SolarWinds recommends checking its release notes aggregator for changes between releases.

After updating, verify that the server reports version 2026.4 and test the sign-in and file transfer workflows your organization relies on.

Security teams should also review recent administrator changes and unexpected file activity, since installing the update does not tell you whether a server was compromised before it was patched.

articles.title: 1Password Hacked – Attackers Breach Backend Systems and Steal Customer Data
articles.description:
1Password disclosed on November 25, 2026, that an attacker compromised an employee’s corporate GitHub account and used it to steal customer data from the company’s backend systems. The stolen records included names, sign-in email addresses, and internal account details. The password manager said the attacker never accessed customer vaults, the passwords stored in them, or […]

The post 1Password Hacked – Attackers Breach Backend Systems and Steal Customer Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
1Password disclosed on November 25, 2026, that an attacker compromised an employee’s corporate GitHub account and used it to steal customer data from the company’s backend systems.

The stolen records included names, sign-in email addresses, and internal account details. The password manager said the attacker never accessed customer vaults, the passwords stored in them, or the keys that protect them. Its apps and services continued to operate normally.

GitHub Compromise Reached 1Password’s Backend

1Password began investigating on November 19 after finding signs that an attacker had gained access to the employee’s GitHub account. The attacker accessed source code and pushed malicious code to backend services, which then downloaded administrative records for a subset of customers.

The company did not disclose how the attacker first gained access to GitHub or give a total count of affected customers.

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and reached 1Password’s continuous integration and delivery system, known as CI/CD. That system builds and deploys software and holds credentials used by the company’s infrastructure.

1Password said the copied code contained no user secrets. In a separate GitHub account compromise, CrowdSec reported that an intruder copied about 170 private repositories. The 1Password incident went further, reaching services that handled customer records.

The downloaded records contained account and user IDs, account creation dates, last sign-in times, public cryptographic keys, and settings used by the Secure Remote Password sign-in protocol. 1Password said those settings cannot be used to access an account.

The records also included tokens from certain emailed invitations, account setup, and recovery links. These tokens were not the same as account recovery keys, which were unaffected.

An exposed token could not grant access by itself. Completing the affected invitation or recovery process required either a single sign-on login or a separate code sent to the user’s registered email address.

1Password said it notified the small number of users who were in those setup or recovery flows and found no evidence that exposed setup tokens were used to take over accounts.

That marks a difference from the 2023 incident involving 1Password’s Okta environment, when the company reported no customer data exposure. The new disclosure confirms that customer account records were copied.

Separate Okta research on AI-driven identity attacks examined disposable-email signups, not the GitHub compromise described by 1Password. Neither disclosure links that activity to this breach.

1Password disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, removed access the attacker had created, and restored clean versions of the affected services.

It also replaced or revoked potentially exposed internal credentials, tightened GitHub and deployment controls, and brought in independent cybersecurity experts. As a precaution, it changed invitation and recovery codes from six digits to ten letters and numbers.

Customers do not need to change anything in their accounts because of the breach, according to 1Password’s incident disclosure. The immediate risk is phishing: a message can use a real name and sign-in address to make a fake invitation or recovery request look genuine.

If one arrives unexpectedly, open the official app or type the website address yourself instead of following the link. 1Password says it will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The U.S. Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has taken some systems offline after confirming unauthorized access to a limited part of its network.

The bureau said the shutdown was a precaution while it investigates the cyberattack. Its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) E-Filing website remains operational, but some services may be temporarily unavailable.

The disruption affects a bureau that collects financial reports used to investigate money laundering, terrorist financing, and other crimes. Banks and other financial institutions use the filing system to submit reports, including suspicious activity reports.

The website’s availability does not mean every filing service is working or that every institution can submit reports through its usual channel.

FinCEN Confirms Cyberattack

Treasury is working with the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and outside forensic examiners to determine what the intruder accessed and the incident’s impact.

A FinCEN official told Reuters that investigators had found no evidence of a breach of the Bank Secrecy Act or beneficial ownership databases. That finding is limited to those databases and reflects what investigators knew while the review was still underway.

FinCEN has not named the systems that were accessed or identified which ones it took offline. It has not said how the intruder got in, how long the access lasted, or who was responsible. The bureau says it is working to restore normal operations but has not given a date for full service.

The incident follows a separate U.S. Treasury breach disclosed in December 2024, when an intrusion involving remote support provider BeyondTrust reached employee workstations and unclassified documents.

Cyber Security News also covered BeyondTrust’s findings on the wider incident, which affected 17 customers of its Remote Support cloud service. Treasury has not publicly linked the earlier breach to the FinCEN cyberattack.

Under its November 24 relief order, FinCEN moved certain deadlines to December 30, 2026. For Bank Secrecy Act reports, the extension applies to financial institutions that used Secure Data Transfer Mode (SDTM), an automated filing channel, as of November 18.

Those institutions have until December 30 to submit covered reports originally due from November 18 through December 29, inclusive. The order does not give every filer a blanket extension.

The same window applies to covered companies required to submit beneficial ownership reports and individuals required to update a FinCEN Identifier. For example, a qualifying report originally due December 15 is now due no later than December 30.

Banks and other financial institutions must still monitor for suspicious transactions and meet all other applicable anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist financing requirements. The order changes when covered reports are due, not what institutions must monitor.

Financial institutions that need to get suspicious activity information to law enforcement quickly can call the Financial Institutions Hotline at 1-866-556-3974. FinCEN says the hotline is unaffected.

For technical filing problems, the order directs filers to the BSA E-Filing Help Desk, while questions about eligibility for relief go to FinCEN’s Regulatory Support Section.

As services come back online, the key distinction for filers is that the website can be open while individual services remain unavailable, and eligibility for more time depends on the order.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added three flaws affecting Drupal Core, Idunno AntiCsrf, and Optimizely Web Experimentation to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on November 24, 2026.

CISA cited evidence that attackers had already exploited all three. The KEV catalog lists November 27 as the federal remediation deadline for each flaw, but the fixes differ.

Drupal has released updates, Idunno users need to replace an unsupported library, and Optimizely customers need to check whether their sites served altered scripts.

Cybersecurity News’ earlier coverage covered CVE-2026-132165, a critical Drupal Core RCE flaw that could let unauthenticated attackers exploit the installer to take over existing websites or execute server-side code, which Drupal patched on November 18.

Its security team later said it had received a report of exploitation on live sites as early as November 19 at 19:00 UTC. Site owners should update to Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22 or 11.4.13, depending on their release branch, or install a later supported release.

Drupal Idunno AntiCsrf Optimizely Flaws Exploited

Drupal says restricting write access to its settings file blocks some attacks but does not fully protect a vulnerable site. The Drupal Core security update also explains the separate flaw fixed in the same releases.

CVE-2026-131914 affects Idunno AntiCsrf through version 0.9.1 Beta. The library was built to help older ASP.NET WebForms applications reject forged requests. It processes untrusted data in a way that can let a remote attacker run code without signing in.

The National Vulnerability Database describes the issue as unsafe deserialization, which occurs here when the library rebuilds software objects from data it should not trust.

No official patch is available. Teams should check deployed ASP.NET applications for the library, remove it where found, and replace it with a supported safeguard against forged requests.

Simply removing the module without a replacement would leave the forms it protected without that defense. Teams should also review application logs for signs of earlier exploitation.

CVE-2026-132224 affected Optimizely Web Experimentation before November 17. A flaw in the signup process let attackers place malicious JavaScript in some customer projects.

Because websites load those scripts from Optimizely, visitors’ browsers could run the injected code even if attackers never accessed the customer’s own web server. Site owners should check Optimizely’s incident notice, identify affected projects, and review what pages loaded their scripts during the incident.

Binding Operational Directive 26-04 applies to federal civilian agencies. As our coverage of CISA’s federal patching rules explains, the shortest deadlines apply when a known exploited flaw is publicly exposed, can be exploited automatically, and gives attackers full control.

The directive also sets rules for checking whether attackers compromised a system before it was fixed. CISA also urges private organizations to prioritize KEV entries. Applying an update or removing a vulnerable component closes the known route in. However, it does not establish whether anyone used it before the fix.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Thanksgiving invitation, a Black Friday discount, or a holiday greeting may look harmless. But behind these familiar messages, cybercriminals are hiding threats that could expose corporate credentials, compromise endpoints, and put sensitive data at risk. 

ANY.RUN researchers uncovered five holiday-themed attacks involving credential phishing, unauthorized remote access software, and malicious scripts.

For businesses, these threats can lead to costly investigations, operational disruption, and increased pressure on SOC teams. 

Let’s examine how these attacks work and what makes them dangerous. 

Thanksgiving Dangers: From Innocent Invitations to Corporate Security Risks 

Thanksgiving-themed messages became the entry point for three distinct attacks investigated by ANY.RUN. From fake event invitations to fraudulent surveys, attackers used familiar holiday communications to steal credentials, collect personal data, and deliver unauthorized remote access software, potentially exposing businesses to account compromise and endpoint security risks. 

Attack 1: Thanksgiving Invitation Targets Corporate Google Workspace Credentials 

A Thanksgiving potluck invitation sent from a US real estate franchise office’s mailbox concealed a credential phishing attack.

The “View & RSVP” button redirected employees to a fake verification page, followed by a fraudulent Google Workspace login form designed to steal corporate credentials. Check full attack chain and gather IOCs 

ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox exposed the redirect chain, iframe-hosted phishing form, and POST requests used to transmit submitted credentials. 

With the help of the powerful Related Threat Context capability available inside the sandbox, analysts identified connections to a broader phishing operation.  

By clicking on a suspicious IOC and pivoting directly to Threat Intelligence Lookup, they uncovered approximately 350 sandbox sessions and over 170 associated domains, drawing on threat data contributed by a community of 700,000+ security professionals and 16,000+ organizations. 

SOC Takeaway: Investigating related infrastructure helps security teams uncover additional phishing indicators, identify connected attacks earlier, and reduce the risk of corporate account compromise. 

Investigate more threats with the same SOC resources and keep rising alert volumes from driving up security costs. Increase SOC Capacity 

Attack 2: Fake Thanksgiving E-Card Delivers Remote Access Software 

A Thanksgiving e-card disguised as a Blue Mountain greeting arrived as a PDF attachment named Invitation RSVP.pdf. Clicking “VIEW INVITATION” redirected recipients through DocSend to a Cloudflare R2-hosted page that automatically downloaded ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi. 

ScreenConnect is legitimate remote access software, but unauthorized installation could give attackers control over corporate devices, putting sensitive data and business operations at risk. 

Check attack chain and gather IOCs 

ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox exposed the full redirect chain and automatic installer download. Researchers also discovered that the page collected visitors’ public IP addresses and transmitted them to a Telegram bot. 

SOC Takeaway: Use behavioral analysis to uncover hidden redirects, automatic software downloads, and suspicious network connections. Detecting these activities early helps SOC teams identify potential remote access threats and reduce the risk of unauthorized access to corporate systems. 

Attack 3: Fake MyChart Thanksgiving Survey Harvests Personal Data 

Attackers impersonated MyChart, a US healthcare patient portal, offering a free medical monitoring kit. An image-based email led recipients to a fraudulent eight-question survey that collected personal information and requested a $10.55 processing fee. Check Thanksgiving picture attachment inside sandbox 

ANY.RUN exposed the multi-stage redirection through a traffic distribution system (TDS) and a fake verification page, showing how attackers concealed the fraudulent destination behind a trusted healthcare brand. 

SOC Takeaway: Pay attention to image-based phishing emails and traffic distribution systems that conceal fraudulent destinations. Identifying these techniques earlier can help security teams detect similar campaigns and limit personal-data exposure. 

Black Friday’s Dark Side: Hidden Threats with Costly Consequences 

The next two cases show how attackers went beyond traditional holiday scams, combining legitimate promotional content with phishing infrastructure and malicious code.

These techniques can make threats harder to detect, giving attackers more opportunities to compromise corporate systems before security teams respond. 

Attack 4: Black Friday Newsletter Conceals Corporate Phishing 

ANY.RUN researchers identified 29 related investigations targeting US businesses, including construction contractors and service providers. 

Attackers combined fake NDA-signing requests with genuine Black Friday promotional newsletters containing 30–46 links. While most led to legitimate websites, a few pointed to phishing infrastructure, making malicious links harder to identify. View the campaign inside sandbox 

Using ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox, researchers uncovered browser fingerprinting through FingerprintJS and conditional redirects to legitimate websites, including SpaceX and USA Today.

These techniques could help attackers conceal phishing activity from automated security checks. 

SOC Takeaway: Don’t trust a clean scan result when investigating suspicious links. Use interactive behavioral analysis to examine fingerprinting and conditional redirects that may conceal phishing activity, helping prevent corporate credential compromise. 

Attack 5: Black Friday Coupon Hides a Malicious Script 

A Word document promising an extra 30% discount at Amazon, eBay, and AliExpress concealed an embedded OLE package containing a malicious VBS script, Voucer.vbs. If executed, the script could expose corporate endpoints to further malicious activity. View analysis and gather IOCs 

The investigation captured the execution chain WINWORD.EXE → wscript.exe → schtasks.exe, revealing attempts to download an additional payload and establish persistence through a scheduled task running every three hours. The payload download failed in all nine observed investigations. 

SOC Takeaway: Watch for unusual child processes launched by Office applications and unexpected scheduled tasks. Detecting these behaviors can help stop persistence attempts before they develop into more serious endpoint security incidents. 

How SOC Teams Can Stay Ahead of Holiday Cyberattacks 

These five investigations show why detecting suspicious activity early and understanding its broader context are essential for protecting business operations. To strengthen detection and reduce security risks, SOC teams should prioritize three steps: 

  • Look beyond initial scan results: Use Interactive Sandbox to examine file execution, hidden redirects, and network activity. AI-powered Tier-1 reports can also summarize findings, speed up triage, and support faster handoffs to Tier-2 teams. 
  • Connect isolated findings: Use Threat Intelligence Lookup to investigate suspicious IOCs, uncover related infrastructure, and identify broader campaigns without spending hours on manual research. 
  • Detect emerging threats before they spread: Integrate Threat Intelligence Feeds into existing security systems to continuously receive fresh malicious indicators. According to ANY.RUN’s internal research, up to 30% of unique malicious IOCs identified in analyzed sandbox sessions were already available in TI Feeds. This gives SOC teams an opportunity to detect known threats earlier, before they require a separate manual investigation. 

Together, these practices help SOC teams reduce repetitive investigations, improve threat visibility, and respond faster while keeping security costs under control. 

Stop Holiday Cyber Threats Before They Become Costly Incidents 

A single successful attack during the holiday season can have consequences long after the celebrations end. For businesses, faster detection and response can make the difference between a contained threat and costly operational disruption. 

ANY.RUN customers have reported 21 minutes less MTTR per incident and 30% fewer Tier-1-to-Tier-2 escalations, helping security teams respond faster, reduce investigation costs, and free up senior specialists for critical threats. 

Give your SOC the speed and visibility to stop hidden threats before they turn into costly business incidents. Strengthen Your SOC Defenses

The attacker also obtained integration tokens and accessed some data from connected Outlook mailboxes. Todoist […]

The post Task Management App Todoist Hacked, Attackers Breach Production Systems appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Task management app Todoist said an attacker breached its production systems on November 23, 2026, and downloaded account records for about 6% of its users.

The records contained email addresses, account creation dates, and older password hashes, not plaintext passwords.

The attacker also obtained integration tokens and accessed some data from connected Outlook mailboxes. Todoist said it blocked the attacker’s access and began notifying affected users on November 24.

Todoist Production System Breach

The Todoist incident report traces the breach to a stolen credential tied to the system that manages changes to its code.

The attacker changed automated workflows in three code repositories, obtained more credentials, and took over an employee’s work account to enter Todoist’s cloud. The attacker could read source code, but investigators found no changes to the application code.

Security monitoring flagged an unexpected administrator account at 17:01 UTC on November 23, hours after the attacker downloaded the account records.

Todoist removed accounts created by the attacker, replaced exposed credentials, and tightened controls on sensitive workflows. A separate cloud intrusion covered by Cyber Security News showed a similar risk: stolen credentials tied to development tools can open access to live systems.

The downloaded passwords were stored as salted SHA-1 hashes. A hash is a stored value used to check a password without keeping the password itself.

A salt adds a random value before hashing, making it harder to test guesses across many accounts at once. But older hashes are still vulnerable to password guessing, as the BigBasket data leak also highlighted.

Todoist retired support for the old method and found no sign that the attacker logged in to accounts in this group. Todoist said the attacker retrieved Todoist API and Slack integration tokens for about 0.003% of users. Targeted searches for credentials in tasks, comments, and attachment names affected about 0.001%.

The company found no bulk download of its task and comment database. Another roughly 0.001% were affected through the Todoist Outlook add-in.

The attacker requested sender details, subject lines, up to 255 characters of message text, and attachment details.

Todoist says users who did not receive a notice do not need to act. If the company disabled your password, use the official Todoist password reset page and change that password anywhere else you reused it.

Google and Apple passwords were not affected. If Todoist revoked an API token used by a script, update the script with the replacement token under Settings → Integrations → Developer.

If you stored API keys or other credentials in Todoist, revoke and replace them with the service that issued them. Deleting a task or comment will not disable a secret someone may have copied.

Todoist says its notices come from no-reply@notify.todoist.com and will not ask you to send a password or install software. If a message looks suspicious, contact Todoist directly rather than replying.

articles.description:
Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) has confirmed its first cases of AI-assisted cyberattacks against organizations in the country. The attacks affected companies and critical infrastructure operators across at least two sectors. In every case known to the agency, the use of AI agents led to a successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems, according […]

The post Switzerland Confirms First AI-Agent Cyberattacks That Successfully Compromised IT Systems appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) has confirmed its first cases of AI-assisted cyberattacks against organizations in the country.

The attacks affected companies and critical infrastructure operators across at least two sectors. In every case known to the agency, the use of AI agents led to a successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems, according to the Swiss NCSC advisory published on November 24.

The agency did not name the victims, identify the sectors or disclose the total number of attacks. The finding describes the cases reported to the Swiss agency, not a success rate for AI-assisted attacks overall. Nor is it a global first.

What makes the warning significant is that the tools can speed up familiar attacks against weaknesses that security teams already know how to fix. The NCSC expects more attacks to succeed as the tools become more widely available.

Switzerland AI-agent Cyberattacks

The Swiss NCSC says attackers used what it calls agentic offensive frameworks. Unlike a chatbot that only offers advice, an AI agent can carry out tasks, assess what happened and adjust its next move.

These frameworks can support authorized security testing, but attackers can also misuse them. The agency highlighted default or easily guessed passwords and known flaws in internet-facing software as common risks, without saying which weaknesses were used in the Swiss cases.

The NCSC said the number of AI agents accessible over the internet had nearly doubled since October 2026. It cited ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI as examples, not as confirmed tools in the Swiss incidents.

In separate cases, Cyber Security News coverage of the FBI’s ARTEX warning noted that some attackers gained elevated access in under three hours. That timing does not describe the Swiss attacks, but it shows why defenders may have less time to act.

The NCSC urges organisations to install critical security updates on internet-facing systems within 24 hours of release. It also advises taking systems off the public internet when direct access is unnecessary and restricting access to approved IP addresses or networks where possible.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s internet exposure reduction guidance likewise recommends identifying exposed systems before deciding which services need to remain reachable.

Webmail, VPNs and other internal services reachable from the internet should require multi-factor authentication or passkeys without exception.

The NCSC also recommends giving users and applications only the permissions they need, monitoring for unusual account activity and changes in data volumes, and testing infrastructure regularly for weaknesses.

In a separate cloud intrusion, Cyber Security News reported that attackers gained access to 3,392 user accounts, illustrating why monitoring account activity matters alongside patching exposed systems.

The Swiss NCSC is sharing technical indicators with critical infrastructure operators and coordinating with national and international partners.

For security teams, the immediate priority is to verify which services are reachable from the internet and whether they can patch critical flaws within a day.

articles.description:
Microsoft has fixed a Microsoft 365 startup issue that left some Windows users staring at a blank white window when they opened Word, Excel, or Outlook. The window showed no text or buttons, and users who couldn’t dismiss it couldn’t use the app behind it. In a November 23, 2026, support notice, Microsoft identified Version […]

The post Microsoft 365 Bug Blocked Users From Opening Word, Excel, and Outlook With Blank White Screen appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has fixed a Microsoft 365 startup issue that left some Windows users staring at a blank white window when they opened Word, Excel, or Outlook.

The window showed no text or buttons, and users who couldn’t dismiss it couldn’t use the app behind it. In a November 23, 2026, support notice, Microsoft identified Version 2611, Build 16.0.20625.20142, as the release that fixes the problem.

Microsoft 365 White Screen Bug

The white screen was a dialog box that appeared when an Office app opened, not an empty Word document or Excel workbook. In a Microsoft Q&A thread on November 22, a Word user said the window prevented them from opening anything underneath it.

Another user reported seeing the same problem the next day. Microsoft also lists PowerPoint, Access, and OneNote for Microsoft 365 in its notice.

Microsoft did not say what caused the dialog to appear, which earlier builds were affected, or how many users ran into it. The notice describes a desktop startup problem and does not identify it as a security incident or a cloud outage.

That distinction matters for Outlook users in particular. During the separate November 12–13 Microsoft 365 outage, users lost access to Exchange Online mailboxes. This time, the symptom Microsoft documented was a blank window blocking access to the installed app.

If at least one Office app still opens, use Microsoft’s normal update route. Open the app and go to File > Account > Update Options > Update Now. In classic Outlook, look for Office Account instead of Account.

If Update Now is missing, check whether Enable Updates appears first. On a work PC where the organization manages Office updates, ask IT to check the installed build and deploy the fix.

If the blank window prevents you from reaching the update menu, Microsoft’s support notice gives a way to update without opening Word, Excel or Outlook.

Save any work you can access, close all Office apps, and open Command Prompt as an administrator. Then run the following command to tell the Office Click-to-Run updater to install the fixed build:

cmd"%programfiles%\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\ClickToRun\officec2rclient.exe" /update user updatetoversion=16.0.20625.20142

After the update finishes, reopen the app that showed the blank window. Check the version and build under File > Account to confirm that Office installed the update, then test whether you can open a document, workbook, or mailbox as usual.

If Outlook opens normally but still cannot upload an attachment, that is a different symptom. Microsoft separately investigated attachment upload failures in New Outlook, and its blank-window notice does not list attachment handling among the problems this update fixes.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
As we move into 2027, SOCs and MSSPs face a growing imbalance between the speed at which threats evolve and the resources available to combat them.

AI-assisted attacks, increasingly sophisticated phishing campaigns, expanding attack surfaces, and growing volumes of security data are putting security teams under pressure. 

The challenge goes beyond improving detection and response. It involves building security operations that can absorb increasing workloads, adapt to emerging threats, and demonstrate measurable business value without continuously expanding headcount or spending. 

What should SOC and MSSP leaders prioritize in 2027, and which innovations can make a tangible difference? 

Here are five practical steps to strengthen defenses, scale security operations efficiently, and turn innovation into measurable business value. 

1. Strengthen Threat Detection to Combat AI-Driven Attacks 

Generative AI has lowered the barrier to cybercrime. Attackers can produce convincing phishing content, personalize social engineering campaigns, and modify malicious code with greater speed.

As AI agents become more capable, the potential for increasingly automated attacks also grows. 

For security teams, this means dealing with more threats that are harder to distinguish from legitimate activity. Traditional detection mechanisms remain essential, but relying exclusively on known signatures and static indicators is becoming increasingly risky. 

SOC and MSSP leaders should prioritize behavioral analysis and contextual detection, giving analysts the ability to understand what a suspicious file or URL actually does rather than relying solely on its reputation. 

With a solution like ANY.RUN Interactive Sandbox, analysts can investigate suspicious objects in isolated virtual environments, interact with threats in real time, and uncover malicious behavior that automated security solutions may overlook.

This speed is particularly valuable as AI-driven threats increase the volume and complexity of investigations without a corresponding increase in analyst capacity.

To strengthen detection proactively, security leaders can also integrate Threat Intelligence Feeds (TI Feeds) into their existing security infrastructure, enabling continuous monitoring for emerging malicious indicators.

2. Make Threat Context an Integral Part of SOC Investigations 

Increasing detection coverage is valuable, but generating more alerts without improving investigation capacity can create additional operational problems. 

Analysts frequently encounter indicators that lack sufficient context. Determining whether a suspicious domain or IP address represents a significant threat often requires multiple searches, reviewing previous findings, and consulting external intelligence sources.

3. Centralize SOC Management to Scale Operations Efficiently 

As organizations expand across regions, business units, and customer environments, maintaining operational visibility and consistency becomes increasingly difficult. 

For MSSPs, every new customer introduces additional investigations, reporting requirements, access permissions, and data privacy considerations.

Without centralized management, growth can lead to fragmented workflows, higher administrative costs, and declining service quality.

  • Centralized Team Management: Manage independent teams, permissions, and shared resources. 
  • Cases and Teamhistory: Organize related analyses, simplify shift handovers, and reuse previous findings. 
  • Team Performance and Threat Landscape Overviews: Monitor investigation activity, detection metrics, and emerging threats across teams and customer environments. 

See how ANY.RUN helps teams reduce MTTR by 20 min and contain threats before they escalate. Accelerate Incident Response
 

Internal SOCs can use Teamspace to connect distributed teams and establish consistent investigation practices, giving managers greater visibility into security activity and enabling more informed resource allocation. 

MSSPs benefit from scalable service delivery, secure customer data separation, greater service transparency, and reduced administrative overhead. 

Ultimately, centralized management allows security leaders to focus less on coordinating individual workflows and more on improving security outcomes, operational efficiency, and customer satisfaction. 

4. Drive Innovation Through Automation and Analyst Development 

As AI enables attackers to operate with greater speed and scale, automation is becoming essential to effective security operations.

The priority should be addressing operational bottlenecks rather than adopting technology simply to keep pace with industry trends. 

Automating repetitive tasks such as alert validation, evidence collection, IOC enrichment, and investigation documentation helps SOCs and MSSPs increase capacity and accelerate response while maintaining human oversight.

5. Align Your 2027 SOC Budget with Measurable Business Outcomes 

Growing cybersecurity requirements do not automatically translate into larger budgets. 

According to IANS and Artico Search, 55% of CISOs reported flat or declining security budgets in 2026. Even for organizations increasing their cybersecurity spending, demonstrating the return on new investments remains essential. 

Before allocating resources to additional technologies, security leaders should examine where their existing budgets and analyst capacity are being consumed.

The objective is not simply to reduce spending but to ensure that every investment contributes to stronger detection, faster response, or greater operational capacity. 

Conclusion: Building a SOC That Can Keep Up with 2027 and Beyond 

In 2027, SOC and MSSP leaders will need to combat increasingly sophisticated threats, manage growing workloads, and scale operations while working within tight budgets. 

The key is to make innovation serve operational needs: automate repetitive tasks, strengthen threat visibility, improve team collaboration, and tie investments to measurable outcomes. 

Success will depend not on how many new technologies security teams adopt, but on their ability to respond faster, maintain investigation quality, and grow sustainably without overwhelming their analysts or budgets.
