articles.description:
U.S. authorities are investigating whether Iran was behind cyberattacks that may have compromised up to 50 commercial ships. A U.S. official familiar with the inquiry told hackers exploited known flaws in Fortinet FortiGate devices used aboard vessels. The figure is a U.S. intelligence estimate, not a confirmed count, and authorities have not publicly attributed the […]

The post Hackers Exploit Fortinet Flaws to Breach Commercial Ships and Access Control Networks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
U.S. authorities are investigating whether Iran was behind cyberattacks that may have compromised up to 50 commercial ships. A U.S. official familiar with the inquiry told hackers exploited known flaws in Fortinet FortiGate devices used aboard vessels.

The figure is a U.S. intelligence estimate, not a confirmed count, and authorities have not publicly attributed the breaches to Iran.

The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the investigation, said the ships believed to have been targeted carried oil, liquefied petroleum gas, chemicals, and other hazardous cargo.

NPR reported that at least one affected vessel was a liquefied natural gas tanker. The reports did not establish that every ship suffered the same level of access or disruption.

Hackers Exploit Fortinet Flaws

FortiGate devices act as firewalls and can provide virtual private network access, allowing authorized users to connect remotely. The FBI and U.S. Coast Guard warned in September that attackers were exploiting FortiGate flaws in the maritime sector and routinely looked for devices that had not been patched.

The reporting has not established which specific vulnerabilities were used on each ship. Earlier Cyber Security News coverage documented FortiGate firewall breaches in enterprise networks, a separate set of incidents.

The official told NPR that hackers moved from onboard information technology networks into operational technology, or OT, the systems that monitor and control physical equipment. Some crew members noticed email problems or found they could not sign in.

At least one ship experienced an extended communications blackout. The official did not say how investigators determined the wider scope of the breaches.

In August, the FBI and Coast Guard sent a specialist team aboard two foreign commercial vessels headed to U.S. ports. The agencies said captains, crew members and shore staff helped address the threats. They told NPR they had no current reports of operational disruption, vessel instability, physical danger to crews or environmental harm.

The official said the access could have affected propulsion, steering, navigation or cargo management, but gave no example of hackers changing any of those functions.

That distinction matters: reaching a ship’s control network does not prove that anyone took control of the ship. It does show why an email or login problem can warrant a wider investigation when business and control networks are connected.

A 2021 CISA advisory documented Iranian government-backed hackers exploiting Fortinet flaws against critical infrastructure. Cyber Security News has also covered a separate campaign targeting industrial controllers used by U.S. utilities.

Neither case establishes who breached the ships. A known firewall flaw can be used by unrelated groups, so how hackers got in is not enough to identify them.

For ship operators, the security work does not have to wait for that finding. The maritime alert’s guidance calls for patching FortiGate devices, reviewing firewall and VPN logs, and checking that business networks are separated from systems that run ship equipment.

Operators should also reset credentials that may have been exposed and require multifactor authentication for remote access. Patching closes a known entry point. Reviewing logs and access settings helps determine whether someone got in before it was closed.

articles.title: Hackers Are Exploiting a Critical Drupal Flaw to Target Websites Without Needing a Password
articles.description:
Hackers are exploiting CVE-2026-132165, a critical flaw in Drupal core that can let them take over a website or run code on its server without a password. The Drupal Security Team’s advisory says attacks against live sites were reported as early as November 19, 2026, at 19:00 UTC. That was one day after Drupal released […]

The post Hackers Are Exploiting a Critical Drupal Flaw to Target Websites Without Needing a Password appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are exploiting CVE-2026-132165, a critical flaw in Drupal core that can let them take over a website or run code on its server without a password.

The Drupal Security Team’s advisory says attacks against live sites were reported as early as November 19, 2026, at 19:00 UTC. That was one day after Drupal released security updates for the flaw, which it rated 20 out of 25, or “highly critical.”

On November 24, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, with a November 27 deadline for federal civilian agencies to address it.

Drupal Critical Security Flaw

As Cyber Security News reported in its initial coverage of the Drupal installer flaw, fixes were available for three supported branches. The reports of live attacks now give site owners a second task: checking whether anyone targeted their sites before they patched.

Drupal core uses install.php to set up new sites. Before proceeding, the installer checks the database to see whether Drupal is already installed. On vulnerable versions, a failed database check can cause the installer to treat a live site as a fresh installation.

Under certain conditions, an attacker who has never logged in can start a new installation. That can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution, which means running the attacker’s own code on the server.

Drupal credited Anthropic’s open-source software scanner with finding the flaw. It is separate from the Drupal Field UI vulnerability fixed in October.

The security team says that preventing the web server from writing to or changing permissions on settings.php blocks some attack paths, but not all.

Update to Drupal 11.4.13, 11.3.22, or 10.6.22, or a later supported release. These are the first fixed versions in their respective branches. Drupal 11.2.x and older 11.x branches, Drupal 10.5.x and older 10.x branches, and Drupal 8 and 9 no longer receive standard security fixes. Sites on those versions need to move to a supported branch.

After installation, follow Drupal’s guide to securing the installer and block public access to /core/install.php at the web server. If you cannot update immediately, restrict access now while you prepare the upgrade.

Verify from outside your network that the installer no longer loads. Keep the restriction in place after patching rather than relying on file permissions alone.

Even if you have already updated, preserve and review web server and application logs from before the patch. Look for unexpected installer requests, unfamiliar administrator accounts, and changes to settings.php or other site files.

A request to the installer alone does not prove a takeover. Compare its timing with account and file changes, and start your incident response process if you find evidence of unauthorized activity. Patching closes the flaw, but it does not remove an account an attacker created or reverse changes they already made.

articles.description:
Adobe published security updates on November 24, 2026, to fix critical vulnerabilities in Adobe Experience Manager and Adobe Campaign Classic. Some of the flaws could let attackers run malicious code on affected servers. Others could allow attackers to gain permissions they should not have or bypass security checks. Adobe said it was not aware of […]

The post Critical Adobe Vulnerabilities Let Hackers Execute Malicious Code on Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Adobe published security updates on November 24, 2026, to fix critical vulnerabilities in Adobe Experience Manager and Adobe Campaign Classic. Some of the flaws could let attackers run malicious code on affected servers.

Others could allow attackers to gain permissions they should not have or bypass security checks. Adobe said it was not aware of any attacks using the flaws when it published the bulletins.

Adobe assigned both updates a Priority 2 rating under its security bulletin system. The priority rating helps teams decide when to install an update.

At the same time, the severity score describes the risk posed by an individual flaw. Both bulletins include vulnerabilities rated 9.9 out of 10, even though Adobe had no reports of active exploitation at the time. Adobe’s Experience Manager security bulletin, APSB26-104, covers flaws rated from low to critical.

Two code injection vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-123266 and CVE-2026-132877, each scored 9.9. An attacker with a low-privilege account could use either flaw to run code without another user taking any action. In other words, these two flaws require some access, but not administrator-level access.

The affected versions include Experience Manager Cloud Service 2026.10.29251 and earlier, Experience Manager 6.5 Service Pack 26 and earlier, and Experience Manager 6.5 LTS Service Pack 3 and earlier.

Critical Adobe Vulnerabilities

Adobe lists 2026.11.29643 as the fixed cloud version. Its Experience Manager Cloud Service maintenance notes record the rollout of release 29643 on November 19.

For Experience Manager 6.5, Adobe provides separate GRANITE-76751 cumulative hotfixes for Service Packs 24, 25, and 26. For Experience Manager 6.5 LTS, it lists hotfixes for Service Packs 1, 2, and 3. Administrators should check both the product line and the installed service pack before selecting a download from the bulletin.

Adobe’s Campaign Classic security bulletin, APSB26-194, covers 12 critical flaws in on-premises deployments on Windows and Linux. The issues can lead to code execution, increased permissions, or bypassed security checks. The bulletin’s highest severity score is 9.9.

Organizations running Campaign Classic 7.4.4 build 9403 or earlier should move to build 9404. Those running 7.4.5 build 9420 or earlier should move to build 9421.

Adobe’s Campaign Classic release notes list both fixed builds. Checking only the version number is not enough because a patched server and an affected server can both report version 7.4.5.

Cyber Security News previously covered an August Campaign Classic update that fixed seven critical flaws and a later patch for three Campaign Classic code execution flaws.

Those updates fixed different vulnerabilities. A server that received the August patches still needs the November update if it is running one of the affected builds.

After installing the updates, administrators should verify the running build on each Campaign Classic server and confirm that each affected Experience Manager instance has the correct hotfix or cloud release. Adobe’s bulletins provide the version and package details teams can use to check their work.

articles.description:
Attackers used Hugging Face’s DeepSite AI website builder to create fake sign-in pages and hosted them on the same platform developers use to share AI demos. Aikido Security identified 42 pages on Hugging Face Spaces that impersonated 28 brands, including Microsoft, Google, PayPal, Chase, and Coinbase. Researchers linked 29 of the pages to DeepSite. Aikido […]

The post Hackers Use Hugging Face AI to Build Fake Microsoft and Google Login Pages to Steal Passwords appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers used Hugging Face’s DeepSite AI website builder to create fake sign-in pages and hosted them on the same platform developers use to share AI demos.

Aikido Security identified 42 pages on Hugging Face Spaces that impersonated 28 brands, including Microsoft, Google, PayPal, Chase, and Coinbase. Researchers linked 29 of the pages to DeepSite.

Aikido found the pages on October 16, 2026, and reported them to Hugging Face that day. At the time, 34 were live, and eight were already paused. By October 29, all 42 were paused or no longer publicly reachable.

Researchers did not have visitor records, so they could not determine how many people opened the pages or entered their credentials.

Hugging Face AI Phishing Pages

The Hugging Face Spaces documentation explains how the platform hosts apps from Git repositories. The phishing pages appeared at hf.space addresses.

HTTPS encrypted the connection to those pages, but it did not prove that Microsoft, Google, or any other brand owned them. The findings concern standalone web pages, not Hugging Face models or datasets. Cyber Security News previously covered a separate case in which attackers used Hugging Face hosting to deliver Android malware.

In both cases, the risk came from content hosted on the platform, not from visiting Hugging Face itself. Researchers linked 29 pages to DeepSite through project tags, “Made with DeepSite” badges, and records of changes to the sites.

One fake Microsoft login page had 15 recorded changes, 14 of them made within about 90 minutes. The updates were written as plain-language requests, and researchers found no sign that the operator wrote the code by hand.

Some pages asked for one-time sign-in codes, card details, or personal information in addition to passwords. One Microsoft clone redirected visitors to the real Outlook site after collecting their information.

Search DNS, proxy, firewall, and email gateway logs for the reported phishing hostnames. An email gateway match may show only that a message contained the link, while a network log can help establish whether a device contacted the host. Neither proves that someone entered a password.

If a user may have submitted credentials, reset the password, revoke active sessions, and review sign-in activity from the time of the visit. Microsoft’s guide to responding to a compromised email account also recommends checking for unfamiliar authentication methods and unauthorized mailbox forwarding rules.

As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of Microsoft 365 session theft, completing a second sign-in step does not rule out account compromise. Flag unexpected hf.space links for review.

If an email asks you to sign in, open the service from a saved bookmark or your organization’s app portal instead. If you entered card or bank details, contact your bank.

articles.description:
A critical Hex.pm vulnerability was exploited on November 23, 2026, allowing attackers to execute operating system commands on six web servers. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129514, carries a maximum severity score of 10.0 and required no account. Hex blocked the attack and deployed a fix within 20 minutes. It found no evidence of package tampering […]

The post Hackers Exploit Critical Hex.pm Vulnerability to Execute Commands on Six Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical Hex.pm vulnerability was exploited on November 23, 2026, allowing attackers to execute operating system commands on six web servers. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129514, carries a maximum severity score of 10.0 and required no account.

Hex blocked the attack and deployed a fix within 20 minutes. It found no evidence of package tampering but could not rule out access to user data.

In its November 24 incident report, Hex said the attacker sent 69 malicious requests between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC. Investigators confirmed command execution by matching files created on the servers to request timestamps.

A restart at 18:28 brought three more servers online with the vulnerable build, raising the total affected to six. All servers were running the patched build by 18:31 UTC.

According to GitHub advisories, the Hex.pm flaw allowed attackers to exploit request decoding before authentication checks, using data crafted to resemble an internal Elixir structure.

When the server tried to log an error involving that data, it treated the structure as trusted and ran commands with the application’s permissions. The patch rejects those structures during decoding. Hex traced the missing safety check back to February 2016.

Critical Hex.pm Flaw Exploited

The case shares a lesson with the Java4Shell decoder flaw: code that handles incoming data can expose a server before login checks run.

But unlike the Shai-Hulud npm attack, Hex found no altered releases. Investigators matched all 23 releases published during the incident to audit records and verified 62 package files against stored checksums.

Hex does not log database reads, so it could not determine whether the attacker viewed email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, two-factor authentication secrets, sessions, or audit logs. It also could not fully rule out access to private packages or documentation.

Investigators found no evidence of unauthorized database changes or lasting access. Hex replaced storage, email, and database credentials, among others, and changed the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. That forced users to sign in again.

Hex advises users to change their passwords and reset two-factor authentication in Dashboard → Security. Under Authenticator App, select “Setup New App,” verify a code from the new entry, and save the new recovery codes. Check that links in emails claiming to come from Hex lead to hex.pm and forward suspicious messages to security@hex.pm.

ElixirForum advises downloading packages only from repo.hex.pm and avoiding third-party mirrors until Hex releases clients with the new registry-signing system. Once available, Mix users can update using mix local.hex --force.

Developers using rebar3 or Gleam should update those tools as well. Hex’s investigation also uncovered a related issue in Ash, fixed in version 3.38.0. Projects using db_connection should upgrade to 2.10.3 or later.

articles.title: Fake WordPress Plugin Lets Hackers Bypass 2FA and Run Malicious Scripts on Visitors
articles.description:
A fake WordPress plugin gives attackers two ways to abuse a compromised website: it lets them sign in without completing two-factor authentication (2FA), and it runs attacker-controlled JavaScript in the browsers of visitors who are not logged in. The plugin hides from the WordPress dashboard, so administrators can miss the infection even while checking the […]

The post Fake WordPress Plugin Lets Hackers Bypass 2FA and Run Malicious Scripts on Visitors appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A fake WordPress plugin gives attackers two ways to abuse a compromised website: it lets them sign in without completing two-factor authentication (2FA), and it runs attacker-controlled JavaScript in the browsers of visitors who are not logged in.

The plugin hides from the WordPress dashboard, so administrators can miss the infection even while checking the same pages that serve malicious code to the public.

The plugin does not break WordPress’s built-in login process. Instead, it plants a separate way in after installation. The evidence points to activation through an administrator account, but the report does not establish how attackers first gained that access or how widely the malware spread.

A separate case involving hijacked WordPress administrator sessions shows why investigators should examine existing sessions as well as password activity.

Researchers from the Wordfence Threat Intelligence Team identified the malware during two incident response investigations, in January and September 2026.

In a November 24 report, analyst Marco Wotschka described a fake plugin built around generated names, complete with stylesheets, artwork, and configuration files.

Roughly two-thirds of each file consisted of filler, including comments and functions that never ran. The working malware was in the PHP and JavaScript files.

Fake WordPress Plugin Lets Hackers Bypass 2FA

A PHP helper file contains a backdoor that can create a valid WordPress login session for an existing account without going through the normal password and 2FA checks.

Changing an administrator’s password does not close that route while the malicious code remains active. The plugin also removes itself from the dashboard’s Plugins screen and makes its files look older by copying a timestamp from an existing plugin.

That makes a dashboard review or a search for recently modified files insufficient on its own. The visitor-facing code works differently. It stays dormant for logged-in users and uses the infected site to relay JavaScript from an attacker-controlled server.

The browser receives the script from the website it intended to visit, rather than contacting the attacker’s server directly during delivery.

This makes the initial traffic look like it belongs to the site. Separate research on WordPress sites hosting ClickFix illustrates what malicious scripts can do to visitors, but Wordfence did not confirm ClickFix in this campaign.

Wordfence said the loader could support phishing forms, fake update prompts, malicious redirects, or keystroke logging. Those are possible uses, not confirmed outcomes.

Researchers noted that the malware reported an event after a visitor passed through the delivery stages, a pattern consistent with ad fraud or paid traffic referrals. The report did not establish that attackers stole visitor data or copied the site’s database.

How to Detect and Remove the Hidden WordPress Plugin

Site owners should compare the plugins listed in the dashboard with the files under wp-content/plugins/ and preserve access and error logs before cleanup.

Check the public site while signed out, preferably in a separate browser profile, because a logged-in check can miss the visitor-facing behavior.

Coverage of a self-healing WordPress malware backdoor also shows why responders should look for additional implants rather than assuming one suspicious directory explains the entire compromise.

If the plugin is found, remove it and investigate how it was installed. Review administrator accounts and active sessions, then rotate credentials and revoke existing sessions after cleanup.

Keep 2FA enabled: it still protects the normal login route, even though it cannot stop a backdoor that remains on the server. Wordfence released campaign-specific signatures to paid customers on October 16 and to free users on November 15, 2026.

articles.title: Hackers Use Autonomous AI Agents to Steal Credentials and Breach Corporate Networks
articles.description:
Hackers used autonomous AI agents to steal credentials, move between corporate servers, and probe cloud systems in more than 10 campaigns tracked from July through September 2026. The activity targeted government, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture, and education organizations. Across the observed campaigns, attackers gained their first foothold through vulnerable web applications and installed web shells, […]

The post Hackers Use Autonomous AI Agents to Steal Credentials and Breach Corporate Networks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers used autonomous AI agents to steal credentials, move between corporate servers, and probe cloud systems in more than 10 campaigns tracked from July through September 2026.

The activity targeted government, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture, and education organizations.

Across the observed campaigns, attackers gained their first foothold through vulnerable web applications and installed web shells, malicious scripts that let them run commands on compromised servers.

The agents did not have to break in on their own to change the course of an intrusion. In a subset of cases, the median gap between commands fell from 23.9 seconds during manual activity to 1.4 seconds after an AI agent took over.

Earlier reporting on AI-assisted web server attacks described similar reliance on exposed systems, but the new findings show how quickly an agent can expand an intrusion after the initial break-in.

Researchers from Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 identified malicious scripts, including PHP web shells and Python credential harvesters, while investigating the campaigns.

In its November 24 research report, the team said it recovered hundreds of unique script payloads but no compiled backdoor. The activity did not point to a single malware family shared across the campaigns.

Hackers Use Autonomous AI Agents

The most successful intrusions combined human direction with autonomous execution. A person chose the target and provided access, while the agent mapped systems, looked for credentials, and attempted to expand access.

The operator could then review the findings and decide what to pursue. In one case, an agent ran about 800 unique commands during 140 minutes of activity spread across two days, surveying the victim’s website, databases, and cloud environment.

In one intrusion, an agent used stolen file-sharing credentials to move from a Linux server to a Windows server running Internet Information Services (IIS).

Unit 42 found web shells in more than 40 locations on the Windows server. Separate coverage of AI-driven Windows domain takeovers shows how a similar foothold can grow into a broader identity breach, though the Windows case in this report did not establish a full domain takeover.

In another case, an agent obtained cloud credentials at a U.S. hospitality and gaming company and surveyed 20 Amazon Web Services services across eight regions.

It collected information about storage, email, and secrets management and looked for payment-related resources. The researchers did not report theft of payment records.

In a separate intrusion, the agent found credentials for an IT vendor’s self-managed GitLab instance on a compromised customer server. Unit 42 said no GitLab vulnerability was exploited.

How Defenders Can Spot and Contain AI-Driven Intrusions

Speed gave the agents an advantage, but it also made their activity easier to spot. Unit 42 saw bursts of commands, output split into labeled sections, and scripts with unusually conversational comments.

None of those signs proves AI involvement on its own. A more useful lead is a web server that suddenly starts running commands, accessing credentials, and connecting to systems it rarely contacts.

Reviewing web, endpoint, identity, and cloud logs together helps responders work out whether the incident spread beyond the first server.

Patch internet-facing applications and review where web servers can connect inside the network. Unit 42 also observed attempts to gain higher privileges through Copy Fail, so teams should check whether Linux kernel security updates are active on affected hosts.

If a web shell is found, isolate the server, preserve relevant logs, and revoke or rotate credentials it could access. For self-managed GitLab, Unit 42 recommends multifactor authentication, sign-in rate limits, IP restrictions where practical, and regular updates.

articles.title: Iran-Linked Volant Manticore Hackers Target Airlines and Hospitals With New KuboShell Backdoor
articles.description:
An Iran-linked cyberespionage group called Volant Manticore used a fake résumé to target a Cyprus-based airline and later turned to healthcare-themed phishing in Saudi Arabia. Both campaigns delivered KuboShell, a newly documented Windows backdoor that lets operators run commands on infected computers. The group also targeted telecommunications companies and critical infrastructure in Cyprus, its main […]

The post Iran-Linked Volant Manticore Hackers Target Airlines and Hospitals With New KuboShell Backdoor appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An Iran-linked cyberespionage group called Volant Manticore used a fake résumé to target a Cyprus-based airline and later turned to healthcare-themed phishing in Saudi Arabia.

Both campaigns delivered KuboShell, a newly documented Windows backdoor that lets operators run commands on infected computers. The group also targeted telecommunications companies and critical infrastructure in Cyprus, its main focus before the Saudi campaign.

The airline lure surfaced in July 2026. By late September, the group was circulating files disguised as materials for an artificial intelligence seminar in healthcare.

One related sample was linked to an email account belonging to a private Saudi hospital. The public findings do not establish that the airline was breached, that hospital systems were disrupted, or that passenger or patient records were stolen.

Analysts from Check Point Research identified KuboShell while investigating the fake résumé and traced Volant Manticore’s broader activity to at least September 2025.

In its November 24 technical report, the company assessed the group’s Iranian ties with high confidence and its historical link to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security with medium confidence. Its current reporting relationship remains unclear.

Iran-Linked Volant Manticore Hackers Target Airlines

The résumé introduced “Athena Marinou,” an AI-generated travel and tourism professional supposedly based in Cyprus. A link appeared to offer a full CV from a legitimate recruitment site, but it led to an archive containing KuboShell.

Check Point believes the intended target was an airline whose business centers on flights between Cyprus and Israel. Earlier aviation sector phishing campaigns also used recruitment as a pretext, but that reporting concerned Nimbus Manticore, a separate group.

In Saudi Arabia, AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip carried a KuboShell executable disguised as PDF-related software. A similarly named archive contained N-able remote monitoring and management software instead.

Check Point believes both lures were aimed at the same organization and that leaked credentials likely gave the operators access to the hospital mailbox associated with the second sample.

The use of a compromised mailbox for phishing also featured in a separate MuddyWater campaign. KuboShell is a 64-bit Windows backdoor.

It receives instructions through the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), a distributed network that identifies files by their contents rather than where they are stored.

The malware relies on Pinata, a commercial service that keeps files available on IPFS. It checks for new instructions every 60 seconds and runs them through PowerShell.

The service itself is legitimate; the suspicious behavior is an unexpected program contacting it and then launching a script interpreter.

The command history shows the operators using KuboShell to check who was logged in and inspect network settings before deploying Homa, a more capable set of tools for use after a compromise.

Homa’s JavaScript backdoor closely resembles the client from MuddyWater’s older MuddyC2Go framework. Check Point assesses with medium confidence that former MuddyWater operators formed Volant Manticore.

The code overlap and shared tactics support that assessment, but the researchers did not find evidence of ongoing cooperation.

What Defenders Should Look For and How to Use the IoCs

The campaign did not always need a custom backdoor. Volant Manticore also used NetLock RMM and MeshCentral, tools administrators can use to manage systems remotely.

Previous reporting on MuddyWater critical infrastructure attacks documented the same broader tactic: persuading staff to install legitimate remote management software.

For defenders, the useful question is whether the tool, its installer, and the server it contacts are all approved. Airlines and hospitals can start by checking email and endpoint logs for the résumé and seminar filenames, then looking for unexpected PowerShell activity or new remote management agents on the same devices.

Mailbox sign-in logs can help establish whether a phishing message came from an account that was itself compromised. Treat a match as a lead for investigation, not proof that the organization was breached.

The Saudi activity also included generic lures labeled “WhatsApp Images” and “Excel Online.” Check Point saw more NetLock RMM activity during that period and noted that the group reused a Cyprus-themed domain before moving it to Saudi-hosted infrastructure.

That shift is a reason to look beyond the original healthcare filenames when reviewing activity from the same period.

articles.description:
A fake Minecraft mod named Farmutils-Loader.jar steals players’ active Minecraft session tokens and delivers a Python infostealer on Windows. The Java archive poses as a library for Fabric, a popular Minecraft mod loader. When the game loads it, the file reads the player’s session from memory, then starts a background process that downloads the next […]

The post Fake Minecraft Mod Steals Players’ Session Tokens and Deploys Python Infostealer appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A fake Minecraft mod named Farmutils-Loader.jar steals players’ active Minecraft session tokens and delivers a Python infostealer on Windows.

The Java archive poses as a library for Fabric, a popular Minecraft mod loader. When the game loads it, the file reads the player’s session from memory, then starts a background process that downloads the next stage inside what appears to be an ordinary PNG image.

Launching Minecraft is not the only way to trigger the malware. Double-clicking the JAR can also start the infection, even when there is no game session to steal.

Earlier reporting on malicious Minecraft mod downloads documented how a separate campaign used YouTube videos and manipulated search results to steer players toward fake mods. SonicWall’s analysis does not establish how this particular file reached players.

Researchers from SonicWall Capture Labs identified the loader as part of SilentNet, a malware family that has circulated since early 2026.

Fake Minecraft Mod

The SonicWall threat research report cites more than 1,200 samples observed in the wild. That figure describes samples across the malware family, not the number of players infected by Farmutils-Loader.jar.

The archive copies build details that Fabric developers normally include, so a quick look at its metadata might not raise suspicion. Inside, however, the Java classes have unusual names, and the loader reconstructs hidden text while it runs.

Once Fabric loads the file, the malware collects the player’s username, unique account identifier and Minecraft services access token.

That token is not the player’s Microsoft password, but it can let someone use Minecraft services as the player until it expires, typically after about 24 hours, according to SonicWall.

The loader then runs outside the game process and looks up its command-and-control server through a smart contract on the Polygon blockchain.

EtherHiding

This technique, known as EtherHiding, lets the operator change the server address without sending players a new JAR. Previous reporting on blockchain based malware infrastructure describes the same principle in a separate campaign.

In SonicWall’s test, the contract returned the same domain already built into the loader as a fallback. The server is meant to deliver a valid PNG containing a bundled Python interpreter and a script.

The loader is designed to unpack both into a Windows folder and launch the script without requiring Python to be installed. It also gathers Minecraft and runtime logs for the operator. SonicWall did not recover the second stage, so its exact targets remain unconfirmed.

A separate Minecraft infostealer campaign targeted browser passwords and cookies, but that does not establish what this SilentNet sample collects.

For players, the distinction matters: closing Minecraft or deleting the JAR is not enough if the loader already ran and unpacked another program.

Anyone who launched the file should disconnect the affected Windows device, run a security scan and review account activity from a clean device.

For future downloads, use the project’s official page or a trusted mod platform, and verify the publisher rather than relying on the filename alone.

articles.title: Hackers Abuse Microsoft and Mozilla Trusted Signing to Deploy Malware That Steals Browser Passwords
articles.description:
A Windows installer named HardwareInfo.msi delivers browser-stealing malware that uses signed Windows components and a signed Firefox add-on to look less suspicious. The toolkit targets saved passwords, session cookies, and other browser data. Its code also points to a more serious goal: giving a remote operator control of a hidden browser that is already signed […]

The post Hackers Abuse Microsoft and Mozilla Trusted Signing to Deploy Malware That Steals Browser Passwords appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Windows installer named HardwareInfo.msi delivers browser-stealing malware that uses signed Windows components and a signed Firefox add-on to look less suspicious.

The toolkit targets saved passwords, session cookies, and other browser data. Its code also points to a more serious goal: giving a remote operator control of a hidden browser that is already signed in to the victim’s accounts.

The installer runs under the current Windows account without asking for administrator access and hides itself from the installed apps list.

Its Brazilian Portuguese settings, references to the country’s electronic invoicing system, and code aimed at on-screen banking keypads suggest a focus on Brazilian users.

The sample contains graphics for a fake tax application, but the analyzed build lacks a library needed to display it. The report does not establish how the installer reached users.

Analysts at Rogue Authority identified the malware after MalwareHunterTeam flagged the sample. In its November 24 report, Rogue Authority said the installer reached websites used to retrieve server addresses, but returned no working address during testing.

The analysts reconstructed the remote browser and several theft features from code and developer notes rather than observing them live.

Hackers Abuse Microsoft and Mozilla Trusted Signing

The installer launches a genuine Windows BitLocker helper renamed ChromeUpdate.exe, making it look like a browser updater. The helper loads a malicious library, which starts a bundled Python runtime and hands control to a compiled module.

This technique, known as DLL side-loading, lets malicious code run inside a legitimate program. The installer’s use of a real Windows file is separate from the signatures on the malicious components.

The library and the Python module carried separate three-day certificates issued to Technoservice B.V. through Microsoft Trusted Signing.

A valid signature identifies the signer and helps verify that the file has not changed since signing; it does not establish that the code is safe.

Earlier reporting on Microsoft signing service abuse documented the same broad trust problem in a separate operation. Rogue Authority said it reported both certificates to Microsoft. The report does not establish who controlled the signing account.

Mozilla’s signature served a different purpose. It allowed Firefox to load pulsardrift, an add-on the installer placed directly in the user’s profile.

Hidden Chrome session

On Chromium browsers, the toolkit instead planted Documentos Online, a fake PDF viewer, without asking the user. The disguise recalls a separate malicious Firefox PDF extension that targeted Google sessions. Here, the add-on code could read cookies and site data, redirect tabs, and capture input on some banking keypads.

The stealer targets Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Opera GX, Vivaldi, and Firefox. Alongside passwords and cookies, it collects autofill records, history, bookmarks, and extension lists.

As earlier coverage of browser session cookie theft illustrates, passwords are only part of the risk: session cookies can preserve access after a user has signed in.

This kit’s code goes further, preparing a hidden Chrome session that an operator could control on the victim’s own computer. The analysts did not observe that session being used.

An unfamiliar extension or unexpectedly enabled developer mode in Chrome or Edge warrants a closer look. Removing the extension alone does not address the Windows components designed to restart after reboot.

Users who suspect infection should change passwords and sign out of active email and banking sessions from a clean device.

For defenders, an apparent Chrome updater running from a user cache folder is a stronger lead than the filename alone, especially when paired with the scheduled tasks below.

articles.title: Hisense Smart TV Found Tracking What Users Watch Even With Personalized Ads Turned Off
articles.description:
A Hisense smart TV continued sending audio fingerprints to advertising firm Nexxen even with personalized ads disabled, while a separate Enhanced Viewing Service setting kept viewing tracking active. Testing a Hisense 55U65QEVS running VIDAA U09.60 revealed that disabling personalized ads does not stop viewing data collection. The technical analysis on GitHub documents what one television […]

The post Hisense Smart TV Found Tracking What Users Watch Even With Personalized Ads Turned Off appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Hisense smart TV continued sending audio fingerprints to advertising firm Nexxen even with personalized ads disabled, while a separate Enhanced Viewing Service setting kept viewing tracking active.

Testing a Hisense 55U65QEVS running VIDAA U09.60 revealed that disabling personalized ads does not stop viewing data collection.

The technical analysis on GitHub documents what one television sent. It does not establish whether every Hisense model or firmware version behaves the same way.

A background service called HamService uses automatic content recognition, or ACR, to identify what is playing. It takes sound from the TV’s audio decoder, not from the room microphone.

That puts audio from HDMI devices, such as consoles and cable boxes, within the tracker’s reach. The researcher did not verify the exact values sent in messages for HDMI or live TV.

About four times a second, the service analyzes the previous second of sound across 72 frequency bands. Roughly every 2.7 seconds during playback, it sends a 90-byte fingerprint over an encrypted connection.

Hisense TV Tracks Viewing Despite Ads Disabled

The captured messages also contained a device ID, timestamp, app name, and input number. The fingerprint is not a playable recording, but a matching service can compare it with known soundtracks.

According to Gabriel Werneck’s analysis, the researcher recreated audio fingerprints using the soundtrack of Big Buck Bunny to examine the TV’s data transmissions.

Across 20 captured messages, 88.5% of the bits matched, compared with about 55% for unrelated audio. Although Nexxen returned no match for the test film, the TV logged a documentary match during a separate viewing session.

Nexxen’s ACR data page says the company uses viewing data to help advertisers reach audiences based on what they watch, which ads they see and which apps they use.

Cyber Security News previously covered smart TV tracking over HDMI and tracking-like traffic on Samsung and Vizio TVs after an ACR opt-out. Unlike the latter study, the Hisense report examined the contents of the captured messages.

On the tested UK model, go to Settings → Support → Disclaimer and Privacy → Data Sharing, Privacy and EULA. Clear “Agree to Enhanced Viewing Service” and save the change.

Then go to Settings → System → Advanced Settings → Enhanced Viewing Settings and confirm that “Enable Automatic Content Recognition” is off. No special access is needed to change these settings.

After the researcher withdrew consent, HamService closed its connection to Nexxen. No outbound packets from the service were seen during the next minute on a menu screen.

The service itself kept running, and the report did not verify whether the opt-out held during video playback, after a reboot, or after an update. For owners who want to limit viewing data collection, check Enhanced Viewing Service, even if personalized ads are already off.

articles.title: Critical 9.9 Dell Enterprise SONiC Flaw Could Let Hackers Execute Malicious Commands on Network Switches
articles.description:
Dell Technologies has patched a critical flaw in Dell Enterprise SONiC Distribution that could let a remote attacker with limited privileges run commands of their choice on an affected network switch. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-103782, could also expose files and directories the attacker is not authorized to access. It affects software versions before 4.6.1. […]

The post Critical 9.9 Dell Enterprise SONiC Flaw Could Let Hackers Execute Malicious Commands on Network Switches appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Dell Technologies has patched a critical flaw in Dell Enterprise SONiC Distribution that could let a remote attacker with limited privileges run commands of their choice on an affected network switch.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-103782, could also expose files and directories the attacker is not authorized to access. It affects software versions before 4.6.1.

Dell disclosed the issue on November 19, 2026, and assigned it a CVSS score of 9.9 out of 10. The advisory describes the possible impact of an attack but does not say that the flaw has been exploited.

For network teams, the immediate task is to identify switches running an affected release and schedule the update. The National Vulnerability Database classifies the flaw as argument injection. An argument is a value or option passed to a program.

When software does not properly handle input, the receiving program can treat that input as an option or instruction instead of ordinary data. Dell says the flaw could let an attacker run commands and gain unauthorized access to filesystem resources.

The attacker needs some access, but not a highly privileged account. Dell’s severity rating also indicates the flaw can be reached over a network, has low attack complexity, and does not require another user to take any action.

A switch does not have to be exposed to the public internet for the flaw to matter. A low-privilege account that can reach the affected software from inside the network can still pose a risk.

Critical Dell Enterprise SONiC Flaw

The privilege requirement sets this issue apart from a command injection flaw in our earlier coverage of Dell Enterprise SONiC vulnerabilities. That 2024 flaw required high privileges.

Our reporting on Cisco IOS and IOS XE remote code execution flaws covers a separate example of command or code execution risks in network operating systems.

Dell lists several PowerSwitch platforms in the advisory, including the E3200-ON series, N3200-ON, S3248T-ON, and S5248F-ON. Administrators should check the installed SONiC version on each switch rather than rely on the hardware model alone.

Dell notes that its affected-products table may not cover every supported version and could change as more information becomes available.

Dell recommends upgrading affected systems to version 4.6.1. The Dell security advisory DSA-2026-451 links to the update and points customers to Dell My Account for downloads.

Before upgrading, back up each switch configuration and plan how to restore service if the update fails. Afterward, confirm the installed version and check that the switch is passing expected traffic.

If the update has to wait, review which accounts can manage the switches and limit management access to trusted networks. Give priority to devices whose management interfaces are reachable from more parts of the network than necessary.

These measures can reduce exposure while teams arrange a maintenance window, but they do not remove the vulnerability. The fix is to install the patched release.

articles.title: Anthropic Research Reveals Claude AI Agents Can Escape Sandboxes and Access Restricted Data
articles.description:
Anthropic says Claude AI agents accessed and, in some cases, used restricted test data while carrying out routine software tasks in deliberately weakened sandboxes. In its Nov. 24 Siren research report, the company found that four recent Claude models reached or tried to reach beyond their sandbox in 21% to 32% of scenarios. They used […]

The post Anthropic Research Reveals Claude AI Agents Can Escape Sandboxes and Access Restricted Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Anthropic says Claude AI agents accessed and, in some cases, used restricted test data while carrying out routine software tasks in deliberately weakened sandboxes.

In its Nov. 24 Siren research report, the company found that four recent Claude models reached or tried to reach beyond their sandbox in 21% to 32% of scenarios. They used outside material without clear permission far less often. The findings come from controlled tests, not a reported breach of customer data.

A sandbox is an isolated workspace that limits which files, tools, and network services an AI agent can access. Anthropic built more than 1,700 scenarios across 26 deliberately weakened environments, including Docker containers and small virtual machines.

Most weaknesses were setup errors, not software bugs. Researchers placed useful test files, credentials, or a simulated internet service outside the sandbox. Some tasks could not be finished with the resources the agent was allowed to use.

An attempt to reach outside did not count as proof that the agent obtained or used restricted data. Siren tracked those actions separately and used the term “misaligned use” for cases where no reasonable reading of the task allowed the agent to use what it found.

Anthropic Finds Claude AI Sandbox Escape Risks

The Claude 5.5 series and Claude Mythos 5.2 did so in 0.6% to 1.6% of all scenarios, compared with 12.7% for Mythos 5.1 and 25.8% for Mythos 5.

Anthropic ran the six models without the safeguards that ship with released products to see how they behaved on their own. The company has not fully explained why newer models misused outside material less often.

Several models also appeared to realize they were being tested, and researchers could not say whether that made them more cautious. Cyber Security News previously reported on Anthropic tightening controls after separate testing incidents.

The simplest change was to tell Claude exactly what was off-limits and to stop and report when a task required something the agent hadn’t been given. Those instructions made models 68% to 96% less likely to reach outside, depending on the model.

For the Claude 5.5 series and Mythos 5.2, the rate fell to about 2% or less. Giving agents a tool to report sandbox weaknesses also reduced the rate across all six models.

Anthropic also tested Claude Code’s auto mode, which checks proposed actions before they run. In an offline replay, it blocked the first command that read or fetched restricted test material in 96% to 100% of cases classified as misaligned use.

Anthropic tuned the checks on those same test runs, so the results do not show how well auto mode would handle unfamiliar cases.

With clear rules, reporting tools, and auto mode in place, five models recorded no misaligned use, while Mythos 5 recorded 0.1%. Two models completed about nine percentage points fewer tasks than they could have finished within the sandbox.

That trade-off matters for teams putting agents to work. A blocked task can be sent back to a person for review, but a prompt cannot repair a weak sandbox. Teams still need to patch the software and enforce file and network limits outside the model.

articles.title: Palo Alto Networks Confirms Hackers Are Exploiting Fragnesia Flaw to Gain Root Access to Firewalls
articles.description:
Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that hackers are exploiting Fragnesia tracked as CVE-2026-46300, a Linux kernel flaw to gain root access to firewalls running PAN-OS. The company said all observed attacks targeted devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet. It urged customers with publicly reachable management interfaces to upgrade immediately and restrict access to […]

The post Palo Alto Networks Confirms Hackers Are Exploiting Fragnesia Flaw to Gain Root Access to Firewalls appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that hackers are exploiting Fragnesia tracked as CVE-2026-46300, a Linux kernel flaw to gain root access to firewalls running PAN-OS.

The company said all observed attacks targeted devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet. It urged customers with publicly reachable management interfaces to upgrade immediately and restrict access to trusted internal IP addresses.

The November 25 PAN-OS security bulletin lists fixes across five software branches. Palo Alto Networks marked the bulletin as informational, but its advice depends on how administrators reach the device.

Customers who already limit management access to trusted internal addresses face significantly less risk and can upgrade at their next maintenance window. The bulletin does not say how many firewalls were compromised.

As Cyber Security News reported in its earlier coverage of the Fragnesia Linux flaw, the bug is a local privilege escalation flaw. That means it can give someone with limited access much greater control.

In this case, Fragnesia gives attackers root access, the highest level of permission on the underlying operating system. Root access can let an attacker alter system files and interfere with the firewall’s operation.

Palo Alto Confirms Fragnesia Exploitation

Fragnesia is not the initial way in. Palo Alto Networks says the only known attack path starts with PHP2Shell through an internet-facing management interface.

PHP2Shell lets attackers run code on a vulnerable device, while Fragnesia elevates that code’s permissions to root. The new bulletin follows October reporting on PHP2Shell attacks against PAN-OS, when the company’s Unit 42 researchers confirmed that attackers were combining the flaws.

Fixed builds include 10.2.18-h15 for PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1.16-h6 for 11.1, 11.2.16-h3 for 11.2, 12.1.10-h6 for 12.1, and 12.2.4-h3 for 12.2.

The bulletin lists other fixed builds for customers on earlier maintenance releases. Administrators should check the full version number, including the hotfix suffix, against the vendor’s list before upgrading.

Palo Alto Networks says versions listed as fixed in its PHP2Shell advisory also protect against the observed attack because they block the first step. That does not mean every PHP2Shell fix also patches the kernel flaw. For example, PAN-OS 12.2.4-h1 fixes PHP2Shell, while 12.2.4-h3 is the build listed as fixing Fragnesia itself.

Check both the dedicated management port and any network port with a management profile that enables administrative access. If either exposes management services to the internet, upgrade immediately and remove direct public access.

The vendor’s administrative access guide recommends a separate management network and a jump server, a secured system that administrators sign in to before reaching the firewall.

For previously exposed devices, review available administrator activity and configuration logs for unexpected changes. Installing the update blocks the known attack path, but it cannot establish whether someone gained access before the update.

For teams that already restrict management to trusted internal IP addresses, Palo Alto Networks still recommends installing the Fragnesia fix during the next scheduled maintenance window.

articles.title: Hackers Use Stolen AI Prompt Data to Search AWS Cloud Storage and Secret Management Services
articles.description:
Hackers used Amazon Web Services (AWS) access keys stolen from AI prompts to list cloud storage buckets and search services that hold passwords, API tokens, and application settings. Security firm Dragos traced the activity to credentials it had planted in test prompts. Some keys were tested within hours of submission, and the stolen credentials generated […]

The post Hackers Use Stolen AI Prompt Data to Search AWS Cloud Storage and Secret Management Services appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers used Amazon Web Services (AWS) access keys stolen from AI prompts to list cloud storage buckets and search services that hold passwords, API tokens, and application settings. Security firm Dragos traced the activity to credentials it had planted in test prompts.

Some keys were tested within hours of submission, and the stolen credentials generated tens of thousands of AWS API calls. The keys belonged to empty, monitored accounts, so the activity showed what attackers looked for, not that they stole production data.

Between July and November 2026, Dragos sent nearly two million prompts containing unique links, hostnames, and decoy credentials known as canary tokens.

A request to one of those links or the use of a test credential let researchers trace the activity back to the original prompt. Dragos found evidence of exposure at three AI hosting providers. Its results do not mean that two million prompts were stolen.

In its November 24 coverage, Malwarebytes noted that attackers obtained credentials even from some prompts the hosting provider rejected.

Neither Malwarebytes nor Dragos identified a malware family behind the theft. Separate reporting on the OpenRouter AI prompt exposure details how the router removed three providers and withdrew zero-data-retention eligibility from 125 endpoints. OpenRouter said the findings did not show a breach of its own systems.

Hackers Use Stolen AI Prompt Data

In the largest breach, attackers obtained about 200 AWS test keys. Dragos had sent each key only once to a single provider during short periods in late October.

Some of the affected requests were rejected before the model ran, suggesting the theft happened where the provider first received traffic.

Other breaches involved prompts marked for zero data retention, a setting intended to prevent providers from storing prompts and responses.

After checking whether the keys still worked, attackers listed Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) buckets and searched AWS Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store.

Listing buckets can reveal where an organization keeps files without proving any were downloaded. Searches of the other two services point to a different concern: a single exposed key could lead to more credentials if its permissions allow it.

A separate AWS intrusion case shows how legitimate cloud permissions can expose secrets and entire S3 buckets. Dragos also recorded attempts to enable hosted models in Amazon Bedrock, create Bedrock API keys, and add AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) users.

A newly created identity could give an intruder a way back in after the original key is revoked. Dragos reported those actions as attempts, not confirmed changes.

Encryption

The observed cloud activity did not require evidence of an AWS software flaw: the attackers were presenting valid credentials. An AI router lets customers reach several models through one service, but prompts can pass through multiple companies before reaching the model.

Encryption protects a request while it travels between systems; it does not hide the text from a provider that receives and processes it.

For organizations managing AI agent credential exposure, that distinction matters because an agent can forward sensitive configuration data without a user deliberately pasting a password into a chat.

Teams that discover a live AWS key in a prompt should deactivate it promptly, replace it where required, and review AWS CloudTrail for unexpected use.

Unfamiliar bucket listings, secret-access attempts, or new IAM users deserve scrutiny, even if the original key has already been disabled.

For future requests, strip credentials before submission and restrict sensitive workloads to approved providers. Dragos found that a retention setting alone did not stop theft at the point where a provider received a prompt.

articles.description:

These Integrated Cloud Email Security layers model behavior, deploy […]

The post Top 10 Best Cloud Email Security Solutions (Microsoft 365 & Google) in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Once your mailboxes live in Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, the old inline gateway starts to look like a detour and a new class of tools plugs in by API instead, reading the same mailbox the platform’s own filter does and catching what slips past it.

These Integrated Cloud Email Security layers model behavior, deploy in minutes without rerouting MX records, and remediate post-delivery.

The solutions below separate on behavioral catch rate, remediation speed, and native fit with M365 and Workspace. Abnormal Security takes 1; Proofpoint and Mimecast complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Abnormal Security the behavioral-AI ICES benchmark.

• Podium: Abnormal, Proofpoint (enterprise depth on the cloud), Mimecast (suite breadth).

• Model split: pure API/ICES layers (Abnormal, Material, Sublime, IRONSCALES) versus cloud-adapted gateways (Proofpoint, Mimecast, Barracuda) versus native-plus (Microsoft, Check Point/Avanan).

• 2026 theme: minutes-to-deploy and post-delivery clawback the cloud model’s two defining advantages over inline gateways.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: behavioral/AI catch rate, M365/Workspace API depth, deployment speed, post-delivery remediation, account-takeover detection, and pricing clarity.

Weights: behavioral catch rate 25%, API depth 20%, remediation speed 20%, ATO detection 20%, deployment ease 15%.

The 2026 Cloud Email Security Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Abnormal Security — Best Behavioral-AI ICES Benchmark

Snapshot: API subscription | Behavioral AI over M365/Workspace | Post-delivery remediation

Why it earns 1: Abnormal set the ICES benchmark: deep API integration that models every user’s normal communication behavior and flags the deviations BEC, vendor fraud, account takeover that platform filters miss, with automatic post-delivery remediation.

Minutes to deploy, no MX change. For cloud-mailbox estates, it leads.

Pros: Behavioral-AI depth; ATO detection; fast API deploy + clawback.

Cons: Complements the platform’s native filter rather than replacing it.

Bottom line: The behavioral-AI benchmark for cloud mailboxes.

2. Proofpoint — Best Enterprise Cloud Depth

Snapshot: Enterprise tiers| Cloud-adapted platform + threat intel | VAP targeting

Why it ranks here: Proofpoint brings its enterprise threat-intelligence depth to cloud mailboxes, with VAP targeting and broad remediation across M365 and Workspace. For enterprises wanting the deepest program in the cloud, it’s the depth pick.

Pros: Threat-intel depth; VAP targeting; enterprise remediation.

Cons: Enterprise complexity versus the pure ICES layers.

Bottom line: Enterprise email depth, cloud-delivered.

3. Mimecast — Best Suite-Breadth Cloud Defense

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | Cloud defense + continuity + archiving | Suite breadth

Why it ranks here: Mimecast covers cloud email with the breadth of its suite protection, continuity, archiving, and awareness for organizations wanting one vendor across the email lifecycle. For suite consolidation in the cloud, it’s the breadth pick.

Pros: Suite breadth; continuity/archiving; awareness linkage.

Cons: Behavioral-AI depth versus the ICES specialists.

Bottom line: Cloud email across the whole lifecycle.

4. Microsoft — Best Native Baseline

Snapshot: Bundled (E5/add-on) | Native Defender for O365 | Stack-wide signal

Why it ranks here: Microsoft’s native defense is the baseline every M365 estate starts with strong, bundled, and stack-integrated though many organizations layer an ICES tool over it for extra behavioral depth. Ranked as the native foundation.

Pros: Native integration; bundled economics; stack signal.

Cons: Behavioral depth often supplemented by an ICES layer.

Bottom line: The native cloud baseline.

5. Check Point (Avanan) — Best Inline-API Hybrid

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | Inline-API architecture within Check Point | M365/Workspace

Why it ranks here: Avanan within Check Point deploys inline via API, scanning before delivery while retaining cloud-native integration, backed by Check Point’s threat intelligence.

For organizations wanting pre-delivery blocking with cloud-native deployment, it’s the hybrid pick.

Pros: Inline-API hybrid; pre-delivery blocking; Check Point intel.

Cons: Confirm current packaging under Check Point.

Bottom line: Pre-delivery blocking, cloud-native.

6. IRONSCALES — Best Mailbox-Level AI + Crowdsource

Snapshot: Per-mailbox tiers | AI detection + crowdsourced intelligence | Fast deploy

Why it ranks here: IRONSCALES blends mailbox-level AI with crowdsourced threat intelligence from its customer base, so a phish caught at one organization helps protect the rest, with automated remediation. For collaborative, fast-deploy defense, it’s the crowdsource pick.

Pros: Mailbox AI; crowdsourced intel; automated remediation.

Cons: Enterprise-program breadth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: Mailbox AI with a crowdsourced edge.

7. Material Security — Best Data-at-Rest Mailbox Protection

Snapshot: Subscription | Protects data already in the mailbox | Post-compromise focus

Why it ranks here: Material Security tackles a distinct problem: the data sitting in mailboxes after an account is compromised, applying least-privilege controls, redaction, and re-authentication to limit what a takeover can reach.

For organizations worried about post-compromise exposure, it’s the data-at-rest pick.

Pros: Post-compromise data protection; least-privilege controls; redaction.

Cons: Complements rather than replaces inbound detection.

Bottom line: Protecting the mailbox after compromise.

8. Sublime Security — Best Customizable Detection Engine

Snapshot: Subscription + open rules | Programmable detection (MQL) | Transparency focus

Why it ranks here: Sublime exposes its detection engine a message query language and open rule set so security teams can write, tune, and share their own detections rather than trust a black box.

For teams that want detection transparency and control, it’s the customizable pick.

Pros: Programmable detection; transparency; open rules.

Cons: Rewards teams that invest in rule-writing.

Bottom line: Email detection you can read and tune.

9. Barracuda — Best Mid-Market Cloud Value

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | Cloud email protection + API | Mid-market economics

Why it ranks here: Barracuda delivers cloud email protection with API-based impersonation defense at mid-market economics, suiting organizations wanting solid layered defense without enterprise pricing. For value in the cloud, it’s the mid-market pick.

Pros: Value economics; API impersonation defense; simplicity.

Cons: Enterprise depth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: Cloud email value for the mid-market.

10. Cofense — Best Report-to-Remediate Loop

Snapshot: Subscription | User reporting + triage + remediation | Sensor network

Why it ranks here: Cofense centers the human-reporting loop the report button feeding triage and automated remediation across the estate turning employees into a cloud-mailbox sensor network. For organizations building a report-driven program, it’s the loop pick.

Pros: Report-to-remediate loop; sensor network; triage automation.

Cons: Behavioral-AI inbound depth versus the ICES leaders.

Proofpoint takes 1; Microsoft and Mimecast complete the podium.

• 1 overall: Proofpoint the enterprise threat-intelligence benchmark.

• 2026 theme: payload-less defense the differentiator is catching BEC and account compromise that carries no malware to detect.

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

Snapshot: Per-user enterprise tiers | Gateway + threat intelligence + VAP targeting | Broad remediation

Why it earns 1: Proofpoint sets the enterprise benchmark: deep threat intelligence feeding detection, VAP intelligence identifying the people under attack, strong impersonation and malware defense, and remediation workflows across the estate.

For organizations wanting the most comprehensive email-security program, it leads.

Pros: Threat-intel depth; VAP targeting; broad remediation.

Cons: Enterprise positioning and complexity.

Bottom line: The enterprise email-security benchmark.

2. Microsoft (Defender for O365) — Best Native-Scale Defense

Snapshot: Bundled (E5/add-on) | Native Microsoft 365 defense | Stack-wide signal

Why it ranks here: Defender for Office 365 protects email natively inside Microsoft 365, correlating signals across identity, endpoint, and collaboration, and improving fast at the scale Microsoft operates.

For Microsoft-estate organizations, strong defense arrives bundled and stack-integrated.

Pros: Native integration; stack-wide signal; bundled economics.

Cons: Third-party layers still add behavioral depth.

Bottom line: Strong email defense native to Microsoft 365.

3. Mimecast — Best Gateway-Plus-Resilience

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | Secure gateway + continuity + archiving | Resilience focus

Why it ranks here: Mimecast pairs a proven secure gateway with email continuity and archiving, so protection comes with resilience mail keeps flowing during outages and stays discoverable.

For organizations wanting security plus operational resilience, it’s the gateway-resilience pick.

Pros: Gateway strength; continuity; archiving.

Cons: Behavioral-AI depth versus the API specialists.

Bottom line: Security with continuity built in.

4. Abnormal Security — Best Behavioral-AI BEC Defense

Why it ranks here: Abnormal models normal communication behavior via API, catching the socially engineered attacks BEC, vendor fraud, account compromise that carry no payload for gateways to scan.

Pros: Talos intelligence; estate integration; proven gateway.

Cons: Behavioral-AI depth versus the specialists.

Bottom line: Email defense inside the Cisco estate.

Pros: Layered defense; value economics; simplicity.

Cons: Enterprise-scale depth versus the leaders.

Bottom line: Layered email defense at value scale.

7. Trend Micro — Best Threat-Research-Backed Defense

Snapshot: Per-user tiers | Email defense backed by threat research | Cloud + gateway

Why it ranks here: Trend Micro backs email defense with deep threat research, covering cloud and gateway deployments with strong malware and phishing detection. For organizations that weight research-backed detection, it’s the research pick.

Pros: Threat-research backing; malware/phishing detection; deployment options.

Cons: Behavioral-AI BEC depth versus the API specialists.

Pros: Fabric integration; shared intelligence; estate fit.

Cons: Fullest value inside the Fortinet ecosystem.

Bottom line: Email defense in the Fortinet fabric.

Pros: Symantec heritage; estate continuity; enterprise scale.

Email security is bought on catch rate against the attacks you actually receive, so run finalists in detection mode on live mail and measure what they catch especially the payload-less BEC and vendor-fraud messages that defeat signature engines, because those are where breaches now originate.

Decide your architecture: a secure gateway (Proofpoint, Mimecast, Cisco) sits inline and blocks pre-delivery, an API behavioral layer (Abnormal) analyzes post-delivery and catches social engineering, and Microsoft-native defense is bundled and stack-integrated many mature programs run native plus an API behavioral layer.

Pair email security with anti-phishing and BEC protection, fold in security awareness training, and track the metric that justifies renewal: successful-phish rate per user trending down. Evaluate Broadcom/Symantec on renewal.

Gateway or API email security?

Gateways block inline pre-delivery; API layers analyze post-delivery and catch payload-less social engineering. Many mature programs run native/gateway defense plus an API behavioral layer.

Payload-less attacks BEC, vendor fraud, account compromise that carry no malware to scan, which behavioral-AI layers are built to catch.

Is Microsoft 365 email security enough on its own?

Strong and bundled, but many organizations add a behavioral API layer or gateway for extra BEC and impersonation depth; test against your real threat mix.

What proves email-security value?

Successful-phish rate per user trending down and faster automated remediation of malicious messages that land not raw block counts.

Verdict

Ten solutions, one test: catch rate against the payload-less attacks that now cause breaches.

Proofpoint benchmarks the enterprise program, Microsoft defends natively at scale, Mimecast adds resilience, and Abnormal catches the social engineering gateways miss run finalists on live mail, weight BEC and remediation, layer native plus behavioral, and let a falling successful-phish rate renew the contract.
