cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Buying a scanner is easy; running one well is a job nobody has time for credentialed scans that don’t break production, results triaged so the team sees the ten findings that matter instead of ten thousand, and false positives filtered before they erode trust.

Managed vulnerability scanning rents that discipline. The services below separate on triage quality, false-positive rate, and whether findings arrive as owned tickets with SLAs or as a raw export. Qualys takes 1; Tenable and Rapid7 complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Qualys the platform-scale managed-scanning benchmark.

• Podium: Qualys, Tenable (coverage-depth heritage), Rapid7 (managed-plus-detection reach).

• Model split: platform-vendor managed services (Qualys, Tenable, Rapid7) versus MDR-adjacent providers (Arctic Wolf, Secureworks) versus specialist scanning services (Outpost24, Intruder, Edgescan).

• 2026 theme: triage over volume the deliverable is a short, owned, false-positive-filtered list, not a scanner dump.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: scan coverage and accuracy, triage and false-positive filtering, SLA and findings delivery, remediation guidance, asset and cloud breadth, and pricing clarity.

Weights: triage/false-positive quality 25%, coverage/accuracy 25%, SLA/delivery 20%, remediation guidance 15%, breadth 15%.

The 2026 Managed Vulnerability Scanning Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Qualys — Best Platform-Scale Managed Benchmark

Snapshot: Platform + managed add-on | Cloud-scale scanning on the Qualys estate | Triage + SLA delivery

Why it earns 1: Qualys pairs its proven cloud-scale scanning platform with managed delivery credentialed and agent-based scans across the estate, triage that filters noise, and findings routed with business context.

For organizations wanting scanning run at platform scale with the vendor behind it, it sets the benchmark.

Pros: Platform scale; triage quality; broad asset/cloud coverage.

Cons: Value tracks scope; confirm managed-tier packaging.

Bottom line: Managed scanning at platform scale.

2. Tenable — Best Coverage-Depth Heritage

Snapshot: Platform + managed | Nessus-lineage coverage depth | Exposure-management context

Why it ranks here: Tenable brings the deepest scanning heritage Nessus-lineage vulnerability coverage delivered with managed triage and exposure-management context that prioritizes what matters.

For organizations that weight detection coverage and accuracy, it’s the depth pick.

Pros: Coverage depth; accuracy heritage; exposure context.

Cons: Confirm managed-service scope versus self-run.

Bottom line: The deepest coverage, managed.

3. Rapid7 — Best Managed-Plus-Detection Reach

Snapshot: Platform + MDR | Scanning tied to detection and response | Managed delivery

Why it ranks here: Rapid7 delivers managed scanning connected to its broader detection-and-response platform, so vulnerability findings and threat detection share one operating picture.

For organizations wanting scanning inside a wider managed-security relationship, it’s the reach pick.

Pros: Scan-detection linkage; platform context; managed delivery.

Cons: Pure-scanning specialization versus the focused services.

Bottom line: Scanning wired to detection.

4. Arctic Wolf — Best Concierge-Managed Delivery

Snapshot: Concierge subscription | Managed scanning within the concierge model | Named team

Why it ranks here: Arctic Wolf delivers managed vulnerability scanning through its concierge security-operations model, pairing scans with a named team that triages and guides remediation.

For organizations wanting a managed relationship over a tool, it’s the concierge pick.

Pros: Concierge delivery; named-team continuity; guided remediation.

Cons: Tool-level configurability versus platform vendors.

Bottom line: Scanning inside the concierge model.

5. Secureworks — Best Threat-Intel-Informed Triage

Snapshot: Managed services | Triage informed by Counter Threat Unit | Prioritization focus

Why it ranks here: Secureworks triages scan results through its threat-intelligence lens, so prioritization reflects what adversaries are actually exploiting, not just CVSS. For organizations wanting intel-informed prioritization, it’s the triage pick.

Pros: Intel-informed triage; exploit-aware prioritization; managed delivery.

Cons: Confirm current services scope/ownership.

Bottom line: Triage shaped by threat intel.

6. Outpost24 — Best Full-Stack Scanning Breadth

Snapshot: Platform + managed | Network, web, cloud, and application scanning | Managed delivery

Why it ranks here: Outpost24 covers the full scanning stack network, web application, cloud, and attack-surface with managed delivery and triage across them. For organizations wanting breadth across asset types under one managed service, it’s the full-stack pick.

Pros: Full-stack breadth; managed triage; attack-surface pairing.

Cons: Platform-scale economics versus the giants.

Bottom line: Managed scanning across the whole stack.

7. Intruder — Best SMB-Friendly Managed Scanning

Snapshot: Subscription tiers | Simplified continuous scanning | SMB/mid-market fit

Why it ranks here: Intruder delivers continuous, simplified vulnerability scanning with noise reduction and clear results aimed at smaller teams without a dedicated VM function. For SMB and mid-market organizations, it’s the accessible managed pick.

Pros: Simplicity; noise reduction; SMB economics.

Cons: Enterprise-scale depth versus the platforms.

Bottom line: Managed scanning for lean teams.

8. Edgescan — Best False-Positive-Free Accuracy

Snapshot: Subscription | Human-validated findings | Low false-positive focus

Why it ranks here: Edgescan blends automated scanning with human validation so findings arrive verified, targeting a near-zero false-positive rate that keeps developer trust intact. For organizations where false-positive fatigue killed the last program, it’s the accuracy pick.

Pros: Human-validated accuracy; low false positives; clear findings.

Cons: Raw scale versus the platform vendors.

Bottom line: Findings you can trust without re-checking.

9. Fortra (Digital Defense) — Best Appliance-Plus-Service Lane

Snapshot: Appliance + managed | Frontline VM (Digital Defense lineage) | Managed delivery

Why it ranks here: Fortra’s Digital Defense lineage pairs vulnerability-management technology with managed delivery, suiting organizations wanting an appliance-plus-service model within the Fortra portfolio.

For Fortra-aligned estates, it’s the appliance-service pick; confirm packaging.

Pros: Appliance+service model; managed delivery; portfolio integration.

Cons: Confirm current packaging under Fortra.

Bottom line: Managed scanning, Fortra-backed.

Cons: Pure-scanning depth versus the focused platforms.

Yes/No Capability Table

Every service can run a scanner; what you’re actually buying is the triage layer that turns ten thousand raw findings into the short, owned, exploit-prioritized list your team will act on so pilot finalists on your real estate and measure the false-positive rate and how findings arrive.

Demand credentialed scanning that won’t break production and confirm the cadence, because an uncredentialed quarterly scan misses most of what matters.

Decide your model: platform vendors (Qualys, Tenable, Rapid7) give scale and integration, concierge providers (Arctic Wolf) give a named team, and accuracy specialists (Edgescan) give human-validated findings for teams burned by false positives.

Insist findings land as owned tickets with SLAs and remediation guidance, not a PDF export, and settle how scanning connects to your broader program.

Track the metric that justifies renewal: mean-time-to-remediate for critical findings trending down, and false positives staying low enough that developers keep trusting the queue. Feed results into your vulnerability management and RBVM programs.

FAQs

What are the best managed vulnerability scanning services in 2026?

Qualys as the platform-scale benchmark, Tenable for coverage depth, Rapid7 for managed-plus-detection, Arctic Wolf for concierge delivery, Edgescan for accuracy, with Secureworks, Outpost24, Intruder, Fortra, and BreachLock by model.

Why use a managed service over running a scanner yourself?

The hard part isn’t scanning, it’s credentialed configuration, triage, false-positive filtering, and routing findings to owners with SLAs managed services rent that discipline so results get acted on.

What matters most in managed scanning?

Triage quality and false-positive rate a short, trusted, exploit-prioritized list drives fixes, while a noisy export erodes developer trust and gets ignored.

Managed scanning or managed vulnerability management?

Scanning finds and triages; full VM adds lifecycle, prioritization, and remediation tracking several of these providers span both. Match the scope to your maturity.

What proves managed-scanning value?

Mean-time-to-remediate for critical findings trending down, with false positives low enough that developers keep trusting the queue.

Verdict

Ten services, one deciding layer: the triage that turns scanner noise into a list worth acting on.

Qualys and Tenable bring platform scale and coverage depth, Rapid7 wires it to detection, Arctic Wolf gives a named team, and Edgescan validates every finding by hand pilot on your estate, measure the false-positive rate, demand owned tickets with SLAs, and let falling time-to-remediate renew the contract.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A penetration test asks “what’s vulnerable?” A red team asks a harder question: “if a real adversary targeted you, would you detect and stop them before they reached the crown jewels?” These engagements emulate specific threat actors end to end initial access through lateral movement to objective and the deliverable isn’t a vulnerability list, it’s a measured verdict on your detection and response.

The firms below separate on threat-actor realism and the value of the purple-team debrief. Mandiant takes 1; CrowdStrike and Bishop Fox complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Google (Mandiant) the incident-informed adversary-emulation benchmark.

• Podium: Mandiant, CrowdStrike (telemetry-grounded emulation), Bishop Fox (offensive-research craft).

• Model split: intel/IR-led emulation (Mandiant, CrowdStrike, Secureworks) versus offensive-research red teams (Bishop Fox, NCC, SpecterOps) versus program-delivery firms (IBM, Coalfire, Trustwave).

• 2026 theme: detection value the best engagements are graded on what your blue team caught, not just what the red team achieved.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: threat-actor emulation realism, threat-intelligence grounding, detection-and-response measurement, purple-team debrief quality, scope (physical, social, cyber), and senior-operator depth.

Weights: emulation realism 25%, detection measurement 25%, intel grounding 20%, debrief quality 15%, operator depth 15%.

The 2026 Red Team Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Google (Mandiant) — Best Incident-Informed Emulation

Snapshot: Scoped engagements | Emulation drawn from frontline breach response | Named threat-actor TTPs

Why it earns 1: Mandiant within Google emulates the exact threat actors it chases in real incidents, so a red-team engagement reproduces the TTPs your likely adversaries actually use, graded against whether your controls detect them.

For organizations wanting the most authentic adversary in a controlled exercise, it sets the benchmark.

Pros: Frontline-IR realism; named-actor emulation; detection grading.

Cons: Premium; demand-driven scheduling.

Bottom line: The adversary emulation drawn from real breaches.

2. CrowdStrike — Best Telemetry-Grounded Emulation

Snapshot: Services | Emulation informed by Falcon threat telemetry | Detection-focused

Why it ranks here: CrowdStrike grounds red-team work in its vast threat telemetry and intel, emulating adversaries with current tradecraft and measuring whether Falcon-era detections fire.

For estates wanting emulation tied to live threat tracking and detection validation, it’s the telemetry pick.

Pros: Telemetry-grounded tradecraft; detection validation; intel currency.

Cons: Fullest value alongside the CrowdStrike estate.

Bottom line: Emulation graded by detection.

3. Bishop Fox — Best Offensive-Research Craft

Snapshot: Scoped engagements | Offensive-research reputation | Creative adversary simulation

Why it ranks here: Bishop Fox brings recognized offensive-research craft to red teaming creative initial access, stealthy movement, and objective-focused operations that stress detection in ways signature-driven tests don’t.

For teams wanting inventive adversary simulation, it’s the craft pick.

Pros: Offensive-research creativity; stealth operations; objective focus.

For organizations wanting full-scope adversary emulation from a research-grade firm, it’s the breadth pick.

Pros: Full-scope emulation; research depth; hard-target capability.

Cons: Premium; scope the specialists.

Bottom line: Full-scope adversary emulation.

Why it ranks here: IBM’s X-Force Red delivers adversary simulation within IBM’s enterprise machine, suiting large accounts that want red teaming inside a broader program relationship and global delivery. For enterprise-scale engagements, it’s the program-delivery pick.

Pros: Enterprise delivery; X-Force Red operators; global reach.

Cons: Boutique agility versus the specialists.

Bottom line: Adversary simulation at IBM scale.

6. SpecterOps — Best Identity-Centric Adversary Sim

Snapshot: Scoped engagements | Identity/AD attack expertise | Detection-engineering focus

Why it ranks here: SpecterOps brings deep identity and Active Directory attack expertise the BloodHound lineage to red teaming, emulating the identity-centric movement real adversaries favor and helping blue teams build detections for it.

For identity-heavy estates, it’s the identity-sim pick.

Pros: Identity/AD attack depth; detection-engineering value; research pedigree.

Cons: Full physical/social scope versus the generalists.

Cons: Confirm current services scope/ownership.

Cons: Bleeding-edge offensive research versus the boutiques.

Demand senior operators by name, because red teaming lives or dies on the people, and make the purple-team debrief where red and blue walk the timeline together a contractual deliverable, since that’s where detection actually improves.

Run emulations against a recognized framework like MITRE ATT&CK so coverage is measurable, and track the metric that justifies the spend: detection coverage across ATT&CK techniques rising, and dwell time in the exercise falling.

Feed findings into your SIEM and detection engineering programs.

FAQs

What are the best red team services in 2026?

Mandiant as the IR-informed benchmark, CrowdStrike for telemetry-grounded emulation, Bishop Fox for offensive craft, NCC Group for full scope, SpecterOps for identity, with IBM X-Force, Secureworks, Coalfire, Unit 42, and Trustwave by model.

How is a red team different from a pentest?

A pentest enumerates and exploits vulnerabilities in a defined scope; a red team emulates a specific adversary end to end and measures whether your detection and response would stop them.

What is purple teaming?

A collaborative debrief where the red team walks the blue team through the attack timeline stage by stage, so defenders build detections for exactly what was missed the highest-value part of the engagement.

Which threat actors should be emulated?

The ones actually likely to target your sector and geography; intel- and IR-led firms map that from real campaigns rather than generic playbooks.

What proves red-team value?

Rising detection coverage across ATT&CK techniques and falling dwell time in the exercise not whether the red team reached the objective, which they usually will.

Verdict

Ten providers, one honest question: would you notice? Mandiant and CrowdStrike emulate the real adversary and grade your detection, Bishop Fox and NCC bring offensive craft and full scope, and SpecterOps stresses the identity paths attackers love scope the right actors, demand named senior operators, make the purple-team debrief contractual, and let rising ATT&CK detection coverage renew the engagement.

The post Top 10 Best Penetration Testing as a Service (PTaaS) Platforms in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The annual pentest was built for a world that shipped software once a year. PTaaS fits the world that ships weekly: a platform that delivers human testing on demand, pipes findings into the tools developers already live in, and retests fixes in days instead of next year’s engagement.

The platforms below separate on tester quality, retest speed, and how little friction they add to the dev workflow. Cobalt takes 1; Synack and HackerOne complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Cobalt the platform-plus-tester-pod benchmark.

• Podium: Cobalt, Synack (vetted-crowd assurance), HackerOne (researcher-scale platform).

• Model split: pod/platform PTaaS (Cobalt, NetSPI, BreachLock) versus crowd-platform (Synack, HackerOne, Bugcrowd, Intigriti) versus automation-blended (Pentera).

• 2026 theme: retest latency the metric that separates real PTaaS from a portal over a traditional engagement.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Criteria: tester quality and vetting, retest speed, platform/dev-workflow integration, scope breadth, real-time findings delivery, and pricing clarity.

Weights: tester quality 25%, retest speed 20%, dev-workflow integration 20%, scope breadth 20%, findings delivery 15%.

The 2026 PTaaS Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Cobalt — Best Pod-Plus-Platform Benchmark

Snapshot: Subscription + credits | Vetted tester pods on a managed platform | Fast retest, dev integrations

Why it earns 1: Cobalt defined modern PTaaS: a managed platform that spins up a vetted tester pod on demand, delivers findings in real time to Jira and Slack, and retests fixes in days, not next year.

The balance of human tester quality and platform speed sets the category benchmark.

Pros: Tester-pod quality; fast retest; strong dev integrations.

Cons: Scope the right pod skills in.

Bottom line: The PTaaS benchmark the category measures against.

2. Synack — Best Vetted-Crowd Assurance

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Vetted researcher crowd on a controlled platform | Continuous coverage

Why it ranks here: Synack delivers crowd breadth under enterprise governance a rigorously vetted researcher network testing through a controlled platform, with continuous assessment and the auditability regulated buyers need.

For assurance at crowd scale, it’s the governance-first pick.

Pros: Vetted-crowd breadth; platform governance; continuous coverage.

Cons: Bespoke pod continuity versus Cobalt-style engagements.

Bottom line: Crowd scale with enterprise control.

3. HackerOne — Best Researcher-Scale Platform

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Largest researcher community | PTaaS + bug bounty

Why it ranks here: HackerOne brings the largest researcher community to a platform spanning PTaaS and bug bounty, so coverage scales and findings flow into developer workflows.

For organizations wanting researcher reach and a bounty on-ramp, it’s the scale platform.

Pros: Researcher scale; PTaaS+bounty breadth; workflow integration.

Cons: Structured-engagement rigor versus pod models.

Bottom line: Researcher scale on one platform.

4. Bugcrowd — Best Crowd-Program Breadth

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Managed crowd programs | PTaaS + VDP + bounty

Why it ranks here: Bugcrowd runs managed crowd programs across PTaaS, bug bounty, and vulnerability disclosure, with triage that keeps signal high. For organizations wanting a managed crowd across multiple program types, it’s the breadth pick.

Pros: Program breadth; managed triage; crowd depth.

Cons: Confirm PTaaS-specific scoping versus bounty.

Bottom line: The managed crowd across program types.

5. Praetorian — Best Enterprise-Depth Offensive Security Testing

Snapshot: Platform + services | Expert-led manual penetration testing | Enterprise-grade offensive security

Why it ranks here: Praetorian combines experienced offensive security consultants with broad penetration testing expertise across applications, cloud environments, APIs, networks, and emerging technologies.

Its approach is suited to enterprises seeking deep, tailored security assessments rather than only automated testing.

For organizations wanting hands-on offensive security expertise with enterprise-scale coverage, it’s the enterprise-depth pick.

Pros: Deep manual testing; broad attack-surface coverage; enterprise-focused expertise; tailored assessments.

Cons: Premium pricing; more consultant-led than fully automated testing platforms.

Bottom line: Expert-led offensive security for enterprise environments.

6. BreachLock — Best Value-Scale PTaaS

Snapshot: Subscription tiers | Human + AI-assisted testing at value economics | Fast delivery

Why it ranks here: BreachLock blends human testing with automation to deliver PTaaS at accessible economics and quick turnaround, suiting mid-market teams needing frequent tests without enterprise pricing.

For value-scale coverage, it’s the budget-conscious pick.

Pros: Value economics; fast delivery; human+automation blend.

Cons: Bespoke depth versus the enterprise specialists.

Bottom line: PTaaS at value scale.

7. Intigriti — Best European Crowd Platform

Snapshot: Platform subscription | European-rooted researcher crowd | PTaaS + bounty

Why it ranks here: Intigriti brings a strong European researcher community and data-residency posture to a PTaaS and bounty platform, suiting organizations with EU compliance and regional-testing needs.

For Europe-centric programs, it’s the regional-crowd pick.

Pros: European crowd; residency posture; PTaaS+bounty.

Cons: Global scale versus the largest platforms.

Bottom line: The European crowd platform.

8. Pentera — Best Automation-Blended Validation

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Automated security validation | Continuous testing

Why it ranks here scoped honestly: Pentera automates adversarial validation safely exploiting the estate continuously to prove what’s exploitable rather than orchestrating human testers.

Ranked here as the automation-blended complement to human PTaaS, strongest where continuous machine validation is the need.

Pros: Automated validation; continuous coverage; exploit proof.

Cons: Human-tester creativity sits with the crowd/pod models.

Bottom line: Continuous validation by machine.

9. Sprocket Security — Best Continuous-Retest Lane

Snapshot: Subscription | Continuous human pentesting | Fast retest focus

Why it ranks here: Sprocket centers continuous human penetration testing with an emphasis on ongoing coverage and quick retests, suiting teams that want a steady testing cadence rather than annual engagements.

For continuous-cadence testing, it’s the retest-lane pick.

Pros: Continuous cadence; retest focus; human testing.

Cons: Crowd/enterprise scale versus the leaders.

Bottom line: The steady-cadence testing lane.

10. HackenProof — Best Crowdsourced Vulnerability Discovery

Snapshot: Crowdsourced platform | Ethical hacker community | Bug bounty and vulnerability discovery

Why it ranks here: HackenProof connects organizations with ethical hackers to identify vulnerabilities through crowdsourced security testing and bug bounty programs.

Its community-driven model offers diverse testing perspectives and continuous vulnerability discovery beyond traditional scheduled penetration tests.

For organizations wanting broader researcher participation and ongoing vulnerability discovery, it’s the crowdsourced testing pick.

Pros: Global ethical hacker community; crowdsourced testing; flexible bug bounty programs; diverse testing coverage.

Cons: Findings depend on researcher participation; results may vary by program scope and engagement activity.

Bottom line: Community-driven vulnerability discovery at scale.

Buying Advice: Measure Retest Latency, Not Portal Polish

The thing that separates real PTaaS from a traditional pentest with a web portal is retest latency how fast a fixed finding gets re-verified so make finalists prove it on your real flaws and measure the days from fix to verified-closed.

Judge tester quality honestly: a slick platform over weak testers finds less than great testers with no platform, so read sample findings and confirm the vetting.

Decide your model: pod-based PTaaS (Cobalt, NetSPI) gives you consistent named testers, crowd platforms (Synack, HackerOne, Bugcrowd, Intigriti) give breadth, and automation (Pentera) gives continuous machine validation many programs pair a crowd for breadth with a pod for depth.

Insist on real-time findings piped into developer tooling, not a PDF at the end, and route fixes with SLAs. Track the metric that justifies renewal: time-to-retest trending down and repeat findings not recurring.

Feed results into your vulnerability management and application security programs.

FAQs

What are the best PTaaS platforms in 2026?

Cobalt as the pod-plus-platform benchmark, Synack and HackerOne for crowd scale, Bugcrowd for program breadth, NetSPI for enterprise depth, with BreachLock, Intigriti, Pentera, Sprocket, and Hackrate by model.

How is PTaaS different from a traditional pentest?

PTaaS delivers human testing on demand through a platform with real-time findings and fast retests, fitting continuous-deploy teams, where a traditional pentest is a point-in-time engagement with a final report.

Pod or crowd PTaaS?

Pod models give consistent named testers and depth; crowd models give breadth and varied perspectives many programs run both, a crowd for breadth and a pod for bespoke depth.

What metric matters most?

Retest latency how fast a fixed finding is re-verified plus tester quality; a fast portal over weak testers isn’t real assurance.

Does PTaaS replace pentest firms?

For continuous coverage as code ships, largely yes; for deep bespoke scope and compliance milestones, traditional engagements still matter see our pentest-companies ranking.

Verdict

Ten platforms, one differentiator: how fast a fix gets re-verified by testers you can trust.

Cobalt benchmarks the pod-plus-platform balance, Synack and HackerOne bring governed crowd scale, NetSPI delivers consultancy depth, and Pentera automates continuous validation measure retest latency on your real flaws, vet the testers, pipe findings into dev tooling, and let falling time-to-retest renew the contract.

articles.title: Remus Stealer Silently Installs Fake Google Sheets Extension to Steal Gmail Messages
articles.description:
Remus Stealer is silently installing a fake Google Sheets extension in Google Chrome to steal Gmail messages from signed-in users. The extension runs in the background on compromised Windows computers, reading new emails and sending their contents to an attacker-controlled server. Despite claims by the malware’s developers, researchers found no evidence that the feature exploits […]

The post Remus Stealer Silently Installs Fake Google Sheets Extension to Steal Gmail Messages appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Remus Stealer is silently installing a fake Google Sheets extension in Google Chrome to steal Gmail messages from signed-in users.

The extension runs in the background on compromised Windows computers, reading new emails and sending their contents to an attacker-controlled server.

Despite claims by the malware’s developers, researchers found no evidence that the feature exploits a Gmail zero-day. It relies on the victim already being signed in.

The developers began promoting the feature on underground forums on November 8, 2026, claiming it could keep reading mail after victims changed their passwords and revoked their sessions.

The distinction matters: unlike Chrome session cookie theft, the Gmail module does not need to copy a session cookie for use elsewhere. It reads mail from inside the browser where the user is already authenticated.

Researchers Vojtěch Krejsa and Jan Rubín of Gen Threat Labs, part of Gen Digital, identified the component behind the claim. Their November 24 technical analysis found that Remus downloads the email interception module after the main malware starts.

The module appeared in only some of the builds researchers examined, so a Remus infection does not necessarily mean the Gmail extension was installed.

Remus Stealer Silently Installs Fake Google Sheets Extension

The module is a 64-bit Windows DLL that carries the extension in a ZIP archive. Gen Digital found that it alters local Chrome profile settings to register the add-on and turn on Developer Mode.

The installation leaves two visible clues on Chrome’s extensions page: a new Google Sheets card marked as unpacked, meaning it was loaded from local files, and a Developer Mode switch that may have been turned on without the user’s knowledge.

The disguise borrows the description of the legitimate Google Docs Offline extension. In a separate analysis of the extension, Invoke RE identified the fake add-on as version 0.5.4 and found no spreadsheet interface.

Although the extension requests permission to access all websites, the email collection behavior documented by both teams targets Gmail. Broad permissions show what an extension could access, not what researchers confirmed it stole.

Once active, the extension checks for unread mail roughly once a minute across up to ten account slots in the same browser session. That means both personal and work accounts could be exposed if they are signed in to the affected Chrome profile.

Activities of extension

The polling differs from the Kimsuky Gmail extension campaign, where a malicious add-on watched for messages as users read or sent them. Remus does not need the victim to open each unread message.

Gen Digital found that the extension sends the sender, subject, message body, victim’s email address, and a campaign identifier to its operator.

Although the code identifies attachment filenames while processing messages, the researchers did not see it send those names or the files themselves.

That still leaves sensitive material at risk: a message body can contain a password reset link, a sign-in code, or details from a private work conversation.

Revoking Gmail sessions stops collection until the user signs in again. If the extension is still installed, it can use the new session, making the theft look as though it survived a password reset.

The PEEP malicious extension case illustrates the same cleanup problem: changing credentials does not remove malicious software from the browser.

Responders should isolate the affected computer, investigate the underlying Remus infection, and revoke sessions and change affected passwords from a clean device before signing back in.

articles.title: Vinci RAT Linked to Microsoft Store Raises Risk of Hackers Remotely Controlling Windows PCs
articles.description:
A Windows user searching for a screenshot tool was redirected to a fake download site and given a Microsoft-signed installer. But instead of installing the Snipping Tool, the installer led to a Microsoft Store app called Setup Assistant. That app opened a backdoor and delivered Vinci RAT, a remote access trojan that can run commands, […]

The post Vinci RAT Linked to Microsoft Store Raises Risk of Hackers Remotely Controlling Windows PCs appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Windows user searching for a screenshot tool was redirected to a fake download site and given a Microsoft-signed installer. But instead of installing the Snipping Tool, the installer led to a Microsoft Store app called Setup Assistant.

That app opened a backdoor and delivered Vinci RAT, a remote access trojan that can run commands, place files on an infected PC, and launch additional malware.

The case stands out because the fake download page did not merely imitate the Microsoft Store. The installation chain led to a real listing published by ETPS Ltd.

That separates it from the fake Microsoft Store pages used in the separate AgtaBackup RAT campaign, where attackers copied the storefront’s appearance. In the Vinci case, reaching the genuine store did not mean the app was safe.

Analysts from eSentire’s Threat Response Unit identified Vinci RAT while investigating an intrusion in early November 2026.

In their November 24 technical report, they said they isolated the affected computer and helped the customer respond. The report documents that intrusion, but it does not establish how many other Windows PCs were infected.

Vinci RAT Linked to Microsoft Store

The first download was Snipping-Tool.exe, a signed installer served by a site posing as a screenshot utility. The file directed the user to Setup Assistant, an app built with Electron, a framework used for desktop software.

The lure fits a broader pattern of fake Windows software downloads that reach people while they are actively looking for a familiar program.

Once installed, Setup Assistant contacted a command-and-control server, or C2, which let the operators send instructions to the app.

It monitored the Downloads folder for specific filenames, including MSTeamsSetup.exe and Readerinstall.exe, and could run PowerShell or JavaScript supplied by the server.

In the investigated intrusion, that access was used to launch a PowerShell loader that retrieved Vinci RAT from a separate domain.

The loader also created a Windows scheduled task that ran every 10 minutes. That gave the malware a way to return without the user reopening Setup Assistant.

The abuse of Windows scheduled task persistence is particularly useful to defenders here: a newly registered task running hidden or encoded PowerShell is more suspicious when it appears shortly after an unexpected app installation.

Vinci RAT gathered the computer name, username, Windows version, and details about installed security tools. It also supported a reverse shell, which lets the infected PC connect out and gives the operator an interactive command prompt.

Malware could run Windows executables

The malware could run Windows executables, DLLs, and PowerShell scripts, with some payloads running directly in memory. Those capabilities describe what the malware could do, not proof that every feature was used in the incident.

The package metadata indicated a June 1, 2026 release, suggesting Setup Assistant may have been available for about five months before the investigation.

eSentire said Microsoft initially replied that the app did not violate its terms after researchers reported it through the Store’s abuse form. The report does not establish whether Microsoft later removed the listing.

For security teams, the strongest lead is the sequence of events: an unexpected Store app, PowerShell activity, a recurring scheduled task, and outbound connections to the reported domains.

If that pattern appears, isolate the device and check endpoint, DNS, and proxy logs to see whether other PCs show the same activity.

For prevention, eSentire recommends restricting Store installs on managed Windows devices through tools such as Intune, AppLocker, or Windows Defender Application Control, and reviewing unfamiliar apps before approving them.

articles.title: Microsoft Declares Code Red After Historic 24-Hour Outage Disrupts Outlook, Teams and Copilot
articles.description:
Microsoft has declared an internal “Code Red” after a nearly 24-hour Microsoft 365 outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Exchange Online on November 12 and 13, 2026. Reuters reported that the company is making it a top priority to prevent major service failures and recover faster when they happen. CEO Satya Nadella publicly apologized. Microsoft […]

The post Microsoft Declares Code Red After Historic 24-Hour Outage Disrupts Outlook, Teams and Copilot appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has declared an internal “Code Red” after a nearly 24-hour Microsoft 365 outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Exchange Online on November 12 and 13, 2026.

Reuters reported that the company is making it a top priority to prevent major service failures and recover faster when they happen. CEO Satya Nadella publicly apologized. Microsoft said neither a cyberattack nor AI agents caused the outage.

Jason Henderson, president of Microsoft 365 Core, told staff that no previous Exchange Online outage had left so many customers without email for so long.

As Cyber Security News reported in its initial Microsoft 365 outage coverage, Microsoft first investigated mailbox access problems in the Americas before warning that users in any region could be affected. The disruption also reached SharePoint and Microsoft Defender XDR.

Windows Defect Took Down Microsoft 365

Microsoft traced the failure to a Windows defect introduced in July on servers that handle incoming connections to Microsoft 365. As our breakdown of Microsoft’s incident report explains, the defect affected Microsoft’s cloud gateways, not ordinary Windows installations.

Internal tasks competed for shared resources until the servers ran short of processing power and memory. Tests missed the problem because it was worse on newer servers with more processor cores.

About 15 hours before the outage, Teams traffic moved to the main gateway it shared with Exchange Online. Nearly 14% of gateway capacity was already unavailable because of a separate issue. As servers stopped responding, automated recovery shifted connections to healthy machines, putting them under the same pressure.

At the worst point, more than 80% of the gateway servers became unresponsive. Exchange Online could not move enough traffic to alternate routes to keep mailboxes available.

Engineers restored an earlier way of handling connections, restarted groups of servers, and gradually brought traffic back. Microsoft also extended the email delivery timeout to 48 hours so messages waiting in queues would have more time to reach recipients rather than being returned as undeliverable.

Microsoft Sets a one-hour Recovery Target

The outage exposed a coordination problem as well as a technical one. Microsoft corporate vice president Amanda Silver told staff that engineers exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats while diagnostic data remained scattered across separate systems. That made it harder for responders to track what colleagues had checked, suspected, and decided to do.

Microsoft plans to limit incoming requests when servers are overloaded and separate traffic by region so failures are less likely to spread. It also plans to use AI agents to help engineers review diagnostic data.

The company aims to restore service worldwide within an hour during future incidents. It is an internal target, not a customer guarantee.

The outage disrupted government operations, delayed trading firms and affected airline communications. The UK Parliament’s debate on the outage put the wider risk in focus: separate apps can still depend on the same infrastructure.

Administrators reviewing their response can look up MO1550821 for the broader outage and EX1550543 for mailbox access in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Microsoft’s public service status page offers another place to check when the admin center is unavailable.

For incident response teams, the practical test is whether staff can reach one another and share updates when Outlook and Teams go down at the same time.

articles.title: CIA and ODNI Reportedly Suffer Cyberattack Exposing Unclassified U.S. Intelligence Information
articles.description:
The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) recently discovered a cyberattack that exposed some unclassified U.S. intelligence information. The intrusion affected a shared network used to analyze publicly available material. The New York Times first reported the breach on November 24, citing U.S. officials and other people […]

The post CIA and ODNI Reportedly Suffer Cyberattack Exposing Unclassified U.S. Intelligence Information appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) recently discovered a cyberattack that exposed some unclassified U.S. intelligence information.

The intrusion affected a shared network used to analyze publicly available material. The New York Times first reported the breach on November 24, citing U.S. officials and other people familiar with the incident.

ODNI told CNN that there had been “no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems.” Officials familiar with the incident said no classified information was affected.

That does not mean the unclassified network stayed online without interruption. A CIA official told the Washington Examiner that the affected network was disrupted and that the issue had been resolved.

The full scope remains unclear. The Times also reported that the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was affected, citing two people familiar with the matter.

Public reports have not identified the specific files or records exposed, how the intruders gained access, or how long they were inside. U.S. officials have not publicly named a person, group, or government responsible.

Intelligence Network Targeted

The system supported open-source intelligence, or OSINT. The CIA and ODNI define this as intelligence drawn from public or commercially available information to answer specific questions.

Their joint 2024–2026 open-source intelligence strategy calls for agencies to coordinate how they acquire that data, share it more widely across the intelligence community, and improve the tools analysts use to make sense of it.

The distinction between open sources and an open system matters. A news report or commercial database may be available outside government, but a shared workspace can show which sources analysts trust, which events they track, and what they have concluded. Those examples show why an unclassified analysis system can be sensitive, not what was exposed in this breach.

A separate incident illustrates the difference. In July 2025, Cyber Security News covered the breach of a contracting portal used by the CIA and other agencies. The unclassified portal, run by the National Reconnaissance Office, held information submitted by vendors supporting intelligence programs.

It was a different system, but the case showed why a platform’s classification alone does not tell readers how sensitive its records may be.

No link established to FBI or USDA incidents

The disclosure follows reports of a possible breach involving the FBI’s National Crime Information Center, a database used by federal, state, and local law enforcement.

That the intelligence breach did not appear linked to that case. The database incident is also distinct from the FBI wiretap and surveillance network incident covered in March.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture also discovered a cybersecurity incident that led it to take some internal applications offline. No public evidence has tied that incident to the CIA and ODNI breach. The timing puts federal network security under scrutiny, but it does not show that the incidents had a common attacker or entry point.

For the intelligence breach, the key unanswered question is whether the intruders reached only source material or also accessed internal analysis and records showing what agencies were studying.

Restoring the network and determining what was viewed or copied are separate tasks. Officials have addressed the disruption, but the public account does not yet establish the full extent of the exposure.

articles.title: McDonald’s Japan Confirms Data Breach – Customer Information and Location Data Exposed
articles.description:
McDonald’s Japan has confirmed that a third party gained unauthorized access to customer information stored in the database behind its official mobile app. In a November 20, 2026, breach notice, the company said the affected records included product purchase histories, internal customer management IDs, IP addresses, and location data from mobile devices used when it […]

The post McDonald’s Japan Confirms Data Breach – Customer Information and Location Data Exposed appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
McDonald’s Japan has confirmed that a third party gained unauthorized access to customer information stored in the database behind its official mobile app.

In a November 20, 2026, breach notice, the company said the affected records included product purchase histories, internal customer management IDs, IP addresses, and location data from mobile devices used when it provided services. McDonald’s Japan said it had not confirmed any unauthorized use of the app or its services as a result of the incident.

The company said the affected data did not include names, email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses, or credit card information registered in the app. It also said the internal customer management ID is different from the membership ID customers use for the app.

The internal ID alone cannot identify a customer. McDonald’s Japan did not disclose how many customers were affected, when the unauthorized access began, or whether the third party copied any records.

McDonald’s Japan Data Breach

The company’s notice concerns access to a database, not the takeover of customer accounts. It also does not link the breach to the unusual McDonald’s iOS app notifications reported days earlier.

That report described unexpected push alerts, while the Japanese disclosure identifies specific types of customer data that a third party accessed. The two reports do not establish a common cause.

Location data can raise privacy concerns even when records do not contain names. As Cyber Security News explains in its guide to location data privacy, access to device location records can reveal more than a single point on a map.

If multiple readings are linked to the same identifier and include precise times and places, they can show where a device regularly goes. That is a possible risk, not a finding about this breach.

McDonald’s Japan did not say how precise the location readings were, whether they included timestamps, or how much history the affected records covered. Nor did it say whether purchase histories could be matched to individual location readings.

The notice describes location information from devices used when services were provided. It does not establish that the database held a continuous record of customers’ movements or that anyone could track them in real time.

As Japanese technology outlet ASCII reported, McDonald’s Japan said it was working to disable the credentials used in the unauthorized access, investigate related systems, and report the incident to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission.

The company has not disclosed what kind of credentials were used or how the third party obtained them. Its work to disable those credentials is separate from its advice to customers about their own passwords.

McDonald’s Japan said customers do not need to change their passwords or take any other special action at this time. It apologized and said it would update the notice as new information became available.

For customers trying to understand their exposure, three questions remain: how many people were affected, how detailed the location records were, and whether anyone took a copy.

Until the company provides more information, the confirmed finding is unauthorized access to some customer records, not confirmed misuse of customer accounts or the app’s services.

articles.title: Critical VMware ESX Flaws Let Remote Attackers Execute Malicious Code on Virtualization Hosts
articles.description:
Broadcom has disclosed 23 VMware vulnerabilities, including two critical flaws that could let attackers run code directly on ESX hosts and a third that could let them access vCenter without signing in. The Broadcom security advisory, VMSA-2026-0011, was published on November 24. It says the flaws were privately reported and does not report active exploitation. […]

The post Critical VMware ESX Flaws Let Remote Attackers Execute Malicious Code on Virtualization Hosts appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Broadcom has disclosed 23 VMware vulnerabilities, including two critical flaws that could let attackers run code directly on ESX hosts and a third that could let them access vCenter without signing in.

The Broadcom security advisory, VMSA-2026-0011, was published on November 24. It says the flaws were privately reported and does not report active exploitation.

The advisory covers VMware vCenter, ESX, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools, and Avi Load Balancer. It also lists VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, Telco Cloud Platform, and Telco Cloud Infrastructure.

Administrators who run those platforms should check the versions of the VMware components they use, rather than relying on the platform name alone.

VMware ESX Host Vulnerabilities

The vCenter flaw, CVE-2026-123903, has a severity score of 9.8 out of 10 and affects VMware Directory Service. An attacker with network access to vCenter could bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access without valid credentials.

That matters because vCenter gives administrators a single place to manage multiple ESX hosts and their virtual machines. Broadcom lists no workaround. Its technical FAQ says turning off Enhanced Linked Mode does not remove the risk.

The flaw is separate from CVE-2026-123890, the vCenter authentication bypass disclosed on November 19. The new advisory also covers three flaws that can disrupt VMware Directory Service.

Another vCenter flaw, CVE-2026-123904, could let someone with access to the backup repository write files with root privileges when vCenter processes certain archives. That could lead to code execution on the appliance.

CVE-2026-123910 and CVE-2026-123911 each score 9.8. Both affect the ESX input/output filter service and could let an attacker who can reach an affected host over the network run code on it.

Neither requires the attacker to first gain access to a virtual machine. That sets them apart from earlier VMware vulnerabilities that required access inside a guest.

A separate virtual USB controller flaw, CVE-2026-123912, does require administrator access inside a virtual machine. It scores 9.3 on Workstation and Fusion, where it could let an attacker run code on the underlying computer.

On ESX, Broadcom says code execution is limited to the sandbox that isolates the virtual machine’s host process.

Fixed Versions

Broadcom lists vCenter 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300, and 8.0 U3m as fixed releases. If you already installed vCenter 8.0 U3m for the earlier advisory, you do not need to reinstall it. Check ESX separately.

The advisory lists ESXi-9.1.2.0-25946735 and ESXi80U3m-25926933 as fixed builds. For ESX 9.0, check the live response matrix before scheduling the update. The initial table marks patches as pending, while the FAQ references an express patch.

Workstation and Fusion users should install 26H1u1. Broadcom recommends Avi Load Balancer 32.1.4 to address all eight Avi flaws. VMware Tools must be updated inside affected virtual machines.

The fixed versions are 13.1.10.0 for the 13.x branch and 12.5.6.0 for the 11.x and 12.x branches. Linux users should check their distribution for open-vm-tools updates.

Prioritize vCenter and ESX systems reachable from untrusted networks. A vCenter update briefly interrupts management access but does not stop running workloads.

The ESX update requires a host restart and does not support Live Patch. Move virtual machines to another host where possible and schedule downtime for workloads that cannot move.

articles.title: Hackers Deploy ZQAgent Backdoor to Run Malicious Commands and Access Files on Linux Servers
articles.description:
A new Linux backdoor called ZQAgent is giving attackers a long-term foothold on compromised servers. It can run commands, move through folders, read files and open network tunnels. It also hides itself to look like a normal system process. The malware was dropped by ARTEX, an AI-driven hacking framework. Most ARTEX intrusions are quick smash-and-grab […]

The post Hackers Deploy ZQAgent Backdoor to Run Malicious Commands and Access Files on Linux Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new Linux backdoor called ZQAgent is giving attackers a long-term foothold on compromised servers.

It can run commands, move through folders, read files and open network tunnels. It also hides itself to look like a normal system process.

The malware was dropped by ARTEX, an AI-driven hacking framework. Most ARTEX intrusions are quick smash-and-grab jobs that steal passwords and leave.

This case is different, because the operator wanted to stay inside the network for a long time. Analysts at NVISO noted the malware during a recent incident response job in Belgium. They also found similar samples reported from Taiwan.

The team said the use of a lasting backdoor is likely the result of instructions from a human operator, not a choice made by the AI tool alone.

Hackers Deploy ZQAgent Backdoor

NVISO found the first sample in /tmp/zqa/systemd-timesyncd, a name picked to look like a normal time service. All known samples talk to the same command servers, the IP address 37.122.150[.]15 and the domain bloonspace[.]com.

NVISO links this setup to a cluster it tracks as FOG0003. Network data from Team Cymru suggests the group used ZQAgent in Asia against government and human-rights groups.

Once it starts, ZQAgent moves itself into a temporary file held only in memory. This makes the process show up as /memfd:a (deleted).

The backdoor then restarts as a detached process that copies the name and command line of the real dbus-daemon tool. A quick look at the process list would show nothing odd.

The malware also protects its own settings. The configuration stays encrypted and is only opened for a moment when needed. Traffic to the command server uses several layers of encryption, including ChaCha20 variants.

The feature list is wide. ZQAgent uses numbered operation codes for each task. These let the operator:-

  • change folders and list their contents
  • move, rename, delete or create files and directories
  • read the first 2048 bytes of any file
  • check the current user and view or kill any process
  • start commands through /bin/sh -c
  • open a full shell through /bin/bash, or /bin/sh if Bash is missing
  • manage TCP and UDP connections

It can even run a program straight from memory. This approach is not new for Linux malware. The Vmcloudoor Linux cloud backdoor uses a similar trick of posing as a trusted agent so admins leave it alone.

Persistence and What Defenders Should Do

ZQAgent survives reboots in two ways. It installs a systemd service and a cron job, and it changes file timestamps on everything it creates, which makes cleanup harder.

A root user gets the binary copied under /usr/lib/systemd/, with the service file in /etc/systemd/system/. Other users get the copy in $HOME/.local/share/, with the service in $HOME/.config/systemd/user/.

If the HOME variable is not set, the malware falls back to /tmp/.local/share/. The service uses the description “Device event journal daemon” and restarts every 30 seconds if stopped.

For normal users, ZQAgent runs loginctl enable-linger so it keeps running after the user logs out. The cron entry uses an @reboot line that runs the file quietly with all output sent to /dev/null.

Linux backdoors that hide in memory and copy trusted names are becoming common. The BPFDoor and Symbiote rootkits also use stealth to stay on servers for long periods. ZQAgent shows that AI-driven tools can now drop this kind of long-term access too.

NVISO warns that LLM-driven tools could soon speed up ransomware and spying. They may cut the time between break-in and ransom from hours to minutes.

The researchers say companies should harden their network edges, split networks into segments, collect security data from every asset, and react faster. They also say automatic isolation of infected systems deserves another look.

Defenders can start with a few checks. Look for the odd dbus-daemon command line and for processes tied to deleted memory files. Search for the “Device event journal daemon” service and unknown cron entries.

Block the listed IP and domain. NVISO also published YARA rules for the backdoor, its service file and its cron job.

For more background on the tool behind this activity, see the report on ARTEX automates enterprise attacks, and the case of a jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent shows how fast these tools can work.

articles.title: Critical ASP.NET AntiCsrf Flaw Exploited in Attacks by triggering a web redirect on vulnerable apps
articles.description:
Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-131914, a critical flaw in Idunno: AntiCsrf, an old third-party library used by ASP.NET WebForms applications. watchTowr Intel reports that it saw attackers trigger web redirects on vulnerable applications to check whether exploitation worked. The flaw allows attackers to run code on an affected server without signing in. ASP.NET AntiCsrf Flaw The […]

The post Critical ASP.NET AntiCsrf Flaw Exploited in Attacks by triggering a web redirect on vulnerable apps appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-131914, a critical flaw in Idunno: AntiCsrf, an old third-party library used by ASP.NET WebForms applications.

watchTowr Intel reports that it saw attackers trigger web redirects on vulnerable applications to check whether exploitation worked. The flaw allows attackers to run code on an affected server without signing in.

ASP.NET AntiCsrf Flaw

The report follows Mandiant’s November 18 disclosure of active exploitation. As Cyber Security News previously reported, the flaw carries a CVSS 4.0 severity score of 9.3 out of 10.

The National Vulnerability Database lists versions through 0.9.1 Beta, including DLL version 0.9.1.0, as affected. The issue is in the optional library, not ASP.NET WebForms itself.

The redirect let attackers check the result, not the weakness that let them run code. A redirect alone does not prove a server was compromised because web applications also redirect visitors during normal use. watchTowr’s public report did not name the affected organizations, disclose the redirect destinations, or say what attackers did after the probes.

Idunno.AntiCsrf was built to prevent cross-site request forgery, where a site tricks a signed-in browser into sending an unwanted request. The flaw lies in how the library reads a security token.

It reconstructs .NET objects from untrusted data before checking whether the token is valid, a weakness known as insecure deserialization. Code that runs through the flaw inherits the permissions of the IIS worker process (w3wp).

No fixed release is listed, so teams should check deployed applications for Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll and review web.config for references to the module.

Prioritize internet-facing applications. Replace the library with a maintained CSRF defense and test that forms still reject requests without valid tokens. If replacement cannot happen immediately, restrict access to the affected application while the work is underway.

For exposed applications, preserve IIS and reverse proxy logs and compare unexpected redirects with endpoint alerts, new files, or unusual processes started by w3wp.exe.

Earlier reporting on attacks against IIS servers covered a separate route involving exposed ASP.NET machine keys. That distinction matters here: rotating keys does not remove the vulnerable library, and removing the library does not tell defenders whether attackers already ran code.

articles.description:
Hackers are still running EvilTokens phishing campaigns to take over Microsoft 365 accounts, even though Microsoft shut the service down on September 22, 2026. London’s Metropolitan Police had arrested two men in connection with the kit eleven days earlier. New phishing hosts kept appearing through October and November anyway. EvilTokens is a phishing-as-a-service kit that […]

The post Hackers Continue EvilTokens Phishing After Microsoft Takedown to Hijack Microsoft 365 Accounts appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are still running EvilTokens phishing campaigns to take over Microsoft 365 accounts, even though Microsoft shut the service down on September 22, 2026.

London’s Metropolitan Police had arrested two men in connection with the kit eleven days earlier. New phishing hosts kept appearing through October and November anyway.

EvilTokens is a phishing-as-a-service kit that was sold on Telegram. Microsoft tracks its developer and support operator as Storm-2992.

The kit was linked to more than 12,000 compromised inboxes across over 10,000 organizations, and it first appeared in a new phishing-as-a-service platform report earlier this year.

It does not fake a login page. It abuses the OAuth device code flow, so victims type a real code on Microsoft’s real sign-in page.

Researchers at VMRay noted the leftover activity in a report published on November 24, 2026. Their hunt began with one indicator from the VMRay UniqueSignal threat feed, dated August 25, 2026. That single lead opened the door to many more hosts.

Hackers Continue EvilTokens Phishing

The kit works by asking Microsoft for a short device code that stays valid for 15 minutes. The phishing page shows that code, often dressed up as an Adobe, DocuSign, OneDrive or SharePoint document, and tells the victim to enter it at microsoft.com/devicelogin.

The attacker’s backend keeps polling Microsoft, and once the victim approves, it receives an access token and a refresh token. This is why the usual advice to check the URL fails.

VMRay’s monthly chart shows how the activity faded but did not stop. Confirmed hosts peaked at 237 in March and 200 in April. The chart then shows four hosts in the last days of September and 25 in October, after the takedown.

A lure page scanned on October 28 was still generating live device codes. Many new hosts now sit on Bunny CDN instead of Workers.dev, although the device code calls still route to a Workers.dev host behind the scenes.

VMRay also warns that some legitimate domains may be compromised and reused to serve the kit. The danger does not end at the sign-in. Microsoft says stolen tokens are used to read email, create hidden inbox rules and register new devices for lasting access.

The kit’s AI features also help pick scam targets by reading the victim’s mailbox and drafting business email compromise messages.

To find the leftover hosts, VMRay searched urlscan for two backend paths unique to the kit, /api/device/start and a /status/ polling call. A second pivot used an odd X-Antibot-Token header, which led to more hosts through FOFA.

Each candidate was then checked in VirusTotal, urlscan and passive DNS before it counted as EvilTokens. The team then grouped the hosts into clusters. One cluster of four hosts pointed to the same e-signing link and used French business names with “portail” in the hostname.

A second cluster used throwaway email domains, dropoffs.org and dropons.com, to register Cloudflare accounts that hosted OneDrive-style lures.

Token theft is already hurting companies, and stolen login tokens helped criminals break into hijacked accounts at 79 organizations in a separate Huntress case.

How Defenders Can Block Device Code Phishing

The best fix is to turn the device code flow off. In Microsoft Entra ID, admins can build a Conditional Access policy under Conditions > Authentication Flows that blocks device code flow for all users and all resources.

Microsoft advises running the policy in report-only mode first to spot legitimate use, then switching it on. Break-glass accounts should be excluded so admins cannot lock themselves out.

Teams that cannot block the flow should filter their Entra sign-in logs for the authentication protocol Device Code. Any sign-in that nobody set up on purpose deserves a look.

The same check works in Microsoft Sentinel with a SigninLogs query that filters AuthenticationProtocol to deviceCode and ResultType to 0. Other groups use the same trick, as a Microsoft 365 device code campaign reported this month showed.

If a suspicious approval turns up, revoke the user’s sessions and refresh tokens and remove any device the account registered. Microsoft has seen operators register a new device within 10 minutes of stealing a token.

Standard session revocation can leave access tokens working for up to an hour, so Microsoft suggests disabling the account for a while instead of relying on a password reset alone. Defenders should also block the indicators below at the web proxy and DNS layer.

articles.title: Hackers Bypass Alpine Linux SSH Authentication Using Just a 257-Byte Password
articles.description:
A flaw in OpenSSH lets remote attackers sign in to certain Alpine Linux accounts without knowing a valid password or holding an SSH key. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 and known as SSHole, affects unpatched servers that use the musl C library, run without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM), and allow SSH password logins. OpenSSH released […]

The post Hackers Bypass Alpine Linux SSH Authentication Using Just a 257-Byte Password appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A flaw in OpenSSH lets remote attackers sign in to certain Alpine Linux accounts without knowing a valid password or holding an SSH key.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 and known as SSHole, affects unpatched servers that use the musl C library, run without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM), and allow SSH password logins. OpenSSH released a fix on November 5, and Alpine shipped patched packages the same day.

Hackers Bypass Alpine Linux SSH Authentication

According to IOTSEC Forum, the 257-byte figure comes from a November 23 lab report. A researcher showed that an unpatched OpenSSH build on Alpine Linux 3.24 accepted a password login for an account with no usable password.

The patched Alpine package rejected the login. The lab result is separate from Cyber Security News’ earlier reporting on active exploitation.

OpenSSH normally checks a password by comparing its hash, a one-way representation of the password, with the value stored for the account. On affected systems, musl’s crypt() function can return an error marker instead of a hash.

That marker can look identical to the stored value that tells Linux an account has no usable password. The unpatched server treated the match as a successful login. It did not recover or guess anyone’s password.

The fix blocks that false match by rejecting stored values that are too short to be valid password hashes. It also changes how OpenSSH copies account data so a later lookup cannot overwrite the value being checked. The OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes credit Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield with reporting the flaw.

An Alpine base image alone does not make a system vulnerable. The risk is on hosts and containers running an affected SSH server with password authentication enabled and the account conditions described in the Alpine Linux security advisory. Containers that do not run sshd and servers that use PAM for authentication are outside this attack path.

Alpine also flagged older tiny-cloud images, covered in our initial OpenSSH bypass report. Those images shipped with an alpine user that could gain root privileges through doas without a password.

Alpine said the images were not exposed on first boot, but later account changes could make them vulnerable. Blocking direct root login does not protect a separate account that can become root.

Check the installed server package revision, not just the upstream version shown in an SSH banner. The first fixed Alpine packages include 10.3_p1-r2 for 3.24, 10.2_p1-r1 for 3.23, and 10.0_p1-r11 for 3.22.

After upgrading, restart the running server with rc-service sshd restart. If patching must wait, verify that key-based access works, set PasswordAuthentication no, and restart sshd. Keep the current session open until a fresh login succeeds.

On exposed systems, review /var/log/messages for Accepted password entries involving accounts meant to use SSH keys only. Compare each event with the account’s settings at the time. Review doas activity and look for newly created users, unfamiliar files, or changes to authorized_keys. A failed login followed by a success is not proof of exploitation.

A password login to an account that should never accept one warrants immediate investigation. Alpine advises treating the system as compromised if you cannot rule out unauthorized access.

articles.title: Hackers Bypass MFA Through Phone Scams to Access Microsoft 365, OneDrive and SharePoint Data
articles.description:
Cybercriminals posing as corporate IT support are calling employees and tricking them into handing over access to Microsoft 365 accounts, even when multifactor authentication (MFA) is enabled. The attackers have used compromised accounts to steal email and files from OneDrive and SharePoint, then contacted employees through Microsoft Teams or email to demand payment. The calls […]

The post Hackers Bypass MFA Through Phone Scams to Access Microsoft 365, OneDrive and SharePoint Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cybercriminals posing as corporate IT support are calling employees and tricking them into handing over access to Microsoft 365 accounts, even when multifactor authentication (MFA) is enabled.

The attackers have used compromised accounts to steal email and files from OneDrive and SharePoint, then contacted employees through Microsoft Teams or email to demand payment.

The calls are a form of voice phishing, or vishing. The caller claims an account setting needs attention and directs the employee to a fake sign-in page made to look like a company portal.

As earlier reporting on Microsoft 365 session theft explains, a successful MFA prompt does not guarantee that the person who approved it is the only one who can use the resulting session.

Researchers at Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 identified malware in a related investigation: a browser extension masquerading as Google Chrome.

The team found it while investigating an activity cluster it calls Helix. The extension was not available through the Chrome Web Store, and Unit 42 did not find evidence that other Com-affiliated groups used it.

Hackers Bypass MFA Through Phone Scams

Unit 42 identified two activity clusters, Vortex and Cinder, in September 2026. Vortex primarily targeted healthcare, pharmaceutical and other medical organizations.

Its callers posed as internal IT support and directed employees to sign-in pages tailored to their employer. The pages acted as a relay between the employee and the real login service, allowing the attackers to intercept authentication information as the employee signed in.

The approach, known as adversary-in-the-middle phishing, does not require the attackers to crack MFA. Instead, the victim completes authentication and the attacker takes advantage of the authenticated session.

Related reporting on passkey-themed Microsoft 365 phishing shows how a supposed security update can make an unexpected call sound like routine IT work. Vortex targeted employees on both corporate computers and personal phones.

Within minutes of signing in, Vortex operators enrolled an unauthorized MFA device. Unit 42 saw a device named Pixel 10a reused across multiple compromised accounts.

The attackers then used scripts to collect Microsoft 365 mailbox, OneDrive and SharePoint data. The device enrollment gave them a way to maintain access beyond the original sign-in.

Cinder took a different route. Unit 42 found that it reused a persistent “keep me signed in” session token without triggering another Duo MFA prompt.

The group used Microsoft Graph, an interface for accessing Microsoft cloud services, to collect SharePoint and OneDrive files.

The findings echo earlier coverage of UNC6671 cloud data theft, where automated collection followed employee session hijacking. Cinder later used a compromised account to send extortion messages by email and Teams.

What Security Teams Should Look For

In the Helix investigation, Unit 42 found that the fake Chrome extension could log keystrokes, steal authentication cookies, read clipboard contents and capture screenshots.

Researchers identified two versions, 1.6.111 and 1.6.112, that communicated with the same remote server. An organization investigating a suspicious call should therefore check browser extensions as well as cloud sign-ins, particularly if an employee recalls being asked to install software.

The timing of events can be more useful than any single alert. Microsoft’s cloud compromise research describes unusual sign-ins followed by new authentication methods, heavy Microsoft Graph activity and bursts of file downloads.

A phone model or software identifier may be legitimate on its own. An unexpected enrollment followed by bulk downloads from the same account deserves closer scrutiny.

Organizations should require employees to verify unexpected support calls through a help desk number they already know. Unit 42 recommends phishing-resistant MFA, tighter help desk verification, browser extension allowlists and alerts for unauthorized exports.

Earlier coverage of Microsoft Entra passkey enrollment highlights why enrollment itself needs protection: a strong sign-in method does not help if the attacker persuades an employee to register it on the attacker’s behalf.

When a takeover is suspected, responders should revoke active sessions, remove unauthorized authentication methods and review mailbox, OneDrive and SharePoint audit records to determine what the account accessed.

Check outbound email and Teams messages as well: both featured in the extortion activity, and a message sent from a real employee account can look trustworthy to colleagues.

In its November 20 alert, the agency confirmed all four flaws were exploited and gave federal civilian agencies until November 23 to patch […]

The post CISA Warns of VMware vCenter, SAP NetWeaver, Cisco Expressway, and Apache Roller Flaws Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added four vulnerabilities affecting VMware vCenter, SAP NetWeaver, Cisco Expressway, and Apache Roller to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on November 20, 2026.

In its November 20 alert, the agency confirmed all four flaws were exploited and gave federal civilian agencies until November 23 to patch them, noting that their impact varies.

Three carry a critical severity score of 9.8, while the SAP flaw is rated 6.5. Its inclusion shows why security teams should weigh evidence of real attacks alongside severity scores when deciding which systems to patch first.

VMware vCenter Server flaw CVE-2026-123890 affects the VMware Directory Service. An attacker who can reach a vulnerable vCenter server over the network can bypass its login checks and gain unauthorized access.

Because vCenter manages multiple virtual hosts, a breach can put more than one system at risk. Broadcom released fixes on November 19.

As Cyber Security News reported in its VMware vCenter zero-day coverage, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant traced attacks to early September, before a patch was available.

CVE-2026-76466 affects Cisco Expressway-C and E clusters, allowing unauthenticated root command execution through hardcoded credentials. Cisco patched the flaw in October 2026 before CISA added it to its catalog.

Apache Roller, an open-source blogging platform, fixed CVE-2026-129448, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw caused by processing untrusted data before authentication, in version 6.1.5.

SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal flaw CVE-2025-42884 can let an attacker without an account redirect a Java lookup and potentially read or change server information.

SAP addressed the issue in its November 2025 security updates under Security Note 3660969. This is separate from the SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer zero-day that CISA listed in April 2025.

CISA’s Binding Operational Directive 26-04 guidance tells federal civilian agencies to prioritize fixes for internet-facing systems when a known exploited flaw can give attackers full control.

The directive also requires agencies to check for signs of earlier breaches and encourages other organizations to use CISA’s KEV catalog to prioritize patches.

Administrators should confirm which versions they run, check which systems are reachable from the internet, and apply the fixes listed in vendor advisories.

For systems that were exposed before patching, security teams should preserve and review available logs for unusual sign-ins, new accounts, or unexpected changes. Installing an update closes the flaw, but it does not tell defenders whether someone used it before the fix went in.
