articles.title: Critical Google Chrome Flaw Could Let Hackers Execute Malicious Code Outside Browser Sandbox
articles.description:
Google released a desktop Chrome security update on November 23, 2026, to fix CVE-2026-134401. This critical flaw could let a remote attacker run malicious code outside the browser sandbox. The Stable update covers Windows, macOS, and Linux. It contains one security fix, and Google says the rollout will take place over the coming days and […]

The post Critical Google Chrome Flaw Could Let Hackers Execute Malicious Code Outside Browser Sandbox appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google released a desktop Chrome security update on November 23, 2026, to fix CVE-2026-134401. This critical flaw could let a remote attacker run malicious code outside the browser sandbox.

The Stable update covers Windows, macOS, and Linux. It contains one security fix, and Google says the rollout will take place over the coming days and weeks.

The update follows the initial Chrome 158 release, which fixed 204 security flaws. Users who installed that earlier release still need the new update. The full build number matters: the National Vulnerability Database lists Chrome versions before 158.0.8127.88 as affected.

Critical Google Chrome Flaw

Google traced the flaw to improper input validation in Variations, a Chrome component that lets the company test changes with groups of users before a wider rollout.

Input validation is the process of checking that data meets expected rules before software uses it. Google reported the issue internally on August 28, 2026, and rated it critical.

The sandbox limits what code handling web content can access on a device. The [National Vulnerability Database record] says a specially crafted HTML page could let a remote attacker run code outside that boundary. Our earlier coverage of a separate Chrome sandbox escape flaw gives readers more context on why that boundary matters.

Google’s release notes do not indicate that the flaw has been exploited in attacks. Additionally, the public record does not clarify whether successful exploitation would grant administrator access. Running code outside the sandbox is a serious issue, but it does not, on its own, prove that an attacker could gain full control of the device.

Google is rolling out Chrome version 158.0.8127.88 or 158.0.8127.89 for Windows and macOS, and 158.0.8127.88 for Linux. To check for updates, open the Chrome menu, select Help, and click on About Google Chrome. After the update installs, select Relaunch. Reopen the About page to ensure that Chrome is running the updated version.

Note that an update downloaded in the background does not protect a browser session that hasn’t been restarted. For IT teams, the currently running version is a more reliable reference than whether the update was offered.

After Chrome restarts, verify the full build number on managed devices, and check again on devices that are still waiting for the staged rollout.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Suzlon Energy disclosed a cyber incident on November 23, 2026. It said it had seen no impact on its business-critical applications at the time of reporting.

In a filing with India’s stock exchanges, the wind turbine maker said it took immediate steps to limit the impact, activated its incident response procedures, and notified the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In).

Suzlon Energy Cyberattack

According to Economic Times, the company did not say when it first detected the incident, how it began or which systems were affected. It also did not say whether anyone accessed or stole customer or employee data.

Suzlon urged stakeholders to avoid speculation. Its statement covers the business applications it relies on. However, it does not separately address the status of turbine controls, remote monitoring systems or power generation.

That distinction matters in the energy sector. Business applications support company workflows, while operational technology, or OT, monitors and controls physical equipment such as wind turbines.

As our coverage of CISA’s guide to tracking industrial equipment explains, keeping an accurate record of these systems helps operators identify what could be affected during an incident. Suzlon has not said whether the incident reached its industrial networks.

Separately, India’s Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has tightened cybersecurity requirements for approved wind turbine manufacturers.

An August ministry notice asked manufacturers to show that they store turbine data in India, keep operational control within the country and prevent live operational data from being sent abroad. The rules predate Suzlon’s disclosure. Our reporting on internet-exposed solar equipment shows why securing connected devices matters across renewable energy.

A separate case involving cyberattacks on Polish wind and solar farms illustrates why operators track communications and generation separately.

In that incident, some facilities lost communications with the distribution network operator, but electricity generation continued. That case is not linked to Suzlon. It shows how one part of an energy network can be disrupted while another keeps working.

For energy operators, guidance on isolating critical systems recommends identifying where business and industrial networks connect and testing whether essential equipment can keep running if those links are cut.

Those are general safeguards, not steps Suzlon said it took. The company’s filing leaves three questions open: which systems were affected, whether any data was exposed, and whether industrial networks were involved.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Anthropic has launched Claude Ship in beta, letting Claude Code review GitHub pull requests, push fixes, and approve changes when a team’s policy allows it.

A pull request, or PR, proposes merging code changes. Claude’s approval does not merge the code by itself. The repository’s permissions and branch rules still determine whether a change can go through.

How Claude Ship reviews and fixes code

Claude Ship combines Anthropic’s Code Review service with two beta tools: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. Code Review checks the proposed changes against the wider codebase and posts its findings on the pull request.

Teams can choose Quick, Standard, or Deep reviews for each repository. Unlike Claude Security’s continuous repository scans, this review starts with the changes a developer wants to merge.

PR Steward can address reviewer feedback, resolve merge conflicts, and work on failed build or test checks. After each push, it explains what changed and how to undo it.

It cannot approve or merge a pull request. To try the workflow, developers can update Claude Code and run /ship in the terminal or desktop app. That extends Claude Code beyond its earlier security guidance during editing into the review process itself.

Claude Approvals uses a policy file stored in the repository. Teams can let Claude sign off on routine changes while routing sensitive changes to a human reviewer. Anthropic recommends starting in observe-only mode so teams can see what Claude would approve before making its decision a required check. GitHub’s branch protection rules can still require code owner approval and passing tests.

A short change is not always low risk. A few lines in an access control rule can change who sees private data. Earlier reports on prompt injection in GitHub comments and security risks in GitHub Actions workflows do not establish flaws in Claude Ship. They do illustrate why teams should keep human review for changes to permissions, approval policies, and build workflows.

Claude Team and Enterprise admins can enable Claude Ship for an entire repository, so developers do not need to run /ship on each pull request.

Admins can set spending limits for Code Review and PR Steward. Tokens bill usage, while /ship counts toward regular Claude Code usage. Organizations using Zero Data Retention, Anthropic’s HIPAA configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys are not eligible.

articles.description:
A vulnerability in the Windows Remote Access API lets an attacker with limited access to a computer run code with SYSTEM privileges. Microsoft fixed CVE-2026-119853 on November 10 as part of its November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates. The company rated the flaw Important and assigned it a CVSS base score of 7.8. Updates cover affected […]

The post Windows Remote Access API Flaw Could Let Hackers Gain Full SYSTEM Control of PCs appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A vulnerability in the Windows Remote Access API lets an attacker with limited access to a computer run code with SYSTEM privileges. Microsoft fixed CVE-2026-119853 on November 10 as part of its November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates.

The company rated the flaw Important and assigned it a CVSS base score of 7.8. Updates cover affected releases of Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server.

Despite the component’s name, this does not allow an attacker to break into a Windows machine over the internet. An attacker must already be able to run code on the affected device, but does not need administrator rights or help from another user.

The flaw matters after that first foothold, code running as SYSTEM can reach protected files and change settings that a standard user cannot.

Windows Remote Access API Flaw

Windows Remote Access Service, or RAS, manages connections such as VPNs. It stores connection settings in profiles and supports software libraries that customize how connections are handled.

Microsoft classifies the flaw as an untrusted search path, meaning a privileged Windows component can load code from a location an attacker can influence. The security failure is not that a user can change their own connection settings. It is that Windows can end up running user-controlled code with the service’s permissions.

In its November 23 write-up, Core Security reported seeing a Windows service host load a researcher-controlled dynamic-link library, or DLL, under the SYSTEM account. The researchers reported confirming the result on Windows 11 Pro 25H2, build 26200.9711, without a live VPN or internet connection.

That finding reinforces the difference between the feature involved and the access an attacker needs. For comparison, PhantomRPC is a separate Windows privilege escalation issue involving a different failure at a service boundary.

Microsoft said it had not observed exploitation when it first published the advisory, although it rated exploitation “More Likely.” A research demonstration shows that the flaw can be exploited under test conditions.

It does not establish that attackers have used it against real systems. That distinction also separates this case from the claims surrounding the Windows SignDrop disclosure.

Administrators should install the applicable November security update or a later cumulative update that includes the fix. The Microsoft security advisory lists update packages and build numbers by Windows release.

For example, Microsoft lists KB5131096 for Windows 10 22H2, bringing it to build 19045.7846, and KB5131090 for Windows Server 2022, bringing it to build 20348.5870. Use Windows release health to check the installed build against that version’s update history. Do not treat changes to VPN profiles as a substitute for patching.

While updates roll out, security teams can review endpoint logs for Windows service hosts loading unexpected DLLs from locations ordinary users can write to. Where that activity appears, check the library’s path and signature, then review any processes the service host started around the same time.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft disclosed a critical Microsoft 365 Copilot vulnerability that could let an attacker with limited privileges gain higher permissions over a network without any action from another user.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-50691, was released on November 19, 2026, and received a CVSS 3.1 base score of 9.9 out of 10. Microsoft says customers do not need to take any action to resolve it.

Microsoft 365 Copilot Flaw

The distinction is that no user interaction does not mean no initial access. The attacker needs some permissions before exploiting the flaw, but does not need another user to click a link, open a file, or approve a request. That separates this issue from SearchLeak, a one-click Microsoft 365 Copilot flaw that Cyber Security News covered in June.

Microsoft classified the weakness as improper authorization, or CWE-285. Authorization is the check that decides what someone can do after the service knows who they are. When that check is missing or applied incorrectly, a user can gain access to a resource or action that their existing permissions should block.

Microsoft’s assessment describes a network-reachable flaw with low attack complexity. It also rates the potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability as high.

In plain terms, a successful attack could put protected data, its accuracy, and access to affected resources at risk. The score also reflects a change in scope, meaning the impact could extend beyond the security boundary of the affected component. These ratings describe potential impact, not confirmed customer harm.

Microsoft’s assessment listed the flaw as not exploited at publication. The Microsoft Security Response Center advisory says no customer action is required, so administrators do not need to install a local update for this CVE.

This flaw is separate from EchoLeak, an earlier Copilot issue that could expose information without user interaction and did not require an attacker to have prior access. Here, the reported impact is higher privileges for an attacker who already has limited access.

The update does not eliminate the necessity of reviewing existing permissions. Microsoft’s Copilot security guidance advises checking SharePoint sites for files shared too broadly and restricting access to only those who need it. This review addresses a separate risk: even if Copilot enforces permissions accurately, it can still make files easier to find for users who already have more access than intended.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-134624, carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3. N-able’s November 22 security advisory identifies build 20261121.1943 as the fix and lists all […]

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
N-able has patched a critical vulnerability in MailAssure, also known as SpamExperts, that lets an attacker with privileged API access reach internal network services through the email security platform.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-134624, carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3. N-able’s November 22 security advisory identifies build 20261121.1943 as the fix and lists all earlier builds as affected.

N-able Mail Assure SSRF Vulnerability

The disclosure follows a November 16 service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of the N-able server breach, the company confirmed unauthorized access to one hosted server and disabled management access while it responded.

Dashboard and API access returned late on November 21. The advisory does not establish how the attacker first gained access to the hosted environment.

The flaw affects a connection check that MailAssure runs for LDAP synchronization when a mail relay is configured. As N-able’s LDAP mailbox sync guide explains, LDAP, short for Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, lets MailAssure query an organization’s directory and keep its mailbox and alias lists up to date. The problem was not with LDAP itself. MailAssure failed to limit where its server could connect during the check.

That makes the flaw a server-side request forgery, or SSRF, classified as CWE-918. A user with the required API privileges can make the MailAssure server connect to internal hosts and ports, learn which services are reachable, and send specially prepared data to them. The distinction matters: internal services do not need to be exposed to the internet for the MailAssure server to reach them.

The risk is similar to that described in Cyber Security News’ coverage of the Zimbra SSRF vulnerability: a trusted server can reach systems that an outside user cannot contact directly. In this case, the severity rating specifies that high privileges are required, but no other user needs to take action. N-able’s advisory describes internal network access, not remote code execution.

Organizations running MailAssure or SpamExperts should verify that their service is on build 20261121.1943 or later. Customers who cannot check the build themselves should ask their provider to confirm that the fix is in place. The National Vulnerability Database entry records the flaw, which CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 23.

Administrators should review who holds privileged API credentials and check available logs for unexpected relay changes or connections from MailAssure to systems outside its normal directory setup. The patch closes the vulnerable connection check, but it cannot show whether someone misused it beforehand. Hosted customers without access to those logs may need help from their provider.

The post AI-Powered Hackers Gain Access to 3,392 User Accounts and Decrypt 50 SSH Private Keys appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An attacker using the CyberStrikeAI framework gained access to 3,392 user accounts and their active session tokens during a four-day cloud intrusion in October 2026.

The operator also decrypted a bastion host’s database to recover 50 SSH private keys. The activity spanned two Amazon Web Services (AWS) accounts and seven Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) clusters, according to a November 23 disclosure.

The scale became clear only after investigators compared the victim’s security logs with more than 3,000 files left exposed on the attacker’s server.

The logs showed activity inside AWS and Kubernetes, while the exposed files revealed what happened in the identity system and on other hosts.

A separate investigation into exposed ARTEX operator servers showed how similar mistakes have helped researchers reconstruct AI-assisted attacks.

Researchers at Wiz identified a custom rootkit, malware designed to hide and maintain access, on compromised Kubernetes nodes. It masqueraded as a font configuration service and used DNS traffic to communicate.

The sample had zero detections on VirusTotal at the time Wiz examined it, but the public report did not disclose a file hash that defenders could use to identify it.

AI-Powered Hackers Gain Access to 3,392 User Accounts

The intruder entered with a stolen session tied to a Terraform runner, a service used to manage cloud infrastructure. That access led to elevated Kubernetes privileges.

Wiz also documented a compromise of the Jenkins build controller and the use of stolen cloud credentials from the attacker’s own server. Those credentials exposed infrastructure records and cloud secrets beyond the systems where they were originally issued.

The attacker’s files showed that forged administrator tokens opened access to the identity provider’s 3,392 users and their live session tokens.

The tokens matter because they can let someone act as an already signed-in user without knowing the password. The figure describes the accounts the attacker could access; the report does not say the operator individually signed in as all 3,392 users.

The operator decrypted the database of a bastion host, a controlled entry point for administrators connecting to private systems, and recovered 50 SSH private keys.

The files also showed that the attacker placed beacons, which can signal back to an operator, on 19 hosts. Wiz did not say that each recovered key was used or that the 50 keys corresponded to 50 separate machines.

The breach also reached the systems that build and deploy software. The attacker extracted GitHub Actions secrets and changed the production Jenkins configuration to run before its approval check, exposing production secrets.

Separate reporting on GitHub Actions credential theft shows why build systems are valuable targets: a single workflow can have access to credentials for several services.

Wiz also found that the operator collected Anthropic API keys from 50 hosts and searched employees’ AI coding-assistant histories for production sign-on credentials.

CyberStrikeAI as the framework

The original Wiz Research report identifies CyberStrikeAI as the framework that ran the operation. Investigators found a copy of ARTEX on the same server, but that does not make the intrusion part of the same campaign as the other attacks discussed in the report.

Wiz also noted csai-escape, csai-pentest-role, and csai-probe as names the operator left on resources in this case. Those strings can help narrow a search, but they are not unique fingerprints.

In a separate campaign, Wiz saw more than 220 proxy IPs used against a single target. That churn helps explain why FBI guidance on ARTEX is more useful alongside behavioral monitoring than as a reason to rely on static blocklists.

For defenders, the strongest leads are unusual administrative sessions, sudden spikes in secret retrieval, and cloud credentials used from unexpected locations. If the logs confirm exposure, invalidate affected sessions and replace the stolen SSH keys and other secrets.

Then review which systems still trust those keys, which build jobs can reach production, and whether any workloads gained privileges they did not need. A password reset alone does not address a stolen SSH key or a compromised build credential.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A scanner hands you ten thousand findings; an attacker needs one chain. Attack path management flips vulnerability lists into graphs showing how a phishing foothold reaches the domain admin through misconfigurations, excess permissions, and credential reuse no single CVE score captures then names the handful of choke points that break the most paths at once.

XM Cyber takes 1; SpecterOps and Palo Alto round out the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: XM Cyber the hybrid attack-path graph and choke-point benchmark.

• Podium: XM Cyber, SpecterOps (BloodHound identity-path depth), Palo Alto Networks (platform-integrated exposure).

• Model split: continuous graph platforms (XM Cyber, Cymulate) versus identity-path specialists (SpecterOps) versus platform modules (Palo Alto, CrowdStrike, Microsoft).

• 2026 theme: choke-point math the value isn’t listing paths, it’s ranking the few fixes that collapse the most.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Criteria: graph modeling depth (hybrid, identity, cloud), choke-point prioritization, continuous versus point-in-time, remediation guidance, integration breadth, and pricing clarity.

Weights: choke-point prioritization 25%, graph depth 25%, continuous coverage 20%, remediation guidance 15%, integrations 15%.

The 2026 Attack Path Management Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. XM Cyber — Best Hybrid Attack-Path Benchmark

Snapshot: Enterprise subscription | Hybrid on-prem + cloud + identity graph | Choke-point scoring

Why it earns 1: XM Cyber models the whole kill chain as one continuous graph on-prem, cloud, and identity together simulating how an attacker actually moves from any entry point to the crown jewels, then scoring the choke points that sever the most paths.

For teams drowning in findings that want the five fixes that matter, it sets the benchmark.

Pros: Hybrid graph breadth; choke-point prioritization; continuous modeling.

Cons: Enterprise positioning; value tracks estate complexity.

Bottom line: The attack-path graph the category measures against.

2. SpecterOps (BloodHound) — Best Identity-Path Depth

Snapshot: BloodHound Enterprise subscription | Active Directory/Entra attack paths | Identity-first graph

Why it ranks here: SpecterOps built the identity-attack-path reference: BloodHound maps the Active Directory and Entra relationships attackers abuse nested group membership, delegation, ACL chains and Enterprise turns that research tool into continuous, prioritized remediation. Where identity is the path, it’s the deepest lens.

Pros: AD/Entra path depth; research pedigree; prioritized identity fixes.

Cons: Identity-centered by design; pair for full hybrid.

Bottom line: The identity attack graph attackers already use.

3. Palo Alto Networks — Best Platform-Integrated Exposure

Snapshot: Cortex/platform module | Exposure paths inside the platform | Unified with security stack

Why it ranks here: Palo Alto folds attack-path and exposure analysis into its broader platform, correlating asset, vulnerability, and identity context already flowing through Cortex. For estates consolidating on Palo Alto, path analysis arrives inside the stack rather than as a separate graph.

Pros: Platform integration; shared context; consolidation economics.

Cons: Fullest value inside the Palo Alto estate.

Bottom line: Attack paths inside the Palo Alto platform.

4. CrowdStrike — Best Endpoint-Identity Path Lens

Snapshot: Falcon module | Endpoint + identity path correlation | Real-time telemetry

Why it ranks here: CrowdStrike draws attack paths from live Falcon telemetry endpoint and identity signals showing real exposure and reachable lateral movement, not just theoretical graph edges.

For endpoint-rich estates on Falcon, the paths come grounded in what’s actually observed.

Pros: Telemetry-grounded paths; endpoint+identity fusion; Falcon integration.

Cons: Network-model breadth versus the graph purists.

Bottom line: Attack paths drawn from live telemetry.

5. Cymulate — Best Validation-Linked Paths

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Attack paths joined to BAS validation | Exposure + proof

Why it ranks here: Cymulate pairs attack-path analysis with its breach-and-attack-simulation engine, so a theorized path comes with proof it’s actually traversable exposure analytics backed by safe exploitation.

For teams that want paths validated, not just modeled, the linkage is the draw.

Pros: Validation-backed paths; BAS integration; exposure analytics.

Cons: Confirm current attack-path packaging scope.

Bottom line: Paths proven, not just plotted.

6. Zscaler — Best Access-Layer Path Reduction

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Path reduction via zero-trust access | Lateral-movement limits

Why it ranks here — scoped honestly: Zscaler attacks the path problem from prevention: its zero-trust access and risk analytics shrink the lateral-movement surface so many paths never exist, with exposure analytics atop the fabric.

Less a standalone graph, more path reduction by architecture ranked as what it is.

Pros: Architectural path reduction; lateral-movement limits; fabric analytics.

Cons: Standalone graph depth sits with the specialists.

Bottom line: Fewer paths by zero-trust design.

7. Microsoft — Best Microsoft-Estate Path Native

Snapshot: Defender/Security Exposure Management | Native attack-path analysis | M365/Azure graph

Why it ranks here: Microsoft Security Exposure Management builds attack-path analysis natively across Defender, Entra, and Azure, mapping how an attacker traverses the Microsoft estate with context the stack already holds.

For Microsoft-centric organizations, the paths come without a new vendor.

Pros: Native M365/Azure paths; stack context; bundled reach.

Cons: Value concentrates in the Microsoft estate.

Bottom line: Attack paths native to the Microsoft stack.

8. Skybox Security — Best Network-Model Path Lane

Snapshot: Platform | Network-model attack paths | Firewall/rule context

Why it ranks here: Skybox models the network itself firewall rules, routing, and connectivity to compute which paths traffic can actually take and where a vulnerability is reachable.

The network-centric path lane for firewall-heavy estates; confirm current availability and packaging.

Pros: Network-model depth; rule/reachability context; policy analysis.

Cons: Confirm current product status and support.

Bottom line: Attack paths computed from the network model.

9. RedSeal — Best Network-Reachability Lane

Snapshot: Platform | Network reachability modeling | Access-path mapping

Why it ranks here: RedSeal maps network reachability which assets can reach which across the topology to show exposure and access paths, strong in segmented and regulated environments. The reachability-modeling lane for network-defense teams.

Pros: Reachability modeling; segmentation validation; compliance fit.

Cons: Identity/cloud path depth versus the hybrid leaders.

Bottom line: The network reachability map.

10. IONIX — Best External-to-Internal Path Lens

Snapshot: Platform subscription | External attack surface to exploitable path | Connected-asset discovery

Why it ranks here: IONIX enters from the outside, discovering the external attack surface and connected assets, then tracing which exposures open an exploitable path inward. The external-to-internal lens for teams whose first risk is the attacker-reachable edge.

Pros: External-surface discovery; path-to-exploit focus; connected-asset reach.

Cons: Internal hybrid-graph depth pairs with the leaders.

Bottom line: The path from the outside in.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Rank the Chokes, Not the Paths

Attack path management earns its budget on prioritization, not enumeration any tool can draw ten thousand paths, but the one worth buying tells you the five choke points that collapse the most, so pilot on your real estate and judge whether the top fixes genuinely break the most routes to your crown jewels.

Decide your dominant terrain: identity-heavy estates start with the AD/Entra specialists (SpecterOps), network-heavy ones with reachability models (Skybox, RedSeal), Microsoft shops native (Microsoft), and consolidators with their platform’s module (Palo Alto, CrowdStrike).

Insist on continuous modeling over point-in-time snapshots, because paths open and close with every config change, and favor tools that validate a path is traversable (Cymulate-class) over ones that only theorize it.

Route choke-point fixes as owned tickets, and track the metric that justifies renewal: paths-to-crown-jewels trending down quarter over quarter.

Feed findings into your CTEM and vulnerability management programs so exposure, path, and fix share one picture.

FAQs

What are the best attack path management tools in 2026?

XM Cyber as the hybrid-graph benchmark, SpecterOps for identity paths, Palo Alto and CrowdStrike for platform-integrated exposure, Cymulate for validated paths, with Zscaler, Microsoft, Skybox, RedSeal, and IONIX by model.

How is attack path management different from vulnerability management?

VM lists and scores individual weaknesses; attack path management chains them into routes an attacker can actually take, then prioritizes the choke points that break the most paths.

What is a choke point?

A node a misconfiguration, a shared credential, an over-permissioned account that many attack paths pass through, so fixing it collapses more risk than patching any single endpoint.

Identity paths or network paths?

Depends on your terrain: identity-heavy estates prioritize AD/Entra path analysis (SpecterOps), network-heavy ones prioritize reachability modeling; hybrid platforms (XM Cyber) cover both.

What proves attack path management value?

Choke-point fixes that measurably reduce paths to crown jewels, with the count trending down not the raw number of paths drawn.

Verdict

Ten tools, three terrains, one test that decides: does it rank the chokes or just draw the paths? XM Cyber benchmarks the hybrid graph, SpecterOps owns identity, Palo Alto and CrowdStrike integrate the platform, Cymulate proves the path is real, and the network modelers map reachability pilot on your estate, insist on choke-point math, model continuously, and let the shrinking count of paths-to-crown-jewels renew the contract.

The post Hackers Plant Backdoors in 6 WordPress Plugins to Steal Passwords and Take Over Websites appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers planted a remote-control backdoor in nine versions of six WordPress plugins from WP connect on November 22, 2026.

The malware could let an attacker steal password hashes, run commands, and take over a website. But WordPress.org blocked the tainted versions before distributing them and closed all six plugins that evening.

The advisory does not report confirmed password theft or website takeovers from the incident.

Wordfence estimated that the six plugins had more than 3,600 active installations combined. That figure describes the plugins’ reach, not the number of compromised sites.

The malicious versions were committed through the developer’s own WordPress.org account. WP connect reported that its account had been compromised, but how the attackers gained access was not clear when the advisory was published.

Researchers at Wordfence identified the malware independently of the WordPress.org Plugins Team. Wordfence’s PRISM monitoring system flagged suspicious changes in two plugins within a minute of each other, and analysts traced the same module to four more. A researcher known as Computeronfire separately reported the backdoor in Air WP Sync.

Hackers Plant Backdoors in 6 WordPress Plugins

The affected releases were Air WP Sync – Airtable to WordPress 2.9.1–2.9.4, WP Sync for Notion – Notion to WordPress 1.7.4, Add-on Brevo for Gravity Forms 2.6.3, Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Airtable 2.5.4, Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Notion 1.6.4, and Orders Sync to Airtable for WooCommerce 1.0.2. The release immediately preceding each plugin’s affected version or range did not contain the backdoor.

Each tainted release loaded a new PHP file that passed itself off as an analytics and update module. An earlier WordPress plugin backdoor case also hid malicious code behind an update-related feature.

In the WP connect incident, Wordfence found the same module across all six plugins, with a slightly earlier draft in Air WP Sync 2.9.1.

The module ran during normal site requests and used WP-Cron, WordPress’s scheduler, to check in every 30 minutes as a fallback. It sent the site URL, software versions, server account name, and previous command output to a remote server.

The module could execute PHP sent back by that server without a WordPress login. It also disabled verification of the server’s TLS certificate.

Backdoor offers multiple capabilities

The backdoor could run shell commands, read or change files, query database tables, and extract usernames, email addresses, and password hashes.

A hash is not a plaintext password, but a stolen hash can be used to test password guesses offline. The malware could also plant a webshell, a script that provides remote access, or set up an hourly task to run malicious code.

As earlier reporting on self-rebuilding WordPress backdoors showed, removing the original plugin does not necessarily remove everything it installed.

WordPress.org’s release hold kept the versions out of the update channel while Gandalf, its automated reviewer, independently detected the malicious code and stopped the rollout.

The incident shows why automated plugin update reviews matter even when a commit comes from a trusted developer account. Wordfence tracks the backdoor as CVE-2026-135202, with a critical CVSS score of 9.8. No patched versions were available at disclosure.

articles.title: Critical Bluetooth Flaw Could Let Hackers Take Control of Trailer Brakes While Driving
articles.description:
A critical Bluetooth flaw in Elecbrakes trailer brake controllers could let someone nearby apply, adjust, or release a trailer’s brakes while it is being towed. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-96805, carries a 9.6 severity score. It requires no pairing, PIN, or action from the driver. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency disclosed the issue […]

The post Critical Bluetooth Flaw Could Let Hackers Take Control of Trailer Brakes While Driving appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical Bluetooth flaw in Elecbrakes trailer brake controllers could let someone nearby apply, adjust, or release a trailer’s brakes while it is being towed.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-96805, carries a 9.6 severity score. It requires no pairing, PIN, or action from the driver.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency disclosed the issue on November 19, 2026, alongside two related vulnerabilities.

Firmware fixes are available for the EB2 and VM1, but owners must start the update themselves in the Elecbrakes app. The older ELBC 2000 also has the flaw and had no fix at disclosure.

The distinction matters because a trailer brake controller governs how much braking force the trailer applies, not how the tow vehicle’s own brakes operate.

Element Digital researchers Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy identified the vulnerabilities after Forck noticed his in-car remote had connected to someone else’s trailer without a pairing prompt.

They tested only equipment they owned, on private property or in a closed setup. Their report describes a product vulnerability, not a malware campaign.

Critical Bluetooth Flaw

The controller uses Bluetooth Low Energy to communicate with the Elecbrakes app and wireless remote. On vulnerable firmware, the controller did not verify that braking instructions came from an authorized device.

Unlike the PerfektBlue automotive Bluetooth flaws, which affected infotainment software, the Elecbrakes flaw directly exposed a function that controls braking force.

In controlled driving tests, stronger unauthorized braking produced noticeably greater deceleration than lighter braking at the same speed. On a public road, unexpected trailer braking could upset the balance of the tow vehicle and trailer.

Earlier reporting on a wireless train braking flaw describes a separate technology but highlights the same safety principle: a brake controller must verify who is giving it instructions.

The second critical vulnerability, CVE-2026-125273, concerns replay: a controller could accept a previously issued instruction again without checking whether it was fresh.

It also scored 9.6. That differs from the Volkswagen Bluetooth hacking demonstration, where researchers exploited infotainment software to access cabin functions and data rather than directly commanding trailer brakes.

The third issue, CVE-2026-124281, scored 6.1 and affects the wireless firmware update channel. CISA warned that inadequate protection could allow unauthorized firmware changes.

The researchers did not install modified firmware on a live controller, so the potential for lasting changes should not be confused with the brake activation they demonstrated in controlled testing.

Firmware Fixes and What Elecbrakes Owners Should Do

Elecbrakes received the report on May 18 and released fixes on July 6. The CISA industrial control advisory directs EB2 owners to install firmware 3.0.4.4.3 or later and VM1 owners to install 1.3.4.2.1 or later.

Open the Elecbrakes app, connect to the controller, and check the installed version. If it is older, start the update manually rather than assuming it has already installed.

The patched controllers restrict braking and access to update mode to an authenticated connection. Initial pairing requires physical confirmation through the tow vehicle’s brake pedal.

The change made older wireless remotes incompatible with the new pairing process, so Elecbrakes offered affected EB2 and VM1 owners free replacement remotes. Owners who use a remote should check whether theirs needs replacing.

All versions of the ELBC 2000 were listed as affected, with no firmware fix available at disclosure. As earlier reporting on legacy Renault vehicle software illustrates, equipment can remain in use long after its software ages.

ELBC 2000 owners should contact Elecbrakes for model-specific guidance and check the app periodically for a remediation update.

The manual update also leaves a gap between releasing a fix and protecting trailers on the road. By late October, Elecbrakes told the researchers that about 60% of daily active EB2 and VM1 users had installed the latest firmware.

That figure does not account for owners who rarely open the app. Fleet operators should verify the firmware on each controller rather than using that rollout figure as evidence that their own units are patched.

articles.title: Hackers Target Check Point Security Management Servers, Putting Corporate Firewall Controls at Risk
articles.description:
Hackers are breaking into Check Point Security Management Servers. These servers hold the rules that decide what traffic a company’s firewalls allow or block. A new campaign has already hit at least 22 organizations worldwide, and the attacker still has access to many of them. Check Point management servers are a high-value target because they […]

The post Hackers Target Check Point Security Management Servers, Putting Corporate Firewall Controls at Risk appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are breaking into Check Point Security Management Servers. These servers hold the rules that decide what traffic a company’s firewalls allow or block.

A new campaign has already hit at least 22 organizations worldwide, and the attacker still has access to many of them. Check Point management servers are a high-value target because they work like a control room for firewalls.

Whoever controls one can read the firewall settings, copy stored credentials, and change the security policy. Confirmed activity ran from

October 17 to November 2, 2026. The victims are in financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing.

Researchers at GreyNoise identified the activity and are tracking it as GreyNoise Threat 13, or GT13. They have not tied it to any known threat group.

They also cannot say whether the attacker is a nation-state or why they chose these targets. The campaign has no clear focus on one region or industry.

Victims sit in the United Kingdom, Germany, France, India, Thailand, South Korea, Australia, the United States, and several other countries.

Hackers Target Check Point Security Management Servers

The attacker used 99 IP addresses. Every one was either an ExpressVPN exit point or a hacked Check Point device. GreyNoise first saw the activity on October 2, when the attacker broke into a Rejetto HFS file server using CVE-2026-61500.

HFS creates session cookies from a weak random number function. By logging in several times in a row, the attacker worked out the secret key and forged an admin cookie, so no password was needed.

That hacked server became a relay box, which GreyNoise calls a “hop.” The attacker used it to run tools and store stolen data. These tools included Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, and Paramiko.

The attacker also ran at least 30 Python scripts. From there, the attacker used CVE-2026-16232, a Check Point SmartConsole authentication bypass, to run scripts on management servers.

The attacker launched more than 100 management tasks, copied the firewall database and the internal certificate authority, and tried to unload security policies, which would turn off the firewall.

This is not the first time Check Point products have been in the crosshairs. Earlier this month, researchers saw hackers who chained Check Point firewall flaws to get root access and wipe files on a VMware ESXi host.

Other recent reports described how hackers abused critical Check Point VPN flaws to get in without logging in. GreyNoise could not tell how the attacker first got into the Check Point servers.

The attacker already had access to them before breaking into the HFS server. The attacker also probed Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS, and domain controllers.

Some of the older flaws they tried, such as the actively exploited CitrixBleed 2 bug, have been public for more than a year. This shows that missed patches elsewhere in a network can still give attackers a way in.

AI Tools, Stealth, and What Defenders Should Do

GreyNoise thinks the attacker used large language models and agentic AI systems to scan for weak systems, run exploits, and write tools. Some odd gaps in the timeline fit this theory.

In one case, an automated download failed and the attacker spent a day fixing it. On November 2, the attacker also tested for a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug, CVE-2026-98432.

The attacker then used the nftables firewall tool to block packets that could trigger it. This kept other hackers from taking over the relay box.

GreyNoise’s view stopped around November 2, but it expects the campaign to continue because the attacker still has access to victim devices.

The company is sharing details with government partners and national security teams (CERTs) to warn victims. One error message pointed to an odd file, /usr/lib/.libproc.so, listed in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may be a hidden implant.

Check Point customers should patch SmartConsole and management servers and limit which IP addresses can reach them. They should also review logs for the indicators below.

Security teams should look for unexpected SSH keys, new certificates, and policy changes. CISA has already added two Check Point flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, so patching should be a top priority.

Check Point also publishes fixes and guidance on its security advisory blog. GreyNoise has the full technical report on its campaign research page.

articles.description:
San Francisco, United States, November 23rd, 2026, CyberNewswire SplitSecure, the cybersecurity technology provider, today unveiled a new access control platform based on secret splitting technology. The platform is intended to replace traditional access controls tools such as password managers, PAM, and vaults. On launch, it supports passwords, passkeys, one-time codes, SAML & OIDC federation, SSH, […]

The post SplitSecure Launches New Access Control Architecture for Humans and AI Agents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
San Francisco, United States, November 23rd, 2026, CyberNewswire

SplitSecure, the cybersecurity technology provider, today unveiled a new access control platform based on secret splitting technology.

The platform is intended to replace traditional access controls tools such as password managers, PAM, and vaults. On launch, it supports passwords, passkeys, one-time codes, SAML & OIDC federation, SSH, x.509 CA, OpenPGP, code signing (Nitro, Google Chrome Extensions), and general secrets vaulting.

The platform is intended for secure organizations of all sizes, including both large enterprise plans and a free plan for teams of up to six.

The access control space today contains a wide variety of tools. A secure organization would typically require a password manager, MFA app, vault, certificate manager, and PAM, among other tools.

But despite their variety, all these tools use a common architecture where clients’ secrets are stored in a singular “vault”. It is this architecture SplitSecure seeks to disrupt, with a new way of storing and using secrets based on secret-splitting.

Secret splitting is the practice of breaking secrets across multiple devices rather than storing them in one location.

This has been common practice in classified government environments for over thirty years but has historically been seen as high-effort and has had only limited adoption in industry.

SplitSecure’s new platform is a significant advance of the state of the art, offering a ready-to-use implementation of techniques that were previously limited to advanced security teams in elite organizations.

Because of this general advancement, SplitSecure is able to replicate the functionality of many common tools.

Its new platform provides password management, MFA, vaulting, certificate signing, and more PAM functionality such as shared accounts and resources.

Supported resource types include passwords, passkeys, one-time codes, SAML 2.0 sign-ons, secrets, certificates, SSH certificates, signing keys, OpenPGP identities, and crypto wallets.

This new technology also offers the particular advantage that it cryptographically guarantees the service provider has no access to client’s secrets.

This is in contrast to traditional PAM tools, in which the provider holds the “keys to the kingdom” at all times and a compromised vendor may be able to compromise client information.

Tristan Morris, CEO of SplitSecure, commented: “We were very ambitious […] we wanted a tool where people didn’t have to trust us as the provider, whereby design they’re the custodians of their own secrets. But we also wanted it to be so easy to use you could imagine a non-technical person using it instead of a password manager. We’ve done that, and it’s amazing to see it launch.”He also noted that SplitSecure’s new platform integrates with common identity providers for an easier transition. “It should always be easy to set up,” he said. “Migration, first time setup, our goal was for that to take under half an hour.” Details on supported security and privacy frameworks are available in the SplitSecure Trust Center.

The free plan of SplitSecure’s new platform, which is available to all customers now, offers access control with the following key differentiators:

  1. Modern Privileged Access: Zero trust, just-in-time access, zero standing privilege, on-demand step-up authentication, multi-party approvals, and quantum resistance come as standard.
  2. Condenses Multiple Tools: SplitSecure can condense two to five tools in the security stack.
  3. No-Vendor-Threat Architecture: Root keys are held exclusively by the customer, so SplitSecure as the vendor has no access to customer secrets.
  4. Built-In Audit and Compliance: Every privileged action are logged automatically with full context on every plan. Paid plans can view the logs for security analysis and forensics.

About SplitSecure

SplitSecure is a cybersecurity technology provider, established to develop and modernize secret splitting technology. After being founded in 2025 by Tristan Morris and Marc Tremblay, it raised $4.7M from Cowboy, Twelve Below, and Cofound Ventures.

Its access control platform combines PAM, password and passkey management, secrets vaulting, and auditing in one product, with root keys held exclusively by the customer. 

SplitSecure’s new access control platform is free for teams of up to six. Learn more at splitsecure.com or read the documentation.

Email: contact@splitsecure.com

Website: splitsecure.com

Contact

Chief of Staff

Slava Pashchenko

SplitSecure

slava@splitsecure.com

articles.title: Critical Node.js simple-git Library Vulnerability Enables Remote Code Execution Attacks
articles.description:
A critical flaw in simple-git, a popular Node.js library for running Git commands, can let attackers run their own commands on a server. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-134815. It affects apps that pass untrusted input into Git arguments. The National Vulnerability Database says simple-git versions before 4.1.0 contain an argument injection weakness, listed as […]

The post Critical Node.js simple-git Library Vulnerability Enables Remote Code Execution Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical flaw in simple-git, a popular Node.js library for running Git commands, can let attackers run their own commands on a server. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-134815. It affects apps that pass untrusted input into Git arguments.

The National Vulnerability Database says simple-git versions before 4.1.0 contain an argument injection weakness, listed as CWE-88. In plain terms, the library does not properly separate user-supplied text from the options it sends to Git. VulnCheck, which assigned the CVE, rated it 9.2 (Critical) on the CVSS 4.0 scale.

The library has a safety guard named allowUnsafePack. It is meant to block dangerous options that make Git run an outside program. Before this fix, the guard only blocked the –exec option for push operations. Attackers can bypass it by adding –exec to other Git actions.

Node.js simple-git Library Flaw

The risk starts when an application lets outside input reach the listRemote() or raw() functions. An attacker who controls those arguments can slip in –exec for ls-remote, archive, fetch-pack or send-pack. Git then treats the value as the name of a remote program and runs it on the host. The result is remote code execution, which means the attacker’s commands run with the same rights as the Node.js process.

The CVSS vector shows the attack needs no login and no user interaction. It also lists high attack complexity and an attack requirement, so a vulnerable app must be set up in a specific way.

Even so, the impact on data, system integrity, and availability is rated high. A researcher write-up from Upwind describes the same bypass of the allowUnsafePack guard.

Two packages from the steveukx/git-js project are affected. These are simple-git below 4.1.0 and @simple-git/argv-parser below 3.0.0. The parser package holds the checks that spot dangerous flags, so both need updating together.

The maintainers shipped the fix in the simple-git 4.1.0 release on 16 November. The notes say allowUnsafePack now blocks –exec for every command except rebase. The release also adds allowConfig and strict options.

It adds a git.cmd helper too, which treats every inserted value as untrusted data that cannot add options or change settings. The maintainers thanked 18 contributors for submitting CVE proposals that shaped these changes. NVD published the record on 22 November.

This is not the first time simple-git has had trouble with argument handling. In 2022, CVE-2022-24433 showed that injecting Git options into fetch() could run commands. Earlier this year, CVE-2026-28292 used a missing case-insensitive regex flag to get around older fixes. The library sees more than 12 million weekly npm downloads.

Another advisory, CVE-2026-6951, covered an incomplete fix that blocked -c but not –config. The pattern is clear. Block lists of bad options are hard to keep complete, because Git accepts many ways to write the same option.

Upgrade to simple-git 4.1.0 and @simple-git/argv-parser 3.0.0 or later. Then run npm ls simple-git to find copies pulled in by other packages, since many projects use it indirectly.

Developers should also stop passing raw user input into listRemote() or raw(). Checking values against a fixed list of allowed repository URLs and branch names is a safer habit. Running the app as a low-rights user adds another layer of protection.

Node.js libraries that run system commands have been a steady source of serious problems. A command injection flaw in the systeminformation package followed the same idea of unchecked input reaching a shell.

Teams should also keep strict control of their dependencies, as shown when the Keyv package compromise reached millions of weekly installs. Use lockfiles, run npm ci in build systems, and review updates before they ship.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 20, 2026, after finding evidence of active exploitation. Cisco says there is no workaround […]

The post Hackers Actively Exploiting Cisco Expressway Vulnerability to Gain Full Root Access appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-76466, a critical vulnerability in Cisco Expressway that lets remote attackers run operating system commands with root privileges.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 20, 2026, after finding evidence of active exploitation. Cisco says there is no workaround and urges customers to upgrade.

Cisco first disclosed the vulnerability on October 21 and assigned it a severity score of 9.8 out of 10. As Cyber Security News reported in its original coverage of the Cisco Expressway vulnerability, fixed software was available before CISA confirmed exploitation. The federal patch deadline was November 23. The catalog entry also directs agencies to follow CISA’s requirements for checking affected devices for signs of compromise.

Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Grants Root Access

The vulnerability affects the database service used by clustered Expressway devices. Cisco’s security advisory points to persistent cookies and a failure to check client certificates even when TLS verification is enabled for clustering.

An attacker who has the required cookies and can reach the affected device over the network can run commands without a normal login. Those commands run as root, the highest level of access on the underlying operating system.

Both Cisco Expressway Core (Expressway-C) and Cisco Expressway Edge (Expressway-E) are affected, whether deployed as virtual machines or physical appliances. For this specific vulnerability, the device must run an affected software release and be part of a cluster. That distinction matters when checking an inventory: the product name and software version alone do not establish whether a device is exposed.

The risk can extend beyond the first device. In a case covered by Cyber Security News, researchers at F6 reported that attackers compromised two internet-facing Expressway devices at one organization and reached two internal cluster members through one of them.

Security teams should therefore check internal members of an affected cluster, even if those devices are not directly reachable from the internet.

Cisco Expressway Fixed Versions

Cisco lists X15.5.20 as the first fixed release for customers running X15.5.3 and earlier. Customers on X14 or earlier must migrate to a fixed release. The update also includes Cisco’s October Expressway security hardening fixes, which address several other vulnerabilities. Cisco credited Stefan Aleksic of Jane Street with reporting the root access vulnerability.

Administrators should verify the installed version on every cluster member after upgrading. If a vulnerable device was reachable from the internet, preserve available logs and review activity on both the exposed device and its internal peers. The update closes the vulnerability, but it cannot tell you whether someone already used it.

articles.title: OpenAI and Cisco Launch Shirudo AI Security Tool to Block Exploits on Linux Servers
articles.description:
OpenAI and Cisco launched Shirudo on November 23, 2026, an open-source security tool designed to block specific exploits on running Linux servers while teams test and deploy permanent patches. In a controlled test, a shield generated by OpenAI’s Codex blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against Elasticsearch without restarting the service. The OpenAI announcement describes Shirudo […]

The post OpenAI and Cisco Launch Shirudo AI Security Tool to Block Exploits on Linux Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OpenAI and Cisco launched Shirudo on November 23, 2026, an open-source security tool designed to block specific exploits on running Linux servers while teams test and deploy permanent patches.

In a controlled test, a shield generated by OpenAI’s Codex blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against Elasticsearch without restarting the service.

The OpenAI announcement describes Shirudo as a way to close the gap between learning about a vulnerability and getting a fix onto every affected system.

That gap can last days or weeks when updates need testing and restarts must be scheduled. An exploit and a legitimate request can also rely on the same Linux operation.

Blocking the operation outright may stop the attack, but it can disrupt the application too. Shirudo is designed to help teams test a narrower safeguard before enforcing it.

Shirudo Protects Running Linux Servers

Shirudo grew out of Tetragon, Isovalent’s runtime security project. It uses eBPF, a Linux technology that lets small programs run at selected points in the kernel.

An AI agent can use those points to observe activity, such as system calls made by a process, or draft a shield that blocks a specific action. Operators can watch how a proposed shield behaves before deciding whether to enforce it.

The approach has a real-world precedent. During its response to the Copy Fail Linux kernel vulnerability, Cloudflare used eBPF to restrict access to the affected kernel feature while keeping it available to a service that needed it.

That response did not use Shirudo, but it illustrates why a targeted control can be more useful than disabling a shared feature across an entire fleet.

Java4Shell Test Keeps Elasticsearch Online

Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, affects the Base64 decoder in certain unpatched OpenJDK builds on supported x86-64 processors. If attacker-controlled data reaches the vulnerable decoder, it can corrupt memory and, under some conditions, allow remote code execution. The flaw is in the Java runtime, not Elasticsearch itself.

For the demonstration, Codex generated a shield in Java bytecode rather than eBPF because the check needed to run inside the application’s Java runtime.

Isovalent reported that the shield added an input check to the decoder in a running Elasticsearch 9.5.5 process. The service logs showed that the check rejected the test input, and Elasticsearch kept running. The result shows that the shield blocked the tested attempt, not that it replaces the OpenJDK update.

Signed Shields and Deployment Limits

For eBPF shields, Linux checks that the loader carries a trusted signature, and the kernel verifier checks the program against its safety rules. A Trusted Platform Module, or TPM, records changes when shields are loaded or removed.

That gives operators signed evidence they can check against what they expect a server to be running. It does not prove a shield works against every attack or leaves every workload unaffected.

The Shirudo GitHub repository lists the project as pre-release. Production targets require a compatible Linux kernel with Shirudo’s patches and a TPM 2.0.

The no-restart benefit applies to shields loaded after the platform is set up, not to the initial setup, which starts at boot. Teams can use the virtual machine quickstart to test signing, loading, verifying, and removing a shield while keeping permanent vendor patches on the rollout schedule.

articles.title: Jensen Huang Returns as NVIDIA CEO Following Unanimous Board Vote
articles.description:
NVIDIA reinstated Jensen Huang as president, chief executive officer, and board director on November 23, 2026, after a unanimous vote. The decision took effect immediately, but an independent board inquiry into reports that a foreign intelligence effort targeted Huang remains open. In its announcement, NVIDIA said the board met with Huang several times and received […]

The post Jensen Huang Returns as NVIDIA CEO Following Unanimous Board Vote appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
NVIDIA reinstated Jensen Huang as president, chief executive officer, and board director on November 23, 2026, after a unanimous vote.

The decision took effect immediately, but an independent board inquiry into reports that a foreign intelligence effort targeted Huang remains open.

In its announcement, NVIDIA said the board met with Huang several times and received input from senior U.S. government officials before deciding that his return posed no national security risk. That was the board’s judgment about reinstatement, not a finding that closed the inquiry.

Harvey C. Jones will remain board chair. Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO after Huang stepped down, will continue as chief financial officer. The vote reversed the board’s position from its November 17 earnings call, when Jones said it did not intend to reinstate Huang.

NVIDIA said Huang supports the independent investigation and has committed to cooperating.

NVIDIA Reinstates Jensen Huang

As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of the original NVIDIA investigation, the board announced the inquiry on November 8 after reports that Huang had been targeted.

A committee made up solely of independent directors is leading the review with help from outside lawyers. At the time, the board said it had no reason to believe NVIDIA secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised.

The reinstatement announcement did not publish findings or give a date for completing the review. The public record does not establish that anyone obtained company information, and the board’s decision to restore Huang to his roles does not settle that question.

The board inquiry is separate from a U.S. investigation involving Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that authorities are examining over possible diversion of restricted NVIDIA chips to China.

NBC News reported that the Commerce Department opened its investigation in 2024 and that the Justice Department later took the lead in the criminal probe.

The Associated Press also reported on a related policy concern: companies can use advanced chips remotely through overseas data centers without taking physical delivery of the hardware.

That difference matters in shared AI infrastructure. Knowing where a server is installed does not necessarily tell a provider who is using its computing power.

Cyber Security News’ AI data center security checklist covers a separate part of that challenge: securing GPUs, firmware, and the hardware supply chain.

Those controls address risks inside the data center, while export compliance addresses who can receive or use restricted technology.

NVIDIA has formed a separate National Security and Export Control Committee, staffed only by independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks.

The committee is bringing in lawyers with national security experience, who will retain specialist advisers. NVIDIA is also starting a search for a chief compliance officer who will oversee compliance across the company and report to the board’s Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee.

NVIDIA says it will continue cooperating with government investigations and inquiries. Huang’s return settles who runs the company, but the independent directors have yet to report what their review found.

The post European Commission Disables Access to EU Academy After Cyberattack Exposes User Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The European Commission disabled public access to EU Academy on Monday, November 23, after confirming that a wider cyberattack exposed users’ personal data.

The online learning platform hosts courses and workshops produced by EU institutions. The Commission posted a notice on the academy’s website, but it did not say how many users were affected or when they could access their courses again.

Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that the academy was affected by the same cyber campaign the Commission disclosed the previous week. The exposed information includes names and email addresses, according to the Associated Press.

EU Academy is the first service in the wider incident for which the Commission has publicly confirmed a leak of users’ personal data. It has not said whether passwords were exposed.

EU Academy Cyberattack Data Breach

At its November 19 press briefing, the Commission said it had taken several applications offline as a precaution and had restored most of them.

The Commission detected the campaign on October 22 and confirmed the incident on October 26 after an initial investigation.

As Cyber Security News reported in its earlier coverage of the European Commission cyberattack, the disruption affected staff tools used for timesheets and medical reimbursements. Those outages do not establish that attackers accessed the records those tools handle.

The Commission confirmed that the campaign used an AI-assisted tool. It has not publicly explained how the attackers first gained access or what role the tool played in the EU Academy data breach.

The distinction matters because identifying a tool used in a campaign does not establish how attackers reached a particular service.

Euronews reported that officials suspect a China-backed hacking group and that the wider attack had not been fully contained by Monday. The report cited people familiar with the investigation.

The Commission has not publicly named the group, so the suspected link to China is not a confirmed finding. Taking EU Academy offline also does not mean the wider incident is over.

The Commission warned EU Academy users to be cautious about unexpected emails or messages and not to share personal information in response.

Users who receive a message about a course, account access, or the breach should open the academy’s website directly instead of following a link in the message. A notice that knows a user’s name or email address is not proof that it came from the Commission.

As Cyber Security News noted in its coverage of the Vimeo data breach, exposed email addresses can help scammers make phishing messages look more credible.

In the EU Academy case, a fake message could claim that learners need to verify their accounts or sign in through a temporary page to regain access to a course. That is a risk to watch for, not a report that such messages have already been sent.

The Commission has yet to disclose how many users are affected, whether the leak included other types of data, or when public access will return. For learners waiting to resume a course, the official academy website remains the place to check for updates.

Until the Commission provides more detail, the confirmed exposure of names and email addresses should not be read as confirmation that login details were also taken.

articles.title: Hackers Hide RevStealer Malware in Fake Claude AI App to Steal Passwords and Crypto Wallets
articles.description:
Hackers are distributing RevStealer, a Windows infostealer, in a fake Claude AI desktop app that promises free access. The download, branded “Claude Opus 5 Free Desktop,” comes in an archive of roughly 101 MB. Running the executable does not open a chat window. Instead, it starts malware designed to steal saved passwords, browser sessions, cryptocurrency […]

The post Hackers Hide RevStealer Malware in Fake Claude AI App to Steal Passwords and Crypto Wallets appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are distributing RevStealer, a Windows infostealer, in a fake Claude AI desktop app that promises free access. The download, branded “Claude Opus 5 Free Desktop,” comes in an archive of roughly 101 MB.

Running the executable does not open a chat window. Instead, it starts malware designed to steal saved passwords, browser sessions, cryptocurrency wallet data, and other information stored on the computer.

The operators distributed the package through GitHub repositories and sites themed around game cheats. Those channels give the download two ways to reach people: as a supposed shortcut to paid AI features or as another unofficial tool offered for free.

A separate fake Claude download campaign used the same brand to lure users, but it was not the RevStealer operation.

Cyberint researchers noted that RevStealer was first observed in September 2026 and described the campaign in an October 18 report.

They did not attribute it to a named threat actor. The findings describe attackers impersonating Anthropic’s software, not a breach of Claude or evidence that Anthropic’s official installer was compromised.

Hackers Hide RevStealer Malware in Fake Claude AI App

The counterfeit app is built with Electron, a framework used by legitimate desktop software. On launch, its loader checks the computer’s memory, processor, hostname, and graphics hardware before unpacking an encrypted component.

It places that component in a randomly named folder under Windows AppData and starts it in the background. Since the executable has no visible interface, a user could mistake the lack of a window for a failed launch.

RevStealer also checks for signs that it is running inside a security researcher’s test environment and attempts to make Microsoft Defender skip scanning AppData.

That change is useful evidence for responders, especially when it appears alongside a suspicious download and an unexpected process running from a user folder.

A separate counterfeit Claude desktop campaign also targeted Defender, but delivered remote-access malware rather than RevStealer.

The stealer collects browser databases and encryption keys, session cookies, Windows Credential Manager entries, password-manager artifacts, and data from cryptocurrency wallets.

It also targets VPN and remote-access credentials, messaging and gaming apps, clipboard contents, screenshots, and selected documents.

For businesses, that mix matters: a single infected workstation can expose both a user’s personal accounts and credentials used to reach company systems. For wallet holders, the risk depends on what sensitive wallet material was stored on the device.

Stolen cookies pose a different problem from stolen passwords. An active session cookie can let someone reuse a login the victim has already completed without facing a fresh multifactor authentication prompt.

Earlier reporting on stolen AI session tokens shows why changing a password is not always enough: some credentials may stay valid until the service revokes them.

Cyberint reported that RevStealer sends stolen data in encrypted records and can obtain a replacement server address through a Polygon smart contract if needed. The malware then deletes itself rather than relying on continued execution to complete the theft.

That means responders may find little left on disk even when endpoint alerts, network logs, or account activity point to a compromise. Cyberint also noted that the malware’s tasking channel can deliver additional components.

If the fake app was run, isolate the computer and use a clean device to revoke active sessions and change exposed passwords.

Organizations should review recent identity and VPN activity, check for unauthorized Defender exclusions, and preserve endpoint and network logs.

If a wallet’s private key or recovery phrase may have been exposed, move funds to a new wallet created on a clean device. For new installations, use Anthropic’s official download page rather than a third-party archive.
