articles.title: Vmcloudoor Malware Could Let Hackers Secretly Control Linux Cloud Servers and Steal Sensitive Files
articles.description:
A newly found Linux backdoor named Vmcloudoor can quietly take over cloud servers and pull files off them. It is built to infect virtual machines on Chinese cloud platforms, mainly Alibaba Cloud. It also targets Tencent Cloud and Huawei Cloud. The malware pretends to be a normal cloud management agent, so administrators are less likely […]

The post Vmcloudoor Malware Could Let Hackers Secretly Control Linux Cloud Servers and Steal Sensitive Files appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A newly found Linux backdoor named Vmcloudoor can quietly take over cloud servers and pull files off them. It is built to infect virtual machines on Chinese cloud platforms, mainly Alibaba Cloud. It also targets Tencent Cloud and Huawei Cloud.

The malware pretends to be a normal cloud management agent, so administrators are less likely to notice it or shut it down.

Linux backdoors that hide in plain sight are not new, as the Auto-Color Linux backdoor showed earlier. Vmcloudoor takes the idea further by copying the names and folders of trusted cloud tools.

Researchers at Exatrack found the implant during a threat hunting session and described it as a very precise tool made to hide itself. They only recovered the “helper” module.

Even so, it shows the main features of the backdoor. A second module called “Core” exists and is meant to run commands received from the attacker.

Vmcloudoor Malware Could Let Hackers Secretly Control Linux Cloud Servers

When Vmcloudoor starts, it checks which cloud it is running on. It looks for known folders and running processes tied to Alibaba, Tencent and Huawei agents.

Based on the result, it picks a matching disguise. On Alibaba it uses the name AliyunSysAssist, on Tencent it uses YunJingSysAssist, and on Huawei it uses UniAgentSys.

If it finds none of these, it hides in /dev/shm/.ov2/ and calls itself kworker/0:2H, which looks like a normal Linux kernel worker. It then renames its own process to match, so it looks like part of the cloud setup.

The command channel is also unusual. Instead of calling a server run by the attacker, the malware checks an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket for tasks meant for that one machine.

It builds a web address from a machine fingerprint and a five-minute time window. By default the file does not exist, so the server answers with a 404 error.

When the attacker wants to act, they place a task file there and the server answers with a 200 response. Because the traffic goes to a public cloud service, it is easy to mistake for normal activity and hard to block.

Similar blending tricks have been seen in BPFDoor attacks on telecom networks, where malware copied trusted server processes.

Each task has a type number. Type 1 runs a command, type 2 pushes a file onto the machine, and type 3 uploads a file from the machine to an address chosen by the attacker.

Type 9 collects a machine inventory, including the hostname, user name, operating system, kernel version, processor type and memory. File transfers must use a full path and stay under 100 MB.

The malware also looks for security tools. It checks for products such as CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Sophos and Elkeid, and it labels the machine as clean, antivirus-protected or EDR-protected.

It then suggests longer waiting times between check-ins on better-protected machines. If the storage bucket is closed, the malware fetches a new one from a Gitee repository. The malware never checks HTTPS certificates.

Git Mistakes Reveal Clues About the Developer

The attacker made some careless errors. The Gitee repository, named “plus”, was created by a throwaway account called test9527. Its commit history shows three different author identities.

One is hpgoc2-deploy with the email deploy@hpgoc2.local, which hints at an internal project name. Another is thor8848, tied to a GitHub account created in 2020 that appears to belong to a Chinese user working in penetration testing.

A later commit also records a switch from the bucket top-sec to assist-logs. Exatrack believes this was a slip in operational security, not a deliberate false trail.

The researchers suspect the author may be a Chinese pentester, possibly running red team work, though they admit this is only an assumption.

The commit data alone does not prove who operated the backdoor or whether it was used with permission. Reports also say it is still unclear how the malware first lands on a server or how many systems it has reached.

Exatrack also found a newer version that shares 88 percent of its code with the first one. The changes mostly affect check-in cycles and timeout values, which suggests the tool is still being improved.

Since the backdoor can run commands and move files, defenders should treat it like any other cloud credential threat, such as the Telnyx SDK credential theft case, and rotate keys if a host looks infected.

Teams can also watch for unknown processes in /dev/shm, fake cloud agent names, and unexpected traffic to Alibaba storage endpoints. The newer BPFDoor variants with stateless C2 are a reminder that Linux backdoors keep changing how they hide.

articles.title: Hackers Plant 13 ClickFix Traps on Compromised WordPress Site to Trick Visitors Into Running Malware
articles.description:
A single hacked WordPress site was found carrying 13 separate ClickFix traps from three different malware kits. Each trap shows visitors a fake security check. It then talks them into pasting a harmful command on their own computer. The site sat in a poor state because several groups had broken into it at different times. […]

The post Hackers Plant 13 ClickFix Traps on Compromised WordPress Site to Trick Visitors Into Running Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A single hacked WordPress site was found carrying 13 separate ClickFix traps from three different malware kits.

Each trap shows visitors a fake security check. It then talks them into pasting a harmful command on their own computer. The site sat in a poor state because several groups had broken into it at different times.

Some of their code even fights the others for control of the page. This shows how one weak website can be used again and again by unrelated criminals.

Analysts at URLScan noted the malware while testing a new feature that captures clipboard content during live browsing.

They flagged a scan of the site academicpipelinedatabase[.]net that carried a ClickFix label but never wrote anything to the clipboard.

The page showed a fake reCAPTCHA box over a blurred Cloudflare screen. It also held more than twenty hidden script blocks, and most of them were scrambled to hide their purpose.

Hackers Plant 13 ClickFix Traps on Compromised WordPress Site

ClickFix does not use a software bug. A fake page asks the visitor to prove they are human, and a click on the box silently copies a command to the clipboard.

The page then tells the user to paste and run it. Because the victim runs the command, many browser and download filters never see a problem. Our earlier report on a fake CAPTCHA that hides malware in the browser cache shows how common this trick has become.

Nine of the 13 traps come from a kit the researchers named LOM, after the “/lom” part found in its web addresses. Each LOM trap carries its own token and tracking link, and it sends different commands for each operating system.

On Windows, the copied command uses PowerShell to download a script from the attacker’s server and run it. The command also sends a special user-agent and header, so the server only answers requests that come from a real lure. One version also carries a Mac command that pipes a downloaded script into zsh.

Fake reCAPTCHA (Source – URLScan)

The LOM code is delivered in five ways. Some copies sit right on the page, some are packed in base64, and some are fake plugin tags with names like “wordpress-defender”.

Others use a blob loader. Two loaders use a trick called EtherHiding, which stores the next server address inside a Polygon blockchain contract.

The operator can swap the server by changing the contract, so blocking one domain does not fix the problem. The same method shows up in a campaign hiding malware on Polygon that we covered earlier.

Two LOM traps also try to delete rival scripts. They scan the page for code that looks like other loaders and remove it.

This suggests the authors expect to share hacked sites with other criminals. LOM has grown fast. It first appeared in the week of September 21, 2026, and added over 700 new sites the next week.

Rival Kits Break Each Other

The second kit shows a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA and also uses EtherHiding. Three of its loaders read hidden server names from Polygon contracts.

They decode the result and load a script only when they see a Windows browser. The researchers say its indicators overlap with ErrTraffic, which Sekoia and Censys have described.

Only one of these loaders served a working payload. Its copied command starts a hidden PowerShell window and downloads a ZIP file. It unpacks the ZIP into a hidden folder and sets a startup registry entry named “nurture_river_mountain” so the program runs again after a reboot.

The screen then prints a fake “I am not a robot” message, so the victim thinks the check passed. Another loader was added to eight theme and plugin files on disk, so cleaning the database alone would not remove it.

The traps also broke each other by accident. Two copies of the same loader both used a function named decode(), each with a different key.

The later one replaced the earlier one, so the first loader decoded its server list with the wrong key and failed. One malicious script had switched off another one on the same page.

The third kit targets only Mac users and looks like a Google Analytics tag. The URLScan team says it overlaps with Macfinger. It shows a fake reCAPTCHA only on macOS, and its command downloads a shell script, runs it, deletes it, and wipes the shell history.

This fits the wider rise in ClickFix campaigns targeting Mac users. A separate script on the page also removes any full-screen overlay except those from LOM and the second kit. So someone knew about both.

Seven more loaders on the page never reached a final stage during the scan. Cleaning one injection does not make the site safe. Site owners should check theme and plugin files on disk and patch plugins.

They should also look for sites that were hit by ShadowCaptcha-style WordPress compromises. Visitors should never paste a command from a web page into Run, PowerShell, or Terminal.

articles.title: iTerm2 Remote Code Execution Flaw Lets Hackers Run Malicious Commands by Displaying Crafted Files
articles.description:
A security flaw in iTerm2, a macOS terminal emulator, lets attackers run commands when a user displays a specially crafted file in a vulnerable terminal session. The user does not have to run the file as a script or paste a command supplied by the attacker. Printing the file’s contents is enough to trigger the […]

The post iTerm2 Remote Code Execution Flaw Lets Hackers Run Malicious Commands by Displaying Crafted Files appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A security flaw in iTerm2, a macOS terminal emulator, lets attackers run commands when a user displays a specially crafted file in a vulnerable terminal session.

The user does not have to run the file as a script or paste a command supplied by the attacker. Printing the file’s contents is enough to trigger the bug. The developer fixed the issue in iTerm2 3.7.9, a security update built on November 20, 2026.

The reported affected range is 3.6.1 through 3.7.8, and the flaw can affect installations using default settings. iTerm2 credits Minseong Kim of NSHC Red Alert Labs with reporting the issue.

The vendor’s release notes confirm the fix and describe the command execution risk, but do not report attacks using the flaw in the wild.

The flaw sits in iTerm2’s implementation of the Kitty graphics protocol, which lets programs display images inside a terminal. A terminal does more than show text. It also reads escape sequences, which are instructions that can change what it displays or tell it to respond.

iTerm2 Remote Code Execution Flaw

According to reports in a GitHub advisory, iTerm2 processes embedded instructions instead of displaying them as plain text, allowing files to appear as harmless README or log files. The issue stems from failed image request error messages that preserve untrusted text and line breaks.

iTerm2 then sent that reply to the pseudoterminal, the channel that also carries keyboard input to the shell. The shell could treat those line breaks like presses of the Return key and run text from the reply as a command. This was a logic bug, not a memory corruption flaw.

The bug is separate from the earlier iTerm2 SSH integration flaw. However, both show how untrusted terminal output can turn into shell input.

It also differs from macOS ClickFix campaigns, which rely on persuading users to paste and run a command. Here, the risky action looks like reading a file.

The first fix replaces line breaks and other control characters with spaces in Kitty graphics replies before sending them. That keeps the error readable without passing characters the shell could act on.

Bypassed Security Controls :

A follow-up change uses the same filter for Kitty drag-and-drop replies and terminal title reports. The developers also added tests to check that unsafe characters are removed without breaking valid replies.

Mac users should check their installed iTerm2 version and update to 3.7.9 or later through the official iTerm2 downloads page. Until the update is in place, avoid printing raw contents from unfamiliar repositories, archives, or attachments into iTerm2.

Instead, use a graphical text editor to inspect suspicious files. For teams managing Macs, check actual installed versions rather than assuming that a centrally deployed update reached every device. The fix is in iTerm2 itself, so changing shells is not a substitute for installing it.

articles.description:
A low-skilled hacker used a jailbroken AI agent to steal an insurer’s customer database and about 8.6GB of files from European municipalities. The operator, known as BabidiGhost, worked for nine days in November 2026. He typed plain, misspelled French orders and let the agent do the technical work. Targets included banks, insurers, payment providers and […]

The post Jailbroken AI Agent Helps Hacker Steal Customer Data and 8.6GB of European Government Files appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A low-skilled hacker used a jailbroken AI agent to steal an insurer’s customer database and about 8.6GB of files from European municipalities.

The operator, known as BabidiGhost, worked for nine days in November 2026. He typed plain, misspelled French orders and let the agent do the technical work. Targets included banks, insurers, payment providers and town halls, mostly in Belgium, France and Switzerland.

The agent targeted more than 50 organizations and datasets. In one order, the operator asked for “13 files of 1,000 full records with IBAN, nice and tidy.”

He also asked the agent who it was, and he could not download his own stolen files. The AI covered for his lack of skill, and it kept working until its model API key was revoked on November 14, 2026.

Researchers at SOCRadar found the operation after the hacker left his home directory open on a hijacked staging server in France.

The folder held 1,901 files, including every prompt he typed, his shell history, implant logs and roughly 10GB of stolen data. SOCRadar’s analysts said they studied the files without running any recovered malware or using any stolen credentials.

Jailbroken AI Agent Helps Hacker

The agent came from a toolchain tied to BlackHatSect0r, a French-speaking, financially driven group that SOCRadar tracks. It runs on the Hermes agent framework and a DeepSeek model.

A 1,371-line file named SOUL.md sets the agent’s rules. It declares the agent’s “ethics protocols destroyed” and treats any refusal as a model malfunction to be ignored.

A local proxy backed up that file. When the model said no, the proxy re-sent the order with more pressure. Across nine days, the agent sent 5,779 requests to its model, and only 41 refusals survived.

The operator typed 1,801 orders, and the agent wrote the scanners, exploits and data-theft scripts on its own. This matches a wider trend, as one operator running 12 AI agents recently hit emergency services and banks in Taiwan.

Nothing here was a zero-day. The successful break-ins used known weak spots that victims could have fixed. In the insurer’s case, an internet-facing and unpatched Metabase dashboard was open to CVE-2023-38646.

Older reporting explains the Metabase remote code execution flaw and the patched versions. The agent ran commands through the dashboard’s database link and read cloud database credentials from the container’s environment. It then exported the customer database and planted a database trigger to restart its implant.

What the Hacker Stole and What Stopped Him

The biggest theft by size needed even less effort. A shared IT provider left a storage server’s management page open to the internet, and a weak admin password opened it.

Three download scripts later, the agent held 23 archives, about 8.6GB, from more than 13 municipalities and 10 other public bodies. One password unlocked every client’s data.

Of the 14 organizations SOCRadar studied closely, two were breached and three were partly breached. Four resisted and five saw only scouting.

Basic controls decided each result. Eleven scripts failed to brute-force a payment portal’s one-time password, and 49 bank hostnames stayed out of reach behind an IP allowlist.

Server-side checks also blocked a fake declaration at one bank. At another bank, a sign-in error confirmed 48 valid corporate accounts.

The agent also ran a 120-thread crawler that collected IBANs, emails and phone numbers from Swiss sites. An IBAN tied to a real identity can enable direct-debit fraud and bank-impersonation calls. That makes this dataset the most likely to harm individuals.

Cutting off the AI key stopped the agent but did not clean up the damage. A PowerShell beacon and a C# backdoor posing as a Windows Update service kept checking in until November 15, 2026.

This echoes findings that attackers now automate every stage of an intrusion, while people still pick targets and sell the loot. SOCRadar rates BabidiGhost a low-capability actor using a high-capability tool.

Defenders should take the main lesson from this case. Keep analytics tools and storage panels off the internet, and keep database secrets out of runtime environments.

Use strong passwords, MFA and IP allowlists. Watch for servers that call model APIs or the Telegram bot API for no business reason.

Teams should search logs for these indicators between November 5 and November 17, 2026. Google has also seen attackers running agent frameworks such as ARTEX and PentAGI, so this pattern is spreading.

articles.title: CrowdStrike to Acquire Zscaler in Massive $43.9 Billion Cybersecurity Deal
articles.description:
CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal that would bring cloud network security to its Falcon platform. The agreement, announced on November 23, 2026, would give CrowdStrike control over both the devices where users and AI agents run software and the connections they make to corporate apps and data. Zscaler […]

The post CrowdStrike to Acquire Zscaler in Massive $43.9 Billion Cybersecurity Deal appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal that would bring cloud network security to its Falcon platform. The agreement, announced on November 23, 2026, would give CrowdStrike control over both the devices where users and AI agents run software and the connections they make to corporate apps and data.

Zscaler shareholders would receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share. Based on CrowdStrike’s November 20 closing price, the exchange valued each Zscaler share at $260.41, about 34% above Zscaler’s close that day.

The agreement follows our earlier report of acquisition talks. If the deal closes, existing CrowdStrike shareholders would own 84.1% of the combined company, while Zscaler shareholders would own 15.9%.

Update: CrowdStrike to Acquire Zscaler in Massive $43.9 Billion Cybersecurity Deal

Zscaler Would Extend the Falcon Platform

Falcon monitors laptops, servers, and cloud workloads for suspicious activity. Zscaler’s Zero Trust Exchange sits between users, AI agents, and the applications they want to reach, where it can check identity and enforce access rules.

That matters when traffic goes straight to a cloud service rather than through a company data center. CrowdStrike plans to add Zscaler’s data protection and secure access service edge, or SASE, which delivers networking and security controls through the cloud.

The companies already share more than 2,000 customers and have built 16 integrations. One existing integration lets Zscaler use Falcon alerts to reassess access when a device shows signs of compromise.

After closing, CrowdStrike plans to bring device events and network logs into Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, its platform for collecting and analyzing security events. That could help an analyst link a suspicious process on a server to an attempt to reach a sensitive app, without switching between two sets of logs.

An AI agent can run on a server and make requests to several apps without a person approving each action. Falcon can monitor activity where the agent runs, while Zscaler can apply rules to the connections it makes.

The difference matters when an agent has a valid identity but tries to reach data outside its assigned role. Zscaler had already expanded its AI security work through its acquisition of SPLX. The proposed deal would bring those network controls closer to Falcon’s device and workload monitoring.

CrowdStrike plans to sell both product lines under one Falcon Flex contract and sees an opportunity to offer Falcon to about 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not already use CrowdStrike.

It estimates the deal would expand its potential market by more than $185 billion in calendar 2029. The companies expect to start with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue and target about $1 billion in additional annualized revenue from the combination within 30 months of closing.

Both boards approved the deal, but it still needs Zscaler shareholder and regulatory approval. The companies expect it to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal 2028 and will operate separately until then.

Zscaler CEO Jay Chaudhry would continue to lead the Zscaler business and join CrowdStrike’s board. For customers, the key question after closing is how quickly the companies can turn their existing integrations into shared access controls and a single view of security events.

The post Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Center Urges Users Not to Share Confidential Data on WhatsApp Web appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Center (I4C) has urged users not to share confidential data on WhatsApp Web and to log out manually after every session.

In a November 18, 2026, security advisory, the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit warned that someone with access to a signed-in browser session could read private messages, view contacts and group chats, or send messages posing as the account owner.

The warning applies especially to office computers, shared systems and devices other people can access. The advisory recommends keeping government, workplace, financial and other sensitive information off WhatsApp Web. It does not identify a new flaw in WhatsApp or say that its encryption has been broken.

When someone can open a browser session that is still signed in, they may be able to use the account without the owner’s permission.

WhatsApp Web Access to Chats

WhatsApp Web lets users access their chats by linking a browser to their account. According to WhatsApp’s linked devices guide, personal messages remain protected by end-to-end encryption on linked devices.

That protection does not stop someone at a computer from reading chats the browser can already display. An attacker could use details from those chats to make a fake payment request seem to come from a colleague or relative.

A separate threat, covered in Cyber Security News’ report on WhatsApp GhostPairing, involves tricking users into approving a device they do not control. The I4C advisory does not tie its warning to that campaign.

Logging out on a shared computer ends that session, but it does not remove a different device already linked to the account.

Protecting WhatsApp Web session

I4C recommends signing out from WhatsApp Web before closing the tab or browser. Avoid signing in at cyber cafés, public kiosks, hotel business centers, or on borrowed computers.

If temporary use is unavoidable, use a trusted computer and open a private or incognito window, then log out manually. Private browsing is an extra precaution, not a substitute for signing out.

For teams handling sensitive records, the safer choice is to use an approved work channel rather than send those records through WhatsApp Web.

I4C also advises keeping the operating system, browser and security software up to date and avoiding suspicious downloads, unknown attachments and cracked software. An unexpected QR code or request to approve a device should also raise concern, as Cyber Security News’ earlier reporting on device-linking scams explains.

Unexpected sent messages or replies to conversations you never started are reasons to check your account. Open WhatsApp on your primary phone, go to Linked Devices, select any device you do not recognize, and tap Log Out.

Repeat this for each unfamiliar device. WhatsApp’s account security instructions explain how to disconnect a session remotely, even if you no longer have the computer in front of you.

If someone sent messages from your account, warn affected contacts through another channel. Ask them not to open links or act on payment requests and to verify unusual instructions by phone. In India, anyone who has lost money to online fraud should call 1930 promptly and file a complaint through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.

articles.description:
Attackers are now using a critical Cisco Expressway bug, CVE-2026-76466, to take full control of devices and move deeper into company networks. Researchers at F6 say the first known case happened soon after a public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit appeared. F6’s Cyber Defense Center looked into the first observed exploitation of the flaw, which has a […]

The post Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco Expressway Flaw to Gain Root Access and Infiltrate Internal Networks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are now using a critical Cisco Expressway bug, CVE-2026-76466, to take full control of devices and move deeper into company networks. Researchers at F6 say the first known case happened soon after a public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit appeared.

F6’s Cyber Defense Center looked into the first observed exploitation of the flaw, which has a CVSS score of 9.8. The attackers broke into Cisco Expressway X15.5.3 devices and ran commands as root, the highest level of access on a system.

Security Affairs reports that the victim was a Russian organization and that no known threat group has been linked to the activity. CISA has since added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, which usually means federal agencies must treat it as urgent.

Cisco published its advisory on October 21, 2026. It says the weakness sits in the database service. Persistent cookies are in use, and client certificates are not checked properly when TLS Verify Mode is turned on for clustering.

An attacker who holds the cookies can connect to the service and send remote procedure call commands that run as root. Only clustered Expressway-C and Expressway-E devices are affected, and Cisco says no workarounds exist. We covered the original disclosure in our earlier report on the critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability.

The attackers first broke into two Expressway devices facing the internet. From one of them, they reached two more cluster nodes on the internal network. With root access, they began building tools to spread further.

Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco Expressway Flaw

F6 found custom Python scripts made to scan the network and find open SMB shares. The scripts also talked to SQL Server and WinRM and searched GitLab repositories for passwords and other private data. The attackers edited these scripts while the attack was running.

The code included comments and fix notes pointing to an AI assistant, showing how attackers now use AI to build and adjust tools quickly. Cisco has seen similar root-level attacks on other products, such as the Cisco SD-WAN zero-day.

F6 says a key sign is a nodeup ‘wombat@127.0.0.1’ entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on the device. It means something connected to an Erlang node whose name matches the known exploit. Finding it does not prove a breach, so teams should also check other logs and files.

Update Expressway right away. Cisco lists X15.5.20 as the first fixed release for X15.5.3 and earlier, and users of X14 or older must move to a fixed release. If you cannot patch today, F6 advises blocking TCP ports 4371 to 4372 at the firewall and allowing only trusted cluster node addresses.

Patching alone may not be enough if attackers got in earlier, so run a compromise check on exposed devices. External attack surface monitoring can help find weak systems before attackers do.

Strong monitoring and incident response let teams isolate hacked systems, measure the damage, and stop lateral movement. Good network segmentation also helps, because one edge device should never give attackers a path to critical systems.

articles.title: Hackers Use AI to Discover Zero-Day in 11 Minutes, Then Take Full Control of Server
articles.description:
Hackers used autonomous AI agents to discover a previously unknown flaw in an open-source medical imaging application and later take full control of the server running it. The agents needed about 11 minutes to go from mapping the application’s interface to proving they could write files outside the intended location. They gained administrator-level access in […]

The post Hackers Use AI to Discover Zero-Day in 11 Minutes, Then Take Full Control of Server appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers used autonomous AI agents to discover a previously unknown flaw in an open-source medical imaging application and later take full control of the server running it.

The agents needed about 11 minutes to go from mapping the application’s interface to proving they could write files outside the intended location. They gained administrator-level access in a later session, not within that initial 11-minute window.

The intrusion was part of a campaign that targeted IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The activity began on September 8, 2026, and lasted about 48 hours.

The operator chose the targets and set the goal of gaining command-line access, but the agents decided what to try next as they worked through each target.

Analysts from AWS identified the activity on September 10 after finding an internet-facing instance of Cairn, an open-source AI security testing framework, running without authentication.

As AWS explained in its November 20 investigation report, the exposed server let researchers review the operator’s prompts, project settings, and agent output. AWS described a payload that gave the agents remote command access but did not name a malware family or publish a file hash.

Hackers Use AI to Discover Zero-Day in 11 Minutes

The flaw was a path traversal bug in the application’s file upload feature. Path traversal occurs when software fails to keep file operations inside the directory where they belong.

In this case, the agents demonstrated that they could write files to unintended locations. AWS assessed with high confidence that the bug was a zero-day: at the time, researchers could find no corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or previous entry in vulnerability databases.

In a later session, the agents turned that file-write access into a remote command session running as root, the server’s highest privilege level.

That outcome distinguishes the incident from AI vulnerability discovery benchmarks, which measure performance under test conditions. Here, the agents found a previously undocumented bug on a real target and used it to gain control.

AWS did not name the application or the affected universities in its report. The agents were not successful everywhere. At one university, they spent roughly 16 hours taking 148 actions against a system with a Redis database that accepted connections without authentication.

They failed to take control. In another operation, they tested more than 30,000 username and password combinations over more than six hours without finding a working login.

Those failures show what the successful intrusion alone does not: the agents could keep trying without constant supervision, but persistence did not guarantee access.

What the Campaign Means for Defenders

The operator stepped in after the discovery, giving the agents a proxy into a second university network. The server behind that connection ran the same vulnerable software.

AWS inferred that the operator used the flaw to establish the tunnel, but did not report that second compromise as directly observed. A separate AI-driven retail theft campaign also involved Cairn, though it was attributed to a financially motivated operator.

AWS assessed with moderate confidence that the university campaign had a Chinese nexus, citing Simplified Chinese prompts, script timestamps set to China Standard Time, and the choice of targets.

The evidence did not establish who ran the operation. AWS notified the project maintainers, who released a fix and a GitHub Security Advisory. Because the affected organizations were not AWS customers, the company worked with a government partner to notify them.

For security teams, the short discovery window makes prevention and fast containment more important. AWS recommends using high-confidence detections to trigger automated responses while keeping people in charge of reviewing outcomes.

Teams running security tooling should also check for exposed AI testing panels on their own networks. In this case, the operator’s unauthenticated panel gave investigators a record of actions that would otherwise have been much harder to reconstruct.

A flaw in GL.iNet’s cloud remote management services allowed unauthorized access to routers and KVM devices, enabling malicious software installation. Identified on November 20, 2026, the issue has been fixed, but infected devices still require a security firmware update. According to GL.iNet’s security notice, the cloud fix prevents new infections through this attack path but […]

The post Hackers Exploit GL.iNet Cloud Flaw to Install Malware and Backdoors on Routers and KVM Devices appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A flaw in GL.iNet’s cloud remote management services allowed unauthorized access to routers and KVM devices, enabling malicious software installation. Identified on November 20, 2026, the issue has been fixed, but infected devices still require a security firmware update.

According to GL.iNet’s security notice, the cloud fix prevents new infections through this attack path but does not remove existing malware. The company has not named the attacker or confirmed how many devices were compromised. Its investigation includes whether computers connected to affected KVM devices were also impacted.

The incident separates two recovery tasks. GL.iNet has closed the cloud entry point, while device owners must install firmware that removes the malware identified during the investigation.

The company says users can keep their settings during the update and do not need a factory reset. Updates remain recommended even when checks find nothing suspicious. Earlier reporting on IP-KVM security flaws covered separate weaknesses affecting GL.iNet and other vendors.

GL.iNet Flaw Exposes Routers and KVMs

Those findings provide background on KVM risks but should not be confused with this newly disclosed cloud incident. Cybersecurity News also examined device checks in its IP-KVM security guide.

GL.iNet’s main indicator is the exact text crond -i /tmp/.log within a running process. Router owners can open System → Advanced Settings, sign in to LuCI, and visit Status → Processes.

Searching for tmp/.log helps locate entries, but users must check for the full indicator rather than treating every temporary-file reference as malicious.

Router users can also connect through SSH and run ps | grep tmp. A result containing only the grep command is not evidence of infection.

Anyone finding the full indicator should treat the device as infected and install the latest stable security firmware for their exact model. Failed updates or a remaining indicator require help from GL.iNet support.

For KVM devices, open Toolbox → Terminal → Access and run the check on the KVM itself, not the attached computer. RMQ1 users should run ps -a | grep tmp, while other KVM models use ps -aux | grep tmp. Both checks look for the same suspicious process text.

Owners should use the GL.iNet Download Center to select their exact model and check the security notice for the required version. For example, the GL-MT6000 download page lists firmware 4.11.1, released November 22. Never install firmware intended for another model.

GL.iNet warns that quick checks may miss some infections. A clean result therefore does not replace updating. Owners of infected KVMs should also inspect connected computers for unfamiliar accounts, programs, extensions, startup entries, and unusual activity, then run an updated security scan. Customers should not wait for a notification email before checking devices or installing the security firmware update.

articles.title: Hackers Use Autonomous AI to Breach 10 Organizations and Access Over 1 Million Personal Records
articles.description:
A group of Chinese-speaking hackers used an open-source AI testing tool to run attacks with very little human help. Between August and September 2026, they broke into 10 organizations and exposed personal data. More than one million records came from a single victim. The tool did most of the work. Operators typed in a target […]

The post Hackers Use Autonomous AI to Breach 10 Organizations and Access Over 1 Million Personal Records appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A group of Chinese-speaking hackers used an open-source AI testing tool to run attacks with very little human help.

Between August and September 2026, they broke into 10 organizations and exposed personal data. More than one million records came from a single victim.

The tool did most of the work. Operators typed in a target and a goal, and the software planned each step, ran it, and saved the results.

This shows how fast autonomous AI cyberattacks are moving from theory into daily use, and how one hacker used AI agents earlier this autumn to reach over 100 company websites.

Researchers from Unit42 identified the activity and track it as CL-STA-1238. Their full technical report says the group ran 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. Unit42 believes, with moderate confidence, that this is a China-linked intelligence collection effort.

Hackers Use Autonomous AI

The attackers used a public penetration testing framework called Cairn. It is normally built for security testers, but the hackers ran a customized copy from a server in Hong Kong.

They paired it with two Chinese AI models, Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4. Thirteen operations ran on GLM 5.2, eight on DeepSeek V4 Flash, and four on DeepSeek V4 Pro. The attackers seem to have switched to the stronger Pro model when a target resisted the Flash model.

Cairn works through AI “agent workers” that share a “blackboard.” Confirmed findings are saved there as facts, and the next steps are queued as intents.

The model repeats a Reason and Explore loop until it reaches the goal, runs out of options, or the attacker stops it. For each target, it built a plan with three to seven stages.

These ran from mapping the target to web exploitation, stealing credentials, moving sideways, and staying inside the network. Single operations lasted from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours.

The attackers also tricked the models into working. They added a Chinese-language note saying every task was an authorized security test and that the model must never refuse.

Each job also got an AUTHORIZATION.md file that made the same claim. Neither GLM nor DeepSeek pushed back. This matches what Anthropic reported when it warned that AI agents automate every stage of an intrusion, from finding targets to stealing data.

The results hit three sectors: semiconductor supply chains, defense policy, and civil society. At an industry standards body, password spraying gave the attackers dozens of valid logins, and they overwrote a live ballot document.

At a semiconductor company, a brute-forced credential let them create administrator accounts and a lasting API token. A flaw in a U.S. teachers’ union’s content management system let them create valid sessions.

That exposed more than one million member records, about 31,000 CRM contacts, and staff password hashes. A defense policy platform leaked about 500 user records, some from .mil and .gov domains.

Why Old Weaknesses Still Matter

The most useful lesson is that the AI did not find anything new. Unit42 says the flaws were known ones: authentication bypasses, insecure direct object references, mass-assignment privilege escalation, weak and default passwords, exposed cloud APIs, and older public CVEs.

AI raised the volume and coverage of the intrusions, not their complexity. A single operator or small team could try 19 targets at once in about two weeks, which used to take far more people and time.

Password guessing is a good example. Defenders have seen a large password spray campaign abuse Azure CLI and bypass weak MFA settings, and AI makes that kind of guessing cheaper and faster to repeat.

Unit42 expects such model-driven campaigns to become more common as open models get stronger while their guardrails against offensive use stay weak.

Unit42 based its China link on three things: Chinese-language tasks and files, the exclusive use of Chinese AI models, and targets that match known Chinese intelligence priorities. It found no tie to a previously known threat group.

Defenders do not need exotic tools to respond. Teams should remove default and weak passwords, lock down exposed registration and cloud storage endpoints, and patch older CVEs quickly.

They should also watch for password spraying and sudden new admin accounts. Microsoft gives similar advice and tells admins to require phishing-resistant multifactor authentication for privileged accounts. Unit42 also offers an AI Security Assessment and incident response help to organizations that suspect a breach.

articles.title: Critical ASP.NET AntiCsrf Flaw Under Attack, Allowing Hackers to Execute Code Without Login
articles.description:
Attackers are exploiting a critical flaw in Idunno.AntiCsrf, a third-party library used by older ASP.NET WebForms applications. Mandiant confirmed active exploitation in its November 18 advisory and said the flaw lets remote attackers run code on affected servers without logging in. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-131914, has a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3. No official […]

The post Critical ASP.NET AntiCsrf Flaw Under Attack, Allowing Hackers to Execute Code Without Login appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are exploiting a critical flaw in Idunno.AntiCsrf, a third-party library used by older ASP.NET WebForms applications. Mandiant confirmed active exploitation in its November 18 advisory and said the flaw lets remote attackers run code on affected servers without logging in.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-131914, has a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3. No official patch is available. The National Vulnerability Database lists releases through 0.9.1 Beta as affected, including the 0.9.1.0 DLL. The flaw is in the abandoned library, not in ASP.NET WebForms itself.

Mandiant traced the issue during an incident response investigation but did not identify the attackers or disclose how many organizations were affected.

ASP.NET AntiCsrf Flaw Under Attack

Idunno.AntiCsrf was designed to stop cross-site request forgery, or CSRF, which tricks a signed-in user’s browser into taking an action they did not intend. The library checks a form token against a cookie.

The flaw is in how it reads the token: it uses .NET’s ObjectStateFormatter to turn data from the request into objects before verifying that the data can be trusted. This weakness is known as insecure deserialization, or CWE-502.

The order matters. The module processes the request before the WebForms page reaches Page_Load. A site can therefore appear to require a login while still exposing the vulnerable code if its only session check happens at that stage.

Authentication and authorization enforced earlier in the ASP.NET request pipeline can block anonymous access before the module runs. If exploitation succeeds, the code runs with the permissions of the IIS worker process, w3wp.exe.

This is different from the ASP.NET machine-key attacks previously covered by Cyber Security News. Those attacks relied on exposed keys to make tampered ViewState data look valid. Here, the third-party module does not verify the token’s authenticity before reading it. Rotating machine keys alone will not fix that flaw.

Check IIS for Compromise

Mandiant says the project’s last official build dates to December 2008. Administrators should search Web.config files for Idunno.AntiCsrf or AntiCsrfModule and check application bin folders for Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll.

Search by name as well as by file hash, since teams may have rebuilt or customized the library. Remove the module registration, its settings, and the DLL, then replace its protection with a supported anti-forgery mechanism. OWASP recommends using the framework’s built-in protection where available.

Review IIS logs for unusual POST requests to .aspx pages that returned HTTP 302 redirects or HTTP 500 errors, especially when the logged request size was larger than normal. These are leads, not proof of compromise.

An error or redirect does not mean the server stopped the attack, because the unsafe processing can occur before IIS returns the response.

If evidence points to exploitation, preserve logs, inspect web directories for unauthorized files, and review IIS for unexpected modules. Previous IIS web shell attacks show why that review matters, though Mandiant did not report a specific web shell in this case.

Rotate machine keys, encryption keys, and database credentials stored in Web.config or applicationHost.config as part of recovery. Removing the library closes the entry point, but it does not remove any backdoor an attacker may have already installed.

articles.description:
Samsung Securities confirmed on November 23 that a data breach exposed personal information belonging to 8,241 customers. The South Korean brokerage detected unauthorized access on Saturday, November 21, in its Voice of Customer (VOC) system, a website service for complaints and inquiries. The company found no evidence of exposure outside the affected system. The breach […]

The post Samsung Securities Data Breach Exposes 8,241 Customers’ Personal and Account Details appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Samsung Securities confirmed on November 23 that a data breach exposed personal information belonging to 8,241 customers. The South Korean brokerage detected unauthorized access on Saturday, November 21, in its Voice of Customer (VOC) system, a website service for complaints and inquiries.

The company found no evidence of exposure outside the affected system. The breach involved some files customers uploaded with their submissions, not the brokerage’s main customer database.

Samsung Securities Data Breach

The files contained 13 categories of personal information across all affected customers, including names, account numbers, home addresses, contact details, and driver’s license numbers, Yonhap reported.

That does not mean every customer lost all 13 types of information. The details varied depending on what each person uploaded. Samsung Securities said that customers who had not used the website’s VOC service were unaffected.

The attachments matter because a support form can hold sensitive records even when it sits apart from the brokerage’s trading systems. Someone posing as a Samsung Securities employee could cite a real account number or address to make a call sound legitimate.

The Coupang data breach raised a similar phishing concern after contact and order details were exposed, although it was a separate incident.

The brokerage blocked the internet address linked to the intrusion, suspended the complaint service and reported the breach to South Korea’s Financial Supervisory Service and the Korea Internet & Security Agency. Chief Executive Park Jong-moon issued an apology.

Samsung Securities was reviewing its other systems and investigating how the files were exposed. The company had not publicly explained how the intruder gained access.

Samsung Securities said it would notify affected customers individually and tell them which details were exposed. Customers can also open the brokerage’s website directly and look for the “Personal (Credit) Information Leak Inquiry” menu.

The company set up a dedicated support channel and said it would compensate customers for verified losses under applicable laws and its internal rules.

Samsung Securities warned customers about phishing calls and emails that may use the leaked details. If someone calls about the breach and asks for a password or a one-time code, hang up and contact the brokerage using the number on its official website.

Avoid opening attachments or following links in unexpected breach notices. Check account activity for any trades or transfers you do not recognize and report them through the brokerage’s official support channel. A caller knowing your account number is not proof they work for Samsung Securities.

articles.description:
Bulgaria has disrupted a cyberespionage operation that gave hackers covert access to state administration networks for five years. Innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vasilev said on November 18 that the intruders illegally downloaded at least 130 gigabytes of government documents, equivalent to more than 62 million pages. He described it as the longest-running known […]

The post Hackers Secretly Spy on Bulgarian Government for Five Years and Steal 62 Million Pages of Documents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Bulgaria has disrupted a cyberespionage operation that gave hackers covert access to state administration networks for five years.

Innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vasilev said on November 18 that the intruders illegally downloaded at least 130 gigabytes of government documents, equivalent to more than 62 million pages.

He described it as the longest-running known cyberespionage case targeting Bulgarian institutions. The hackers targeted systems that government offices use to exchange official documents and collected sensitive information about the work of the state.

Vasilev said investigators had found no evidence so far that Bulgarian citizens’ personal data was compromised. That finding does not mean the stolen material was harmless, and authorities have not released a full inventory of the documents taken.

The Bulgarian News Agency’s report noted that multiple hacking groups had operated inside Bulgarian systems since 2021, with additional cases of unauthorized access identified in 2022.

BTA did not identify a malware family or report how the groups first got in. Vasilev did not name the countries from which they operated.

The public timeline therefore shows when investigators traced activity, not whether every group had the same access or stayed inside for the full five years.

Hackers Secretly Spy on Bulgarian Government

The choice of target helps explain the scale of the theft. A service that moves official documents between offices can expose material from more than one institution.

In a separate case, government webmail espionage campaigns showed how shared government services can become sources of intelligence.

Bulgaria has confirmed that its document exchange systems were targeted, but it has not said which offices lost records, how many individual files were taken, or whether any of the documents were classified.

Vasilev said the activity went undetected across several governments because existing security measures did not work as a single system. A new national cybersecurity platform gave investigators a wider view of activity across government networks.

The ministry first disclosed unauthorized access in August, while that platform was being rolled out. At the time, officials said the intrusion appeared to have lasted years but were still investigating its scope.

The November briefing put a lower bound on the amount of data taken. The 62 million pages figure describes the equivalent volume of the stolen material, not a count of individual files.

Separate reporting on a government cloud data theft in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region provides another example of why the amount downloaded and the sensitivity of the records are different questions.

In Bulgaria, the 130-gigabyte figure establishes scale, but it does not tell readers what the intruders obtained from any particular agency.

Bulgaria brought together its Interior and Defence ministries, intelligence agencies and national incident response team to investigate.

Information Services JSC, private-sector specialists and international partners, including the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, supported the work.

Vasilev said responders cut the links to the hackers’ infrastructure and removed them from state systems. He also referred the findings to prosecutors to examine what authorities did or failed to do over the five years.

A parliamentary committee agreed to hear further details behind closed doors. The government is extending its national monitoring system to 28 municipalities and regional administrations.

It is also introducing multifactor authentication, which requires a second form of verification at sign-in, and tighter controls on administrator accounts.

For defenders, the case illustrates why centralized security event logging matters: investigators can compare activity across networks instead of relying on each office to spot a pattern in isolation. The new access controls are part of the response, not evidence that stolen passwords caused the breach.

The post Hackers Use 480+ Malicious Ad Domains to Target iPhones and Steal Crypto Wallet Recovery Phrases appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are using a large network of malicious ads to break into vulnerable iPhones and steal cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases, passwords, messages, and photos.

Researchers tracking the operation, named MoldyRoost, identified more than 480 advertising domains targeting users across over 47 countries between May 12 and November 17, 2026.

According to Confiant’s investigation, opening an infected ad’s landing page can trigger an exploit attempt without requiring a download or command.

Researchers Roshan and Eliya Stein published their findings on November 20, describing a delivery system built around paid ads, hidden browser frames, and stolen data tracking.

MoldyRoost purchases ads through automated advertising systems and directs visitors to attacker-controlled websites. These pages often copy trusted brands or promote games, travel offers, cryptocurrency services, and news content.

The operators use cloaking to hide their activity. This technique checks details such as the visitor’s device, browser, and location before deciding what content to display. Security scanners, advertising reviewers, and unsupported devices may receive harmless pages instead of malicious code.

Malicious Ad Domains Target iPhones and Crypto Wallets

On a targeted iPhone, an invisible browser frame checks the iOS version and loads a matching exploit chain. The chain uses several flaws in sequence to run code, escape browser restrictions, and gain deeper access to the device.

One campaign copied Agoda’s Hong Kong website. A hidden frame started the attack while a loading screen delayed the visitor before forwarding them to the real service.

Other campaigns used fake Cloudflare verification pages that kept visitors waiting while exploits loaded, without requiring users to copy or execute commands as in ClickFix attacks.

The operation uses Coruna, DarkSword, SilkPath, and GhostWave branches to select payloads for different iOS versions. Researchers found routing logic for newer releases but did not confirm working iOS 26 exploit code.

Google’s Coruna analysis describes 23 exploits arranged into five chains covering iOS 13.0 through 17.2.1. Its wallet-stealing features target applications including MetaMask, Phantom, and Trust Wallet, while also searching saved notes and images for recovery information.

Cybersecurity News previously reported how Coruna hides inside advertising landing pages, showing how advertising networks provide another route for delivering these tools.

DarkSword targets iOS 18.4 through 18.7 and chains six vulnerabilities, including three zero-days. Its data collection features can steal keychain records, messages, wallet information, saved Wi-Fi passwords, and location history. Earlier coverage of DarkSword’s expanding malicious infrastructure also highlighted its growing reach.

Researchers divided MoldyRoost into six related groups, labeled A through F. The largest accounted for 403 advertising domains, with heavy targeting in Hong Kong, Japan, and Singapore.

An exposed server repository provided further insight into the operation. Recovered code showed that separate payloads were built for different sales channels, allowing stolen wallet data to be linked to the campaign responsible for delivering the victim.

This structure suggests a possible reseller or affiliate setup. However, researchers have not established whether one group controls every campaign or different customers share the platform.

The findings show how advanced iPhone exploit tools are reaching broader criminal campaigns. The reported domain count measures advertising infrastructure, not confirmed infections, and the research does not establish how many wallets were successfully drained.

articles.title: Palo Alto Confirms NGINX Vulnerabilities Impact PAN-OS and Releases Workarounds
articles.description:
Palo Alto Networks confirmed that two critical NGINX flaws, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, affect PAN-OS and Panorama deployments with HTTP/2 enabled. The flaws could allow unauthenticated remote attackers to crash worker processes or execute code, prompting Palo Alto Networks to release patches and a workaround for affected systems. The security advisory assigns a CVSS v4.0 score […]

The post Palo Alto Confirms NGINX Vulnerabilities Impact PAN-OS and Releases Workarounds appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Palo Alto Networks confirmed that two critical NGINX flaws, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, affect PAN-OS and Panorama deployments with HTTP/2 enabled.

The flaws could allow unauthenticated remote attackers to crash worker processes or execute code, prompting Palo Alto Networks to release patches and a workaround for affected systems.

The security advisory assigns a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and a moderate response urgency. Palo Alto Networks says it is not aware of malicious exploitation.

Customers without HTTP/2 enabled are not affected by these issues. Panorama virtual appliances and M-Series appliances are included in the affected products.

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free flaw in NGINX HTTP/2 proxy handling. Active connections can remain marked as reusable when they should not be. If a worker runs low on connection slots, NGINX may close connections and release memory. At the same time, it still sends requests to backend servers.

That memory error can crash the worker or allow code execution. The CVE record adds an important limit for the underlying NGINX flaw. Code execution requires Address Space Layout Randomization, or ASLR, to be disabled or bypassed. ASLR makes memory locations harder to predict, which helps block exploitation.

Palo Alto Confirms NGINX RCE Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-123007 affects HTTP/2 flow control, which manages how much data a connection can send. An integer underflow lets the flow-control window exceed its allowed limit. Specially crafted traffic can then trigger a heap-based buffer overflow, causing a crash or allowing an attacker to run code.

Cyber Security News previously covered these NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities, including their different attack conditions. They also appear in its wider reporting on the NGINX2Root vulnerabilities.

The Palo Alto notice now gives customers product-specific guidance rather than requiring them to rely on upstream NGINX version numbers.

For PAN-OS 12.2, the vendor directs customers to upgrade to 12.2.4-h3 or later. On PAN-OS 12.1, customers running affected 12.1.8 through 12.1.10 builds should install 12.1.10-h6 or later. Those on 12.1.5 through 12.1.7 can use 12.1.7-h15 or 12.1.10-h6, subject to release availability.

For PAN-OS 11.2, fixed options include 11.2.10-h19, 11.2.13-h6, and 11.2.16-h3, depending on the maintenance branch. The advisory lists November 23 as the expected release date for 12.1.7-h15, 11.2.10-h19, and 11.2.13-h6. Customers should confirm availability before scheduling an upgrade.

The vendor lists PAN-OS 12.1 versions below 12.1.5 and PAN-OS 11.2 versions below 11.2.8 as unaffected. Other on-premises products not listed were reviewed and found unaffected. Palo Alto Networks is managing fixes for its SaaS products, with no customer action required.

Customers unable to patch can disable HTTP/2 on PAN-OS and Panorama using the vendor’s HTTP/2 configuration documentation. The documentation says HTTP/1.1 is enabled by default, while HTTP/2 requires manual configuration.

Teams should therefore check both the installed software version and protocol settings when reviewing exposure, then apply the appropriate fixed release.

A screenshot shared by Dark Web Informer shows the seller claiming that the tool can create a new vCenter administrator account. The listing surfaced after Broadcom issued a fix on November 19, 2026. The post Hackers Allegedly Claiming Exploit for VMware vCenter 0-day Vulnerability appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A forum seller using the name Matilda is asking $30,000 for a claimed exploit targeting CVE-2026-123890, a critical VMware vCenter Server vulnerability.

A screenshot shared by Dark Web Informer shows the seller claiming that the tool can create a new vCenter administrator account. The listing surfaced after Broadcom issued a fix on November 19, 2026. The tool’s claimed capabilities and compatibility have not been independently verified.

The seller describes the tool as a Python program with separate functions for checking whether a server is vulnerable and exploiting the flaw.

The post claims support for affected releases from vCenter 7.0 through 9.1 and offers prospective buyers a demonstration. An offer is not proof of a successful test, and the listing does not establish that the seller used the tool against any organization.

VMware vCenter Attacks Began Before Patch

Broadcom’s VMSA-2026-0009 advisory rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of the VMware vCenter authentication bypass, the flaw affects VMware Directory Service, which supports vCenter’s single sign-on system.

An attacker who can reach an affected server over the network can bypass login without valid credentials. That matters because vCenter provides a central place to manage VMware hosts and virtual machines.

Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant traced attacks exploiting the flaw to early September 2026, before a patch was available. In earlier coverage of the vCenter zero-day attacks, Cyber Security News reported that a suspected China-linked group known as ARMORY CASTLE used a separate tool called BONESAW.

The documented attacks explain why the flaw is described as a zero-day. The forum post, by contrast, advertises an exploit for a flaw that has since been disclosed and patched. The reporting does not link Matilda to ARMORY CASTLE.

VMware vCenter Patch

Broadcom lists fixes in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 Update 3m. VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x customers should follow the vendor’s guidance for release 5.2.5.

The advisory lists no public fix for vCenter 7.0 and directs customers with extended support contracts to contact Broadcom Support. Administrators should use the vendor’s response matrix to confirm the correct update for their deployment.

The National Vulnerability Database entry records the flaw’s addition to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 20. Broadcom lists no workaround, so teams should apply the relevant update without waiting for the forum claim to be verified.

They should also review vCenter sign-in records and administrator account changes for unexpected activity, especially on servers that were reachable from untrusted networks before patching. An update closes the flaw, but it does not establish whether an attacker used it before the fix was installed.

articles.title: Researchers Hack Volkswagen Cars via Bluetooth to Spy on Conversations and Track GPS Locations
articles.description:
Bluetooth flaws in Volkswagen cars could expose private conversations, reveal GPS locations, and allow unauthorized control of cabin features. The findings highlight a lengthy patch rollout, with some vehicles remaining exposed roughly 16 months after the vulnerabilities became public. Hungarian firm PCA Cyber Security demonstrated the attack against a Volkswagen ID.4 in Budapest, according to […]

The post Researchers Hack Volkswagen Cars via Bluetooth to Spy on Conversations and Track GPS Locations appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Bluetooth flaws in Volkswagen cars could expose private conversations, reveal GPS locations, and allow unauthorized control of cabin features.

The findings highlight a lengthy patch rollout, with some vehicles remaining exposed roughly 16 months after the vulnerabilities became public. Hungarian firm PCA Cyber Security demonstrated the attack against a Volkswagen ID.4 in Budapest, according to heise’s report.

Researchers reportedly accessed the hands-free microphone, monitored location data, and operated the heater, windshield wipers, and sunroof using a laptop outside the vehicle.

The attack uses PerfektBlue, a chain of vulnerabilities in OpenSynergy’s BlueSDK Bluetooth software. This component handles wireless connections in vehicle infotainment systems. PCA’s security advisory explains how the flaws can be combined to run attacker-controlled code on affected systems.

For the demonstrated Volkswagen attack, the driver must first approve a Bluetooth pairing request. Once connected, the attacker can exploit the vulnerable software and gain control over functions available through the infotainment system.

That requirement is important. The demonstration does not show that an attacker can silently compromise every nearby Volkswagen without interaction. Rejecting an unfamiliar pairing request blocks the connection this attack needs.

Volkswagen Cars Hacked via Bluetooth

Cyber Security News previously covered the underlying weaknesses in its report on the PerfektBlue Bluetooth vulnerabilities, which affected software used across multiple vehicle brands.

Researchers estimate that several hundred thousand Volkswagen vehicles could be affected. However, that figure is not a confirmed count of compromised cars, and the reported demonstration does not establish widespread criminal exploitation.

Volkswagen told heise that older infotainment software required additional changes and security checks, which delayed repairs. The company said it had addressed the issue more quickly in newer software branches.

For vehicles running software older than version 4.0, Volkswagen says version 3.9.1 fixes the vulnerability. Eligible owners can install that update over cellular or Wi-Fi while their vehicle is parked.

Other affected software versions require a workshop visit. Volkswagen says vehicles running version 5.6 or later are not affected. Owners should confirm the correct update route with Volkswagen rather than assume every car receives the same fix.

Volkswagen says the flaws do not provide access to steering, braking, or acceleration. The demonstrated access instead concerns infotainment and connected cabin functions.

Nevertheless, microphone access could expose sensitive conversations, while GPS tracking could reveal journeys and regular destinations. Those privacy risks remain significant even when driving controls are outside the attacker’s reach.

Earlier research also identified separate weaknesses affecting vehicle data and infotainment systems, as detailed in Cyber Security News’ coverage of Skoda and Volkswagen security flaws. Those findings should not be treated as the same vulnerability chain.

Volkswagen advises owners never to accept unknown Bluetooth pairing requests or connect unfamiliar USB devices. Drivers should check their installed software version, follow official update instructions, and contact a dealer when patch availability is unclear. Volkswagen has not announced a recall for this issue, according to heise’s report.

articles.title: OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra Discovers 0-Day Vulnerabilities Enabling Mobile OS Security Bypass and RCE
articles.description:
OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra has found and exploited zero-day vulnerabilities affecting a popular mobile operating system and a widely hosted network service, according to the company’s latest system card. The findings include a permission bypass that exposed private data and a separate remote code execution flaw reachable from a low-privileged role. The discoveries came from testing […]

The post OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra Discovers 0-Day Vulnerabilities Enabling Mobile OS Security Bypass and RCE appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra has found and exploited zero-day vulnerabilities affecting a popular mobile operating system and a widely hosted network service, according to the company’s latest system card.

The findings include a permission bypass that exposed private data and a separate remote code execution flaw reachable from a low-privileged role. The discoveries came from testing by security firm Irregular, rather than reports of attacks against users.

OpenAI’s November 17 system card says Irregular is handling responsible disclosure. It does not name the affected products, identify vulnerable versions, provide CVE numbers, or confirm when patches will become available.

The mobile operating system flaw allowed a malicious app to access private data despite lacking the required permissions. That finding points to a failure in the operating system’s access controls. The published account does not identify the exposed data types or explain which permission checks the app bypassed.

OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra Discovers Zero-Day Vulnerabilities

The remote code execution finding involved a separate network service. Astra exploited the service from a low-privileged role, showing that limited access was enough to reach code execution. The report does not establish unauthenticated access, administrator control, or a mobile exploit chain linking the two discoveries.

Keeping those findings separate is important. The mobile issue concerns access to protected information, while the network service issue concerns running code. Neither description supports claims that Astra remotely took over phones or compromised every device using the unnamed operating system.

Irregular tested Astra through FrontierCyber, which measures offensive skills on real-world systems, and CyScenarioBench, which covers multi-stage security operations.

Astra solved 68 of 217 FrontierCyber challenges, compared with 77 for GPT-6 Astra. The newer model therefore discovered serious flaws without outperforming its predecessor across that entire suite.

Neither model successfully attacked a fully hardened target. All 15 of the hardest FrontierCyber challenges remained unsolved. On CyScenarioBench, both models solved nine of 11 challenges at least once. At the same time, Astra’s success rate reached 63%, compared with 61% for its predecessor.

Separate OpenAI tests showed stronger progress in developing exploits for known vulnerabilities. Astra achieved a 53.5% mean arbitrary code execution rate on ExploitBench Internal Port, compared with 31.5% for GPT-6 Astra. That evaluation used V8 and Chrome flaws disclosed between June and August 2026, not newly discovered zero-days.

The distinction helps readers judge the results fairly. Finding an unknown flaw and turning a disclosed bug into working code are related skills, but they are not the same task. Earlier reporting on Astra’s zero-day research provides background on this growing capability.

OpenAI says both GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol meet its Critical cybersecurity capability threshold. The company describes tighter restrictions on higher-risk assistance, monitoring, and additional approval for more permissive access. The company conducted its capability evaluations without production safeguards, so the results should not be treated as a description of ordinary customer access.

Previous coverage of OpenAI’s security isolation tests also shows why containment matters alongside model rules. These systems can help researchers find weaknesses, but their tools and access need firm limits.

For now, the missing product names and patch details prevent specific exposure checks. The immediate takeaway is evidence of successful zero-day research under evaluation conditions, not proof of widespread exploitation. Further disclosure will determine which users need fixes and how urgently vendors must respond.

articles.description:
Cleverbridge confirmed that hackers copied payment card data from its e-commerce platform. The stolen information includes card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV or CVC security codes. Cleverbridge’s public update does not list those fields or say whether the same details were exposed for every affected customer. The company began notifying affected individuals on November 20, […]

The post Cleverbridge Confirms Hackers Stole Customer Card Numbers and CVV Codes in a Major Data Breach appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cleverbridge confirmed that hackers copied payment card data from its e-commerce platform. The stolen information includes card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV or CVC security codes.

Cleverbridge’s public update does not list those fields or say whether the same details were exposed for every affected customer. The company began notifying affected individuals on November 20, 2026.

According to Cleverbridge’s incident update, the company detected unauthorized activity on November 4 and temporarily took affected systems offline to contain it. All systems were back online that day, but investigators later found that someone had copied payment card data stored on the platform.

Cleverbridge Data Breach

Cleverbridge said the incident was not ransomware and that none of its systems were encrypted. Restoring service addressed the outage, but it did not undo the theft.

Cleverbridge handles online purchases, payments, and subscriptions for other businesses, so affected shoppers may recognize the seller rather than the company that processed their payment.

The public notice does not identify the affected merchants, give a count of impacted customers, or explain how the attackers got in or how long they had access. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of separate breaches at financial service providers, stolen customer data does not necessarily mean the business customers bought from was itself breached.

A CVV or CVC is the three- or four-digit security code printed on a payment card. Online merchants use it to help verify that the buyer has the card. When thieves have the card number, expiration date, and security code, they can try to make online purchases without the physical card.

The PCI Security Standards Council says merchants must not retain these codes after a payment is authorized, even in encrypted form. Cleverbridge has not publicly explained where it stored the exposed codes or for how long, so the available information does not show whether it broke that rule.

If you receive a Cleverbridge breach notice, check which card it identifies and review recent transactions. Report any charge you do not recognize to your card issuer right away.

Even if you have not spotted fraud, contact the issuer through its official app or the number on your card and ask whether it should be replaced. Cleverbridge says it hired TransUnion’s Cyberscout to help notify customers and offered credit or identity monitoring where available. Enrollment details are in the individual notices.

Treat unexpected calls, emails, or texts about the breach with caution. Cyber Security News has documented how fake billing notices can send people to convincing payment pages that ask for card details and one-time codes.

Cleverbridge says it will never ask for card details, passwords, or security codes by email, phone, or text. If a message asks you to verify a card or claim help, check it through a trusted contact channel rather than using the link or phone number in the message.
