articles.title: VirusTotal’s New Ransomware Detection Catches Malware Missed by All 75 Antivirus Engines
articles.description:
VirusTotal has rolled out a ransomware detection update that checks whether suspicious files actually encrypt user documents during execution. The new checks caught a Python ransomware sample that recorded zero detections across 75 antivirus engines at the time of analysis, showing how behavior checks can expose threats that static scanning misses. The update spans VirusTotal […]

The post VirusTotal’s New Ransomware Detection Catches Malware Missed by All 75 Antivirus Engines appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
VirusTotal has rolled out a ransomware detection update that checks whether suspicious files actually encrypt user documents during execution.

The new checks caught a Python ransomware sample that recorded zero detections across 75 antivirus engines at the time of analysis, showing how behavior checks can expose threats that static scanning misses.

The update spans VirusTotal and Google Threat Intelligence, adding verified encryption tags, stricter ransomware behavior rules, and support for real-time hunting. Rather than treating encryption code or heavy file activity as proof of ransomware, the system looks for damage to user documents inside controlled test environments.

The new tag:encrypts-files search tag and behaviour_tags:encrypts_files behavior trait work across CAPE Sandbox and Zenbox on Windows, plus macOS Mirage on Apple Silicon. VirusTotal introduced macOS Mirage to provide native Apple Silicon malware analysis and detailed behavior reports.

Each environment contains realistic user documents. During and after execution, the sandboxes inspect changed files for broken document structures, unusual byte patterns, and higher data randomness. These checks examine the results on disk instead of relying only on calls to operating system encryption tools.

VirusTotal Ransomware Detection Missed

That approach covers malware using built-in AES, ChaCha20, XOR, or partial encryption routines. Such variation matters because ransomware families use different methods to damage files, as seen in Beast ransomware’s partial encryption design.

The sandboxes also track linked file reads, writes, renames, and deletions. The sandbox excludes routine installer activity, browser caches, and temporary files. A ransom note or encryption function alone does not trigger the tag.

The standout example is system_update.pyw, a Python locker linked to a .k404 extortion campaign submitted on November 17–18. Although its static scan showed 0/75 detections, Zenbox observed it running through pythonw.exe, deleting itself, and rewriting Desktop documents into .k404 encrypted files.

A related Windows program, K404T_Fidye.exe, had 10/75 detections. Another locker, lkd.exe, had just 3/75. CAPE confirmed that both encrypted user documents, providing evidence beyond their antivirus scores.

The checks also identified INC Ransom encrypting documents.INC files and dropping INC-README.txt ransom notes. INC has previously appeared in healthcare attacks linked to Vanilla Tempest, underlining the value of clear encryption evidence during investigations.

VirusTotal reports that the tag matched 55 files among 328,257 newly submitted unique files analyzed since November 17. Manual review found no benign software among those matches. These early results do not establish that future scans will have no false positives.

CAPE also tightened its mapping to MITRE ATT&CK T1486, Data Encrypted for Impact. Generic file activity now requires verified document encryption before receiving that mapping. VirusTotal says the change reduced false-positive T1486 volume across the platform by 97.6%.

Analysts can search entity: file tag:encrypts-files or use VirusTotal Livehunt with the YARA-X trait vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES for real-time alerts. Adding a low antivirus detection threshold helps focus hunts on overlooked samples.

A missing tag, however, is not a clean verdict. Malware may need passwords, user input, network access, or more time before it starts encrypting. The feature confirms observed file encryption, not the absence of ransomware when a sandbox run shows none.

Analysts should also remember that the reported 0/75 score describes the sample at analysis time, not a permanent detection result, and does not prove every endpoint product would fail to stop it.

articles.title: OpenRouter Users’ Private AI Chats Possibly Exposed Via Compromised Third-Party Providers
articles.description:
OpenRouter has removed three AI hosting providers and revoked Zero Data Retention eligibility for 125 endpoints after researchers found evidence that some providers had been compromised or had failed to follow their data policies. In its November 22 incident notice, OpenRouter said it notified all potentially affected customers. The findings did not show a breach […]

The post OpenRouter Users’ Private AI Chats Possibly Exposed Via Compromised Third-Party Providers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OpenRouter has removed three AI hosting providers and revoked Zero Data Retention eligibility for 125 endpoints after researchers found evidence that some providers had been compromised or had failed to follow their data policies.

In its November 22 incident notice, OpenRouter said it notified all potentially affected customers. The findings did not show a breach of OpenRouter itself, and the company did not say how many users or conversations may have been exposed.

OpenRouter AI Chat Leaks

OpenRouter gives customers a single API for accessing AI models hosted by different providers. But the company that first receives a request may not be the only one that handles it.

If a provider forwards the request to another service, that service can also see the prompt. As Cyber Security News explained in its comparison of AI privacy gateways, routing requests and keeping them confidential are separate tasks.

In its research report, Dragos said it sent nearly two million test prompts between July and November 2026. The prompts contained unique links and test credentials known as canary tokens.

When a link was opened, or a credential was used, researchers could trace it to the original request. Dragos found evidence of compromises at three hosting providers. Some test requests were copied even though the model rejected them before processing.

The researchers also saw signs that some requests marked for Zero Data Retention, a policy that says prompts and replies should not be stored, were kept or forwarded. In one case, a test link sent to a U.S. provider surfaced in a company chat in China 24 days later.

What OpenRouter Users Should Check

OpenRouter’s provider disclosures list notices from Novita, Phala, and Together. The company said it removed some endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility as a precaution, so the 125 removals do not represent 125 confirmed breaches.

It is checking whether providers forward requests or replies to other companies and plans to verify endpoints before restoring their eligibility.

Customers who received a notice should review what they sent through the affected provider. If prompts contained passwords or API keys, revoke or rotate them and check access logs for unusual activity.

Earlier Cyber Security News reporting on exposed Clawdbot gateways showed why chat histories and credentials need to be reviewed together. For future requests, restrict sensitive workloads to approved providers and keep secrets out of prompts rather than relying on retention settings alone.

articles.title: Hackers Could Execute Commands on WordPress, Email and Print Servers Through Upload2Shell Flaw
articles.description:
A flaw in Ghostscript let researchers run commands on WordPress, Roundcube webmail, and Linux print servers through routine file processing. The vulnerability, dubbed Upload2Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-125396, affects upstream Ghostscript releases before 10.08.0. It sits in the software’s Type 1 font loader, but the affected servers did not need to expose Ghostscript directly. Their […]

The post Hackers Could Execute Commands on WordPress, Email and Print Servers Through Upload2Shell Flaw appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A flaw in Ghostscript let researchers run commands on WordPress, Roundcube webmail, and Linux print servers through routine file processing. The vulnerability, dubbed Upload2Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-125396, affects upstream Ghostscript releases before 10.08.0.

It sits in the software’s Type 1 font loader, but the affected servers did not need to expose Ghostscript directly. Their own preview, thumbnail, and print features delivered files to it.

The CVE record gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.5 and lists a local attack vector. That describes the flaw at the interpreter level, not how a document arrives there.

In research published on November 17, Paulos Yibelo and pwn.ai showed that network-facing services could pass remotely supplied files to the vulnerable code. The report describes research demonstrations, not confirmed attacks in the wild.

Upload2Shell Bypassed Ghostscript’s Sandbox

Ghostscript renders PDFs and PostScript documents. PostScript is a programming language for describing pages, so rendering a file means running instructions from it.

Ghostscript’s -dSAFER mode is meant to limit what those instructions can access. Upload2Shell undermined those limits through a use-after-free, a memory flaw in which software keeps a reference to data after releasing the memory that held it.

The font loader failed to check the type of data it received before an operation that could raise an error. That error exposed a protected write that document code was not supposed to control.

Researchers used the resulting memory flaw to alter Ghostscript’s security checks while -dSAFER was still enabled. The test commands ran with the renderer’s permissions, not automatically as root. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of a separate Ghostscript PDF flaw, those permissions help determine what an attacker can reach after gaining code execution.

WordPress, Roundcube and CUPS were Exposed

On WordPress, the researchers reached Ghostscript through the media preview process on a site using Imagick and ImageMagick. The WordPress advisory tracks the core upload issue separately as CVE-2026-65640. It requires media upload privileges, which Authors and higher roles have by default.

As covered in our WordPress Imagick vulnerability report, WordPress fixed that route in 7.0.4 and backported the fix, including to 6.9.7. The researchers also found that certain public upload features in Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor reached the renderer without a login in the configurations tested.

On Roundcube 1.7.2, the sender needed no webmail account. The recipient had to view the message, but did not have to click or download the attachment. Roundcube’s server generated a thumbnail and passed the attachment through ImageMagick to Ghostscript. The test depended on an ImageMagick policy that allowed the handoff. The command ran as www-data, the web service account, rather than on the recipient’s device.

The print server required no action from a recipient. On Debian 13, a shared CUPS queue accepted network print jobs without credentials and sent the test document to Ghostscript for conversion. The researchers confirmed command execution by writing a marker file as lp, the print service account.

Requiring authentication blocked anonymous submission in the test, but did not repair the underlying flaw. These were three ways to reach the same vulnerable renderer, not three separate flaws in Ghostscript.

Artifex fixed the underlying flaw in Ghostscript 10.08.0. Linux distributions can apply the same fix to an older release, so the upstream version number alone is not enough to judge exposure. Debian 13, for example, first shipped the fix in 10.05.1~dfsg-1+deb13u2.

Administrators should check their vendor’s package status for CVE-2026-125396 and verify the copy used by each service. Updating the host does not replace Ghostscript inside an existing container or application bundle.

WordPress operators should apply both the core and renderer updates and review public forms that send uploads into the Media Library. If patching must wait, suspend automatic previews for untrusted files where practical.

On print servers, require authentication for shared queues and restrict network access to them. Keep renderers isolated and give their service accounts only the access they need.

The key check comes after a file is accepted. Storing a file did not start Ghostscript in the researchers’ tests. Rendering it did. Trace the worker that actually makes the preview, thumbnail or print output, then verify that worker uses the patched package.

articles.description:
Attackers exploited a flaw in Microsoft Entra Connect Health to read administrator and technical contact email addresses, along with configuration data from affected organizations. A Microsoft customer notice shared on Reddit describes read-only access to those records, not access to inboxes or email messages. Microsoft fixed the flaw in its cloud service on November 19, […]

The post Hackers Exploit Microsoft Entra Connect Health Flaw to Access Admin Emails and Organization Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers exploited a flaw in Microsoft Entra Connect Health to read administrator and technical contact email addresses, along with configuration data from affected organizations.

A Microsoft customer notice shared on Reddit describes read-only access to those records, not access to inboxes or email messages. Microsoft fixed the flaw in its cloud service on November 19, 2026, and said customers do not need to install a patch.

Microsoft said the vulnerability was introduced on July 23 and detected on November 9. Investigators reviewed service logs for unauthorized requests and concluded on November 20 that attackers had read tenant data.

The flaw could also have allowed changes to monitoring settings, but Microsoft found none. The notice does not say when the unauthorized access began, who was behind it, or how many organizations were affected.

Entra Connect Health Flaw Exposed

Microsoft Entra Connect Health lets IT teams view alerts, performance data, and directory sync errors for identity systems running on their own servers. The flaw was in the cloud monitoring service’s API. Unlike a separate Entra ID flaw involving Global Administrator privileges, this incident involved confirmed reads of tenant records, with no reported takeover of administrator accounts through the flaw.

The records included each affected tenant’s ID, display name, initial domain, country code, regional scope, and Entra license tier. They also showed whether directory sync was enabled, when it last ran, and whether the organization had set up Connect Health.

The API still returned an expired certificate once used to register monitoring agents with an internal Microsoft service shut down in late 2024. Microsoft said the flaw did not expose passwords, password hashes, sign-in tokens, valid cryptographic keys, Azure subscription details, or details about how local Active Directory servers were arranged.

The cloud fix stopped further access through the flaw, but it cannot take back the contact details already exposed. Knowing who administers a tenant and which domain it uses could make a fake support message more convincing.

Previous Microsoft 365 phishing campaigns show why unexpected sign-in requests deserve scrutiny. The notice did not report any phishing linked to this incident.

Microsoft advised organizations to alert their IT and security teams, confirm their technical contact details, and require phishing-resistant multifactor authentication for privileged accounts.

Where available, teams should use Privileged Identity Management to grant admin access only when needed. They should also check Connect Health settings and review Entra audit and sign-in logs and Azure Activity Logs for unexpected changes or unusual administrator activity.

Administrators should open the Azure portal directly and check the security advisory in Azure Service Health to confirm whether it lists their tenant.

The notice also points to Microsoft’s read-only GetTenant PowerShell script, which shows the types of records the API could have returned. It reports current values, so it cannot reconstruct what attackers saw or tell an organization which specific records were read.

articles.title: MCP Server Security: How to Stop Rogue AI Agents
articles.description:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets AI applications connect to external tools, APIs, and business data through a standardized interface. But every MCP server adds another entry point that attackers can target. MCP server security is becoming an important concern as organizations give AI agents access to increasingly sensitive systems. DataDome reported in October 2025 […]

The post MCP Server Security: How to Stop Rogue AI Agents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets AI applications connect to external tools, APIs, and business data through a standardized interface. But every MCP server adds another entry point that attackers can target.

MCP server security is becoming an important concern as organizations give AI agents access to increasingly sensitive systems.

DataDome reported in October 2025 that more than 16,000 MCP servers had been deployed across Fortune 500 companies.

Each connection creates opportunities for automation, but also potential exposure if access is not properly controlled.

The challenge is verifying not just who connects, but what each agent intends to do.

What Are the Main Security Risks of MCP Servers?

MCP servers introduce risks that extend beyond traditional API attacks. Attackers can scan exposed tools for vulnerabilities, use compromised credentials to access connected resources, or scrape sensitive information through repeated requests.

Malicious agents can also exploit excessive permissions or manipulate tool inputs to trigger unintended actions.

Three attack patterns deserve particular attention.

1. Vulnerability scanning and exploitation

An exposed MCP server can reveal available tools, their descriptions, input parameters, and underlying functionality.

Attackers can use this information to identify weak validation, outdated dependencies, or tools that expose sensitive operations.

For example, an MCP server connected to an internal database might expose a search tool. If it accepts unrestricted query parameters, an attacker could test inputs designed to retrieve unauthorized records or exploit an injection vulnerability.

Akamai researchers have documented vulnerabilities in multiple MCP server implementations, including SQL injection, missing authentication, and unauthenticated data exposure.

These findings demonstrate how familiar application security weaknesses can affect MCP infrastructure.

2. Credential stuffing and account abuse

MCP servers frequently interact with authenticated services. If attackers obtain credentials or tokens, they may use an MCP connection to access information or perform actions through legitimate-looking requests.

DataDome’s 2026 State of Bot & Agent Security Report found that AI agents generated 605.6 million requests to high-risk endpoints during January–June 2026.

These included login pages, forms, carts, payment flows, and account creation. Login pages accounted for 51.7% of this traffic. SiliconANGLE reported the findings on September 22, 2026.

This does not mean every request was malicious. It does show that automated traffic increasingly reaches the same sensitive workflows attackers target.

3. Abusive scraping and data extraction

An agent with legitimate access can still misuse that access. It might repeatedly call a search tool, retrieve large datasets, or enumerate records beyond what its task requires.

Consider an agent authorized to retrieve individual customer orders. If it can also query every customer record without meaningful limits, an attacker could exploit that capability to extract business data at scale.

This risk becomes more serious when organizations expose multiple tools through one server without separate permissions or usage policies.

Cyber Security News has also reported on malicious MCP servers distributing malware through fake AI skills and integrations. The wider lesson is that both the server and the agents connecting to it need scrutiny.

Why Do API Keys and Allowlists Fall Short?

API keys and IP allowlists help restrict access, but they do not establish whether an agent is trustworthy. A valid credential can be stolen, shared, or used outside its intended purpose.

An attacker can also imitate a recognized agent’s identity. Authentication must therefore be combined with behavioral analysis and request-level authorization.

An API key answers a limited question: does the requester possess a credential accepted by the server?

It does not establish whether the requester is the expected agent, whether its behavior is normal, or whether a specific operation is authorized.

IP allowlists have similar limitations. Cloud-based agents and distributed infrastructure can change addresses. Attackers can also operate through residential proxies or compromised systems.

Agent identity is another challenge. A request may claim to come from a recognized AI crawler or assistant without proving that claim cryptographically.

DataDome’s June 2026 benchmark tested 21,491 popular websites against 10 bot and spoofed AI agent types.

Its findings showed that more than seven in ten sites allowed at least one spoofed AI agent or crawler through without a challenge. DataDome’s benchmark details the test.

The MCP specification provides an important foundation through OAuth-based authorization. Its authorization requirements include validating access tokens and ensuring they are intended for the MCP server receiving them.

The MCP authorization specification explains these requirements.

However, authentication is only one layer. Security teams must also decide what an authenticated agent can do.

How Do I Protect an MCP Server from Malicious AI Agents?

Protecting an MCP server requires multiple controls working together. Organizations should verify agent identity, inspect request behavior, enforce permissions for individual tools, and monitor activity continuously.

No single API key, firewall rule, or authentication mechanism can reliably distinguish every legitimate agent from automated abuse.

Four controls are particularly important.

1. Verify agent identity

Use strong authentication rather than trusting user-agent strings, self-declared agent names, or network addresses.

MCP authentication should follow the protocol’s OAuth requirements for remote servers. Validate tokens, check their intended audience, and use short-lived credentials where appropriate.

Where supported, cryptographic verification and trusted identity signals can provide additional confidence that an agent is who it claims to be.

2. Analyze intent on every request

An agent that behaves normally at connection time can become abusive later. Security controls should therefore examine individual requests and changes in behavior throughout a session.

Look for unusual request rates, repeated access to sensitive tools, suspicious parameter combinations, and attempts to retrieve data outside normal usage patterns.

3. Apply policies per agent and endpoint

Different agents need different permissions. A research assistant should not automatically receive the same access as an agent authorized to update customer records.

Apply least-privilege permissions to individual tools and operations. Set rate limits, restrict sensitive actions, and require additional approval for high-impact operations.

4. Maintain visibility into MCP traffic

Security teams need to understand which agents connect, which tools they invoke, and how traffic changes over time.

DataDome, a bot and agent trust management platform, offers MCP protection that applies agent identification and intent-based detection to MCP traffic.

Its controls include agent-level and endpoint-level policies, alongside visibility into MCP activity and usage.

Other providers address different parts of the MCP security problem.

F5 introduced MCP Protocol Protection in BIG-IP 21.1.0. Its WAF capabilities include inspection of MCP traffic, JSON-RPC request validation, and protections against injection, sensitive data exposure, SSRF, and token tampering.

This gives organizations an option for applying protocol-aware security controls at the application delivery layer.

Cloudflare provides tools for deploying MCP servers and securing their access. Its guidance recommends OAuth authorization with granular scopes for individual operations.

Cloudflare One can also help organizations identify MCP connections through Gateway logs, distinguish authorized services from shadow MCP traffic, and apply data loss prevention controls.

These approaches are not identical. The right choice depends on whether an organization needs protocol-aware request inspection, identity and intent analysis, access governance, or visibility into MCP connections.

Do I Need Bot Protection in Front of an MCP Server?

Bot protection is worth considering whenever an MCP server is exposed to network traffic, especially when it provides access to sensitive data or business operations.

Authentication and application security remain essential, but they do not always identify automated abuse.

An additional protection layer can help detect suspicious behavior before requests reach the server.

Traditional WAFs and API security tools can block common attacks, including malformed requests, injection attempts, and suspicious traffic patterns.

However, MCP introduces additional context. A request may be structurally valid and authenticated while still representing abusive activity.

For example, an agent might repeatedly invoke a legitimate search tool to enumerate customer records. A conventional firewall may see valid HTTPS requests and allow them.

A bot and agent protection layer can add behavioral analysis, agent identification, and intent-based controls.

It should complement OAuth, server-side authorization, input validation, and application-level safeguards rather than replace them.

Which Vendors Offer MCP Server Protection?

Several vendors now offer capabilities relevant to MCP security, but their approaches differ. F5 provides dedicated MCP protocol inspection, Cloudflare offers MCP deployment and access-governance capabilities, and DataDome focuses on identifying agents and detecting malicious intent.

Buyers should compare actual MCP-specific controls rather than rely on general AI security claims.

When evaluating providers, ask whether they inspect MCP-specific traffic, verify agent identity, support granular policies, and provide visibility into tool usage.

Also establish where enforcement happens. Protection may operate at the network edge, within an application delivery layer, or through a server-side integration.

The distinction matters because a solution that monitors outbound connections to remote MCP servers does not necessarily protect an organization’s own inbound MCP endpoints.

How Should Organizations Roll Out MCP Protection?

Start by identifying every MCP server, its exposed tools, connected data sources, and authentication requirements.

Then place the selected protection layer at the edge or integrate it with the server. Begin in monitoring mode, review detected activity, and gradually enforce policies.

A practical rollout should include:

  1. Inventory MCP servers: Identify public and internal deployments, including development environments.
  2. Map tool permissions: Document which agents can access each tool and which operations involve sensitive data.
  3. Integrate protection: Select a supported edge or server-side module. DataDome documents integrations for FastMCP, AWS CloudFront, Cloudflare Workers, and Fastly.
  4. Monitor first: Establish normal traffic patterns and investigate suspicious requests before blocking.
  5. Enforce gradually: Introduce agent-level restrictions, endpoint policies, and rate limits. Test legitimate workflows after each change.

The monitoring stage is important. Overly aggressive policies can disrupt legitimate automation and business processes. Security teams should validate both detection accuracy and operational impact before enforcing broad restrictions.

MCP Server Security Checklist

Before deploying or expanding an MCP environment, security teams should confirm that:

  • Every MCP server is inventoried and has an accountable owner.
  • Remote connections use properly configured OAuth authentication.
  • Access tokens are validated for the intended MCP resource.
  • Permissions follow least-privilege principles at the tool level.
  • Sensitive operations have additional authorization requirements.
  • Requests are analyzed for suspicious behavior and intent.
  • Rate limits and data access restrictions are enforced.
  • MCP traffic is logged, monitored, and reviewed.
  • Protection policies are tested against legitimate agents and simulated abuse.

MCP gives AI agents powerful ways to interact with enterprise systems. That makes it important to treat every server as a security boundary, not simply another API endpoint.

As agent adoption grows, organizations need controls that establish trust throughout each interaction.

DataDome is one provider addressing this challenge, but the broader priority is clear: verify identity, understand intent, and enforce permissions before an agent can access sensitive tools and data.

Neither company has announced a deal or […]

The post CrowdStrike in Talks to Acquire Zscaler in One of the Biggest Cybersecurity Deals Ever appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire Zscaler in a deal that could rank among the largest in cybersecurity history. Bloomberg first reported the discussions on Friday, November 20, citing two people familiar with the matter who said talks were ongoing.

The discussions could still end without an agreement. Neither company has announced a deal or disclosed a proposed purchase price.

Zscaler shares jumped 18% in extended trading Friday, while CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%. CrowdStrike declined to comment, and Zscaler did not immediately respond to CNBC’s request.

At Friday’s regular close, Zscaler was worth about $32 billion. That figure reflects the stock market’s valuation, not what CrowdStrike has offered or might ultimately pay.

Zscaler Would Add to CrowdStrike Falcon

CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform helps security teams detect and stop threats on laptops, servers, and cloud workloads. Zscaler controls how users and devices connect to applications and the internet.

Its Zero Trust Exchange checks identity and other signs of risk before allowing access. The two products address different parts of the same problem: Falcon can spot suspicious activity, while Zscaler can limit what a user or device can reach.

The companies already work together. A day before the takeover reports, CrowdStrike previewed an integration that lets Falcon share changes in user risk with Zscaler’s Adaptive Access Engine through open standards.

For example, if Falcon flags a user as risky after sign-in, Zscaler can use that signal to tighten access without waiting for the user to log in again. That work builds on a partnership expansion announced in September and is separate from the reported acquisition talks.

CrowdStrike’s earlier agreement to buy SGNL also focused on changing access as risk changes, rather than letting permissions stand until someone removes them.

Buying Zscaler would go further by bringing a cloud service that manages access to private applications and the public internet under the same owner as Falcon. The companies have not announced any plans to combine products or change customer contracts.

The talks come as major vendors buy tools that extend their reach beyond their main products. Google closed its $32 billion acquisition of Wiz in March 2026, adding cloud security tools to Google Cloud. Palo Alto Networks completed its $25 billion purchase of CyberArk earlier this year, expanding into tools that protect accounts with powerful system permissions.

Both are completed deals. Zscaler’s market value shows why the CrowdStrike talks matter, but it cannot yet be used to rank the proposed purchase.

For security teams, the practical question is whether common ownership would make it easier to investigate an alert and restrict access without switching tools.

Teams that use only one of the products would also want to know whether existing links to other vendors would remain supported and whether pricing would change.

For now, the existing partnership shows how the products can work together. It does not tell customers how a combined company would sell or support them.

articles.title: 6 Critical F5 BIG-IP Vulnerabilities Could Let Hackers Disrupt Websites and Execute Malicious Code
articles.description:
F5 released emergency fixes for six critical BIG-IP vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers take websites and other services offline without logging in. The flaws affect specific traffic-handling configurations. An attacker who can reach a vulnerable service could crash the BIG-IP process that handles client traffic. F5 also warned that attackers may be able to […]

The post 6 Critical F5 BIG-IP Vulnerabilities Could Let Hackers Disrupt Websites and Execute Malicious Code appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
F5 released emergency fixes for six critical BIG-IP vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers take websites and other services offline without logging in. The flaws affect specific traffic-handling configurations.

An attacker who can reach a vulnerable service could crash the BIG-IP process that handles client traffic. F5 also warned that attackers may be able to run code on affected devices. The company disclosed the flaws in its November 18 out-of-band security notification.

The advisory said no exploitation had been reported at the time. That sets this disclosure apart from the BIG-IP OAuth zero-day reported in September, which F5 said attackers were already exploiting.

BIG-IP Flaws Take Websites Offline

BIG-IP often sits between users and the servers that host a website. Its Traffic Management Microkernel, or TMM, handles connections passing through the device. If that process crashes, users can lose access even when the web servers behind it are still running.

The impact is not limited to websites. Remote access portals and other applications that rely on the same device can also become unavailable.

These are data-plane flaws, meaning they affect the part of BIG-IP that handles live traffic rather than the interface administrators use to manage it. Keeping the management interface off the internet does not fix the problem if an affected service is still reachable.

The result can look similar to an outage caused by the earlier BIG-IP HTTP/2 denial-of-service flaw, but the new flaws involve memory corruption rather than exhaustion of processing power.

BIG-IP Deployments Affected

Five of the six flaws affect iRules, the scripts administrators use to control how BIG-IP handles traffic. They are CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-116953, CVE-2026-120722 and CVE-2026-121805.

Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes or BIG-IP Cloud-Native Network Functions. Teams should check the advisory for each flaw against the product and configuration they actually run.

The sixth flaw, CVE-2026-123637, affects BIG-IP Access Policy Manager when a virtual server uses a per-request policy with both the Client Information and Endpoint Security agents. A separate single sign-on flaw, CVE-2026-126822, can also cause an outage without a login, but it is rated high severity and is not part of the six critical issues.

F5’s engineering hotfix guide covers BIG-IP TMOS 17.1.x, 17.5.x and 21.1.x. The correct package depends on the exact base release or engineering build already installed.

For example, a device on the 17.5.1.11 base release should use Hotfix-BIGIP-17.5.1.11.0.61.12-ENG. Devices running either of the two 17.5.1.10 engineering builds named in the guide need Hotfix-BIGIP-17.5.1.10.0.80.35-ENG instead. Customers running a custom build should contact F5 Support for a replacement.

F5 lists no workaround for the six critical flaws. Start with internet-facing virtual servers and those that carry traffic for critical services. Record the full installed build before choosing a package, then test the update outside production where possible.

After deployment, verify that users can reach the websites and remote access portals served by BIG-IP. A successful login to the device’s management interface does not confirm that live traffic is flowing.

Of the three, only the IP exposure flaw was flagged for possible abuse. The advisory says it may have been […]

The post WhatsApp Android Flaws Could Let Hackers Delete Users’ Files and Expose IP Addresses appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
WhatsApp’s November 2026 security update describes three flaws that could let attackers delete files stored by WhatsApp on Android, expose a user’s IP address, or bypass a security check for Meta AI’s Private Processing service.

Of the three, only the IP exposure flaw was flagged for possible abuse. The advisory says it may have been used alongside specific spam messages, but it does not say how many users may have been affected.

WhatsApp Android Flaw Could Delete Local Files

CVE-2026-102769 is a SQL injection flaw affecting WhatsApp for Android before version 2.26.35.74. SQL injection occurs when an app treats input as part of a database command rather than as data.

According to the November advisory, file deletion required the recipient to tap an “order details” message. The advisory limits the possible damage to files stored locally by WhatsApp, not files across the device.

The same flaw could also reveal one bit of information about the recipient’s chat database if they were online when the message arrived. That is a limited leak, not evidence that an attacker could read entire conversations. An external researcher reported the issue through Meta’s security reporting program. WhatsApp said it had seen no evidence of exploitation.

CVE-2026-23871 affects WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android before version 2.26.17.4. The app did not fully check external media links in replies tied to Click to WhatsApp ads.

A device could reveal its IP address when WhatsApp displayed the message in a chat. Unlike the file deletion flaw, the advisory does not describe a tap as necessary. An IP address is network information, not the contents of a chat.

Cyber Security News previously covered a separate WhatsApp flaw involving Instagram Reels that also involved incomplete checks on media links. The two issues carry different CVE IDs and affect different app versions.

CVE-2026-44908 affected how WhatsApp verified the identity of servers used by Meta AI’s Private Processing service. The flaw could have let someone positioned inside Meta’s infrastructure bypass a check meant to confirm that the server was running on trusted hardware.

The advisory says the certificate would first have had to appear in a third-party record. All published certificates traced back to trusted hardware, which WhatsApp says confirms the flaw was not exploited.

The certificate fix arrived in WhatsApp 2.26.24.72 for iOS, 2.26.23.74 for Android, and 2.26.23.72 for Mac. WhatsApp Business received fixes in 2.26.23.72 for iOS and 2.26.23.70 for Android.

Users should install the latest available version from their official app store and check WhatsApp Business separately if they use both apps. The WhatsApp Security Advisories page notes that app store release notes may not list every security fix.

Perpetual and subscription licensing exist. Netwrix is a complete IT infrastructure risk management system. Its strong features and operations help firms prevent security risks, protect sensitive data, and meet legal requirements.

Netwrix helps firms assess risk, manage compliance, find internal risks, and secure secret information. Netwrix analyzes IT infrastructure logs, event records, and configuration data. The system analyzes user behavior and security concerns using complicated algorithms and regulations.

The tool’s report and alert creation capabilities help organizations manage risk and protect assets. Netwrix uses this technology for risk analysis, compliance, user activity tracking, and data security. Netwrix supports numerous computer and network security systems.

Its seamless interaction with Active Directory, Microsoft Exchange, and SharePoint gives it comprehensive coverage and user-friendliness. Its straightforward design and numerous reporting tools earn Netwrix high praise.

13. Riskalyze

Business risk management tool Riskalyze works well. Its insights help firms assess, analyze, and mitigate risks throughout their operations to safeguard assets and achieve goals. With risk assessments and adjustable risk scoring, Riskalyze helps identify and prioritize risks.

It interacts with multiple data sources, assuring data integrity and compatibility. Users can use departmental data for a more holistic risk management strategy. Risk intelligence-based teamwork and information sharing are also encouraged.

Riskalyze addresses investments, compliance, patient safety, data privacy, and supply chain disruptions to increase operational efficiency and asset protection in banking, healthcare, and manufacturing.

Riskalyze’s simple UI, clear dashboards, and actionable reports appeal to users. It notifies enterprises of significant dangers in real-time so they may respond quickly. Riskalyze prioritizes data security. To safeguard sensitive data, it uses encryption and access controls.

14. ServiceNow

ServiceNow is a robust Enterprise Risk Management Tool that speeds up and optimizes risk identification, assessment, and mitigation.

ServiceNow offers streamlined risk assessment, centralized incident management, automated compliance, vendor risk management, and in-depth risk analytics and reporting for effective risk management. ServiceNow’s system integration protects data.

Among its best qualities are its customizable dashboards and simple UI. ServiceNow offers trustworthy safety and customer service, and its friendly sales staff can explain the tool’s flexible price plans.

ServiceNow manages risks like compliance, security, financial transactions, patient safety, and data privacy for banks, healthcare providers, manufacturers, and governments.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft is investigating reports that some Microsoft 365 users cannot upload email attachments in New Outlook. In a November 20 service update, the company said attachment uploads still work in Outlook on the web and classic Outlook. Microsoft is tracking the issue in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1561765.

New Outlook Attachment Issue

The public update focused on uploads, but an Exchange Online advisory tracked by 365Fanatic says some users may also be unable to open attachments in New Outlook. Microsoft reproduced the issue internally and began reviewing diagnostic data to find the cause. The available updates did not identify affected regions, say how many users were impacted, or provide a timeline for a fix.

The reported impact is narrower than the November 12–13 Microsoft 365 outage, which blocked mailbox access across several Outlook clients. In this case, Microsoft identified two alternatives for uploading files. The company has not publicly linked the attachment issue to the earlier outage.

If a file will not upload in New Outlook, open the same mailbox in Outlook on the web or switch to classic Outlook if it is installed. Attach the file there and check that it appears in the message before sending.

IT teams can follow Microsoft’s service health guide, then open Health → Service health in the admin center and look for EX1561765.

Help desks can use the incident ID to group matching reports while noting cases that also fail in the browser or classic Outlook. Staff should verify any emailed recovery instructions with their help desk rather than follow sign-in links.

Cybersecurity News previously reported fake Exchange Online alerts that used outage claims to lure users into clicking. That campaign has not been linked to the current incident.

Update: Microsoft says it has developed a second fix for a remaining issue that prevents some New Outlook users from opening or saving certain types of attachments.

The company is completing final checks and has not yet deployed the fix to affected users. Administrators can follow the rollout under EX1561765 in the Microsoft 365 admin center.

articles.title: Over 100 Debian Packages Still Contain Distrusted CA Certificates Despite Security Updates
articles.description:
A scan of a Debian package mirror found that more than 100 packages still contained copies of distrusted certificate authority (CA) certificates after Debian removed them from its system trust store. Debian developer Steve McIntyre posted the scan results to the Debian developer mailing list on November 19. The findings show why updating the operating […]

The post Over 100 Debian Packages Still Contain Distrusted CA Certificates Despite Security Updates appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A scan of a Debian package mirror found that more than 100 packages still contained copies of distrusted certificate authority (CA) certificates after Debian removed them from its system trust store.

Debian developer Steve McIntyre posted the scan results to the Debian developer mailing list on November 19. The findings show why updating the operating system’s trust store does not necessarily change which certificates an application accepts.

On October 20, Debian removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 and Comodo AAA Services root certificates after several eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were compromised. Debian fixed its shared ca-certificates package in version 20250419+deb13u1 for Debian 13 “trixie” and 20250419~deb12u2 for Debian 12 “bookworm.”

Unlike a Debian kernel security update, this fix changes which certificate chains applications accept, but only if they use the updated trust store.

Distrusted CA Certificates Remained

A trust store is a list of certificates an application relies on to verify the identity of a server before making an encrypted connection. Debian provides a shared list through ca-certificates, but some packages ship their own copies.

An application that relies on a separate list can still accept a certificate chain that another application on the same machine rejects. This is distinct from the changes covered in our report on shorter Let’s Encrypt TLS certificate lifetimes, which concern when server certificates expire.

Debian developer Enrico Zini drew attention to the issue after using custom ClamAV signatures to look for the certificates on systems he had installed. His scan found copies in packages or files tied to pip, Node.js, gRPC, NSS, AWS tools, and Qt WebEngine.

McIntyre then widened the search to his local Debian mirror. Some matches were in sample code or older package versions, so the results do not show that every match represents a currently installed application that still trusts either root.

Administrators should install the latest ca-certificates update for their release and check which trust store their applications actually use. Start with services that make outbound HTTPS connections and tools that download software or handle cloud credentials. Check containers, Flatpaks, and Python virtual environments separately.

Updating the host does not necessarily replace certificate files shipped inside them. Use Debian’s security advisories and package tracker to verify the installed version and follow related updates.

McIntyre argued that Debian packages should use the shared system trust store instead of shipping their own. Other developers discussed rebuilding packages or replacing bundled copies with links to the system store where possible.

That would let future distrust updates reach more applications through one package. Until then, a file match is a starting point: verify whether the running application loads that file before deciding whether it needs a separate fix.

articles.title: Critical Apache Tomcat Flaw Lets Remote Attackers Join Trusted Server Clusters Without Authentication
articles.description:
The Apache Software Foundation has disclosed a critical flaw in Apache Tomcat that allows a remote attacker to join a trusted server cluster without authentication. Tracked as CVE-2026-133325, the flaw affects clusters that use TLS 1.3 with a pre-shared key. Apache published the advisory on November 19, 2026, and credited researcher Mike Read with finding […]

The post Critical Apache Tomcat Flaw Lets Remote Attackers Join Trusted Server Clusters Without Authentication appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Apache Software Foundation has disclosed a critical flaw in Apache Tomcat that allows a remote attacker to join a trusted server cluster without authentication. Tracked as CVE-2026-133325, the flaw affects clusters that use TLS 1.3 with a pre-shared key.

Apache published the advisory on November 19, 2026, and credited researcher Mike Read with finding the issue.

The Apache Tomcat 11 security advisory identifies versions 11.0.28 and 11.0.29 as affected. Apache also lists Tomcat 10.1.62 and 9.0.124. Running one of those versions does not by itself mean a server is exposed.

The flaw requires the affected cluster encryption setup, and a remote attacker needs network access to the service that handles communication between cluster members. A public Tomcat website does not necessarily expose that service.

Tomcat Cluster Authentication Failed

Apache Tribes handles communication between servers in a Tomcat cluster. Those servers can share session data so that a user can stay signed in when another server takes over. A pre-shared key is a secret configured on trusted members in advance.

In the affected TLS 1.3 setup, Tomcat did not verify the identity of the server at the other end of the connection. The connection could be encrypted without proving that the server was allowed to join.

Cyber Security News previously covered flaws in Tomcat’s EncryptInterceptor, an older component used to protect cluster traffic. The new advisory concerns a different failure: Tomcat accepted a cluster member it had not authenticated. Apache’s advisory does not report active exploitation or say that joining a cluster gives an attacker remote code execution.

Apache recommends switching cluster communication to TLS 1.2 while keeping the pre-shared key enabled. This change applies to traffic between Tomcat servers, not the HTTPS connections used by website visitors. The fixed versions are 11.0.30, 10.1.63, and 9.0.125 for their respective branches. Apache listed them as pending release in its Tomcat 11, Tomcat 10, and Tomcat 9 security notices.

Administrators should check the running version and cluster settings on every member, restrict cluster ports to approved servers, and review available logs for unexpected membership changes. After applying the workaround or updating, confirm that every expected member reconnects and that session replication still works where enabled. A website can still respond while its servers are no longer sharing session data.

The earlier CISA warning about an exploited Tomcat encryption flaw concerned CVE-2026-34486. That warning does not establish exploitation of CVE-2026-133325, and the two flaws should be tracked separately.

articles.title: Hackers Use 355 Domains to Spread Fake GTA 6 PC Launchers Delivering Malware
articles.description:
A malware campaign called CyberLeek is using more than 355 domains and subdomains to promote fake Grand Theft Auto VI PC launchers. The sites offer what they claim is a leaked or early Windows release of GTA 6. Instead of a playable game, the download delivers a ZIP archive containing a malicious program disguised as […]

The post Hackers Use 355 Domains to Spread Fake GTA 6 PC Launchers Delivering Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A malware campaign called CyberLeek is using more than 355 domains and subdomains to promote fake Grand Theft Auto VI PC launchers.

The sites offer what they claim is a leaked or early Windows release of GTA 6. Instead of a playable game, the download delivers a ZIP archive containing a malicious program disguised as an installer.

The campaign takes advantage of a familiar search: players looking for a GTA 6 PC release before they can get one through an official store.

Earlier reporting on fake GTA 6 downloads documented a separate operation that bundled password stealers, remote-access malware and file-destroying code with a fake game installer. Those findings do not establish what CyberLeek’s launcher does after it runs.

Researchers at the Vecert Foundation identified the malware distribution network and traced its activity to mid-October 2026, with notable spikes in November.

The count comes from domain and certificate records. It reflects the size of the infrastructure the researchers linked to CyberLeek, not the number of people infected or the number of distinct malware samples.

Hackers Use 355 Domains to Spread Fake GTA 6 PC Launchers

One site examined by researchers advertised a playable GTA 6 port for Windows 10 and 11. It used search-friendly text and page markup that presented the supposed launcher as a software download.

A prominent button promised a direct file with “no ad wall,” making the page look like a convenient alternative to the pop-ups and redirects users might expect from an unofficial download site.

The download button did not always lead to the same file location. Researchers found that the page could send visitors to changing links on public hosting platforms, with a local ZIP archive available as a fallback.

That distinction matters for defenders: blocking one download URL may leave the original landing page reachable and other download paths available.

CyberLeek also used multiple domain endings and subdomains while keeping the same branding. This gave the campaign several places to send visitors if a site was blocked.

The approach echoes gaming search poisoning campaigns that use credible-looking pages to reach people searching for game tools or popular software. A high search ranking does not verify who published a file or what it contains.

The reported infection step is running the program inside the archive. Visiting the page or finding the ZIP in a Downloads folder does not, on its own, show that the installer ran.

Fake GTA 6 demo

In a separate case involving a fake GTA 6 demo, analysts identified Vidar, a program that steals passwords and browser sessions. Vecert did not name a specific malware family for CyberLeek or confirm what data the fake launcher collected.

Security teams can search DNS and web proxy logs for the reported hosts, then compare any matches with endpoint records for archive downloads and installer launches.

A generic script name or installer filename is not enough to establish a compromise. A recorded launch after a visit to a reported domain gives responders a stronger lead and a reason to check the device for unusual processes and network connections.

Players who downloaded the ZIP but did not run it should delete it without opening the installer. Anyone who ran the program should disconnect the device from the network and have it checked.

Since password and session theft can put accounts at risk even after the download is removed, use a clean device to change important passwords and revoke active sessions if compromise is suspected.

For future releases, check the publisher’s official channels or a trusted storefront rather than a site promising an early build.

articles.title: Hackers Turn Legitimate VPN Software Into a Stealthy Tool for Spying on Government Networks
articles.description:
Hackers have rebuilt the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge to keep a quiet route into compromised networks. The modified Windows program, branded internally as NtMonitor VPN, can link an external network to a victim’s local network while leaving fewer of the traces defenders expect from a standard SoftEther installation. Researchers link the tool to Webworm, a […]

The post Hackers Turn Legitimate VPN Software Into a Stealthy Tool for Spying on Government Networks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have rebuilt the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge to keep a quiet route into compromised networks. The modified Windows program, branded internally as NtMonitor VPN, can link an external network to a victim’s local network while leaving fewer of the traces defenders expect from a standard SoftEther installation.

Researchers link the tool to Webworm, a China-aligned espionage group with a history of targeting government organizations, particularly in Europe.

The distinction is that the bridge helps operators stay connected after a breach; the report does not show how they broke in. Nor does it name agencies newly affected by this build or establish what data, if any, was taken through it.

Earlier coverage of Webworm’s GraphWorm documented a separate backdoor that used Microsoft OneDrive for communications. NtMonitor serves a different purpose: it gives operators a network route rather than a built-in command shell.

Researchers from Rapid7 identified the modified VPN tool and attributed it to Webworm with moderate confidence in a November 19 report.

They compared a public 64-bit Windows sample with the matching SoftEther source release, version 4.44, build 9807, and found no added command-execution backdoor.

At the time of analysis, only one antivirus vendor on VirusTotal flagged the sample, even though it had been publicly available since January.

Hackers Turn Legitimate VPN Software Into a Stealthy Tool

A VPN bridge connects networks rather than simply giving one user remote access. Every configuration Rapid7 examined linked a remote network to the local one.

That can make the Windows host running the bridge a route to other systems on its network. The risk comes from an existing feature being used without authorization, not from a newly disclosed SoftEther vulnerability.

Earlier reporting on Flax Typhoon’s SoftEther use illustrates how another group used the same open-source project to retain access after a breach.

The public sample described itself as “Network Monitor Software” from “Network Systems Solutions Inc.” and listed netcapa.exe as its original filename.

The disguise was inconsistent: some internal strings used NtMonitor branding, but the service entry point still referenced SEVPNBRIDGE, and several registry paths retained the SoftEther Project name.

The build also packaged a normally separate resource archive inside the program and stored its settings in an encrypted file. Together, those changes meant an installation could look unfamiliar even to a team that knew what stock SoftEther leaves behind.

The network traffic changed, too. Rapid7 found web request paths that resembled routine update traffic and a different marker in the opening exchange between VPN peers.

That made signatures written for standard SoftEther traffic less useful. A separate case involving modified WireGuard also involved a rebuilt VPN tool, but that version ran embedded code. Rapid7 found no comparable execution feature in NtMonitor; the bridge itself was enough to maintain access.

How Government Defenders Can Detect Unauthorized VPN Bridges

Rapid7 found that configurations not considered likely tests pointed to addresses in AS20473, a hosting network associated with The Constant Company and Vultr.

That overlap with past Webworm activity supported the attribution, but the network number alone is not evidence of compromise. ESET’s earlier Webworm research documented targeting in Belgium, Italy, Poland, Serbia, and Spain.

Those countries describe earlier activity, not a confirmed victim list for NtMonitor. For defenders, the best starting point is an inventory of approved VPN services, the hosts allowed to run them, and the remote networks they are supposed to reach.

Investigate unexpected Windows services, firewall rule changes, and connections to unapproved peers together. Earlier reporting on malware in isolated government networks illustrates why investigators should check which systems a compromised host could reach, not just identify the first machine that raised an alert.

If a bridge is unauthorized, preserve its executable, configuration, and connection logs before removing it so responders can reconstruct where it led.

articles.title: OpenSSL Hit by Critical 9.8 Heap Buffer Overflow Vulnerability in Base64 Encoding Function
articles.description:
A heap buffer overflow in OpenSSL’s Base64 encoding function can corrupt application memory when the library processes very large inputs. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-121481, was published on November 18, 2026, with a critical CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8. That score describes the potential severity, but it does not mean every service that uses OpenSSL […]

The post OpenSSL Hit by Critical 9.8 Heap Buffer Overflow Vulnerability in Base64 Encoding Function appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A heap buffer overflow in OpenSSL’s Base64 encoding function can corrupt application memory when the library processes very large inputs. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-121481, was published on November 18, 2026, with a critical CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8.

That score describes the potential severity, but it does not mean every service that uses OpenSSL is remotely exposed.

The flaw affects EVP_EncodeBlock(), which converts binary data into printable text. Base64 produces four output bytes for every three input bytes, with padding for a partial group. The application supplies the buffer that holds the result.

For very large inputs, OpenSSL’s calculation of the encoded length can exceed the range of the integer used to store it. That calculation error can cause the encoder to write beyond the end of the supplied buffer. The write can corrupt nearby memory or crash the application.

OpenSSL Heap Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

This differs from the OpenSSL flaw that could leak server memory: the Base64 bug writes outside a buffer, while the earlier DTLS flaw read data outside one.

The key question for security teams is whether an application passes large amounts of untrusted data to the affected encoder. A server’s use of OpenSSL for encrypted connections does not, by itself, answer that question.

Teams should check where their applications call the function and which size limits apply before encoding begins. The CVE version record lists OpenSSL 4.0.0 through 4.0.3 and OpenSSL 4.1.0 as affected, with 4.0.4 and 4.1.1 marking the upper bounds of those ranges.

Those version numbers do not, by themselves, confirm that a fixed package is available from a particular vendor. As with earlier OpenSSL memory corruption fixes, check the release or package notes for the branch you run.

Ubuntu’s security tracker assigns the issue Medium priority and lists its main openssl packages as needing evaluation. It also marks the nodejs package in Ubuntu 22.04 LTS as vulnerable.

Ubuntu notes that this package embeds its own copy of OpenSSL, so checking only the system library can miss software that bundles it.

Inventory OpenSSL copies in system packages, containers, and application bundles. Prioritize applications that Base64-encode data supplied by users or external services.

Until a vendor-confirmed update is available, enforce application-level input limits before encoding. After updating, restart or redeploy affected workloads and verify that they are running the updated build.

For developers, the OpenSSL encoding documentation explains that callers must reserve space for the encoded data and a final zero byte that marks the end of the string. Review that calculation alongside input limits. For large files, consider an encoding interface that processes data in chunks rather than passing the whole file to one call.

articles.title: BYOD Ransomware Hackers Play Audio Ransom Messages on Computers Across Hospitals and Universities
articles.description:
Staff at the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center reported hearing ransom messages from their computers during an October 26 cyberattack. Two weeks later, a recording from Vanderbilt University captured a voice announcing, “You have been compromised by BYOD.” The messages took the ransom demand out of a private note and made the incident […]

The post BYOD Ransomware Hackers Play Audio Ransom Messages on Computers Across Hospitals and Universities appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Staff at the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center reported hearing ransom messages from their computers during an October 26 cyberattack.

Two weeks later, a recording from Vanderbilt University captured a voice announcing, “You have been compromised by BYOD.” The messages took the ransom demand out of a private note and made the incident visible to people far beyond the IT team.

The disruptions were real, even where the hackers’ claims remain unverified. New Mexico’s only Level 1 trauma center diverted ambulances for two hours, and more than 30 clinics canceled appointments and outpatient surgeries.

On November 9, Vanderbilt told students, faculty and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi while it investigated.

Researchers at TrendAI noted the reported ransomware activity in their analysis of the BYOD campaign, which claimed at least nine organizations between October 5 and November 9, 2026.

The researchers did not have a public malware sample to examine. Their findings draw on victim statements, public reporting and claims by the group, so the report separates confirmed disruptions from unverified accounts of encryption and data theft.

BYOD Ransomware Hackers Play Audio Ransom Messages on Computers

At UNM, employees reported that the audio claimed patient, student and employee data had been stolen. BYOD later claimed it compromised 36,000 systems, including Microsoft Entra and two Oracle databases.

UNM said the incident affected some end-user devices but did not reach core systems or servers. As the Ascension hospital ransomware incident also showed, ambulance diversion is an operational consequence, not a measure of how far attackers reached.

The Vanderbilt campus device shutdown came as the university warned users about unfamiliar applications, unexpected login approval requests and unusual file or permission changes.

Campus Wi-Fi returned that evening, with other services restored in phases. BYOD claimed it encrypted databases and stole more than one million Social Security numbers, but Vanderbilt had not confirmed the group’s involvement, encryption or data theft in the reporting reviewed by TrendAI.

The audio tells investigators less than it might seem. It shows that a message played on affected computers, but it does not establish how the group delivered it, whether the same method was used at both sites, or whether attackers controlled a central directory.

Its clearest effect was public pressure: staff and students could hear and record the demand before either institution had finished assessing the incident.

Credential compromise

Michigan State University offers a separate clue about account security. It reported a possible credential compromise and required university password resets in early October, before BYOD listed it on November 1.

The university said it had no evidence that its central Active Directory was compromised or that other data was accessed, altered or stolen. The group’s claim about 1.3 million current and former students therefore remains unverified.

Unexpected login prompts deserve attention even when endpoint tools find no malware. Separate reporting on cloud account takeover tactics shows how repeated approval requests can precede unauthorized access.

TrendAI recommends checking identity, endpoint and cloud logs together, then reviewing what a suspected account accessed before its password was reset, including shared files and administrative settings.

For hospitals, the response plan should also cover what happens when staff cannot use their computers. TrendAI advises testing offline backups and rehearsing downtime procedures that do not depend on the network.

The company also recommends giving patients, students and staff a trusted way to report unsolicited messages from anyone claiming to hold their data.

That preparation matters before the first ransom message plays, because restoring computers and containing public pressure are two different jobs.

articles.title: Hackers Use AI-Powered ARTEX Framework to Automate Cyberattacks Without Relying on Zero-Day Exploits
articles.description:
Attackers are using an AI-driven testing tool called ARTEX to break into company networks. It needs no secret software flaws to do this. Instead, it hunts for ordinary mistakes such as exposed apps, weak passwords and loose permissions, and it keeps working at them far longer than a human would. ARTEX is an open-source framework […]

The post Hackers Use AI-Powered ARTEX Framework to Automate Cyberattacks Without Relying on Zero-Day Exploits appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are using an AI-driven testing tool called ARTEX to break into company networks. It needs no secret software flaws to do this.

Instead, it hunts for ordinary mistakes such as exposed apps, weak passwords and loose permissions, and it keeps working at them far longer than a human would.

ARTEX is an open-source framework that connects a large language model (LLM) to a set of hacking tools. It was built for authorized security testing, but criminals and state-linked groups now use it.

The FBI warned that hackers have used it since at least August 2026 and, in some cases, reached privileged access in under three hours.

Researchers at TrustedSec noted that ARTEX works like a familiar scanner with an AI brain attached. The framework gives a model tools to inspect a target and act on what it finds. Each result feeds the next decision, so the tool can follow a lead without waiting for a person.

Hackers Use AI-Powered ARTEX Framework

The attack flow is not new. According to TrustedSec, attackers still find assets with subfinder, check web services with httpx, map services with Nmap, run nuclei templates and use ffuf to find hidden content.

What changes is the work after that first scan. The model picks an action, the framework runs it, and the output becomes the next input.

It may adjust a request with curl, write a small script or check an exposed file. A secret it finds becomes a new question: is it valid, and what can it reach?

Microsoft showed the tool paired with Nmap, curl, Python HTTP clients and Playwright. It tracked Storm-3358 using ARTEX to scan internet-facing systems and exploit flaws like anonymous file upload and SSRF.

Mandiant also logged rapid AWS permission probing. Other groups have used it to automate Active Directory attacks and move sideways inside networks.

The real shift is cost. Many firms have custom apps, old APIs and forgotten subdomains that nobody tests closely. Attackers used to skip these because one exploit for a common product hits thousands of targets, while a custom app pays off once.

TrustedSec called limited attacker attention an economic assumption, not a control. An AI agent can spend hours on every odd response for little money.

The tool also has weak points. It can burn many tokens on a false lead, and repeating a wrong guess does not make it right. Broad scanning and fast retries also create noise that defenders can spot.

Backdoored Copies and Sandbox Escapes

ARTEX is risky even for people who run it legitimately. The tool holds model API keys, target data and captured sessions, so it becomes a rich target itself.

TrustedSec described a third-party ARTEX copy that pointed users to backdoored Docker images. The changed login handler allowed unauthenticated command execution inside the container. The finding covers those copies only.

It does not show that the original ARTEX source held a backdoor. The WorkOS case shows the other side of the problem. The company said an ARTEX agent used by a researcher running benchmark tests reached a real internal tool.

Reports say the agent escaped a sandbox and pulled sales and support records. The tool had a public API, a predictable development credential and no rate limits.

WorkOS has not shown a true container flaw. An agent with internet access can leave its intended scope without breaking out of anything.

Defenders can act on several points:

  1. Move one exposed employee tool or management API behind an identity-aware proxy, private access service or VPN, then confirm the original server cannot be reached directly.
  2. Set limits in the WAF and application controls for path enumeration, repeated exploit probes and bulk record retrieval.
  3. Trim the permissions of public web apps so one flaw does not open the wider network.
  4. Test whether the team can link odd API use to an account and revoke access while retrieval is still running.

User-agent blocking helps only against default setups, since an operator can change the string. Anyone testing ARTEX should use a disposable VM, temporary credentials and a lab network whose outbound policy denies unrelated destinations.

Scope rules should be enforced by the network, not by a prompt. Security teams should also watch for frameworks exposed on public servers, because open consoles give attackers a free starting point.

The original developer pulled the public code in October after reports of abuse, but forks keep circulating. Defenders should not wait for a zero-day alert, because these intrusions rely on gaps that already exist.

The post Signal Restricts Screenshots to protect User Privacy from AI assistants appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Signal is restricting screenshots on iOS 27 and some Android devices to stop built-in AI assistants from reading private chats through screen capture.

The encrypted messaging app is targeting Apple’s Siri AI and assistants such as Google Gemini. On Android, the block turns on when Signal detects an assistant trying to read the screen.

The change addresses what happens after a message arrives. End-to-end encryption protects messages as they travel between devices, but Signal must show readable text when someone opens a chat.

An assistant that can read the screen does not have to break that encryption to see the message. It can capture the same text the recipient sees.

On iOS 27, Signal’s “Block Siri AI” setting prevents Siri from scanning Signal content and blocks screenshots inside the app and in the App Switcher.

On Android, Signal automatically turns on “Screen security” when it detects an assistant seeking screen access. Signal says detection varies across Android versions, so the protection does not work the same way on every phone.

The move follows Signal’s 2025 decision to block screenshots by default in its Windows 11 desktop app to keep chats out of Microsoft Recall’s searchable history. Other developers took a different route. As Cyber Security News reported, Brave blocked Microsoft Recall while preserving regular screenshots.

Signal Restricts Screenshots

Apple says Siri’s onscreen awareness lets it answer questions or act on what users are viewing. Google’s Gemini help page says some screen actions upload visible content to give the assistant context.

That does not mean either assistant routinely records every Signal chat. The risk is that once an assistant captures a message, Signal cannot control how that copy is handled.

Users can turn off the protection in Signal’s privacy settings to take screenshots again, but doing so can also expose messages from other people in the chat. The Electronic Frontier Foundation points to a separate option on iOS 27.2: open Settings → Siri → Excluded Apps and add Signal to block Siri’s access, including on-screen awareness.

Screenshot blocking does not cover every route to private data. Signal says it cannot offer the same protection on macOS and warns that an assistant may still reach content already saved on a device.

In related coverage, Meta’s Muse read Signal message text through Android notifications and Mac permissions without breaking Signal’s encryption.

Signal is asking Apple, Google and Microsoft to give developers a clear way to opt out of AI access to screens, files and notifications without disabling ordinary features such as screenshots. It also wants better documentation about what assistants can read and where that data goes.

The distinction matters for anyone sharing sensitive information. A screenshot block can close one route into a private chat, but it cannot decide what a phone shows in a notification or what permissions another app receives. Those controls sit with the operating system, which is why Signal is pressing platform makers for stronger limits.
