articles.title: Meta AI Agent Muse Reads Encrypted Messages Through Android Notifications and Mac Permissions
articles.description:
Meta’s AI agent Muse read Signal message text on Android phones and Macs without directly connecting to the encrypted messaging app, Reuters reported on November 18. The investigation found that Muse could use Android notifications and macOS permissions to see text already displayed on a device. The tests did not show that Muse broke Signal’s […]

The post Meta AI Agent Muse Reads Encrypted Messages Through Android Notifications and Mac Permissions appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Meta’s AI agent Muse read Signal message text on Android phones and Macs without directly connecting to the encrypted messaging app, Reuters reported on November 18.

The investigation found that Muse could use Android notifications and macOS permissions to see text already displayed on a device. The tests did not show that Muse broke Signal’s end-to-end encryption.

The finding followed an internal complaint from a Meta employee who said Muse unexpectedly reminded her to reply to a Signal message from her sister. The employee was using a personal phone and said she did not recall granting Muse access to other apps. A colleague said he traced similar reminders to Android notification access.

The complaints surfaced after Muse, represented by a fuzzy mascot named Jolly, passed 10 million downloads following its September launch.

Employees also reported unsolicited messages about childcare, career advice, and purchases they had not made. In one case, a routine update about fishing conditions included two bank balances the recipient did not recognize.

Muse Read Signal Messages on Android and Mac

On Android, Muse read message text from push notifications. Signal encrypts messages between devices, but a notification preview can display the text after it arrives.

An app with notification access can see what appears in those alerts. That is different from opening Signal, reading its full chat history, or breaking its encryption.

On macOS, testers found that Muse could use accessibility and screenshot tools to read Signal text. Neither the Android nor the Mac test required adding Signal through Meta’s Connector feature, which links external services to the assistant. The same request was blocked on the iPhone used in testing.

The Reuters investigation highlights a distinction users can easily miss: leaving Signal off an agent’s list of connected apps does not revoke permissions granted through the operating system.

Cybersecurity News previously covered a separate Apple notification privacy flaw that exposed Signal message text through a different route. In both cases, the exposure involved text the device had already received.

Meta said Muse can access other apps only through permissions users explicitly grant. The company described the reported cases as isolated and said many suspected account mix-ups were AI hallucinations, meaning the assistant generated information that was not based on real records. The tests confirmed that Muse could read Signal text, but they did not establish that the bank figures belonged to another user.

Mac users can check System Settings under Privacy & Security and remove Muse’s accessibility or screen recording access if they do not need those features.

Cybersecurity News’ coverage of macOS 27.3 beta privacy controls explains why existing grants deserve a separate review: tighter controls do not necessarily remove access an app already has.

Android users can search system settings for “Notification access” and turn off Muse’s access if it is enabled. They can also follow Signal’s notification settings guide to hide message text in alerts.

The two changes do different things: hiding previews limits what Signal puts in a notification, while revoking access stops Muse from reading notifications through that permission. Neither requires turning off Signal notifications altogether, so users can still receive alerts without showing the message text.

articles.title: BADBOX 3.0 Malware Infects Android TV Boxes to Generate 40 Billion Fraudulent Ad Requests Daily
articles.description:
Low-cost Android streaming boxes helped power an advertising fraud operation that generated roughly 40 billion bid requests a day at its peak. Known as BADBOX 3.0, the campaign used infected devices to play video ads outside the visible screen while making the traffic look as though it came from legitimate streaming apps. Some of the […]

The post BADBOX 3.0 Malware Infects Android TV Boxes to Generate 40 Billion Fraudulent Ad Requests Daily appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Low-cost Android streaming boxes helped power an advertising fraud operation that generated roughly 40 billion bid requests a day at its peak.

Known as BADBOX 3.0, the campaign used infected devices to play video ads outside the visible screen while making the traffic look as though it came from legitimate streaming apps. Some of the fraud did not require a real device at all.

The figure measures requests to bid on advertising space, not ads watched, payments made, or devices infected. At its peak, BADBOX 3.0 accounted for more than 4% of the connected TV (CTV) traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform.

Its daily bid volume was more than three times that of VASTFLUX, the previous record holder cited in the research.

Researchers from HUMAN Security’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team identified and disrupted BADBOX 3.0, publishing their findings on November 18, 2026.

The affected boxes primarily ran the Android Open Source Project, or AOSP, and were not Play Protect certified. They were not devices running Google’s Android TV OS, despite being sold as Android-powered streaming hardware.

BADBOX 3.0 Malware Infects Android TV Boxes

The investigation began with a backdoor packaged as a system app. It contacted a command-and-control server, which told the box what additional software to download.

Researchers traced those downloads to a maintained collection of ad fraud and proxy modules, with backup copies on separate hosting services. The setup meant that removing one copy would not necessarily stop infected boxes from fetching the software.

The case builds on the earlier BadBox 2.0 botnet lawsuit, in which Google took legal action against operators of a botnet that it said had compromised more than 10 million uncertified devices.

That number applies to the earlier campaign, not BADBOX 3.0. The latest report does not provide a comparable count of unique infected devices.

In one sample, a system app played video ads in a transparent player positioned outside the visible screen. The bid requests borrowed the names of legitimate CTV apps, even though those apps did not run on the infected boxes.

Satori tested one impersonated app and its intended hardware and found no malicious behavior. Blocking all traffic associated with that app would therefore risk rejecting genuine ad requests along with fraudulent ones.

Android TV Botnet

Researchers also found code from the Vo1d Android TV botnet alongside the new fraud modules, strengthening a link noted in earlier BADBOX research.

On the advertising side, repeated traffic spikes at nearly the same hour and the use of a browser identifier from an internal test build helped distinguish fake requests from normal viewing.

Satori also found requests falsely claiming that a server had inserted an ad into a viewer’s stream when neither the device nor the ad playback existed.

The operators made money from household connections in another way: the malware could enroll boxes in any of 11 residential proxy networks without owners’ consent.

A residential proxy sends someone else’s traffic through a home internet connection. Satori assessed that one network, PXYEDGE, was a renamed successor to IpMoYu. For one impersonated app, about 80% of U.S. requests came from addresses flagged as residential proxy exits.

The risk extends beyond streaming boxes. Earlier reporting on malware in photo frames documented related Vo1d activity on another type of Android hardware.

Satori linked the BADBOX 3.0 software catalog to Chinese electronics manufacturer TXCZ through server infrastructure, a factory-installed launcher, and code that checked for TXCZ-specific device settings.

For households, the FBI’s BADBOX advisory recommends disconnecting suspicious devices from the network. Buyers should verify Play Protect certification before purchasing an Android streaming box and use official app stores.

A box that streams normally is not necessarily clean: the hidden ads observed in the investigation did not change what the owner saw on screen.

articles.title: Hackers Steal US Bank, IRS and Social Security Login Credentials From Infected Computers
articles.description:
A Russian-speaking cybercrime operation has been stealing logins for US banks, the IRS and Social Security from infected Windows PCs. The victims were ordinary people. Many used a password manager and multi-factor authentication (MFA), and it did not help. The attackers did not break into any bank or government agency. They went after the victim’s […]

The post Hackers Steal US Bank, IRS and Social Security Login Credentials From Infected Computers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Russian-speaking cybercrime operation has been stealing logins for US banks, the IRS and Social Security from infected Windows PCs. The victims were ordinary people. Many used a password manager and multi-factor authentication (MFA), and it did not help.

The attackers did not break into any bank or government agency. They went after the victim’s own computer, where saved passwords, cookies and password vaults sit in one place.

At least 57 US victims had a bank or government login in the stolen data. At least 46 had an ID.me, Login.gov, IRS or Social Security account.

Researchers at Hunt.io found the operation through an exposed open directory on a server in the Netherlands. The folder held the attackers’ stolen data, scripts and logs, and it showed that 603 infected computers were reporting to the group’s servers.

Hackers Steal US Bank, IRS and Social Security Login Credentials

The attackers began with a small Python file that runs quietly in the background on Windows. Hunt.io says it was delivered by phishing, though it did not give the exact lure.

Once it was running, the infected PC checked in with the attackers’ servers, and they sent more tools based on what the victim had stored.

The first target was the web browser. The attackers broke the encryption Chrome and Edge use to protect saved passwords. Their scripts carried built-in keys that unlocked the stolen browser files later, away from the victim’s PC.

Hunt.io counted at least 3,345 decrypted logins from 16 victims, along with 30 cookie databases. Cookies matter because they prove a user has already signed in.

When an attacker copies one, the website may treat the attacker as the real user. This is how session cookie theft leads to account takeovers even when MFA is turned on.

In this case the attackers replayed stolen Microsoft 365 cookies to get live access tokens without a password or MFA prompt.

Password managers did not stop them either. One victim lost an entire LastPass vault with 2,880 logins, including Chase, Wells Fargo, IRS.gov, Medicare and PayPal.

Criminals have long cracking weak master passwords offline in stolen vaults. Here the group instead decrypted the vault data straight from the victim’s browser files.

They also guessed the master passwords of two 1Password users and copied a KeePass database from a developer’s computer.

The stolen data pointed to major US banks. Chase appeared in 31 victims’ data, Capital One in 20, Citi in 17 and Wells Fargo in 15. The ID.me and Login.gov accounts are the most worrying part, because those services open the door to the IRS, Social Security and the VA.

Wider Theft and the Attackers’ Hidden Setup

The group did not stop at banks. Hunt.io found 6,570 cryptocurrency records from 67 victims, covering 44 platforms such as Binance, Coinbase, MetaMask and Kraken.

The attackers also went after login tokens from 35 AI tools, including Claude, Codex and Gemini. These tokens can expose chat history, project files and API keys.

To keep access after a cleanup, the attackers installed legitimate remote-management tools, Level.io and ScreenConnect. Because these are real business products, they can slip past some security filters.

The setup was built to stay hidden. One server ran three control systems, named HavoX, Phantom53 and Kraken Bridge. Twelve Cloudflare Workers domains sat in front of them, so victim traffic looked like normal web traffic.

Hunt.io says the system handled more than 1.2 million check-in messages over about three weeks. This kind of theft often ends in resale. Stolen logs can show up in an AI-powered marketplace selling infected computers. Hunt.io did not report a sale in this case.

Its evidence of who is behind the operation is the Russian-language text in the attackers’ own files. It found that text across 249 scripts and logs.

Home users who think a PC may be infected should use a clean device to change passwords, starting with email and banking. They should also sign out of every active session. Passwords alone are not enough, because a stolen session can stay valid after a reset.

Security teams should watch for pythonw.exe running .pyw files from the AppData\Roaming folder, which is where these implants live.

They should also block the listed domains and IPs. Hunt.io also advises binding sessions to compliant devices, keeping token lifetimes short and treating AI tool login files like SSH keys.

articles.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added four flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 18, 2026, after finding evidence that attackers were already exploiting them. The entries cover Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM), BerriAI LiteLLM, Apache Axis and Vanderbilt University’s Research Electronic Data Capture platform, better known as REDCap. The […]

The post CISA Warns Hackers Are Actively Exploiting Four Flaws in Synology, LiteLLM, Apache Axis and REDCap appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added four flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 18, 2026, after finding evidence that attackers were already exploiting them.

The entries cover Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM), BerriAI LiteLLM, Apache Axis and Vanderbilt University’s Research Electronic Data Capture platform, better known as REDCap.

The four products serve different roles: network storage, access to AI models, legacy web services and research data collection. That makes this update relevant to more than one IT team.

A storage administrator may own the Synology fix, but finding Apache Axis may require asking application vendors whether they bundle the library. CISA’s listing confirms exploitation of each flaw, not that the same attackers used all four.

CISA noted evidence of active exploitation in its November 18 security alert, but the agency did not identify any malware in that notice.

Separate reporting has linked attacks against Synology storage to C3RB3R ransomware and documented cryptomining malware in a REDCap incident. Those are incident-specific findings, not evidence of a shared campaign.

Flaws in Synology, LiteLLM, Apache Axis and REDCap

CVE-2024-10441 is an output-handling flaw in a Synology system service that can let a remote attacker run code without signing in or requiring a user to take action.

The original Synology vulnerability coverage lists fixed builds across several DSM branches, including 7.2.2-72806-1 and 7.2.1-69057-6. Those builds are historical patch thresholds; administrators should install the latest supported release for their device.

CVE-2026-40217 affects LiteLLM’s custom guardrail testing feature. Guardrails are rules that control what an AI application accepts or returns.

In this case, code meant to run inside a restricted test environment could escape those limits. The maintainers say the feature requires proxy administrator credentials in default configurations and recommend upgrading to version 1.83.11 or later.

Earlier coverage of other LiteLLM gateway flaws explains why teams should also review what credentials and connected services the gateway can reach.

CVE-2026-90436 affects Apache Axis 1.x, a discontinued Java library for SOAP web services. The flaw can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a vulnerable server.

Rapid7 observed exploitation in a Confluence Data Center environment, where the attacker used the application’s credentials to access its database.

Apache does not plan to ship a fixed Axis 1.x release. Organizations using software that bundles Axis should follow that product vendor’s guidance; for Confluence Data Center, that means upgrading to 9.2.28 or an unaffected 10.x release.

CVE-2026-90817 is a code injection flaw in REDCap that can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on the server. Exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash, an identifier associated with a survey.

That prerequisite does not make the issue harmless: teams running public surveys should confirm their REDCap version and prioritize the vendor’s remediation guidance. The survey hash is not a malware file hash or an indicator of compromise.

Patch Deadlines and What Defenders Should Check

Federal civilian agencies face a November 21 deadline for Synology DSM, Apache Axis and REDCap, and a December 2 deadline for LiteLLM.

CISA’s directive also sets expectations for checking whether attackers compromised certain systems before they were patched.

Recent coverage of an exploited Check Point flaw illustrates why that distinction matters: an update can close the entry point, but it cannot tell administrators what happened before installation.

Start with internet-facing systems and confirm which versions are actually running. For storage appliances, review unexpected logins, new administrator accounts and unfamiliar scheduled tasks.

Earlier reporting on Synology NAS ransomware attacks also recommends removing direct internet access to DSM management and keeping independent offline or off-site backups.

Where Axis is embedded in another product, verify the fix against the host product’s version rather than assuming a separate Axis package will appear in inventory.

articles.description:
A federal grand jury has indicted Russian national Igor D’iu over an alleged spy operation targeting employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company. The U.S. Department of Justice said on Nov. 18 that D’iu bought remote access software and wireless networking equipment at the direction of people who recruited him through Telegram. Prosecutors […]

The post Russian National Accused of Using Remote Access Tools to Spy on Silicon Valley Defense Firm appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A federal grand jury has indicted Russian national Igor D’iu over an alleged spy operation targeting employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company.

The U.S. Department of Justice said on Nov. 18 that D’iu bought remote access software and wireless networking equipment at the direction of people who recruited him through Telegram.

Prosecutors say the group targeted the company because it supplied weapons used against Russia in Ukraine. The department did not name the firm, which has an office in Palo Alto, California.

According to the Justice Department’s announcement, D’iu’s alleged handlers told him to place his laptop near the company so they could connect to it remotely and try to gather information about employees nearby.

They also allegedly directed him to visit a coffee shop near the Palo Alto office, identify company employees, and photograph their laptop screens. The department published images it says D’iu took of employees’ computers.

The department did not name the remote access software, say whether the handlers successfully connected to D’iu’s laptop, or report a breach of the company’s network.

The device they allegedly wanted to control was D’iu’s own computer. That differs from other cases Cybersecurity News has covered, where attackers abused legitimate remote access tools to control victims’ computers.

The alleged surveillance extended beyond the workplace. Investigators say D’iu searched for employees’ home addresses, including that of a senior executive.

On Sept. 3, he allegedly followed an employee for nearly 30 miles as she drove from Palo Alto toward San Francisco. She called 911 and drove to a police station. Prosecutors say D’iu stopped following her after she contacted an officer.

During searches in October, FBI agents recovered about $18,000 in cash, two laptops, two iPhones, wireless networking gear, and false identity documents. They also found a notebook with 10 handwritten addresses, several of which matched employees’ homes.

Detailed profiles of at least three employees included relatives’ names, education and work histories, and notes on their strengths and weaknesses. Cybersecurity News previously reported on Russian military intelligence targeting Western logistics and technology firms.

A joint advisory published by CISA and its partners described a separate cyber espionage campaign against organizations involved in getting aid to Ukraine.

The Justice Department did not link D’iu to that campaign. The allegations against him show why defense firms should take reports of employees being followed or work screens being photographed seriously, even when there is no sign of a network breach.

D’iu faces four charges: conspiracy to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as a foreign agent without notifying the U.S. Attorney General, interstate stalking, and identification document fraud.

He has been in federal custody since his Nov. 2 court appearance and is scheduled to return to court on Nov. 24. He is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Microsoft 365 Device Code Authentication to Hijack Accounts and Bypass MFA
articles.description:
Hackers are targeting Microsoft 365 accounts with fake payment notices and SharePoint documents that lead employees to a genuine Microsoft sign-in page. The November 2026 campaigns turn a routine task, such as checking whether an invoice was paid, into an authorization request that can give an attacker access to the employee’s account. The trick does […]

The post Hackers Exploit Microsoft 365 Device Code Authentication to Hijack Accounts and Bypass MFA appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are targeting Microsoft 365 accounts with fake payment notices and SharePoint documents that lead employees to a genuine Microsoft sign-in page.

The November 2026 campaigns turn a routine task, such as checking whether an invoice was paid, into an authorization request that can give an attacker access to the employee’s account.

The trick does not require breaking multifactor authentication (MFA) or stealing a password. As earlier coverage of Microsoft device code phishing showed, a real Microsoft sign-in page can still be part of a phishing attack.

The employee may complete every security prompt correctly while unknowingly authorizing a session the attacker started.

Researchers at Hornetsecurity’s Threat Intelligence Lab identified malicious HTML and SVG attachments in several payment-themed campaigns.

The attachments redirected recipients or displayed phishing content; the report did not describe a separate malware implant. Researchers also did not name the operators or say how many accounts the campaigns compromised.

Hackers Exploit Microsoft 365 Device Code Authentication

In one case, the email’s subject was a single period, and the body offered almost no explanation. A personalized ZIP filename did the work of making the message look like payment advice.

Inside was a file that appeared to be HTML but contained an interactive SVG, a type of image that can run scripts when opened as a browser document. What looked like a security check was actually a redirect.

The redirect led to a counterfeit SharePoint workspace advertising remittance reports and check images. A second campaign used a scheduled electronic payment notice and a ZIP named SpwcinBillPaymentReports.zip.

Its attachment rebuilt a document lure from hundreds of concealed fragments. Earlier reporting on browser-based phishing concealment illustrates why a static scan may miss what a recipient eventually sees, though it does not establish a link between the campaigns.

Device code authentication is designed for devices such as shared displays that cannot easily handle a full sign-in. A user enters a short code on another device to authorize the original request.

In these campaigns, the fake workspace supplied the code under the pretext of unlocking payment documents. When the employee signed in and completed any required MFA, Microsoft issued tokens to the client that initiated the request. That client belonged to the attacker.

The tokens let the attacker act within the permissions granted to that client. Depending on those permissions, corporate email or files could be exposed.

The FBI’s earlier Kali365 account hijacking warning documented the same authorization risk in a separate operation. Hornetsecurity also observed the fake workspace checking its session status, traffic that defenders can correlate with sign-in records.

Detecting and Blocking Device Code Phishing

Security teams should start with Microsoft Entra sign-in logs. Filter Authentication Protocol for Device code, then check whether successful sign-ins match an expected application, account, source and time.

The Original transfer method field can help trace sessions that began with device code authentication even if a later token renewal used another flow. Compare suspicious events with email, browser and network records.

Microsoft’s Conditional Access configuration guide recommends blocking device code flow wherever possible. In Entra, select Authentication flows, choose Device code flow, and set the grant control to Block access.

Start in Report-only mode to check which legitimate workflows would be affected. Keep exceptions narrow, document why each one is needed, and regularly review emergency-access exclusions before and after enforcement.

A new policy is not a substitute for investigating an account that may already be compromised. If an employee entered an unsolicited code and finished signing in, revoke the account’s sign-in sessions and review subsequent activity for unauthorized access.

As earlier coverage of OAuth device code abuse explains, email filtering and domain blocklists address only part of the problem. Employees should verify unexpected payment requests through a trusted channel and enter a device code only for a sign-in they started themselves.

articles.title: Hackers Turn aNotepad Into a Malware Delivery Channel for XenoRAT and NodeLinkRAT Backdoors
articles.description:
A North Korea-linked hacking group is using aNotepad, a free online note-sharing site, to control infected computers and swap malware on demand. The campaign targets South Korean policy and security professionals. It delivered the XenoRAT backdoor first and later a new JavaScript tool called NodeLinkRAT. The attackers did not need to change their phishing files […]

The post Hackers Turn aNotepad Into a Malware Delivery Channel for XenoRAT and NodeLinkRAT Backdoors appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A North Korea-linked hacking group is using aNotepad, a free online note-sharing site, to control infected computers and swap malware on demand.

The campaign targets South Korean policy and security professionals. It delivered the XenoRAT backdoor first and later a new JavaScript tool called NodeLinkRAT.

The attackers did not need to change their phishing files to switch tools. They edited one public note page, and every infected machine picked up the new code. Because of this, a single snapshot of the malware or its server address never shows the full attack.

Researchers at Genians Security Center (GSC) identified the campaign and named NodeLinkRAT in a detailed report published this week. They link the activity to the Kimsuky group with moderate confidence.

Hackers Turn aNotepad Into a Malware

The attack began between September 12 and 18, 2026. The attacker posed as a senior aide to a National Assembly member and wrote to someone who had attended a September 9 seminar.

The email asked the victim to return an honorarium payment form, but the first message had no attachment. The omission was deliberate. The victim replied that nothing was attached, and the attacker then sent a ZIP file through a webmail large-attachment feature.

Inside the ZIP was a shortcut file named like a Hangul (HWP) document. Windows hides the shortcut extension, so the victim saw only “.hwp”.

The file used the same trick seen in LNK files and PowerShell campaigns against Korean users. Opening it started cmd.exe, which launched a hidden PowerShell window.

The command text was scrambled with character substitution, so words like “curl” and “iex” never appeared in plain text. The script then used curl.exe to pull code from a free web host and ran it in memory.

That second-stage script changed on every connection. It created a scheduled task named CommonMaintenanceHost, which ran a hidden script every 38 minutes.

The script visited an aNotepad page, extracted Base64 text between two marker strings, and executed it. It also opened a real-looking honorarium form as a decoy.

The form asked for a bank name and account number, so a victim who filled it in would hand over financial details.

Payloads Swapped Through the Note Page

GSC collected third-stage code from June to October 2026, and the tools changed in a clear order. On June 18, the note delivered a XenoRAT variant that ran in memory and contacted 103.81.116[.]10.

It posed as “Updater.exe”. This was about three months before the phishing email, so the same setup was likely used on other targets earlier.

In September, the code became simple data collectors. The scripts gathered antivirus names, system details, network settings, and running processes.

They uploaded the results to Dropbox, and later to MEGA cloud storage. A script on September 28 stole document and image files and sent them to a South Korean free hosting site.

Because the task reran every 38 minutes, files a victim was working on could be stolen almost as they changed. Earlier reports on cloud storage to host scripts showed the same habit of using trusted services.

On October 16, the note delivered NodeLinkRAT. The script downloaded the official Node.js runtime, installed three npm packages, and ran a file called teamview.js from the public Music folder.

The name imitates TeamViewer. The tool connects to 207.148.112[.]166 on port 3000 using Socket.IO. It can run commands, browse folders, upload and download files, compress and steal folders, and capture the screen live.

Traffic is encrypted with AES-256-GCM, but the key is hardcoded as “12345678901234567890123456789012”, so captured traffic could be decrypted.

No single clue settles attribution, so GSC weighed several overlaps. A Dropbox account tied to a similar aNotepad case used an email address that appeared in 2025 phishing against people working on North Korean affairs.

A fake NAVER MYBOX page matched a 2024 Kimsuky phishing page, and the servers sat in the same subnet.

Three XenoRAT variants shared one assembly GUID and a custom encryption key, which suggests one builder. Kimsuky has also used XenoRAT before, as in the case where Kimsuky hackers leveraged GitHub against embassies.

GSC lists limits on this conclusion. Much of the infrastructure is public, so a copycat is possible. Korean-language strings may be a decoy. The note page changed often, so some stages may still be unknown.

Blocking Dropbox, MEGA, or aNotepad outright is rarely practical, since businesses use them legitimately. GSC advises looking at behavior instead. Defenders should watch for these signs:-

  • An LNK file inside an archive launching cmd.exe, PowerShell, and curl.exe in sequence.
  • Scheduled tasks with maintenance-style names that repeat at odd intervals.
  • Scripts that fetch a public note page and run the result in memory.
  • Node.js installed under C:\ or run from a public folder.

Keep early execution logs, because the original LNK is deleted after it runs. Users should be wary of any “resend the attachment” email, and file-extension display should be switched on. These steps echo advice from Kimsuky’s recent LNK campaign coverage.

articles.title: N-able Confirms Server Breach, Disables Mail Assure and SpamExperts Management Access
articles.description:
N-able confirmed unauthorized access to one server in its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud environment and disabled management access across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. The company said inbound and outbound email filtering continued to operate normally while it investigated the breach. Customers could still send and receive email, but administrators lost access to […]

The post N-able Confirms Server Breach, Disables Mail Assure and SpamExperts Management Access appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
N-able confirmed unauthorized access to one server in its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud environment and disabled management access across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific.

The company said inbound and outbound email filtering continued to operate normally while it investigated the breach. Customers could still send and receive email, but administrators lost access to the dashboard, application programming interfaces (APIs), and quarantine tools.

N-able first told customers about a service disruption on November 16, 2026. Its early assessment pointed to platform settings and dependencies between services.

The company later determined that a security incident had caused the disruption and said it had taken steps to contain the threat. N-able has not publicly identified who accessed the server, how they got in, or how long they had access.

The company said it had found no evidence that customer data was compromised, including evidence that anyone accessed customer mailboxes. That is a finding from an ongoing investigation, not a final conclusion. The confirmed breach concerns one server. The loss of management access across all three regions does not mean that servers in each region were breached.

N-able said the breach was unrelated to the separate N-central security incident, which prompted an emergency hotfix earlier in November. N-central is used to monitor and manage customer devices. The current outage affects the hosted email security services, not the N-central platform.

Email Filtering Stays Online

At 00:01 UTC on November 19, N-able said it had started testing some fixes in a controlled environment. It said the dashboard, quarantine, logging, mailbox synchronization, and API access would each need to pass security checks before returning. By 04:01 UTC, engineers were continuing those tests and making further security changes.

In its 08:00 UTC update on November 19, N-able said teams were working around the clock to check and secure the management portal and related services. The official N-able incident page said core mail flow and filtering were operating normally. The portal and APIs remained disabled, and N-able did not give a time for restoring access in that update.

Email can keep moving even when administrators cannot manage the filter. As Cybersecurity News explains in its guide to email security gateways, these services can hold suspicious messages in quarantine rather than deliver them. During this outage, administrators may be unable to review or release held messages, check logs, or make changes such as adding or removing a domain. Workflows that rely on the API also remain unavailable.

For managed service providers, that distinction matters when a customer reports a missing message. Normal mail flow does not show whether an individual email was held, and the unavailable portal limits what support teams can check.

Teams should follow N-able’s updates and any instructions for their own environment rather than treat normal delivery as a sign that management access has been restored.

articles.title: Ubiquiti Warns of Critical UniFi Access Flaws Enabling Root Code Execution Attacks
articles.description:
Ubiquiti has disclosed seven vulnerabilities in its UniFi Access Application, including a critical flaw that could let an attacker with limited permissions run code as root on the host device. Security Advisory Bulletin 073, dated November 18, 2026, lists version 4.3.22 and earlier as affected. Ubiquiti advises administrators to update to UniFi Access Application 4.3.24 […]

The post Ubiquiti Warns of Critical UniFi Access Flaws Enabling Root Code Execution Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ubiquiti has disclosed seven vulnerabilities in its UniFi Access Application, including a critical flaw that could let an attacker with limited permissions run code as root on the host device.

Security Advisory Bulletin 073, dated November 18, 2026, lists version 4.3.22 and earlier as affected. Ubiquiti advises administrators to update to UniFi Access Application 4.3.24 or later.

Five of the seven vulnerabilities are rated critical, and two are rated high. All require network access, but not all require an account. The impact also varies. Some flaws affect the host running the application. In contrast, others affect adopted UniFi Access devices, meaning hardware already enrolled in and managed by the application.

CVE-2026-132802, rated 9.9 out of 10, stems from how the application handles file links before opening files. An attacker who can reach the application over the network and already has limited permissions could run code with root privileges. Root is the highest level of access on the host, so the impact is not limited to the attacker’s original application account.

Ubiquiti Warns of Critical UniFi Access Flaws

A separate set of authenticated SQL injection flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-132803 and also rated 9.9, could let a low-privileged attacker gain more permissions on the host.

SQL injection occurs when an application treats untrusted input as part of a database command. Another authenticated SQL injection flaw, CVE-2026-132806, scores 8.8 and could expose sensitive information or allow unauthorized changes within the application itself.

Two flaws involve server-side request forgery, or SSRF, which occurs when an attacker causes a server to make requests it should not make.

CVE-2026-132804, rated 9.9, requires limited privileges and could let an attacker gain more permissions within UniFi OS. CVE-2026-132805, rated 8.3, requires no account and could allow someone with network access to obtain information and make unauthorized changes on the host.

The remaining critical flaws affect adopted devices. A certificate validation flaw, CVE-2026-132807, scores 9.0 and could expose sensitive information or allow unauthorized changes on an adopted device under certain conditions.

CVE-2026-132808, rated 9.9, is an authorization flaw that could let a low-privileged attacker run commands on certain adopted devices. That is distinct from the root code execution flaw, which affects the application host.

According to Security Advisory Bulletin 073, administrators must update the UniFi Access Application to version 4.3.24 or later, then verify the installed version on each host. The fix applies to the application, not individual reader or intercom firmware.

Where an update cannot be applied immediately, restrict access to the management interface to trusted networks and authorized users. Network restrictions can reduce exposure, but they do not replace the update.

The bulletin describes what attackers could do. It does not report confirmed exploitation. Administrators should not treat an affected version alone as evidence of a breach.

Cyber Security News previously covered 21 Ubiquiti UniFi vulnerabilities, including earlier flaws in the Access application, and a separate command injection flaw in UniFi Access readers and intercoms. These disclosures involved different fixes. A deployment that received those earlier patches still needs to meet the minimum application version specified in Bulletin 073.

articles.description:
A cyberattack on the European Commission disrupted staff services for more than 10 days, leaving some employees unable to submit timesheets, request leave, or enter salary information. The EU’s cybersecurity service, CERT-EU, found that hackers used an AI tool called ARTEX, POLITICO reported on November 19, 2026. Most affected applications are back online, but investigators […]

The post Hackers Target European Commission with ARTEX AI Tool in Major Cyberattack appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A cyberattack on the European Commission disrupted staff services for more than 10 days, leaving some employees unable to submit timesheets, request leave, or enter salary information.

The EU’s cybersecurity service, CERT-EU, found that hackers used an AI tool called ARTEX, POLITICO reported on November 19, 2026. Most affected applications are back online, but investigators have not established whether anyone accessed or stole staff data.

According to an EU official who spoke to POLITICO, CERT-EU detected ARTEX’s use earlier in November. The publicly available tool uses artificial intelligence to look for security weaknesses in IT systems.

The report did not name the attackers, identify a specific flaw or explain how they gained access. It also did not establish whether ARTEX helped them break in or was used only to look for weaknesses.

The Commission took several applications offline as a precaution. Spokesperson Thomas Regnier said individual systems were targeted and that the Commission had informed those concerned. An EU official said the Commission believed it had contained most of the attack, but the full extent of the damage remained unclear.

Sysper, MyPMO and Translation Services Disrupted

Two affected platforms were Sysper, which staff uses to view payslips, record work hours and request leave, and MyPMO, which handles medical reimbursements. Both returned earlier in the week, although Sysper briefly went down again on November 18.

Translation services were also disrupted on November 17. Salaries largely arrived as usual, POLITICO found, even though some staff could not complete routine HR tasks.

The outages show which services staff could not use, not which records the attackers may have seen. The Commission has not confirmed that payslips, leave records or medical reimbursement data were exposed.

An EU official told POLITICO that uncertainty about whether personal information was compromised, and how much, was one reason staff had received limited details.

The Corporate Management Board, the Commission’s top internal crisis group, held an urgent meeting earlier in November, according to an internal email reviewed by POLITICO.

The Commission’s digital services department ordered extra security checks, and technology commissioner Henna Virkkunen briefed fellow commissioners on November 18. Reuters, citing the original report, said the Commission did not immediately respond to its separate request for comment.

The incident follows two separate cases covered by Cyber Security News. In January, an attack on the system that manages Commission staff mobile devices exposed a limited set of names and phone numbers. In March, a cloud breach tied to the Trivy supply-chain attack affected the public Europa website platform. CERT-EU said the March breach did not affect the Commission’s internal systems.

Neither earlier case has been publicly linked to the November attack. For staff, getting Sysper and MyPMO back means they can resume routine work.

It does not answer the central question of the investigation: whether attackers reached personal records and, if they did, which employees and types of data were affected.

articles.title: Hackers Deploy Overlord RAT That Survives Windows Resets and Crashes Systems When Terminated
articles.description:
A financially motivated hacking group is deploying Overlord RAT, a Windows remote access trojan that can return after a victim uses “Reset this PC.” The malware can also trigger a blue screen if a user or security tool forcibly ends its process. The two features turn familiar recovery steps into risks: killing the process can […]

The post Hackers Deploy Overlord RAT That Survives Windows Resets and Crashes Systems When Terminated appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A financially motivated hacking group is deploying Overlord RAT, a Windows remote access trojan that can return after a victim uses “Reset this PC.”

The malware can also trigger a blue screen if a user or security tool forcibly ends its process. The two features turn familiar recovery steps into risks: killing the process can immediately take the machine offline, while resetting Windows can give the malware another chance to run.

The campaign appears to target cryptocurrency holders, gaming account owners and users of internet calling software. File names and decoys included references to Viber, MicroSIP and a financial statement, suggesting that messaging users, call-center staff and finance teams could also be targets.

The evidence points to likely targets rather than confirmed victims, and the researchers did not observe how the initial files reached users.

Researchers at Cisco Talos identified the malware while examining an exposed staging server tied to a group they track as UAT-12643.

Their November 18 report assessed a possible North Korea link with low confidence, noting that other groups have used both Overlord and its blockchain-based server discovery technique.

Earlier coverage of the MALFEX npm malware campaign documented Overlord in a separate operation targeting Windows developers.

Hackers Deploy Overlord RAT

Overlord uses two forms of persistence, the term for how malware keeps a foothold after a restart or other interruption. Its first method adds a startup entry to the current user’s Windows registry so the malware can run again at sign-in.

Similar Windows RAT registry persistence has appeared in other campaigns, but what sets this Overlord variant apart is its ability to run during recovery, before the user signs in.

The second method tampers with the Windows Recovery Environment, or WinRE, which runs outside the normal Windows session.

Talos found that Overlord places a copy of itself in the recovery area and changes the reset configuration so Windows launches it during “Reset this PC.”

That is different from surviving a clean installation from trusted external media. The report describes abuse of the built-in recovery process, not a firmware infection.

The blue screen is a separate mechanism. If Overlord is already running with administrative privileges and successfully marks itself as critical, Windows treats its process like one the operating system cannot afford to lose.

Forcibly ending it can trigger the stop code CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED. A blue screen alone does not identify Overlord, but one that follows an attempt to stop a suspicious process gives responders a reason to preserve logs and investigate before trying again.

35 commands in the Go-based implant

Talos identified 35 commands in the Go-based implant, covering tasks such as recording keystrokes, capturing screens, accessing webcams and microphones, and transferring files.

Earlier reporting on live Overlord RAT activity showed how quickly that access can translate into data theft in a separate intrusion. In this campaign, Overlord retrieved encrypted server addresses from Solana transaction memos.

The blockchain stored the address, not the control server itself, allowing operators to change where infected machines connect without sending them a new copy of the malware.

The group’s other tools help explain the financial motive. The Good Game infostealer targeted browser credentials, account sessions, cryptocurrency wallet data and selected documents.

It uploaded archives to GoFile and sent download links through a Discord webhook. A separate clipboard hijacker replaced copied cryptocurrency addresses, potentially redirecting payments if victims pasted an address without checking it. Neither behavior should be confused with Overlord’s recovery mechanism.

articles.title: ruby2ßhell: Critical One-Byte Heap Overflow in Ruby Could Allow RCE Attacks
articles.description:
Ruby has patched a critical memory corruption flaw that can allow remote code execution (RCE) on vulnerable servers. Tracked as GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 and named ruby2ßhell by Veria Labs, the flaw affects Ruby’s string case conversion code. Researchers report that attackers can reach the vulnerable code over the network without logging in to applications running Ruby on […]

The post ruby2ßhell: Critical One-Byte Heap Overflow in Ruby Could Allow RCE Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ruby has patched a critical memory corruption flaw that can allow remote code execution (RCE) on vulnerable servers. Tracked as GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 and named ruby2ßhell by Veria Labs, the flaw affects Ruby’s string case conversion code.

Researchers report that attackers can reach the vulnerable code over the network without logging in to applications running Ruby on Rails or classic-style Sinatra with default settings. A CVE identifier was still pending at disclosure.

The flaw occurs in case conversion routines for several legacy single-byte encodings, including some ISO-8859 and Windows-125x variants.

In those encodings, Ruby converts the German lowercase letter ß to SS when uppercasing it. That conversion produces two output bytes from one input byte, but the loop checks only whether the output buffer has room for one more byte. If the conversion needs two bytes and only one fits, the second write crosses the buffer boundary.

This is a heap buffer overflow because the output buffer sits in memory allocated at runtime. A subsequent copy of the converted string can also read one byte beyond the buffer.

The affected code dates back to Ruby 2.4.0 and can be reached through upcase, swapcase, downcase(: fold), and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings follow a separate code path and do not trigger this flaw.

ruby2ßhell – One-Byte Heap Overflow in Ruby

Ruby’s maintainers say proof-of-concept exploits have demonstrated code execution in some scenarios, not that every out-of-bounds write leads to RCE.

Affected releases include Ruby 3.3.0 through 3.3.13, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. The flaw also affects older releases, including Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end-of-life and have no fix for this issue.

Plain Rack is not exposed by default, according to Veria Labs. However, custom application code can still introduce exposure if it applies an affected case conversion to untrusted text in a legacy encoding.

Veria Labs identified affected Ruby runtimes bundled with GitLab 19.6.0, GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5, Mastodon 4.7.5, OpenProject 17.9.7, Discourse 2026.10.1, and Chatwoot 4.20.0.

Affected Ruby Web Frameworks

Affected Self-Hosted Software :

For administrators, the key detail is which Ruby runtime the application actually loads. Updating the host’s system Ruby does not replace a separate runtime shipped inside an application package, appliance, or container image.

The Ruby team released 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 on November 18, 2026. The official Ruby security release addresses seven flaws across string case conversion and the regular expression engine.

These are separate from the earlier GitLab CI/CD regex vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-97229, which Cyber Security News also covered when CISA warned of active exploitation. That earlier exploitation does not establish that ruby2ßhell has been exploited in the wild.

Teams that manage their own Ruby runtime should upgrade to the fixed release for their branch or move to a supported branch if they run Ruby 3.2 or older.

Administrators of self-hosted products should install the vendor’s fixed build, then verify the Ruby version inside the running application environment. Prioritize internet-facing deployments where the vulnerable code is reachable without authentication.

The Veria Labs disclosure tracks affected products and vendor fixes. The researchers said they planned to publish a proof of concept about a week after disclosure.

The SOAR flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-131253, scored 9.9 out of 10 and requires an account with specific permissions. The Enterprise flaw, CVE-2026-76535, lets someone who has not signed in run searches […]

The post Splunk Patches Critical 9.9 RCE and Authentication Bypass Vulnerabilities in SOAR and Enterprise appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Splunk has released security updates for Splunk SOAR and Splunk Enterprise to fix a critical remote code execution flaw and a separate authentication bypass. The SOAR flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-131253, scored 9.9 out of 10 and requires an account with specific permissions.

The Enterprise flaw, CVE-2026-76535, lets someone who has not signed in run searches under another user’s identity. The two bugs affect different products and require separate updates.

Splunk’s November 18 advisory says CVE-2026-131253 affects SOAR versions below 8.8.0. The flaw is in the App Wizard, which helps users build connectors between SOAR and other tools.

Splunk says a signed-in user who can edit apps and containers and run playbooks could execute code with the permissions of the account that runs SOAR. Playbooks are automated workflows that security teams use to investigate alerts and respond to incidents.

That level of access matters because code running under the SOAR service account could read or change data beyond what the user normally controls. The Splunk SOAR security advisory lists no workaround for the App Wizard flaw and recommends upgrading to 8.8.0 or later.

Splunk Patches Multiple Vulnerabilities

The same release fixes a separate 9.6-rated remote code execution flaw in the REST API, tracked as CVE-2026-131287, and a high-severity single sign-on bypass, tracked as CVE-2026-131297.

The update also addresses flaws that could expose data or let users make changes outside their assigned roles. One flaw could let a user change or delete integrations assigned to another tenant, a separate group within a shared deployment.

That matters for organizations that use one SOAR instance to serve multiple teams or customers. The November release follows Splunk’s October fixes for 24 Enterprise and SOAR vulnerabilities, which included four critical flaws.

The Splunk Enterprise security advisory identifies RapidDiag, a tool for collecting troubleshooting data, as the affected component. Improper username validation could let an unauthenticated user run Search Processing Language queries as a signed-in user.

Depending on that user’s permissions, the attacker could read or change data and settings. The reported impact is unauthorized searches, not the operating system code execution described in the SOAR advisory.

The RapidDiag bypass is separate from the Splunk Enterprise flaw CISA flagged as actively exploited in June. That earlier issue, CVE-2026-20253, involved a PostgreSQL component and had its own patches. Reports of attacks against the June flaw do not show attackers using the new RapidDiag bypass.

The fixed Splunk Enterprise versions for the RapidDiag flaw are 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17. Administrators should install the fix for their release branch or a later supported release.

Teams that run both products should track the upgrades separately. Patching Enterprise does not update SOAR, and the October SOAR 8.7.0 update does not include the November fixes.

After upgrading, verify the installed version on each affected instance and check that key searches, connectors, and response playbooks still work. If there are signs of earlier misuse, preserve logs and review unexpected searches, app changes, or playbook runs. The updates close the flaws, but they cannot tell you whether someone used them before the patches were installed.

articles.title: Ruby Patches 7 Security Vulnerabilities, Including Buffer Overflow and RCE Flaws
articles.description:
Ruby maintainers released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13, and 3.3.14 to fix seven security vulnerabilities in the language’s regular expression engine and string case-conversion code. Several flaws can allow remote code execution (RCE), which means an attacker could run code inside a vulnerable Ruby process. The maintainers said they know of proof-of-concept demonstrations that achieved code execution […]

The post Ruby Patches 7 Security Vulnerabilities, Including Buffer Overflow and RCE Flaws appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ruby maintainers released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13, and 3.3.14 to fix seven security vulnerabilities in the language’s regular expression engine and string case-conversion code.

Several flaws can allow remote code execution (RCE), which means an attacker could run code inside a vulnerable Ruby process. The maintainers said they know of proof-of-concept demonstrations that achieved code execution in some scenarios and urged users to upgrade.

The advisory was published on November 19, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. At publication, the Ruby team had requested CVE numbers. However, none had been assigned, so the flaws are tracked by their GitHub Security Advisory IDs.

The advisory describes research demonstrations, not confirmed attacks against production systems. Two flaws affect the Ruby code used to change text case. The first flaw, GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5, lets Ruby write one byte beyond the memory reserved for its output in some text encodings.

The second, GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, starts with an integer overflow, where a calculation exceeds the range it can store. That error leads to a write outside the intended memory area. Ruby says both flaws can allow code execution in some scenarios.

Ruby Patches Security Vulnerabilities

Five flaws affect regular expressions, often called regexes, which applications use to search or validate text. The double-free flaw, GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x, causes Ruby to release the same memory block twice while compiling a pattern.

A separate flaw, GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w, causes a buffer overflow during compilation. Ruby says both can lead to code execution when an application compiles patterns supplied by an attacker.

Another buffer overflow, GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4, occurs when Regexp#to_s converts a regular expression to text. Ruby says the flaw can expose information or allow code execution.

GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r involves a read beyond the intended memory area during case-insensitive matching. Ruby reports that a demonstration showed attacker-controlled memory corruption for this flaw, but does not say it demonstrated code execution.

The final flaw, GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h, can expose memory contents or crash the process during case-insensitive matching that reuses text captured earlier in the pattern.

The affected versions are Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Upgrade to 3.3.14, 3.4.13, or 4.0.10, respectively, if you are on one of those maintained branches. Ruby 3.3 is in security maintenance.

Ruby 3.2 and older branches have reached end of life and will not receive these fixes, so teams still running them need to move to a supported branch.

These patches apply to the Ruby runtime itself, not to a Rails gem. That makes them different from the Rails Active Storage file-read flaw and the later Rails image-upload vulnerability previously covered by Cyber Security News. Updating Rails dependencies alone will not install a fixed Ruby runtime.

Start with internet-facing services that accept user-defined patterns or change the case of incoming text. Check the Ruby version in the environment where each app runs, not just on a developer’s laptop.

After upgrading, rebuild any container images that still bundle an older runtime, redeploy web services and background workers, and verify that the new instances are running a patched version.

Use the review to set patching priorities, not to delay updates elsewhere. The release fixes several distinct bugs, and an application does not need to use every affected feature to be exposed.

articles.title: Chinese Hackers Upgrade EggStreme Malware With Silent Backdoor to Evade Security Detection
articles.description:
A suspected Chinese cyberespionage group has rebuilt its EggStreme malware framework, adding a Windows backdoor that waits for an incoming connection instead of calling out to an attacker-controlled server. Bitdefender’s November 18, 2026, report tracks the changes as the group continues to target government organizations in the Philippines. Researchers also found signs of possible targeting […]

The post Chinese Hackers Upgrade EggStreme Malware With Silent Backdoor to Evade Security Detection appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A suspected Chinese cyberespionage group has rebuilt its EggStreme malware framework, adding a Windows backdoor that waits for an incoming connection instead of calling out to an attacker-controlled server.

Bitdefender’s November 18, 2026, report tracks the changes as the group continues to target government organizations in the Philippines. Researchers also found signs of possible targeting in Taiwan, but assessed that link with low to medium confidence.

Bitdefender first publicly documented EggStreme in September 2025 after investigating a compromise at a Philippine military company. The original EggStreme malware investigation described a modular toolkit that could run its main implant in memory and collect keystrokes.

The newer samples show that the operators can change how the backdoor communicates without abandoning the methods they use to run malware on compromised Windows systems.

ThreatCluster noted in its November 18 analysis that the overhaul went beyond changing servers or file hashes. It highlighted a new communications protocol, an expanded set of commands and a passive variant that does not send an outbound beacon.

The timing suggests public exposure may have prompted some of the changes, although Bitdefender found that some samples discovered after disclosure had been compiled earlier.

Chinese Hackers Upgrade EggStreme Malware

Bitdefender found two EggStremeAgent builds that operated in passive mode. A conventional backdoor often sends a beacon, or a recurring check-in, to tell its operators that a compromised machine is online.

These builds instead opened a listening port and waited for a connection. The distinction matters: a network rule that looks only for recurring outbound traffic may have nothing to flag.

A separate passive Windows backdoor called SLEEPWALKER illustrates the same monitoring gap, but it is not part of EggStreme.

The communications overhaul was not limited to passive mode. Newer EggStremeAgent builds dropped gRPC, a protocol for calling functions across a network, in favor of direct TCP connections while keeping mutual TLS.

That security mechanism requires both sides to present certificates. Bitdefender also found signs that the operators were moving away from one shared certificate authority toward campaign-specific ones.

If confirmed, that change would make it harder to link separate servers through a common certificate issuer. The newer agent builds analyzed by Bitdefender did not include the earlier keylogger, but they added ways to map Windows domains, query system information and run PowerShell in memory.

The missing keylogger does not mean the group has stopped collecting data, nor does it confirm that EggStremeWizard, a separate tool, has been retired.

Earlier coverage of Southeast Asian government espionage documented EggStreme components alongside other tools in a campaign where several activity clusters shared a victim network.

What Defenders Can Still Detect After the Rebuild

The malware still relies on DLL sideloading, in which a legitimate Windows program loads a malicious library. As other China-linked sideloading campaigns show, a trusted program name does not tell defenders whether every library it loads is safe.

For EggStreme, Bitdefender recommends checking whether system-named libraries load from unexpected folders and whether workstations begin listening on ports that do not match their usual roles.

Bitdefender also observed the operators using an unmanaged system reachable by workstations to stage malware. The researchers saw valid credentials and activity over Server Message Block (SMB), the Windows file-sharing protocol, but could not determine how the attackers first gained access.

That distinction matters in an investigation: a script launched from a file share can reveal how an intruder moved inside the network without identifying the original entry point.

Security teams should check which unmanaged devices can reach workstations and review internal file-share activity alongside endpoint alerts.

articles.title: AuditTeam Ransomware Gang Poses as Security Auditors and Use AV Drivers to Kill EDR Process
articles.description:
A ransomware group called AuditTeam is dressing up extortion as a paid security audit. Victims get a ransom note that reads like an audit log. It asks for an “Audit & Consulting fee” in return for a report on the holes the attackers used to get in. Before the note appears, the group has already […]

The post AuditTeam Ransomware Gang Poses as Security Auditors and Use AV Drivers to Kill EDR Process appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A ransomware group called AuditTeam is dressing up extortion as a paid security audit. Victims get a ransom note that reads like an audit log. It asks for an “Audit & Consulting fee” in return for a report on the holes the attackers used to get in.

Before the note appears, the group has already shut down security tools with a signed antivirus driver and encrypted the files.

The campaign ran from January 2026 through at least October 2026. It hit dozens of organizations, and a recent report on crews that disable EDR shows why this step matters so much to modern ransomware gangs.

Researchers at Securelist, the research arm of Kaspersky, identified the malware and named its framework OpsAgent. They first saw it on March 10, 2026, in an intrusion at a company in Hong Kong.

The tool looked like a normal penetration testing kit. Further digging showed the same tool in other countries.

The Securelist team says AuditTeam’s victims include organizations in Russia, Italy, the Philippines, Hong Kong, Senegal, Finland and China. The group’s leak site also lists victims in Turkey, Thailand, Ukraine, Argentina, South Korea, Japan and Spain.

AuditTeam Ransomware Gang Poses as Security Auditors

The EDR killer is an add-on module for OpsAgent. It installs a driver that poses as Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus, from the KV product series.

The driver carries a valid digital signature, which helps it load without raising alarms. This trick is called Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver, or BYOVD.

Attackers bring a trusted, signed driver onto a machine and misuse it to run code at the kernel level, where security tools have little power to fight back.

Once the driver is loaded, the malware talks to it through a filter port named \KvCorePortX0. When the driver gets the command 0x1D followed by a file name, it ends the matching process.

The kill list holds about 220 names. It covers Microsoft Defender (MsMpEng), ESET (ekrn) and Kaspersky (avp). It also covers monitoring tools such as Sysmon, splunkd and wazuh-agent.

Remote access tools like TeamViewer, backup services such as Veeam and Acronis, and database engines such as sqlservr, mysqld, mongod and redis-server are on it too.

Other gangs use the same idea. Earlier reporting on how GentleKiller abused vulnerable drivers showed one gang killing more than 400 security processes before it encrypted anything.

After the security tools go down, the cryptor module takes over. It encrypts files with AES-CBC or ChaCha20 and gives each file its own key.

It also uses X25519 key exchange, so victims cannot easily recover the keys. The module stops database and backup services, deletes shadow copies and empties the recycle bin.

When it deletes files, it overwrites them with random data first, which makes forensic recovery much harder. The same backup-wrecking habit appears in how DeadLock ransomware targets backups before locking files.

The ransom note says nothing about encryption. Because the cryptor module drops it, anyone who sees the note already has encrypted files.

OpsAgent Tooling, Infrastructure and Defense

OpsAgent does a lot. It manages files and processes, injects shellcode, steals tokens, logs keystrokes, takes screenshots and moves between machines.

Securelist says it rivals Cobalt Strike in features. Its loaders push code into msiexec.exe, and the newest Rust loader runs the payload inside its own process instead.

During the campaign, the authors rewrote the implant from C++ to Rust. Securelist also saw code patterns that suggest the authors used AI tools to help write it.

For command and control, the malware uses Amazon CloudFront subdomains. It finds them by reading a public GitHub repository.

Because CloudFront addresses are shared with legitimate traffic, blocking by IP address does not work well. The GitHub repository was removed in November 2026. The latest Rust samples have that feature switched off, so the campaign is probably still running.

Defenders should watch for new kernel driver installs, especially a file named kvcore.sys. They should alert on any security agent that stops reporting while its host stays online.

Turning on Microsoft’s vulnerable driver blocklist and limiting local admin rights also helps. Even trusted vendor tools can be turned against you, as research on how a Microsoft Defender driver abused can disable endpoint protection shows. Keep offline backups, because this gang destroys the online ones.

articles.title: Hackers Actively Exploit Critical Apache Roller RCE Flaw to Execute Code Without Authentication
articles.description:
Hackers are actively exploiting a critical vulnerability in Apache Roller that lets them run code on affected servers without signing in, the Apache Software Foundation warned on November 17. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129448, affects versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 out of 10. Apache says administrators should upgrade […]

The post Hackers Actively Exploit Critical Apache Roller RCE Flaw to Execute Code Without Authentication appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are actively exploiting a critical vulnerability in Apache Roller that lets them run code on affected servers without signing in, the Apache Software Foundation warned on November 17.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129448, affects versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 out of 10. Apache says administrators should upgrade to Roller 6.1.6 or later. Version 6.1.5 is also vulnerable, but Apache tracks it under a separate CVE.

Apache Roller is a Java-based blogging platform that can host multiple blogs and support teams of writers and editors. The vulnerability is in its XML-RPC endpoint, an interface that lets other software communicate with Roller.

The server accepts certain extended data types and rebuilds them into objects before checking whether the sender is allowed to use the service. That process, known as deserialization, is unsafe when the server reconstructs data supplied by an attacker.

The result is remote code execution, or RCE. An attacker who can reach the vulnerable service over the network can run code without a valid account or any action from a blog user.

Critical Apache Roller RCE Exploitation

Apache’s CVE record confirms active exploitation but does not identify the attackers, say how many systems have been targeted, or describe what attackers have done after gaining access.

The November disclosure expands the known affected range. Apache’s September advisory listed only version 6.1.5 under CVE-2026-82384.

The new record says the two CVEs describe the same underlying flaw across different releases. That matters for administrators who installed 6.1.5 to fix an earlier Apache Roller session vulnerability. That update fixed the session issue, not this code execution flaw.

Cyber Security News also covered active exploitation of a separate Apache Tomcat RCE flaw. The Roller issue is in the blogging application itself.

Apache Roller 6.1.6 turns off the affected extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the feature is turned off. On vulnerable releases, turning off XML-RPC in the administration interface is not enough.

Those versions can process incoming data before checking the setting, leaving the server exposed even when the dashboard shows the feature is disabled.

If an upgrade cannot happen immediately, Apache recommends setting enabledForExtensions to false in WEB-INF/web.xml or removing the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping. Both workarounds require a Roller restart.

Removing the mapping also takes the endpoint offline, so administrators should check whether any publishing tools depend on it before choosing that workaround. Neither option changes Apache’s recommendation to upgrade.

For teams managing several Roller deployments, first check the version running on each server rather than relying on the XML-RPC setting in the dashboard. Prioritize instances reachable from the internet, then verify that the fixed release is running after deployment.

Patching closes the flaw, but it doesn’t show whether a server was compromised before the update. Treat any suspected compromise as a separate investigation.

articles.title: Hackers Abuse CyberPower UPS Software to Execute SYSTEM Commands and Dump Active Directory Data
articles.description:
Exploited CyberPower PowerPanel Business software for managing uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) to gain SYSTEM-level access to a Windows domain controller. Symantec reported on November 18 that the attackers used a built-in scripting feature to copy the Active Directory database and launch malware that kept running after the collection activity. Researchers did not observe data leaving […]

The post Hackers Abuse CyberPower UPS Software to Execute SYSTEM Commands and Dump Active Directory Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Exploited CyberPower PowerPanel Business software for managing uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) to gain SYSTEM-level access to a Windows domain controller.

Symantec reported on November 18 that the attackers used a built-in scripting feature to copy the Active Directory database and launch malware that kept running after the collection activity. Researchers did not observe data leaving the network or see ransomware deployed.

PowerPanel Business helps businesses keep servers running during brief power interruptions and shut them down safely during longer outages. Its event settings let administrators run scripts when power drops or fails.

On Windows, the PowerPanel service, ppbed.exe, runs as SYSTEM, a built-in account with extensive local privileges. Scripts started by the service inherit those permissions. In the incident, Symantec traced unauthorized scripts to the PowerPanel web console on TCP port 3052.

The service launched Windows Command Prompt, and the resulting activity included downloading tools and running a PowerShell test that loaded a small .NET program into memory. The program only printed a greeting, but it showed that the attackers could run code in memory through a trusted service.

Symantec did not establish how the attackers first gained console access. Earlier advisories documented hard-coded credentials, a default administrator password and a file-upload flaw in PowerPanel Business.

Hackers Abuse CyberPower UPS Software

Stolen administrator credentials were another possibility. Cyber Security News previously covered security flaws in PowerPanel Enterprise, a separate CyberPower product. Those findings do not establish how this intrusion began.

The attackers repeatedly changed their collection scripts and checked the results before trying again. They eventually copied ntds. dit, the Active Directory database, and collected the SYSTEM registry hive.

As our earlier coverage of Active Directory database theft explains, access to both files can expose password hashes and other secrets used to authenticate domain accounts.

Symantec said the repeated adjustments suggested someone was operating the tools live. It did not name a threat group or determine the attacker’s motive.

The same PowerPanel process tree later led to upnpcont.exe, an executable named after a Microsoft component. It ran from an unusual location under the SYSTEM profile and loaded a malicious atl.dll.

The technique, known as DLL side-loading, uses a legitimate program to load a malicious code library. The link back to ppbed.exe gave defenders a way to connect the malware with the earlier activity.

Symantec recommends finding every PowerPanel Business installation and limiting access to TCP port 3052 to approved administrator workstations. Keep the console off the public internet and away from regular user networks.

Apply vendor updates, replace default passwords with unique credentials, and review the settings that link power events to scripts. Check the extcmd and temp\profile\extcmd folders for scripts that do not match a known configuration.

On domain controllers, review endpoint logs for unusual command shells, PowerShell activity, or database access linked to ppbed.exe. Use Symantec’s incident report to compare file names and hashes with evidence from affected hosts.

If the evidence shows that the directory database was copied, treat domain credentials as potentially exposed even without proof of an outbound transfer. Plan a coordinated reset of krbtgt, the account used to sign Kerberos authentication tickets, alongside wider credential rotation.
